Claim: The two elder-money monitoring products found, Carefull and EverSafe, sell through banks, credit unions and advisors and publish no count of paying families; Carefull, the best funded, raised a $16.5M Series A in October 2023.
Evidence: Carefull Series A $16.5M announced October 12, 2023, led by Fin Capital with Bessemer, TTV Capital, Commerce Ventures, Montage Ventures and Alloy Labs; total funding $19.7M including a $3.2M seed in February 2021; more than 35 financial institutions and advisor groups; 25 employees; no user count (WealthManagement.com) | Carefull site (2026): $29.99 per month for two people; says it can never access funds or move money; monitors accounts at over 12,000 institutions; business-page logos include Synovus, C&N, SECU, Merck, OceanAir, Tucoemas, Edward Jones, Osaic and MassMutual; no family or user count. In July 2022 the product was a consumer app at $9.99 to $12.99 per month with no disclosed users (Financial Planning) | EverSafe (Elderscan, LLC) monitors bank, investment and card accounts and all three bureaus, lets members name trusted people as an extra set of eyes, includes $1M identity-theft coverage and a 30-day trial, discounts Raymond James clients 20% and their family members 30%, and describes itself as nearly a decade old; no user count on either page fetched
Implication: A priced consumer caregiving-money product exists but shows no disclosed consumer scale and leans on institutions as buyers, so a bank should read it as a retention feature it could buy, not proof that mid-life caregivers pay for a bundle.
Caveats: Merged from caregiving-A findings 1 and 3. Round figures are company-reported via trade press (WealthManagement.com is the primary record of the round; FinTech Futures, Business Wire and CUInsight returned 403 to the researcher). Carefull's logo walls mix monitored institutions and partners and the page does not say which are formal partners. Absence of a disclosed user count is not proof of small scale. The move from consumer app to institutional buyer is the compiler's and researcher's inference from two dated sources, not a stated pivot. Neither product gives delegated payment access.

Claim: True Link Financial, the one elder and disability money product found with disclosed scale, claims 250,000+ families served and $1 billion a year in prepaid-card purchases and now also sells trust administration and white-label family banking to banks and credit unions.
Evidence: True Link site: 250,000+ families served (no date or definition); $1 billion in card purchases annually (active and inactive cards as of 7/31/2023); $1.67 billion AUM, 27,000+ trust beneficiaries and 36+ pooled trusts, all as of 01/31/2025 | Product lines: prepaid card with spending rules; investment and trust administration; integrated and white-label family banking for banks and credit unions; Ledger software for representative payees and professionals | The same page also carries an older block ($1B+ AUM, 17,000+ beneficiaries, 25+ pooled trusts as of 1/24/2023), so its figures are internally inconsistent across sections
Implication: A delegated-spending card for a vulnerable adult has reached six-figure family counts but has drifted toward fiduciary and bank white-label work, which suggests the bank role is as a buyer or distributor of the tool rather than a builder of a new consumer company.
Caveats: Company marketing page, not a filing; True Link sells into the space. Families served is undefined and undated; card volume is a flow, not revenue. The corpus already excludes True Link's 102 million financial-caregivers figure for the same seller interest.

Claim: As of October 2026 Chase and Bank of America publish a trusted-contact option that gives the contact no access to the account, and neither their pages nor a Wells Fargo elder-abuse guide describes view-only or delegated caregiver access.
Evidence: Chase financial-abuse page: a Trusted Contact is someone the customer authorises Chase to reach if something seems wrong; the contact does not have access to the money; view-only or delegated access not mentioned; power of attorney mentioned only as a planning document and as an abuse warning sign | Bank of America elder-services page: trusted contact must be 18 or older; the bank may discuss suspicious activity, contact details, health status and the identity of a guardian, executor, trustee or POA holder; the contact cannot see balances, transact or change the account; set-up needs a financial-centre appointment with photo ID; the only delegated arrangement described is power of attorney | Wells Fargo elder-financial-abuse PDF (text extracted locally by compiler): advises sending duplicate account statements to a trusted person and keeping a durable power of attorney among planning documents; no product feature described
Implication: The large-bank answer to the adult child running a parent's money is an advisory contact plus advice to get a power of attorney, which leaves a native view-only or delegated account open for mid-life customers whose parents hold deposits.
Caveats: From caregiving-A finding 4 (Capital One part moved to caregiving-09). Not mentioned on a page is not proof of absence: banks run POA, joint and convenience-account processes in branches and by phone. Wells Fargo was checked through one guide only. Page dates are not shown. The Wells Fargo PDF does not parse through WebFetch; the compiler extracted it locally.

Claim: Caregiver support that is already bundled and priced as a service is sold to employers: Cariloop says it supports over 2 million employees worldwide, and Wellthy sells care concierge and backup care through employers, health plans and families without disclosing covered lives.
Evidence: Cariloop site (2026): employer-sponsored caregiver coaching and backup care with flexible subsidies and fast reimbursement; supports over 2 million employees worldwide; claims 3x employer ROI and 79% of employees avoiding unplanned leave or PTO, no method; public benefit corporation and B Corp | Wellthy site (2026): Care Concierge and Backup Care from 200+ care experts; separate employer, health-plan and family pages; employer logos include Best Buy, Cisco, Meta, Salesforce and Workday; claims 3.6x employer ROI, no method; no covered lives or funding stated | Both deliver human navigation and care services; neither is a money product, and the revenue is employer-paid
Implication: Where the caregiving bundle T10 imagines already exists, the payer is the employer and the product is human help, which cuts against a bank pricing it to consumers; Debit-Primary Spenders mostly lack these employer benefits.
Caveats: Vendor claims; employees supported is eligibility, not usage, and ROI figures have no method. Wellthy's funding round could not be verified (release host returned 403 to the researcher) and is not cited.

Claim: Bright Horizons, the largest childcare provider found, earned $2,933.6M in fiscal 2025, of which full-service centre care was $2,081.1M and back-up care $728.0M, with families paying about 90% of centre revenue and employers sponsoring the channel, and no financing layer in its segments.
Evidence: Form 10-K for fiscal 2025: total revenue $2,933,607 thousand; full-service centre-based care $2,081,119 thousand (71%); back-up care $727,988 thousand (25%); educational advisory $124,500 thousand (4%) | 1,010 centres (597 North America, 413 elsewhere), capacity about 115,000 children; more than 1,450 employer clients including more than 220 Fortune 500 companies; back-up network of more than 5,500 providers | Tuition paid by families is about 90% of full-service segment revenue
Implication: Families already pay a provider at billion-dollar scale through an employer-shaped channel, so a childcare finance product would insert into a flow providers and employers own; the higher-income, employer-sponsored families it serves are not the Debit-Primary segment.
Caveats: Segment totals span the US, UK, Netherlands, Australia and India. Only the first 100,000 of about 287,000 characters of the 10-K were read by researcher and compiler. Skews to employer-sponsored, higher-income families. A second EDGAR browse URL in the slice was a filing index, not a source of these figures, and was dropped.

Claim: The tax-advantaged way to pay for childcare is gated by the employer: in 2026, 43% of private-industry workers had access to a dependent care FSA (22% in service occupations, 62% in management and professional), and in March 2025 13% had employer childcare benefits.
Evidence: BLS National Compensation Survey factsheet: dependent care reimbursement account access 46% of civilian workers and 43% of private-industry workers in 2026, up from 38% in 2017; 22% in service occupations versus 62% in management, professional and related occupations; take-up not reported | BLS Employee Benefits release (September 25, 2025, March 2025 reference): childcare benefits available to 13% of private-industry workers; 8% in establishments under 100 workers, 10% at 100-499, 30% at 500 or more | Pointer only: Upwards, a childcare benefits platform, reported a $21M Series B (February 17, 2024; total $43.3M) and nearly 3 million families and 520+ employer clients, with costs split among employer, employee and state subsidy (press-release copy on Pulse 2.0); Vivvi lists 13 campuses, mostly in New York City, plus an employer backup-care network
Implication: The channel for childcare money is the employer and the state, and it is thinnest for service workers, which fits Debit-Primary Spenders poorly and leaves a bank no natural point of entry.
Caveats: Access is not use; BLS gives no FSA take-up or dollars. The factsheet and the release use different reference years. Upwards figures are company-reported through a press-release reposting site (Business Wire returned 403), kept as a pointer only. Vivvi's Series B and Kinside's reported acquisition could not be verified and are not cited.

Claim: Paid family caregiving for low-income households runs through state Medicaid: every responding state paid family caregivers in some circumstances in 2025, 1915(c) waivers bar states from paying participants directly, and a fiscal intermediary runs the payroll.
Evidence: KFF 2025 state survey (fielded April-July 2025, published January 5, 2026; every state but Florida responded): all responding states pay family caregivers in some circumstances; 44 states allow payment of legally responsible relatives through waivers, 6 through the state plan; 11 states run structured family caregiving at roughly $40 to $70 a day (American Council on Aging rates quoted by KFF); over two-thirds of states could not report the share of waiver participants paid as family carers | CMS training deck on Financial Management Services in 1915(c) waivers: the waiver authority prohibits states from paying participants directly; the FMS acts as fiscal intermediary, makes payments, and can run payroll and tax withholding | MACPAC June 2025 report, chapter 5: states must establish information and assistance including FMS for self-direction; in 2023, 44 states had at least one self-direction programme with budget authority; most beneficiaries choose to hire family members, friends or others they know | Entrants act as agencies, not banks: Givers enrols and pays family caregivers through state programmes and can act as the licensed agency (App Store listing, 11 ratings) and announced a $3.5M seed and a caregiver debit card in August 2022 (fintech.global); Papa charges $30 an hour direct and is a benefit in some Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and employer plans
Implication: For low-income caregivers the money is a Medicaid programme with required intermediaries holding the employer and tax roles, so a consumer bank's role shrinks to the receiving account; Debit-Primary caregivers are the people paid this way.
Caveats: Merged from caregiving-A finding 8 and caregiving-B finding 8. KFF reports policy, not usage or dollars. The CMS deck is undated (post-2020). The direct-payment bar is stated for 1915(c) only. Both PDFs return binary through WebFetch; the compiler verified them against local extracts. Givers' seed round comes from trade press as the primary record of the event; its current status is unknown. Medicaid changes in the 2025 budget act were not assessed.

Claim: In its March 2016 report the CFPB recommended that banks offer opt-in view-only access for authorised third parties and routinely offer convenience (agency) accounts without survivorship, and later CFPB guides list a convenience account and a trusted contact as caregiver options, so no rule bars the account the corpus candidate describes.
Evidence: CFPB Recommendations and report for financial institutions on preventing and responding to elder financial exploitation (March 2016): honour powers of attorney unless state law gives a basis to refuse; offer opt-in features including withdrawal limits, alerts and view-only access for authorised third parties; offer multi-party accounts without survivorship; describes a monitoring feature letting a designated family member watch for irregularities; recommends routinely offering convenience accounts as an alternative to joint accounts | CFPB guide Considering a financial caregiver (dated 3/2021): trusted contacts do not have access to the money; a convenience or agency account lets a helper deposit, withdraw and write checks without changing ownership or giving survivorship; formal roles listed include power of attorney, guardian, trustee and SSA representative payee or VA fiduciary | CFPB trusted-contact advisory (document dated 4/2022): calls its recommendations voluntary and says a trusted contact cannot view the account or transact without other legal authority such as guardianship or power of attorney | CFPB Ask CFPB page (last reviewed June 27, 2023): lists informal help, a convenience account, a trusted contact and a power of attorney as the ways a family member can help with banking
Implication: The regulator has invited a bank-native view-only and delegated account for ten years and few large banks show one, which keeps the candidate open for mid-life adult children of a parent with deposits, but marks it as an account feature regulators want every bank to have rather than a moat.
Caveats: All items are voluntary recommendations, not rules. Standing as of October 2026: all four CFPB URLs still resolve (October 26, 2026), and none of these items appears among the 67 guidance documents the CFPB withdrew on May 12, 2025 (Federal Register 2025-08286, read via govinfo; the notice lists some bulletins by number only, so an unnamed match cannot be fully excluded). No later withdrawal was found in a Federal Register API query of CFPB withdrawals from 2025 onward. The three PDFs return binary through WebFetch; the compiler extracted them locally and confirmed the quoted points. The trusted-contact file name says 2021-11 but the document is dated 4/2022.

Claim: On Capital One's public pages as of October 2026, a power-of-attorney request can be filed online with an eligibility decision within 7 business days sent by mail, 360 Checking lists joint holders and beneficiaries as its sharing options, a forms page carries an Authorized Signer Modification Form, and no page fetched mentions a trusted contact, view-only access or a convenience account.
Evidence: capitalone.com/power-of-attorney: options are power of attorney, conservatorship or guardianship, and other financial authority; submit details on the principal and agent and upload documents online; eligibility decided within 7 business days of receipt; outcome sent by mail; no trusted-contact or view-only mention | 360 Checking features page lists only adding beneficiaries and adding a joint account holder; the joint-holder help page describes an online invite needing a one-time passcode and says branch accounts must be changed in a branch, with no survivorship or liability language | Bank forms page lists an Account Owner and Beneficiary Change Form and an Authorized Signer Modification Form, and no power-of-attorney, trusted-contact or conservator form | Elder-financial-abuse page mentions a durable power of attorney and connecting online accounts to pay bills and review statements; no trusted contact, delegated access, view-only access or holds
Implication: On the additive screen, POA intake and an authorised-signer form already exist, so the new work would be a caregiver-designed view-only or delegated layer on existing deposit accounts, not a new company, for mid-life customers whose parents bank with Capital One.
Caveats: From caregiving-B finding 2 plus the Capital One part of caregiving-A finding 4. Help pages summarised by a fetch tool; not mentioned is not proof of absence, and internal trusted-contact or authorised-signer processes may exist. What an authorised signer can do on a consumer account was not described on the forms page. The agent instruction PDF returned 403 to the researcher and is not cited.

Claim: Under Virginia's Uniform Power of Attorney Act a person presented with an acknowledged power of attorney must accept it or request a certification, translation or opinion of counsel within seven business days, may refuse only on listed grounds, and faces a court order and attorney fees for unlawful refusal, while the CFPB reports banks still refuse POAs for reasons state law does not support.
Evidence: Code of Virginia 64.2-1618: accept or request certification within seven business days of presentation, then accept within five business days of receiving it; may not require a different form; refusal grounds include actual knowledge of termination, a refused certification, a good-faith belief the power is invalid, and a good-faith adult protective services report about the agent; unlawful refusal can bring a court order and reasonable attorney fees and costs | CFPB 2016 report: consumers and elder-law attorneys report institutions refusing POAs because they were not on the institution's preferred form or were not executed within a given period; a 2002 Uniform Law Commission survey found 63 percent of surveyed attorneys had difficulty getting third-party acceptance and 17 percent called it frequent; Florida law bars requiring a different form | Uniform Law Commission fact sheet (copy in February 2023 Vermont legislative testimony): the act aims at greater protections against abuse and shielding innocent parties from liability; completed 2006
Implication: Fast, lawful POA acceptance is a service-quality edge state law already requires, not a legal privilege, and a state-by-state patchwork raises the cost of doing it nationally for adult children whose parents live in another state.
Caveats: One state's enactment; adoption count of the uniform act and non-adopting states' rules not verified. The 2002 attorney survey is 24 years old and reached only through the CFPB footnote. No US complaint-volume data on POA refusals found. The CFPB and Vermont PDFs return binary through WebFetch; the compiler extracted them locally and confirmed the quoted points.

Claim: Federal law protects a bank that reports suspected elder exploitation but gives it no authority to hold funds: the 2018 Senior Safe Act grants immunity for good-faith disclosures by trained staff about people 65 or older, FINRA Rule 2165 hold rights reach only broker-dealers, and about half of states let banks hold or delay transactions.
Evidence: Public Law 115-174 section 303 (May 24, 2018; 12 U.S.C. 3423): covered financial institutions include depository institutions and credit unions; covered agencies include state and federal financial regulators, law enforcement and adult protective services; senior citizen means not younger than 65; exploitation includes acts by a caregiver or fiduciary; immunity attaches to disclosure by trained staff, not to holding funds | FINRA Rule 2165: members may hold a Specified Adult's account (65 or older, or 18 or older with an impairment) for up to 15 business days, extendable by 10 and then by 30 more if reported to a state regulator, agency or court; trusted contact notified within two business days; effective February 5, 2018, amended effective March 17, 2022 | ABA Banking Journal (March 31, 2025) on an ABA Foundation bank survey: roughly half of states have hold laws for depository institutions; 54.5% of respondents in those states had used them; nearly 90% of banks in states without one said a law would help. DOJ Elder Justice page (updated November 5, 2024) announces a state temporary-hold-law resource developed with an FTC advisory group
Implication: A national bank giving adult children delegated access would carry exploitation exposure with no federal safe harbour for stopping a payment and a state patchwork on holds, which argues against building this as a stand-alone company.
Caveats: Section 303 text is past the first 100,000 characters of the congress.gov page; the compiler confirmed it against the researcher's saved copy (_pdf/publ174.htm). The ABA survey figures are bank self-report with undisclosed sample, reported by industry trade press secondhand because the report was not fetched; rated down for that. The state list linked from the DOJ page returned Page Not Found, so the current count and 2025-2026 state laws are unverified. No federal bank hold rule was found; that is an absence, not proof.

Claim: FinCEN's June 2022 advisory reports over 62,000 elder-exploitation SARs in 2020 and over 72,000 in 2021, and a family member was involved in 46 percent of elder-theft cases in a random sample of SAR narratives from 2013 to 2019, so the adult child with access is also the main documented theft channel.
Evidence: FinCEN advisory FIN-2022-A002 (June 15, 2022): over 62,000 EFE SARs in 2020, an estimated $3.4 billion in suspicious transactions per the CFPB (up from $2.6 billion in 2019); over 72,000 in 2021; filers asked to use the key term EFE FIN-2022-A002 and tick the elder-exploitation box | Same advisory: in a statistically significant random sample of SAR narratives, a family member was involved in 46 percent of elder-theft cases reported 2013-2019 | CFPB data spotlight (published November 15, 2021): 62,014 EFE SARs in 2020; $3.4 billion with the top 1 percent by amount excluded; a checking or savings account or a money transfer in more than half; depository institutions filed nearly 60 percent (58.8%); no perpetrator relationship reported
Implication: Delegated access is the channel through which a documented share of elder theft runs, so any such account must be built around monitoring the delegate, a fraud capability a deposit bank already has and an app does not; this is both the exposure and the bank's best right-to-win argument.
Caveats: SAR counts are filings, not losses; the 46 percent covers elder theft only, not scams, and comes from a 2019 FinCEN analysis quoted in the advisory. No SAR count after 2021 retrieved. The FinCEN PDF returns binary through WebFetch; the compiler extracted it locally and confirmed the figures.

Claim: The informal workarounds for helping a parent bank carry documented loss and estate risks, while the formal structures already exist and are insured: a parent who shares a card and PIN is fully liable for the helper's transfers, a joint owner can withdraw for their own use, and FDIC insures agent and POA-operated accounts as the owner's single account.
Evidence: CFPB 2016 report: under Regulation E, a consumer who gives another person a card, PIN or other access device and authorises transfers is fully liable for that person's transfers, even beyond what was intended | Same report: a joint owner can withdraw money for his or her own use, the joint owner's creditors may reach the account, and on death the money may pass to the joint owner; the CFPB recommends routinely offering convenience accounts instead | FDIC Your Insured Deposits: an account titled to one owner where another person (for example a power of attorney or custodian) can withdraw is insured as a Single Account; accounts opened for one person by an agent, nominee, guardian, custodian or conservator are Single Accounts; pass-through coverage needs the relationship expressly disclosed in the bank's records; joint co-owners must have equal withdrawal rights
Implication: The safety case for a native delegated account is real, but because convenience, agency and POA accounts are existing insured forms, the idea is a better-designed existing account rather than a new category.
Caveats: Regulation E reading is from the 2016 CFPB report, not the regulation text or current official interpretation. The FDIC page is a consumer brochure; 12 CFR part 330 not retrieved. No data on how many families share cards and PINs. A clause in the slice saying joint accounts need no family relationship was not on the FDIC page as summarised and was removed. An Ask CFPB source in the slice is moved to caregiving-08.

Claim: Under the 2025 budget act the dependent care FSA limit rose from $5,000 to $7,500 for 2026 and the child and dependent care credit's top rate rose from 35 to 50 percent from tax year 2026, but the credit stays non-refundable and the FSA exists only where an employer offers it.
Evidence: IRS Publication 15-B (2026) What's New: the annual dependent care FSA limit was raised from $5,000 to $7,500 for 2026 ($2,500 to $3,750 if married filing separately) | IRS child and dependent care credit page: for tax year 2026 the credit is 20% to 50% of qualifying expenses, 50% at AGI of $15,000 or less tapering to 35%, lower above $75,000 ($150,000 joint) but not under 20%; expense limit $3,000 for one person and $6,000 for two or more; the credit is non-refundable | IRS provisions page lists the Child and Dependent Care Credit enhancement as Section 70405 (top rate 35 to 50 percent from tax year 2026); no dependent care assistance provision is listed there | IRS Topic 602: qualifying persons are dependent children under 13 and a spouse or dependent incapable of self-care who lived with the taxpayer more than half the year; care must let the taxpayer work or look for work
Implication: The policy lever on childcare is the tax code and employer payroll, which pay at a filing or payroll event with no financing gap, and a non-refundable credit gives nothing to households with no income tax liability, where the corpus finds the highest burden (Debit-Primary Spenders).
Caveats: The statutory section for the FSA change is not on the IRS pages fetched. The 2026 employer-provided childcare credit (section 45F) change was not on the pages fetched and is not claimed. A credit-advance or FSA-claims feature was not tested for demand. The adult-dependent rule narrows any eldercare relevance to a co-resident person incapable of self-care.

Claim: In 2019-2021 families below the poverty line paid a median 23 to 27 percent of income for child care, against 7 to 8 percent for families at 300 percent of poverty or more.
Evidence: DOL National Database of Childcare Prices: full-day care takes 8.9 to 16 percent of median family income, at 2022 annual prices of $6,552 to $15,600 across 2,512 counties | Census SIPP via Chicago Fed: families below poverty paid a median 23 percent of income in 2019 and 27 percent in 2021; families at 300 percent of poverty or more paid 8 percent, then 7 percent | Families at 100-199 percent of poverty went from 12 to 17 percent; HHS treats 7 percent as affordable; median weekly cost rose from $160 to $189 between 2019 and 2021
Implication: The pain is real and acute, but it is a price-to-income ratio that a loan or smoothing product cannot fix for the debit-primary, low-income households where it bites hardest.
Caveats: Corpus row 1 (Observed/Administrative). NDCP prices stop at 2022, before the post-2024 funding-cliff price wave. SIPP figures come via a Chicago Fed microdata analysis, not a raw Census table.

Claim: In the 2025 analysis, 46 percent of US children under 6 lived in a licensed child care desert, down from 51 percent in 2018, with remote rural areas at 70 percent.
Evidence: A desert means more than three young children per licensed slot; 46 percent in 2025, 51 percent in 2018 | Remote rural 70 percent, all-rural 65.6 percent; majority-Hispanic communities 52.2 percent; 43.5 percent of children under 6 in poverty live in a desert | State spread from about 5 percent in DC to 96 percent in Alaska
Implication: Where the pain is worst the constraint is that no licensed slot exists, which no financing product can supply; this cuts against T21 for the debit-primary segment.
Caveats: Corpus row 2. Center for American Progress is an advocacy organisation; kept because it names its data (state licensing files, ACS 2019-2023) and partners. Unlicensed care is unmeasured.

Claim: More than $52 billion of supplemental CCDF funding was appropriated in fiscal years 2020-2021 with expenditure required by September 30, 2024, and state officials told GAO that keeping the changes depends on securing non-federal money.
Evidence: GAO-24-106258: more than $52 billion in supplemental CCDF funds in FY2020-2021; remaining funds had to be spent by September 30, 2024 | Five-state review: states widened eligibility, cut co-pays, raised provider rates and worker pay | State officials said sustaining some changes may need non-federal funding; no replacement mandate
Implication: The why-now for child care cost is a public funding event, so the cause sits in state policy, which weakens the case for a bank-built product across both segments.
Caveats: Corpus row 4. Single source; GAO documents mechanism and intentions, not realised closures or prices. Compiler spot-check: $52 billion and September 30, 2024 confirmed on the page (October 26, 2026).

Claim: In Household Pulse waves from September 2022 to May 2023, about 40 percent of working women living only with children under five did not pay for child care at all.
Evidence: Chicago Fed analysis of Census Household Pulse (nine waves): about 40 percent of working women living only with children under five pay nothing for child care | 78 percent of relative-care arrangements and 97 percent of Head Start involve no payment | The highest-income households are almost twice as likely to pay as the lowest and, when paying, pay nearly three times as much
Implication: Where households do not buy paid care there is no payment stream to finance or smooth, so T21 has the thinnest base in the debit-primary segment.
Caveats: Corpus row 5. Single source; arrangement type is household-reported. The 78 and 97 percent figures are for households with one child and one arrangement. Compiler spot-check: 40, 78 and 97 percent confirmed on the page (October 26, 2026).

Claim: BLS counts 7.6 million of 38.2 million US unpaid eldercare providers in 2023-24 as parents of a child under 18 at home, and other sources place sandwich caregivers at 28 to 29 percent of caregivers.
Evidence: BLS ATUS 2023-24: 7.6 million of 38.2 million eldercare providers were parents of a minor child at home; Table 9 shows 55.3 percent of those were caring for a parent, 86.0 percent employed, 72.0 percent full time | NAC 2019 (n=328 sandwich): 28 percent of caregivers were sandwich caregivers; AARP/NAC 2025: 29 percent | Pew (8,750 adults, fielded September 2025, published August 27, 2026): 25 percent of all adults are sandwiched, 54 percent of those in their 40s
Implication: The dual-obligation state is large and concentrated in midlife, so a caregiving transition would reach a sizeable share of existing customers in their 40s and 50s.
Caveats: Corpus row 6. Definitions differ across BLS, NAC/AARP and Pew; directional only. NAC part-funded by MassMutual; AARP gives no sample. Compiler spot-check of Table 9: 7,616 thousand, 86.0 and 72.0 percent confirmed; the table labels 55.3 percent as caring for a parent, not specifically one's own parent, so the corpus wording was softened. A PMC reanalysis source in the corpus row was not used here.

Claim: In HRS panel data for 2002-2014, spousal caregivers aged 59-66 held 50 percent less in IRA assets and 39 percent less in non-IRA assets than married non-caregivers.
Evidence: GAO-19-382 (HRS 2002-2014): spousal caregivers 59-66 had 50 percent lower IRA assets, 39 percent lower non-IRA assets and 11 percent lower Social Security income than married non-caregivers | GAO estimates roughly one in 10 Americans a year cared for a parent or spouse across 2011-2017
Implication: A measurable balance-sheet gap shows up before retirement, giving a bank a dated signal, though the data are old and cover spouses as well as parents.
Caveats: Corpus row 12. GAO warns caregiving may not be the cause. Data end in 2014. Compiler spot-check: 50, 39 and 11 percent confirmed on the page (October 26, 2026).

Claim: ASPE microsimulation for adults turning 65 in 2021-2025 finds the top income quintile averages $75,400 of lifetime out-of-pocket long-term care spending versus $15,400 for the bottom quintile.
Evidence: ASPE (2022, DYNASIM4, 2020 dollars): average lifetime LTSS cost $120,900; families pay 37 percent out of pocket; 14 percent spend $100,000 or more; unpaid family care valued at $204,000 on average | Only 5.7 percent of the top quintile will receive Medicaid LTSS versus 35.4 percent of the bottom | About 10 percent of the top quintile can expect out-of-pocket spending above $250,000
Implication: Elder-care cost is a large, unevenly insured exposure, but it concentrates in upper-income households outside the debit-primary segment and is a services and insurance problem more than a deposit-bank one.
Caveats: Corpus row 18 (Wave 3B). A forward projection, not an observed outcome; quintile is a simulated income measure.

Claim: Candidate (adult children running a parent's money): a bank account structure giving adult children who pay a parent's bills or act under a power of attorney delegated or view-only access is an unserved category, shown by a CFPB figure of about 22 million people 60 or older having named a power of attorney (a 2013 release with no stated method), while the leading bank-side product, a trusted contact, is voluntary and gives no access.
Evidence: CFPB release (October 29, 2013): about 22 million people 60 or older have named someone in a power of attorney; launched the Managing Someone Else's Money guides (agents under POA, guardians, trustees, government benefit payees); no method stated | Financial institutions filed 62,014 elder-exploitation SARs in 2020 involving about $3.4 billion (up from $2.6 billion in 2019); a checking or savings account or money transfer in more than half; depository institutions filed nearly 60 percent; FINRA requires brokerage trusted-contact efforts while the CFPB trusted-contact advisory for banks is voluntary | BLS ATUS 2023-24: 7.6 million parents of minors give unpaid eldercare, 55.3 percent caring for a parent and 86 percent employed
Implication: A family-run account for mid-life adult children between caregiving and transfer; it fails if few adult-child caregivers use informal workarounds or would switch for delegated access, or if a trusted-contact feature on existing accounts closes the gap.
Caveats: Corpus candidate row 12. Correction: the corpus dated the 22 million figure to 2020; the compiler confirmed it is from an October 29, 2013 CFPB release with no method, so Vintage is 2013. SAR data do not record the perpetrator's relationship. No row measures how many adult children pay a parent's bills or their willingness to pay. True Link's 102 million figure excluded as seller-sourced. Overlaps transfer (T06); home here only when the trigger is a living parent. Research rows caregiving-03 and 08 to 13 bear on it.

Claim: In 2025, one in four US parents of children under 13 used paid childcare, and among families paying for both, median monthly childcare ($1,083) was over half the median housing payment ($1,900), a pain driven by the price of care rather than a missing financial product.
Evidence: SHED 2025: one-fourth of parents of children under 13 used paid childcare in the past week (35% at $100,000+ income); median weekly spend $250, $350 at 20+ hours; median monthly childcare $1,083 against median housing $1,900 among families paying both, $1,517 at 20+ hours; most such families spent at least 50% as much on childcare as on housing (PDF pp. 6, 28) | SHED 2025: 41% of non-working mothers of under-13s said childcare contributed at least in part to not working, against 25% of non-working fathers; 44% of part-time working parents said childcare contributed to working part time (PDF p. 30) | SHED 2024: 24% of parents of under-13s used paid childcare; median weekly $240, about $960 a month (2024 report, PDF p. 30)
Implication: Childcare cost is large for the minority who pay for it, but a bank can shift timing, not the price, and no willingness-to-pay evidence exists, so T21 likely dies or folds into benefits claiming (dependent-care FSA, tax credits) under T10.
Caveats: Cause is the wage bill of care, not a product gap. SHED measures past-week use, so it excludes families priced out of care. Dependent-care tax and benefit rules and any 2025 budget act childcare provisions were not researched. T14-A found no 2024-2026 childcare-finance venture round. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Neither Huntington nor True Link has published an enrollment, household, deposit, partner-count or retention figure for delegated caregiver banking: five Huntington earnings calls from October 2025 to October 2026 never name Caregiver Banking or True Link.
Evidence: Huntington calls Q3 2025 (17 Oct 2025), Q4 2025 (22 Jan 2026), Q1 2026 (23 Apr 2026), Q2 2026 (23 Jul 2026) and Q3 2026 (22 Oct 2026): no mention of Caregiver Banking or True Link; Q3 2026 has Brant Standridge listing recently built features such as family and team banking and AI-powered savings goals, with no number | Company-wide figures only: Q3 2026 total production of checking households up 35% year over year; Q2 2026 checking household acquisition up 31% with the Cadence footprint | True Link's September 2025 release names partner types only (banks, credit unions, nonprofits, government programmes), says it has served over 250,000 families and cites an 80+ NPS with no method; its news page adds 250,000+ families and $175M of fraud prevented yearly, company-wide, with no partner count or retention figure | EDGAR lists one Form D for True Link Financial, Inc. (CIK 0001718716), filed 12 Oct 2017
Implication: The family-authority kill test (Huntington enrollment under 1% of consumer checking households by August 2027) cannot be run from public records, so the Feature verdict is left where it was and the next step is a True Link vendor-diligence call or Capital One's own POA data.
Caveats: Transcripts are a third-party mirror (stockanalysis.com). Huntington's FY2025 10-K was fetched but only the XBRL front matter was readable; its business section and the 10-Qs, investor-day deck and earnings supplements were not searched in full. Absence from calls is not absence of an internal figure. True Link is a seller into this space; its fraud-prevented figure has no method. Two Business Wire releases (Feb 2026 Forbes Fintech 50, Dec 2025 caregiver survey) returned 403 or 429 and are not used. Merges researcher findings uptake-1 and uptake-3.

Claim: A Huntington and True Link award release says one-third of account holders in the family-banking offering are new to Huntington and switched for it, and that the offering has grown deposits, with no count, dollar figure, base or period.
Evidence: Quoted: one-third of account holders are new to Huntington and switched specifically for this offering; since launching in early 2025 the offering has protected families, brought new households to the bank and grown deposits | Not given: enrollment, number of new households, deposit total, whether the one-third is of accounts or balances, or the period | Tied to the 2026 Banking Tech Award for Best Bank-Fintech Partnership, dated 18 June 2026 on True Link's news page
Implication: The first quantified claim for the live case points to acquisition of new-to-bank households, not retention of existing owners, which softens the no-demand-evidence objection but leaves the Feature verdict where it was until the base is disclosed.
Caveats: Both parties are interested (vendor and bank in an award press release). The page is a syndicated copy of a Business Wire release that returned 403 (mirror). The release says the offering launched in early 2025, while 04_stress.md dates Huntington's launch to August 2025; not reconciled. Account holders may mean caregiver or owner; one-third of a tiny enrollment is possible. It does not address attrition of enrolled owners against matched non-enrolled owners, which is the kill test.

Claim: Checking-or-savings complaint narratives mentioning power of attorney numbered 113, 146, 152 and 75 in 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 to mid-August, and narratives mentioning a caregiver 17, 13, 34 and 21.
Evidence: Power of attorney: 486 total; 40.3, 49.5, 29.5 and 40.0 per 10,000 checking-or-savings narratives (researcher arithmetic on narrative counts of 28,017 / 29,484 / 51,448 / 18,775); issue split managing an account 350 of 486 (72%), closing an account 84 | Caregiver: 85 total; 6.1, 4.4, 6.6 and 11.2 per 10,000 narratives (researcher arithmetic); managing an account 54 | Paraphrased cases: agents with notarised POA refused or stalled for weeks while a bedbound parent's bills went unpaid; POA documents repeatedly not on file; a family member using a POA to drain an account; a hired caregiver taking funds
Implication: About 150 narratives a year show a recurring failure at the account (valid agents refused or stalled), real but narrow against roughly 50,000 checking-or-savings narratives a year, so it neither reopens nor kills anything and points the family-authority feature at POA onboarding.
Caveats: Same archive provenance and opt-in limits as transfer-92. Power of attorney appears in many non-caregiving contexts (travel, business, collection letters) and no manual coding was done; caregiver is a narrow word. No threshold for these terms exists in 04_stress.md; the count is for sizing only. Researcher set T10 here, although the 04_stress.md feature it bears on (family authority over a parent's accounts) carries no Opportunity ID.

Claim: Wealthfront's fiscal 2026 10-K (year to 31 January 2026) reports cash management revenue of $271.7M, about 74% of total revenue, on $45.4B of off-balance-sheet cash management assets and 1.4M funded clients, earned as a negotiated share of what program banks pay on swept deposits.
Evidence: 10-K FY2026: cash management revenue $271.7M vs $230.9M (up 18%); cash management assets $45,361M at 31 Jan 2026 vs $42,411M; annualised cash management fee rate 0.62% vs 0.64%; cash management about 74% (FY2026) and 75% (FY2025) of total revenue | Same 10-K: 1.4M funded clients, $94.1B platform assets, average platform assets per client about $66,000, annual client retention over 95%; platform net deposits fell to $6,659M in FY2026 from $17,714M (down 62%) | Same 10-K: each program bank pays a gross amount 'based on a negotiated percentage multiplied by the program deposits'; part goes to clients as interest and the rest is Wealthfront's fee | S-1 (2025): cash management was about 71%, 75% and 76% of revenue in FY2024, FY2025 and the six months to 31 Jul 2025; cash management assets $46,579M at 31 Jul 2025; fee rate 0.60% for those six months (0.65% a year earlier); the disclosed fee may range from 0% to 2% annualised by program bank
Implication: A yield-seeking cash sweep reaches company scale at a robo-adviser serving mass-affluent clients, which supports T03 as a business, but the winner is a non-bank paid out of program banks' deposit margin, so a deposit bank would be selling against its own funding (mass-affluent, not debit-primary).
Caveats: Company's own disclosure of its own metrics. Wealthfront is a robo-adviser; the cash account is an acquisition product for a wider platform and the filing does not show cash-only clients or whether cash came from other banks (migration vs new money). Fee rate is compressing (0.65% to 0.60% to 0.62%) and depends on the rate cycle. Merged from crosscut-A 1 (10-K) and the S-1 figures in crosscut-B 2. The 10-K exists (filed after the 2025 IPO) and every figure was confirmed in the filing text.

Claim: Robinhood's Cash Sweep held $32.8B of off-balance-sheet user cash at 31 December 2025 and earned $229M in 2025, about 5% of $4.47B total net revenues, and is the subject of a class action alleging non-Gold users were paid an unreasonable rate.
Evidence: FY2025 10-K interest-earning assets table: Cash Sweep (off-balance sheet) $32,786M at 31 Dec 2025 vs $26,064M at 31 Dec 2024; 2025 Cash Sweep revenue $229M; annual yield 0.74% (0.84% in 2024) | Same 10-K: total net revenues up 52% to $4.47B; Funded Customers 27.0M. Cash Sweep share about 5.1% of revenue (my arithmetic: 229 / 4,470) | Q3 2025 10-Q: Cash Sweep revenue $64M for the quarter (vs $46M) and $172M for nine months (vs $129M) against $3,190M nine-month total net revenues | 10-K legal proceedings: Dey v. Robinhood Markets (N.D. Cal., filed Oct 2024) alleges breach of fiduciary duty and California unfair competition for failing to pay a reasonable rate to non-Gold accounts on cash swept to program banks; a motion to dismiss was granted in part and denied in part on 28 Apr 2025
Implication: At the largest retail brokerage the sweep is a small spread line attached to a trading relationship and already draws litigation over the rate paid, which supports the reading that sweeps are features rather than companies (mass-affluent investors).
Caveats: Company disclosure. Revenue is a spread on balances and moves with rates. The year-end balance and full-year revenue were a gap in crosscut-A; the compiler extracted them from a local copy of the 10-K. The reported November 2025 wind-down of the non-Gold sweep was not found in the 10-K text and is not used. The class action is an allegation, not a finding.

Claim: Schwab's fiscal 2025 10-K says client moves from sweep cash into higher-yielding alternatives in 2022-2023 forced it onto higher-cost funding that hurt net income, with bank supplemental funding down 49% from its May 2023 peak by end-2024, and that it recouped through its own money market funds and managed products.
Evidence: Risk factor: rapid rate rises in 2022 and 2023 brought a significant decrease in clients' allocation to sweep cash and more investment in higher-yielding alternatives at Schwab such as fixed income and proprietary purchased money market funds; Schwab extensively used higher-cost funding, which hurt net income (paraphrase) | MD&A: bank supplemental funding ended 2024 at $49.9B, down $29.7B (37%) in the year and down 49% from May 2023 peak; reallocation from sweep further decelerated in 2024; bank deposit account fee revenue $729M in 2024; BDA balances $87.6B at 31 Dec 2024, down 10% | 2025: net interest revenue $11.8B, up 28%, mainly from lower interest expense as supplemental funding was cut; asset management and administration fees $6.5B, up 14%, partly from growth in managed investing solutions and money market funds | Risk factor: a rise in rates may reduce bank deposit account fee revenue as clients reallocate out of BDA balances into higher-yielding alternatives, 'as we experienced in recent years'
Implication: The one large disclosed case of customer cash moving to yield shows the cost lands on the holder's funding and is recouped only by owning the destination product, which a deposit-only bank lacks, so moving customer money to yield is a margin-cannibalising feature for a bank, not a standalone business (mass-affluent balances).
Caveats: Schwab is a broker with bank subsidiaries and its sweep is brokerage cash, so the comparison to Capital One deposits is by analogy. Company's own account of its own experience. The 10-K gives no dollar amount of cash that realigned. Verified against a local copy of the filing text.

Claim: As of October 2026 the CFPB's 2024 Section 1033 data-rights rule has its compliance dates stayed by the 29 October 2025 Forcht Bank order, the reconsideration is at the 22 August 2025 advance-notice stage on the CFPB's own page, and a proposed rule was sent to OIRA by 6 August 2026 without public text.
Evidence: CFPB compliance page (last modified 6 Jan 2026): compliance dates stayed on 29 Oct 2025 in Forcht Bank, N.A. v. CFPB, No. 5:24-cv-304-DCR (E.D. Ky.); the CFPB announced plans for a proposal to extend compliance dates | CFPB reconsideration page: advance notice issued and published 22 Aug 2025 (90 FR 40986, docket CFPB-2025-0037) on four issues, including who can act as a consumer's 'representative' and how fees may be assessed; no proposed rule shown | Consumer Finance Monitor (6 Aug 2026): per OIRA, the CFPB submitted an NPRM titled 'Personal Financial Data Rights Reconsideration' for review; content not public; whether data providers may charge third parties is the most contested issue | No September or October 2026 publication of that proposal was found by the researcher or on the CFPB pages
Implication: A cross-institution treasury or agent product has no settled right to read other banks' data on consumer authorisation and may face access fees set in incumbents' favour, which favours products built on a bank's own account holders over a multi-bank agent (all segments; bears equally on T08).
Caveats: The OIRA fact is from a law-firm-run publication summarising reginfo.gov; reginfo.gov and the Federal Register were not opened. The CFPB compliance page is dated January 2026, so its silence is not evidence about October. Court status after the injunction (appeal) not re-verified from a court record. Updates corpus finding 7 (not carried separately).

Claim: Section 4(a)(11) of the GENIUS Act (Public Law 119-27, approved 18 July 2025) bars stablecoin issuers from paying holders interest or yield solely for holding, use or retention, platform rewards were still being fought over in the CLARITY Act in May 2026, and Capital One's FY2025 10-K says the Act may let competitors compete for funds otherwise deposited with banks.
Evidence: Public Law 119-27, Sec. 4(a)(11) 'Prohibition on interest': no permitted or foreign payment stablecoin issuer shall pay the holder any form of interest or yield (cash, tokens or other consideration) solely in connection with holding, use or retention; approved 18 Jul 2025 | Consumer Federation of America (8 May 2026): the Tillis-Alsobrooks amendment to the CLARITY Act (Section 404) opens with a yield ban but lists activity-based rewards; CFA says GENIUS was silent on third-party platforms such as Coinbase and the exceptions largely legalise yield | Capital One 10-K FY2025 risk factor: the GENIUS Act provides a legal framework for stablecoins 'which may allow new and existing competitors to compete for funds that may have otherwise been deposited with banks'; stablecoins and tokenized deposits named among alternative payment mechanisms | No source confirmed CLARITY Act floor passage or signature by October 2026
Implication: The statute shields deposits only against issuer-paid yield, so a platform-paid stablecoin reward sits in an unresolved zone that could pull idle cash from banks, raising the chance that someone else offers the yield sweep if a bank does not (mass-affluent and crypto-active customers).
Caveats: CFA is an advocacy group and its reading of Section 404 is a characterisation; bill text and October 2026 status not verified (congress.gov 403). OCC rulemaking under GENIUS not fetched. The Capital One quote is a company risk factor, not a regulator statement.

Claim: The FDIC Board on 3 March 2025 withdrew its 23 August 2024 brokered-deposit proposal, while Wealthfront's S-1 lists reclassification of sweep balances as brokered deposits as a risk that could make program banks refuse them, and Capital One already holds $19.2B of brokered deposits.
Evidence: FDIC FIL-6-2025 and press release (3 Mar 2025): Board withdrew the brokered-deposits proposal published 23 Aug 2024 (parts 303 and 337), saying it would have significantly disrupted many aspects of the deposit landscape; future action requires a new proposal; the FIL does not mention sweeps | Wealthfront S-1 risk factor: a change in regulatory treatment of cash sweep programs, 'for example treating our cash sweep program balances as brokered deposits', or in FDIC insurance interpretation, could make program banks less willing to accept balances | Capital One 10-K FY2025 funding table: total deposits of $475.8B at 31 Dec 2025 include brokered deposits of $19.2B ($11.6B a year earlier)
Implication: For the own-the-sweep candidate the nearest FDIC constraint on sweep programs is gone, but the sweep fee is earned by the intermediary and paid by the bank holding the deposit, so a bank that sweeps its own customers' cash out gives up the deposit and a bank that keeps it earns no fee (mass-affluent savers).
Caveats: Direction is read against the own-the-sweep candidate (corpus finding 10), not T03 as written. The withdrawal removes a proposal; it is not a safe harbour, and 'withdrawal helps sweeps' is the researcher's inference from the S-1 risk factor. crosscut-B said the brokered figure was the Other segment's; the 10-K footnote attaches it to total deposits (corrected). The Wealthfront revenue figures from the same S-1 are in crosscut-01.

Claim: Exchange Act section 3(a)(4)(B)(v) exempts a bank from the broker definition when it effects transactions in a program investing deposit funds in a no-load money market fund, while the New York AG's May 2025 suit against Capital One (360 Savings frozen at 0.3% while 360 Performance Savings reached 4.35%) marks the disclosure risk of steering customers between yields.
Evidence: 15 U.S.C. 78c(a)(4)(B)(v) 'Sweep accounts': a bank is not a broker when it effects transactions as part of a program for investing or reinvesting deposit funds into a no-load, open-end registered investment company that holds itself out as a money market fund | Section 3(a)(4)(B)(ii): trust and fiduciary transactions are excepted only in a trust or regularly examined fiduciary department, with conditions on compensation and solicitation | NY AG press release (14 May 2025): Capital One froze 360 Savings at 0.3 percent while raising 360 Performance Savings (introduced Sept 2019) to as high as 4.35 percent; employees were told not to mention the new product unless asked; $10,000 from Sept 2019 earned $186 over five years versus $1,090; the AG sought restitution, damages, disgorgement and penalties
Implication: A bank can run a default sweep into money market funds under a statutory exception a non-bank app cannot use without a broker-dealer or program banks, a real edge for the own-the-sweep candidate, but the same bank carries a documented deposit-rate disclosure exposure, so the product must tell customers about the yield gap it was built to manage (mass-affluent).
Caveats: Direction read against the own-the-sweep candidate. Only subsections (B)(ii) and (B)(v) were read; the Investment Advisers Act bank exclusion, Reg R and 12 CFR 9 were not researched. Whether the exception covers an agent that selects funds, rather than a fixed program, is untested. The NY AG matter is an allegation; its $425M class settlement (final approval April 2026, appeal pending) is in the franchise file and was not re-fetched.

Claim: Rocket Companies' FY2025 10-K reports 4.58M Rocket Money paying subscribers at year-end (4.12M in 2024, 3.02M in 2023) and Rocket Money revenue of $390M in 2025 ($297M in 2024, $199M in 2023), earned as subscription and service fees.
Evidence: 10-K key metrics: Rocket Money paying subscribers at period end 4,583K (2025), 4,117K (2024), 3,017K (2023): 11% growth in 2025 after 36% in 2024 (my arithmetic) | 10-K Other income breakdown: Rocket Money revenue $390M (2025), $297M (2024), $199M (2023), described as subscription revenue and other service-based fees; total Other income $1,976M (2025) | 10-K: Rocket Money offers subscription cancellation, budget management and credit score improvement; Q4 2025 earnings exhibit lists it as one of five brands with Rocket Mortgage, Redfin, Rocket Close and Rocket Loans
Implication: The consumer-scale found-money business is a paid subscription-cancellation app owned by a non-bank and growing at about $390M of revenue, which shows people pay for bill and subscription clean-up but as a fee-based app, not as bank loyalty funded by a share of recovered value (broad debit-primary and young segments).
Caveats: Company disclosure. Paying subscribers is a subscription count, not money recovered; no dollars recovered are disclosed. Revenue per subscriber (about $85-90 a year by my arithmetic on 390 / average of 4,117 and 4,583) is derived, not disclosed. crosscut-A said revenue was not broken out; the 10-K does break it out (corrected).

Claim: Benefits Data Trust, a Philadelphia nonprofit that ran public-benefit screening for seven states, ended operations on 24 August 2024 and laid off all 273 staff, after relying on grants and donations to cover the cost of its government contracts.
Evidence: WHYY: as of 24 Aug 2024 BDT laid off all 273 employees and shut its call centre; the CEO's statement said financial distress 'could not be relieved in a timely manner'; it had benefit-screening contracts in Colorado, Maryland, Michigan, New York, North Carolina, South Carolina and Pennsylvania and claimed to have helped deliver $10B in benefits over two decades | WHYY: fiscal 2022 revenue $45M including $32M grants; a $20M unrestricted MacKenzie Scott grant; about half of revenue was donations covering the cost of government contracts | Route Fifty (2024): an open letter from about 120 former staff blamed leadership mismanagement and said the group served more than 120,000 people in 2023
Implication: The proven benefits-finding operator ran on government contracts and philanthropy and could not sustain itself, so the benefits-recovery side of T04 has no revenue-funded precedent (low-income debit-primary households).
Caveats: Local news and trade press used as the primary record of a closure; no IRS 990 was fetched. Cause disputed between the organisation (finances) and ex-staff (mismanagement). A nonprofit, so not a venture failure, and a share of recovered value was not its model.

Claim: The FTC's October 2024 Click-to-Cancel rule is off the books after court action, the FTC restarted with an advance notice on 11 March 2026 and lists no proposed rule, and its January 2025 DoNotPay order ($193,000) bars claims that an AI service can substitute for professional services without evidence.
Evidence: FTC Negative Option Rule page: final Click-to-Cancel rule announced 16 Oct 2024; stay petition denied 13 Dec 2024; 12 Feb 2026 Federal Register notice 'Revision of the Negative Option Rule ... To Conform These Rules to Federal Court Decisions'; advance notice announced 11 Mar 2026, published 13 Mar 2026 (docket FTC-2026-0265); no later proposed rule listed | FTC DoNotPay case page: complaint and consent agreement 25 Sep 2024; decision and order 17 Jan 2025; finalisation announced 11 Feb 2025; $193,000 payment; notice to 2021-2023 subscribers on the limits of its law-related features; ban on claiming it can substitute for any professional service without evidence; it marketed 'the world's first robot lawyer' | CFPB junk-fees page (last modified 28 May 2026) carries the Acting Director Vought accomplishments report and a deregulatory-agenda link and does not mention the overdraft or late-fee rules (whose reversal is in crosscut-22)
Implication: No federal rule will force cancellation ease or fee refunds within a year or more, so a bank-run found-money product cannot lean on regulation to create the money to find, and any AI claim of recovered savings must be substantiated or invite an FTC order (debit-primary households who bear fees).
Caveats: The FTC page names no court or vacatur date; the Eighth Circuit vacatur comes from a law-firm summary not fetched. The DoNotPay case page still shows status 'Pending' while listing a final order. DoNotPay concerned legal-services claims, not money recovery, so it is an analogy for substantiation duties. Merged crosscut-A 6 (DoNotPay) into crosscut-B 6.

Claim: Capital One Shopping already covers the shopping half of found money (free coupons, price drops and cash-back offers paid from merchant commissions) with no subscription, refund or unclaimed-property function on its pages, while state unclaimed-property programs return property free through NAUPA's MissingMoney.com and many states regulate third-party finders.
Evidence: capitalone.com/shopping (fetched 2026-10-26): checks for deals and coupons as you shop online; free; no mention of subscriptions, refunds, class actions or unclaimed property | capitaloneshopping.com (fetched 2026-10-26): 'Capital One Shopping earns a commission when you make eligible purchases from merchants and we may share those commissions with you as rewards'; offers include price drops, activation bonuses and percentage cash back with per-offer caps | NAUPA: no fee to search for and claim unclaimed property through an official state program; MissingMoney.com is a free all-state search run by NAUPA; finders usually charge a percentage of the find, some states limit the maximum fee, and many require finders to register or be licensed; no recovery totals beyond 'billions' | The largest overpayment pool in the corpus (overdraft and NSF fees, crosscut-21) is revenue to banks, so a bank finding it returns its own income
Implication: Found money looks like a feature attached to an existing product rather than a company: the recoverable pools are free from the state, already served by an enterprise tool, or the bank's own fee income, so the surviving form is narrow (subscription and fee surfacing inside the app) for debit-primary customers.
Caveats: Product pages are marketing; absence of a feature on a page is not proof it does not exist. NAUPA is a state-official association giving general guidance; no state fee-cap figure is cited. Subscription and benefits pools were not sized. Merged the Capital One Shopping bullet from crosscut-A 5 into crosscut-B 7; the 'often capped at $1,000' wording was dropped because the caps are per offer.

Claim: Visa's December 2025 release reports only 'hundreds' of agent-initiated transactions and predicts millions of consumer agent users by holiday 2026, Mastercard's September 2025 release says all US cardholders would be enabled for Agent Pay by the holidays, and neither discloses consumer counts or volume.
Evidence: Visa (18 Dec 2025): hundreds of controlled, real-world agent-initiated transactions completed with partners; more than 100 partners, over 30 building in the Visa Intelligent Commerce sandbox, over 20 agents and enablers integrating; US pilots with Skyfire, Nekuda, PayOS and Ramp in closed beta; 'Visa predicts that millions of consumers will use AI agents to complete purchases by the 2026 holiday season' | Visa (21 Oct 2026): a B2B agentic pilot with BILL and Billtrust is 'currently live and processing end-to-end transactions'; no counts or volume | Mastercard (10 Sep 2025): by the holiday season all US Mastercard cardholders will be enabled for Agent Pay, Citi and U.S. Bank cardholders first; no transaction counts | Capital One (12 Mar 2026): Chat Concierge, an auto-buying chat tool, converted leads 55% better than a leading competitor on Q1 2025 results (company-reported); its agentic-AI explainer describes agents processing payments only as an illustration; no Capital One agent-payments product was found
Implication: Ten months after launch the networks disclose only hundreds of transactions and a forecast, so no one runs consumer-scale agent payments yet, and the networks, not issuing banks, hold the agent credential layer (all segments).
Caveats: Consumer line: OUTSIDE. Network agent tokens, sandboxes and protocols are infrastructure; the Capital One items are consumer-facing but are not agent payments. A launch announcement is vendor belief, not usage; 'enabled' means eligible, not used. The Visa survey figure cited by the researcher was not found on the fetched page and is not used. The Mastercard release PDF loaded directly (HTTP 200) and was verified; no local extract was needed.

Claim: OpenAI moved ChatGPT Instant Checkout into merchant apps in March 2026, the x402 protocol site shows 75.41M transactions worth only $24.24M in its 'Last 30 Days' panel, and Google's AP2 launched in September 2025 with 60-plus collaborators and no usage figures.
Evidence: Digital Commerce 360 (6 Mar 2026): an OpenAI spokesperson said 'Instant Checkout is moving to Apps, where purchases can happen more seamlessly', echoing an earlier report by The Information; Shopify and Etsy were among the first checkout participants in 2025; no volume figures | x402.org (fetched 2026-10-26), 'Last 30 Days' panel: 75.41M transactions, $24.24M volume, 94.06K buyers, 22K sellers; about $0.32 per transaction (my arithmetic) | Google Cloud (16 Sep 2025): AP2 announced with more than 60 collaborating organisations and a public GitHub specification; no usage or consumer availability stated
Implication: The only disclosed agent-payment volume is sub-dollar machine-to-machine traffic and the one AI-lab consumer checkout retreated, so a consumer bank has no demonstrated consumer agent-payment market to become the default in.
Caveats: Consumer line: OUTSIDE. Protocols (x402, AP2) and an AI lab's checkout are infrastructure or someone else's consumer surface. The x402 figure is a 30-day dashboard panel with no stated window dates; the researcher's 'last updated 2026-08-25' was not on the page fetched 2026-10-26, which showed identical figures, so the panel may be stale. x402.org is a protocol foundation site; traffic may include test or automated calls and says nothing about consumers. OpenAI item is trade press as the record of a product change; weak uptake as the reason is reported inference.

Claim: Under 12 CFR 1005.2(m) a transfer by a person the consumer furnished with the access device is not 'unauthorized' until the consumer notifies the bank, no US regulator statement applying Reg E to agent payments was found, and a Fed governor (29 September 2026) and Capital One's FY2025 10-K both describe agent liability as unsettled.
Evidence: Reg E 1005.2(m): an unauthorized EFT is one initiated by someone other than the consumer without actual authority and with no benefit to the consumer; it excludes a transfer by a person who was furnished the access device by the consumer, unless the consumer has notified the institution; commentary: a consumer who gives a device and authority to someone who exceeds it is 'fully liable' until notice; a device obtained through fraud or robbery makes the transfer unauthorized | Governor Waller, Sibos 2026 (29 Sep 2026): 'Who is on the hook if an agent makes the wrong purchase?'; existing liability frameworks 'could potentially be adapted'; fraud systems calibrated to human behaviour 'may not translate well to agents'; no adoption figures and no mention of Regulation E | Capital One 10-K FY2025: agentic commerce may increase fraud losses and change when merchant or issuer is liable; legal frameworks for autonomous agents 'remain nascent, with limited direct guidance'; activists and regulators have sought to expand banks' duty to hold customers harmless for scam-induced authorised transactions | UK FCA: Payments Regulatory Priorities (March 2026) will consider whether regulation needs to change to support agentic AI payments; FCA speech of 19 Oct 2026 (drafted text) promises a framework on agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution, without allocating liability
Implication: The bank that authenticates and limits an agent carries exposure it cannot yet price (scam-induced 'authorised' transfers sit with the consumer under the text, while regulators press banks to absorb them), so a consumer agent-permissions product is a liability decision before it is a growth decision (all segments; debit-primary customers least able to absorb a loss).
Caveats: Consumer line: INSIDE. Liability, notification and dispute handling on the consumer's own account is the consumer-facing layer. Applying 1005.2(m) to an AI agent is the researcher's reading of the rule text, not a regulator statement; whether an agent-held token is an 'access device' 'furnished' by the consumer is untested. The commentary text was confirmed on the CFPB eRegs page by the compiler. No CFPB, OCC or FDIC statement on agent payments was found; a reported January 2026 CFPB advisory was second-hand and not used. EU AI Act not researched.

Claim: Mastercard's FY2025 10-K says it enabled all US Mastercard cardholders for Agent Pay in 2025 on its tokenization and dispute-management capabilities, Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol is a merchant-side signature standard silent on liability, and Capital One now runs the Discover, PULSE and Diners Club networks ($401.8B of 2025 volume) but discloses agentic commerce only as a fraud and liability risk.
Evidence: Mastercard 10-K FY2025: launched Mastercard Agent Pay, enabling AI-assisted and fully automated agent payments across its acceptance network, building on tokenization (including Agentic Tokens) and dispute management; 'In 2025, we enabled all U.S.-based Mastercard cardholders to participate', global launch scheduled for early 2026 | Visa Trusted Agent Protocol developer page: a cryptographic standard (RFC 9421 signatures) to help merchants tell legitimate agents from bots and crawlers; no mention of liability, disputes, chargebacks or consumer authorisation | Capital One 10-K FY2025: for bank-issued cards on the Global Payment Network 'a portion of the amount that merchants pay ... is passed through to the Bank'; Global Payment Network volume $401,775M in 2025; the only agentic mentions are the fraud and liability risk factor | No Capital One or Discover agent-payments announcement was found by either researcher
Implication: Agent credentials, registration and disputes at the network level are infrastructure the networks already ship and the sponsor rules out, so a bank's consumer role shrinks to agent approvals, limits and dispute handling in its own app; Discover helps only if Capital One writes agent rules on its own volume, which it has not disclosed (debit-primary customers on the Discover network are where it controls issuer and network).
Caveats: Consumer line: STRADDLES. The evidence (tokens, agent protocols, network rules) is OUTSIDE; the residual role named in the Implication (approvals, limits, disputes in the bank app) is INSIDE. 'Enabled' means eligible, not used; no usage figure found. Mastercard 10-K verified from the SEC PDF (identical to the researcher's local extract ma_ars.pdf). Network rulebooks on issuer duties were not opened. The inside/outside line is the researcher's judgment.

Claim: In an account-level panel of 12.1 million credit-union deposit accounts through 2023, accounts above $25,000 (about 10% of accounts, about 70% of dollars) showed no statistically detectable balance response to deposit-rate spreads, while smaller accounts did.
Evidence: NBER WP 34742, 12.1M accounts at 154 US credit unions through 2023: accounts under $25,000 show a semi-elasticity of about -9.0% per 1pp of rate spread; accounts above $25,000 about -0.005, statistically insignificant | Same paper: excess bunching at a bank's own rate-step threshold falls from 11% at $1,000 to 4.4% at $25,000 to insignificant at $50,000 | FDIC National Rates (as of 17 Aug 2026): national average savings rate 0.38% against high-yield offers above 4% APY | CNBC Select/Dynata (Sept 2023, n=1,151): 82% report not using a high-yield savings account (corroborating only)
Implication: Idle high-balance cash that ignores rate gaps is real, which supports the 'money sits' premise of T03, but the same inattention is what a bank is paid for, so it supports the problem and cuts against the bank as the fixer (mass-affluent; debit-primary hold too little).
Caveats: Working paper, not peer-reviewed; credit-union members are a proxy for the upmarket segment; CNBC figure sponsor-run. Spot-checked by the compiler: 12.1M accounts, the $25,000 definition and -0.005 confirmed in the PDF. Original Territory ID: independence (sheet line 64). Paired with crosscut-17 (H1 objection).

Claim: US money market fund net assets reached a record $6.4 trillion at end-2023 on a record $1.2 trillion of net inflows, with retail investors more than half of the full-year increase and institutions about 80% of the March 2023 surge.
Evidence: OFR blog (26 Mar 2024): MMF net assets $6.4T at 31 Dec 2023; $1.2T inflows in 2023, the largest on record | About 40% of net inflows arrived in March 2023, the month of the SVB and Signature failures | Retail investors more than 50% of the 2023 net asset increase; institutional investors 80% of March inflows
Implication: This is the H1 money-market objection to inattention as a moat: large cash did move to money market funds in 2023, so a treasury product competes with out-of-bank alternatives that already exist, and the open question for T03 is who owns the sweep (affluent households, not debit-primary).
Caveats: H1 objection kept visible as Mixed on T03. The corpus row calls this compatible with crosscut-16 (different dollars); the wave-3 shortlist says that reconciliation is inference and no source measures where 2023 inflows came from by depositor type; treat as unresolved. Single year's flow. Spot-checked by the compiler: $6.4T, $1.2T, ~40%, >50% retail, 80% institutional all confirmed. Original Territory ID: independence (sheet line 88).

Claim: Cumulative deposit beta rose from -0.03 in Q1 2022 to 0.51 by Q2 2024, reaching about 0.4 within about a year in this cycle against about three years in 2015-2019.
Evidence: St. Louis Fed (27 Sep 2024) and NY Fed Liberty Street (Apr 2023): cumulative beta -0.03 (Q1 2022) to 0.51 (Q2 2024); deposit rates kept rising after fed funds flattened | Beta about 0.4 by Q4 2022, a level the 2015-2019 cycle took three years to reach | Q4 2022 spread between average fed funds (3.7%) and average interest-bearing deposit rate (1.4%) was a modern high
Implication: Deposit pricing already moves toward rate without any consumer agent, so the treasury gap may be narrowing on its own (all balance tiers).
Caveats: Different datasets (Call Report/UBPR vs FR Y-9C); beta is a bank-side aggregate and says nothing about who moved. Original Territory ID: independence (sheet line 87).

Claim: Chase household bank balances were up only 23% against 2019 versus a roughly 40% trend expectation as of May 2025, while the top income quartile's broader cash reserves grew as its bank balances fell.
Evidence: JPMorgan Chase Institute (17 Jul 2025; 4.7M Chase households, active checking, $12,000+ income): median bank balances up 23% vs 2019 against about 40% expected | Highest-income households' bank balances 3% negative year on year in May 2025 while broader cash reserves (investments, CDs, money market) grew 1-2% (low-return scenario) to 4% (moderate-return scenario) | The Institute reads lower bank balances as households investing and seeking return elsewhere, not distress; brokerage use rose across income groups from 2020
Implication: Upper-income households already move cash toward yield without an agent, which weakens 'trillions idle' for them and points T03 at the debit-primary segment, where the gain per household is small.
Caveats: Chase customers only; income quartile is a proxy for liquid assets. Spot-checked by the compiler: 23%, 40%, -3% and 4.7M confirmed; the corpus's '1-4%' blends two scenarios and is restated. Original Territory ID: income (sheet line 181).

Claim: A Dallas Fed research note (25 Aug 2026) models that a 10 percent rise in deposit rate beta would cut banks' duration-risk appetite by about $700 billion, driven by tokenized deposits, with agentic AI named only as a possible enabler.
Evidence: Dallas Fed (Levy and Ramaswamy, 25 Aug 2026), back-of-envelope sensitivity: a 10% increase in beta (baseline about 0.44) reduces 10-year-equivalent duration-risk appetite by about $700B, assuming a four-year deposit weighted average life | Driver is tokenized deposits with instant settlement; agentic AI named only as a theorised enabler of switching without depositor action | A Curinos perspective claiming affluent households are most exposed to agentic switching has no disclosed data and is not used as evidence
Implication: The corpus holds no measured agent-driven deposit movement; the only agent link is a scenario, so T08 and T03 cannot lean on it for demand (all segments).
Caveats: Consumer line: OUTSIDE. A bank balance-sheet and tokenized-deposit scenario, not a consumer product. Scenario conditional on retail tokenized-deposit adoption that does not exist; Curinos is a bank-advisory vendor. Original Territory ID: independence (sheet line 65).

Claim: Banks and credit unions collected an estimated $12.1 billion in overdraft and NSF fees in 2024 and $12.4 billion in 2025 after Congress overturned the CFPB's 2024 overdraft rule.
Evidence: NCLC analysis of call reports: about $12.1B in 2024 and an estimated $12.4B in 2025 (extrapolated from the top 20 banks); JPMorgan Chase $1.1B and Wells Fargo $924M in 2025 | CFPB overdraft rule (issued 12 Dec 2024, effective date 1 Oct 2025) never took effect after congressional disapproval, per NCLC (page dated 3 Jun 2026) and the CFPB rule page
Implication: A large recurring fee pool exists that customers overpay into, but a bank that finds and returns it gives up its own fee revenue, so the pool supports the pain and cuts against bank-as-finder (debit-primary bear most of it).
Caveats: NCLC is an advocacy organisation and 2024-2025 totals are its extrapolation. Spot-checked by the compiler: NCLC $12.1B, $12.4B, $1.1B and $924M confirmed. The CFPB Data Spotlight URL in the corpus row now returns 404, so it and its 2019-2023 figures ($11.96B to $5.83B, -51%) were removed. Original Territory ID: rupture (sheet line 254).

Claim: The CFPB overdraft rule was nullified via CRA resolution (signed 9 May 2025) and the $8 credit-card late-fee rule was vacated by consent judgment on 15 April 2025.
Evidence: Overdraft rule finalized Dec 2024, nullified by S.J. Res. 18 signed 9 May 2025, before its 1 Oct 2025 effective date | $8 late-fee rule finalized 5 Mar 2024, vacated by consent judgment 15 Apr 2025 in N.D. Texas | Fed SHED 2024 (n above 12,000): 6% of adults with $100,000+ income paid an overdraft fee in the past year vs 16% under $25,000
Implication: With federal fee caps gone, no regulator forces the fee relief a 'bank finds what you overpay' product would ride on, and the exposed customers are lower-income debit-primary.
Caveats: Dates cross-checked in the corpus on the CFPB page plus two law-firm and association summaries (pointers for dated facts). Another compiler's check found the CFPB resource page gives 12 May 2025 for the disapproval signing; the date discrepancy is unresolved here. Original Territory ID: income (sheet line 187).
