Claim: Candidate 'own the sweep': households with balances above $25,000 do not respond to rate spreads inside their bank, yet cash moved out of bank balances into money market and investment products in 2023-2025, which implies the contested object is a bank-run default sweep for balances above $25,000 rather than a rate match.
Evidence: Sheet line 64 (NBER WP 34742): accounts above $25,000 show a semi-elasticity of about -0.005, indistinguishable from zero | Sheet line 88 (OFR, Mar 2024): $1.2T net MMF inflows in 2023, retail more than half | Sheet line 181 (JPMorgan Chase Institute, Jul 2025): top-income households' bank balances fell 3% in May 2025 while cash reserves including money market and CDs grew | Wave-3 shortlist H1: the reconciliation (brokerage sweeps move idle cash with no separate customer decision) is inference; no source measures where 2023 inflows originated by depositor type
Implication: Falsifiable form: households with more than $25,000 in bank deposits would accept a bank-run default sweep to a yielding instrument at a stated yield gap, and the bank would retain more net revenue than it loses on spread; killed if sweep-eligible balances show no uptake in a bank's own pilot or spread loss exceeds retained balances (mass-affluent, not debit-primary).
Caveats: An inference across three rows, not a corpus finding; segment proxies differ. Adjacent to T03 (the sponsor's version is a cross-institution agent; this is a bank-run default). Research rows bearing on it: crosscut-01, 03, 06, 07. Original Territory IDs: independence (lines 64, 88), income (line 181).

Claim: Unpromoted candidate, consumer stablecoin savings: Osero, a Cayman-based stablecoin savings provider founded in 2025, raised a $13.5M seed reported 13 May 2026, but it sells an SDK to wallets and neobanks, and the category already sits on the sponsor's Framework C ring 3 list.
Evidence: CB Insights: Osero founded 2025, Grand Cayman; $13.5M seed reported 13 May 2026, headline says led by Sky Ecosystem; investors listed include Sky Frontier Foundation, Plasma and stablewatch | CB Insights describes an SDK that lets wallets, neobanks, custodians and stablecoin holders earn yield, so the main customer is a distributor | The sponsor brief (Section 6, Framework C) lists tokenized deposits among ring 3 new-to-world models
Implication: Not a missed territory: it maps to the sponsor's ring 3 list and, for households, to T03 Household Treasury.
Caveats: Single aggregator page; round date inferred from the page's news date. Investors are the protocol ecosystem it serves (Sky, Plasma), a direct interest. Offshore. GENIUS Act yield rules were not checked.

Claim: The CFPB stopped publishing consumer complaint narratives on 14 August 2026, and as of 26 October 2026 neither the public API nor the live bulk file carries a narrative field, so an Internet Archive capture of 15 August 2026 is the last public narrative record.
Evidence: CFPB newsroom notice dated 14 Aug 2026: the Bureau is ceasing publication of unverified complaint narratives and visualizations, which it calls discretionary; previously published narratives are treated as public domain for FOIA and are being disclosed in its FOIA Reading Room | Compiler check 26 Oct 2026: an API query for mortgage returns 485,091 hits with no complaint_what_happened field in records; the live bulk file (358,644,221 bytes, modified 26 Oct 2026) has 15 columns and no narrative column | Internet Archive CDX lists a 200 capture of the bulk file at 20260815141332 (record length 1,414,994,469) and a later one at 20261022003117 (356,116,504); the 15 Aug capture carries the narrative column, with 110,695 of 198,015 complaints (55.9%) in the four product groups dated 2023 carrying a narrative (arithmetic from the saved JSON totals)
Implication: Every narrative-based kill test (transfer-92, transfer-93, caregiving-92, partnerships-90) rests on this frozen copy and cannot be refreshed; structured fields are the only live complaint series.
Caveats: The archive file is a third-party copy (Internet Archive), not a CFPB-served file; its row counts were not reconciled to a CFPB-published total, and the local download (1,415,011,387 bytes) differs slightly from the CDX record length, which measures the archived record rather than the payload. WebFetch is blocked from web.archive.org; the capture was confirmed by curl (HTTP 206 on a byte-range request) and the CDX listing. The consumerfinancemonitor.com post is a law-firm blog, kept as a pointer; the CFPB notice is the primary.

Claim: In September 2026 prospectuses and the June 2026 Goldman Sachs filing, the sweep-oriented classes of large government money funds pay intermediaries 3 to 50 bps in service and administration fees, and 85 to 105 bps only on classes that add a 12b-1 fee, while FINRA Rule 2341 caps service fees at 0.25% and bars the no-load label above 0.25% of charges.
Evidence: Federated Hermes Government Obligations Fund summary prospectuses (30 Sep 2026): Service Shares GOSXX 12b-1 none, other expenses 0.35%, total 0.50%, 0.45% after waiver; Capital GOCXX 12b-1 none, other 0.33%, total 0.48%, 0.30% after waiver; Cash II GFYXX 12b-1 0.35%, total 0.91%, 0.85% after waiver; Cash Series GFSXX 12b-1 0.60%, total 1.10%, 1.05% after waiver | Federated 485(b) filing (24 Sep 2026): Service Fees up to 0.25% to intermediaries, or Account Administration Fees up to 0.25% to banks that are not broker-dealers or advisers, not both on one account | Goldman Sachs Trust 485(b) (11 Jun 2026), Financial Square funds: Administration up to 0.25%; Capital 0.15%; Preferred 0.10%; Select 0.03%; Service 0.25% service plus 0.25% shareholder administration; Cash Management 0.50% plus 0.30% 12b-1; Resource 0.50% plus 0.15% 12b-1. Fidelity Treasury Portfolio Select (30 May 2026) 12b-1 0.05%, 0.23% net; Morgan Stanley Tax-Exempt Wealth (27 Feb 2026) no 12b-1, 0.20% net | FINRA Rule 2341: (d)(5) no sale of a fund whose service fees exceed 0.25% of average annual net assets; (d)(2)(E)(i) asset-based sales charge above 0.75% barred; (d)(4) no no-load label if sales-related charges and service fees exceed 0.25%
Implication: The fee a fund can pass to a sweep provider is 15 to 25 bps on ordinary service or administration classes and 50 bps at the outer edge before 12b-1, which sets the revenue side of the own-the-sweep kill test far below any deposit spread benchmark.
Caveats: Fee-table figures are maxima or class totals, not the fee any bank receives, which sits in negotiated intermediary agreements; no disclosed fee paid to a bank intermediary was found. Fund sponsors are interested parties. Rule 2341 binds FINRA members, not a non-member bank. Reading the no-load term in the Exchange Act sweep exception (15 U.S.C. 78c(a)(4)(B)(v)) through Rule 2341(d)(4), which would cap a bank-run sweep near 25 bps, is the researcher's inference and was not tested against SEC or OCC guidance. Dreyfus/BNY, JPMorgan and Schwab sweep classes were not tabulated. Merges researcher findings sweep-1 and sweep-2.

Claim: Sweep intermediaries disclose earning 122 bps (Schwab, 2025), 74 bps (Robinhood, 2025) and 62 bps (Wealthfront, fiscal 2026) on deposits swept to program banks, the market price of the spread a bank keeps on a swept dollar.
Evidence: Schwab FY2025 10-K: bank deposit account fees $977M (2024 $729M) on average BDA balances $80,329M; average net yield 1.22% (0.84% 2024, 0.68% 2023); 78% of balances fixed-rate; balances are swept off balance sheet to the TD Depository Institutions under the 2023 IDA agreement | Robinhood FY2025 10-K: Cash Sweep (off-balance sheet) $32,786M at year end, average $30,912M, revenue $229M, annual yield 0.74% | Wealthfront FY2026 10-K (year to 31 Jan 2026): cash management revenue $271.7M on average cash management assets $43,886M ($45,361M at period end); annualised fee rate 0.62% (0.64% prior year)
Implication: Program banks pay intermediaries 60 to 122 bps for deposits, three to five times what a no-load fund class can return, which sets the spread side of the own-the-sweep test and points to the kill.
Caveats: These are sweeps into bank deposit programmes, the reverse flow of a bank sweeping out to a fund, but they price the same spread. Schwab's yield reflects fixed-rate contracts set in earlier rate regimes. Each company reports its own metric. The researcher's line that Schwab says fee revenue may be less than the net interest it could earn holding the balances itself was not found in the extract and is removed. LPL's client cash revenue ($1,657.8M on $50.9B average balances) was not used as a rate because the filing does not say whether it is net of client interest.

Claim: On 17 January 2025 the SEC settled cash-sweep cases with Wells Fargo Clearing ($28M), Wells Fargo Advisors Financial Network ($7M) and Merrill Lynch ($25M), citing yield gaps of almost 4 percentage points, while LPL disclosed that the SEC closed its sweep inquiry on 23 January 2026 without recommending action.
Evidence: SEC press release 2025-16: $60M combined for failing to adopt and implement policies reasonably designed to prevent Advisers Act violations on cash sweeps; bank deposit sweep programmes were the only sweep option for most advisory clients at Wells Fargo Advisors and Merrill; the yield gap to other options at times reached almost 4 percent | LPL FY2025 10-K: SEC request for information in August 2024 on the cash management programme for corporate advisory accounts; on 23 Jan 2026 the SEC said it had concluded its investigation and did not intend to recommend enforcement; client lawsuits over sweep programmes continue
Implication: The enforcement target is a default sweep where the firm keeps the spread, so a bank-run default sweep to a third-party fund would face the same steering question; this adds conduct risk to the arithmetic kill and to Capital One's open 360 Savings settlement.
Caveats: These are advisory (fiduciary) account facts and a single-option default, which do not map one to one onto a retail deposit customer. Morgan Stanley's reported closure of its sweep inquiry came only from secondary press and is not cited. No FINRA action on sweep disclosure was found.

Claim: On public documents the fee a money fund can pay for a bank-run sweep (15 to 25 bps typical, 50 bps at most before 12b-1) sits below every spread benchmark available (62 bps Wealthfront, 74 bps Robinhood, 122 bps Schwab, about 230 bps Capital One segment proxy), so the bank gives up 35 to 205 bps per swept dollar unless most swept dollars would have left anyway.
Evidence: Fee side (crosscut-91): 3 bps (Goldman Select) to 50 bps (Goldman Service) before 12b-1; 85 to 105 bps only on 12b-1 classes a no-load-restricted sweep likely cannot use | Spread side (crosscut-92, franchise-90): 62, 74 and 122 bps intermediary yields; about 230 bps Capital One Consumer Banking net interest income per average deposit dollar, a ceiling | Researcher arithmetic at a 25 bps fee: give-up 35 bps (against 60), 97 bps (against 122), 205 bps (against 230); only a 50 bps fee against a 60 bps spread narrows it to 10 bps | Researcher arithmetic, break-even share p of swept dollars that would otherwise leave, fee > (1 - p) x spread: at 25 bps p must exceed 80% (122 bps spread) or 89% (230 bps), and 58% against a 60 bps spread
Implication: The kill criterion as written (fee below spread) is met, so own-the-sweep dies as a revenue case before any pilot; it survives only as a defensive feature if outbound-flow data show that more than about 80% of swept dollars would otherwise leave, and the NBER low-rate-response evidence points the other way.
Caveats: Analyst arithmetic across non-identical settings: fund-class maxima against program-bank prices and a segment proxy, not Capital One's internal funds-transfer price, which the kill criterion names and which is not public and could differ either way. A bank might negotiate revenue share outside the prospectus. Spread benchmarks carry the reporting firms' interest. The break-even ignores the relationship value of a retained customer, which no row measures.

Claim: Visa's 18 April 2026 Core Rules treat an agentic payment provider as the Cardholder, make the cardholder responsible for the provider's actions as if they had initiated the transaction, and add no agent-specific dispute condition.
Evidence: Section 4.1.24.10 (p.260, ID# 0031176, last updated Oct 2025): a Cardholder is responsible for any actions taken by an Agentic Payment Provider as part of an Agentic Transaction as if the Cardholder initiated the Transaction; the glossary entry for Cardholder treats the provider as the Cardholder for an Agentic Transaction | Section 4.1.24.3 (ID# 0031169): before transacting, the provider must obtain cardholder consent, state when the payment instruction expires and obtain the cardholder's acknowledgement of responsibility; initiators of agentic transactions are not considered Merchants (glossary) | Dispute chapter: the only agentic edits are agentic-payment-provider login IDs accepted as evidence under Dispute Condition 10.4 (Other Fraud, Card-Absent) and section 5.4.2 (ID# 0008771), which bars merchants from making cardholders waive dispute rights on agentic transactions; a full-text search of the 923-page edition finds no dispute condition for agent scope or agent error
Implication: The T08 kill test is not met on the Visa side: agent-error liability lands on the cardholder, not on the agent operator or merchant, so scope disputes fall to the issuer-cardholder relationship, which keeps the issuer app's dispute and evidence slot open but leaves the verdict at Feature.
Caveats: Visa's public edition omits some proprietary content, so absence from the text is not absence from all Visa documents; the Dispute Management Guidelines and Visa Intelligent Commerce specifications were not read. Network rules bind members and providers, not consumers; Reg E and Reg Z still govern the consumer against the issuer, and how the two interact is the researcher's reading. The compiler verified the quoted sections in the researcher's local extract and confirmed the live PDF is byte-identical (same MD5). Merges researcher findings agent-1 and agent-2.

Claim: Visa's rules require issuers to pay for agentic transactions processed per the cardholder's instructions and bar systematic or wholesale declines that include agent traffic, leaving per-customer controls as the issuer's lever.
Evidence: Section 1.7.6.1 (ID# 0006558): an issuer must pay the acquirer for valid-card transactions, including an Agentic Transaction processed in accordance with the cardholder's payment instructions | Section 1.7.4.1 (ID# 0029326): an issuer must not block, refuse or decline authorisation requests, token provisioning or transactions in a systematic or wholesale manner; a footnote includes transactions by Agentic Payment Providers among the covered categories; exceptions for immediate fraud threat, law or special programmes | Section 4.1.24.3 requires the provider to retain consent and credential terms and supply them to the cardholder or issuer on written request; 4.1.24.8 requires an order confirmation available to the cardholder for at least 120 days
Implication: A customer-set limit is not systematic blocking (researcher's reading), so a narrow permissions-and-limits feature in the bank app is permitted, but the network supplies the consent record, leaving the app's distinct content as the customer-facing control surface; the verdict stays at Feature.
Caveats: The reading of wholesale is the researcher's; Visa has not said so. Applies to Visa-brand cards only, not Mastercard or Discover.

Claim: Mastercard's rule text on agent disputes could not be read in this pass, and its public statements through July 2026 describe Agent Pay and Verifiable Intent as feeding existing chargeback processes rather than a new liability rule.
Evidence: mastercard.us and mastercard.com rules and Chargeback Guide URLs returned 403 on every fetch, so no version date or agent wording was obtained | Mastercard Q2 2026 call (30 Jul 2026, Motley Fool transcript on Webull): Agent Pay uses tokenisation, Zero Liability Protection and dispute resolution; CEO Michael Miebach said Verifiable Intent, developed with Google, allows a cardholder to challenge a transaction; token penetration over 40% of switched transactions (not agent-specific) | Worldpay analysis (undated, after April 2026): properly authenticated tokenised agent transactions follow existing rules with the issuer carrying fraud risk and chargeback rights intact; no liability shift exists yet; disputes where an agent misreads instructions are unallocated | Shopappy (13 Sep 2026), citing Mastercard's 3 Aug 2026 Signals report Encoding Trust: neither network is expected to have a binding agent-dispute rule before holiday 2026, the first more likely in the April 2027 cycle
Implication: The Mastercard half of the T08 network-liability test remains unresolved: every available account routes agent disputes into existing chargeback processes with no named agent reason code, weakly consistent with the kill, but no rule text was seen, so the verdict stays at Feature.
Caveats: No primary rule text. Mastercard is interested in its own statements; Worldpay is a processor with a stake in acceptance; Shopappy is a content site of unknown standing and the Mastercard report it cites was not fetched (pointers only). The transcript is a third-party copy. Someone with Mastercard Connect access should search the Chargeback Guide and Transaction Processing Rules for agent terms.

Claim: As of 26 October 2026, Visa's and Mastercard's latest earnings materials give partner counts and launches but no count of consumer agentic transactions, enabled cardholders or merchants, and the next releases (27 and 29 October 2026) were not yet out.
Evidence: Visa FQ3 2026 call (28 Jul 2026, FactSet corrected transcript): the CEO said Visa is in the very early stages of a major adoption curve and that agentic commerce is a when, not an if; announcements include Agent Score and partnerships with OpenAI and Meta; no agentic transaction count | Visa notice: FQ4 and full-year 2026 results on 27 Oct 2026 after market close, webcast 2:00 pm PT; Mastercard notice dated 8 Oct 2026: Q3 2026 results and call on 29 Oct 2026 at 9:00 am ET | Mastercard Q2 2026 call: more than 30 industry leaders at the launch of Agent Pay for Machines; it's early days; no volumes; Digital Transactions (29 Jan 2026) on Mastercard's Q4 2025 reports no agentic figures and quotes the CEO that scaling is hard to predict
Implication: No consumer agent-usage figure exists, so the demand half of the T08 kill test is unresolved pending the 27 and 29 October releases; on the evidence so far the demand case has nothing behind it and the verdict stays at Feature.
Caveats: Absence of a figure in disclosures, not a measured zero. Company disclosure; the Mastercard transcript is a third-party copy; Digital Transactions is trade press. The earlier-sweep figures (Visa hundreds of transactions in Dec 2025; Mastercard all US cardholders enabled) were not re-verified here. PayPal and Stripe agent volumes were not found. Direction corrected from the researcher's Supports (set against the proposition that usage is tiny) to Contradicts, relative to the T08 hypothesis.

Claim: No 2026 CFPB, OCC, Fed or FTC statement on liability for AI-agent-initiated payments was found, while the UK FCA's March 2026 payments priorities commit it to consider whether regulation needs to change to support agentic AI payments.
Evidence: FCA Regulatory Priorities: Payments (March 2026): working with HM Treasury on modernising payment-services regulation, including considering whether change or development of regulation is needed to support agentic AI payments | Bratby Law (posted 22 Jul 2026, updated 25 Oct 2026): under PSRs 2017 reg 67 (consent), 75 (burden of proof) and 76 (refunds), whether an agent's payment is authorised turns on the scope of the delegation; neither the PSRs nor the APP reimbursement regime allocates loss to the party that supplied the agent | US: searches returned only law-firm and trade material; the Davis Wright Tremaine paper made with the Consumer Bankers Association (January 2026) lists gaps in current legal and regulatory frameworks as a key insight
Implication: With no US ruling and the UK still reviewing, liability for an agent's mistake under Reg E or Reg Z is unassigned in law, so the issuer's exposure and any value in clear agent controls both persist and the verdict stays at Feature; Debit-Primary Spenders carry the exposure if Reg E treats a delegated agent as a furnished access device (researcher's reading).
Caveats: The UK is not US jurisdiction. Bratby is author commentary, not the regulator. The DWT landing page gives no detail on authorisation or liability (the full PDF was not read) and the CBA is a bank trade group with an interest. US absence is from search, not a docket review of consumerfinance.gov, occ.gov or federalreserve.gov. The FCA PDF is encrypted and would not parse through WebFetch; the compiler extracted it locally and confirmed the sentence. Geography changed from UK to Multi-region because the claim covers both.

Claim: The fees T01 targets are large but the headline is loose: BEA puts US broker commissions and related costs at about $170 billion in 2024, and the CFPB puts median total loan costs on a purchase mortgage at $6,684 in 2023.
Evidence: Fed FEDS Note 'Commissions and Omissions' (Banerjee and Paciorek, May 2025): over 5 million home sales a year over the past decade, about $1.5 trillion annual volume; BEA estimates commissions and related costs at about $170 billion in 2024 (0.6% of GDP); average buyer-agent rate about 2.7% today from MLS data. | DOJ statement of interest (Case 2:24-cv-02374, Doc. 115, filed 12/19/25) repeats the same five million sales, $1.5 trillion and $170 billion figures. | Compiler-labelled arithmetic, not a sourced figure: $1.5 trillion x 2.7% x 2 sides is roughly $80 billion, about half the $170 billion headline, so 'related costs' carry much of the BEA total. | CFPB 2023 HMDA report (Dec 2024): median total loan costs on purchase loans $6,684 in 2023, up 12.3% from $5,954 in 2022; 56.6% of purchase loans paid discount points. CFPB closing-cost RFI (May 2024): origination fees and title fees are the two largest disclosed closing-cost categories; title premiums typically 0.5-1% of price; more than 200 fee types seen on closing disclosures.
Implication: The fee pool is tens of billions a year, large enough for a venture case, but the commission-only figure is unresolved and the lender-side costs a bank would natively touch are thousands per loan, not tens of thousands.
Caveats: The $170 billion is a BEA national-accounts estimate that includes undefined related costs; the authors warn BEA leans on five-yearly Economic Census data. The 2.7% is a buyer-agent rate from MLS data covering about half of listings, and the total-is-twice-the-buyer-rate assumption is the Fed note's. The roughly $80 billion figure is compiler arithmetic shown only to bound the commission-only pool; it is not a sourced number. The CFPB HMDA report gives the 2022-2023 rise as 12.3% in one place and 12.2% in another. DOJ is a litigant repeating the Fed figure. DOJ and CFPB PDFs were read from locally extracted text. No HMDA 2024-2025 cost figures were sourced (FFIEC blocked).

Claim: The 2024 NAR settlement changed how buyer-agent pay is offered but did not cut it: offers of compensation were barred from MLSs and written buyer agreements required from 17 August 2024, and Redfin's closed-deal series shows the average buyer-agent commission back at 2.43% in Q2 2025.
Evidence: NAR (26 Nov 2024): court granted final approval of the Sitzer/Burnett settlement; practice changes took effect 17 August 2024 (no MLS offers of compensation; written buyer agreements before touring); release covers over 1.4 million members and brokerages with 2022 volume of $2 billion or less. | DOJ statement of interest (filed 24 Nov 2024) objected to the written-agreement-before-touring provision on antitrust grounds and said sellers feel pressure to offer the customary 2.5-3% to buyer brokers. Fannie Mae Selling Notice (15 April 2024): no immediate Selling Guide change; seller-paid buyer-agent commissions paid under local common and customary practice need not count toward the 2-9% interested-party-contribution limits. | Redfin (Aug 2025): average buyer-agent commission 2.43% in Q2 2025 versus 2.38% a year earlier, after a low of 2.36% in Q3 2024; 2.52% for homes under $500,000. | Consumer Policy Center (2 Nov 2025): of 281 buyer agents interviewed in 26 metros, 95% quoted 2.5-3%, and two-thirds said they would accept a lower rate if a seller insisted.
Implication: The settlement is a why-now for transparent buyer-side pricing, but commissions held, so a low-fee entrant must win buyers who are not shopping on price; this matters most to Young Consumers buying under $500,000, where rates are highest.
Caveats: NAR is a defendant and DOJ an adversary to the settlement; the settlement text was not opened. Redfin competes on lower commissions and its sample excludes most Redfin-represented buyer deals. CPC does not state field dates or funding. The status of the settlement appeal in 2026 was not confirmed from a primary record. No 2026 closed-deal commission series was found.

Claim: Rocket Companies already owns the end-to-end chain (Redfin brokerage and search, Rocket Mortgage, Mr. Cooper servicing, Rocket Title and Rocket Close) after closing Redfin on 1 July 2025 and Mr. Cooper on 1 October 2025, and posted a 2025 net loss.
Evidence: Rocket 10-K FY2025: consideration transferred about $1,742 million for Redfin and $16,973 million for Mr. Cooper; goodwill attributed partly to synergies from integrating Redfin's brokerage and home-search platform with Rocket's mortgage and real estate ecosystem; Rocket Title Insurance Company sits inside the group. | Rocket 10-K FY2025: total revenue, net $6,695 million (2024: $5,101 million); net loss $(234) million (2024: net income $636 million); real estate services revenue $404 million (2024: $54 million); Rocket Close revenue $391 million. | Rocket 10-Q Q2 2026: six-month real estate services revenue $453 million (2025: $25 million); Rocket Close closings 190 thousand units versus 33 thousand Redfin real estate transactions in H1 2026; six-month net income $526 million versus a $(178) million loss a year earlier. | The 10-K warns synergies may not be realised in the expected timeframe or at all.
Implication: The bundle the hypothesis describes exists under a licensed non-bank owner, so a bank would be an entrant against an integrated incumbent and the open question is whether the bundle earns more than its parts.
Caveats: Company filings; Rocket discloses no attach rate or per-buyer take across brokerage and mortgage. The Redfin and Rocket Close unit counts measure different things (Redfin includes sell-side). Only two quarters of Redfin are in the record. Rocket is not a bank.

Claim: Versions of the thesis that hold home inventory have the largest documented losses: Zillow wound down Zillow Offers on 2 November 2021, Redfin decided to wind down RedfinNow in November 2022, and Opendoor lost $1.3 billion in 2025 on an 8.0% gross margin.
Evidence: Zillow 10-K FY2021: on 2 November 2021 Zillow decided to wind down Zillow Offers; gross profit hit by a $211.0 million Homes inventory write-down. | Zillow 10-K FY2022: 2021 net loss $(528) million, of which loss from discontinued operations (Zillow Offers) $630 million. | Redfin 10-K FY2024: decided in November 2022 to wind down RedfinNow; inventory liquidated by Q2 2023. | Opendoor 10-K FY2025: revenue $4,371 million, gross profit $350 million (8.0% margin), net loss $(1,300) million (2024: $(392) million; 2023: $(275) million); 11,791 homes sold; accumulated deficit $5.0 billion.
Implication: A bank pursuing T01 should capture fees without owning the asset; the inventory-risk variant has a multi-billion-dollar loss record.
Caveats: The $630 million is the discontinued-operations line, not a company-stated total Offers loss. Opendoor's net loss includes items beyond resale. The hypothesis as written does not require buying homes, so this bounds one variant only.

Claim: The origination and title layers are cyclical and tech-first entrants could not hold margin through the trough: total originations fell from about $4.6 trillion in 2021 to about $1.5 trillion in 2023, Better's funded volume fell 73% to $3.0 billion in 2023, and Doma lost $302.2 million (2022) and $124.4 million (2023) before a cash sale in 2024.
Evidence: Urban Institute Housing Finance at a Glance (Sept 2026), Fannie Mae and MBA estimates of single-family originations ($ billions, refi share): 2021 4,570 and 4,436 (58% and 62%); 2023 1,503 and 1,458 (15%); 2025 1,956 and 1,953 (29%); 2026 forecasts 2,121 and 2,123. Rates rose to 6.7% in August 2026. CFPB HMDA: purchase originations 3.2 million in 2023 versus 4.1 million in 2022 (down 21.3%). | Better 10-K FY2023: funded loan volume $3.0 billion versus $11.4 billion in 2022 (about 73% decline); net loss $536.4 million versus $877.1 million. Better 10-K FY2025: funded volume $4.7 billion, net loss $165.9 million; 2020 was the only year with an annual operating profit. | Doma 10-K FY2023: total revenues $310.9 million versus $400.0 million; GAAP net loss $124.4 million (2023) and $302.2 million (2022); going-concern doubt raised and then alleviated by financing. Doma 8-K (27 Sept 2024): acquisition closed at $6.29 cash per share.
Implication: Any T01 revenue case built on 2021 volume is overstated; a new entrant should plan for a flat, rate-driven pool near 2025 levels.
Caveats: 2026-2027 values are forecasts; FNMA and MBA series are estimates not directly comparable to HMDA. Better's 2022 loss includes listing and warrant items not isolated. Doma's 10-K also shows a different net-loss line in a summary table ($95.3 million and $187.3 million); the $124.4 and $302.2 million figures are the GAAP net loss in the reconciliation and risk factors. HMDA 2024-2025 purchase counts are unsourced (FFIEC blocked).

Claim: A bank cannot simply own the realtor and referral fees: a 2001 Fed-Treasury proposal to let financial holding companies do real estate brokerage was blocked by Congress and the current Regulation Y finder rule excludes activity needing a real estate broker licence, and RESPA Section 8 bars referral fees among affiliated settlement providers.
Evidence: Treasury testimony (May 2002): the proposal was published in the Federal Register in January 2001; comment period closed 1 May 2001; 34,735 comment letters, mostly from brokers, and letters from 160 Members of Congress. Earlier testimony (May 2001) found a threshold case that banks and brokers compete. | CRS RS21104 (July 2003): the Consolidated Appropriations Resolution FY2003 (P.L. 108-7) barred Treasury funds for issuing the rule; H.R. 111 had 236 cosponsors. 12 CFR 225.86 (eCFR, current): a finder may not engage in any activity requiring a licence as a real estate agent or broker. | 12 U.S.C. 2607: no fee or kickback for referring settlement business; penalties up to $10,000, one year, and three times the settlement charge; affiliated business arrangements allowed with disclosure. 12 CFR 1024.15: written disclosure, no required use, and only bona fide ownership returns. | Redfin 10-K FY2024: brokerage, mortgage and title each require a state-specific licence; Rocket 10-K FY2025 cites RESPA and state law risk including revocation of licences.
Implication: The realtor-fee leg of T01 is closed to a bank holding company or must run through a non-bank partner, and inside a bundle each affiliate earns only on its own work, which narrows the capture story to lending and possibly title.
Caveats: No formal withdrawal notice was found and whether the appropriations rider continued after FY2004 was not confirmed. The eCFR reading covers the finder authority only. Cornell LII mirrors the U.S. Code. Rocket and Redfin are not bank holding companies, so the brokerage limit does not bind them. State attorney-closing rules were not sourced from a statute (gap).

Claim: The one input a deposit bank has that the integrated non-banks rent is funding: Rocket finances on $14.2 billion of funding facilities and $10.4 billion of senior notes and Zillow Home Loans on repurchase agreements, while Capital One left mortgage origination in 2017.
Evidence: Rocket 10-K FY2025 balance sheet: funding facilities $14,155 million (2024: $6,801 million); senior notes, net $10,423 million; deposit income $616 million is earned on servicing-related custodial deposits, not a retail deposit base. | Zillow 10-K FY2025: Zillow Home Loans finances originations through master repurchase agreements; purchase loan origination volume $4,721 million; Mortgages revenue $199 million of $2,583 million total (compiler arithmetic: about 7.7%). | Capital One exited mortgage and home equity origination (announced 2017) and sold Discover Home Loans in November 2025, per the round-1 franchise file (T00-A), not re-fetched here.
Implication: Cheaper funding is the only bank-native edge visible in T01, but no source shows funding cost decides purchase-mortgage share, and Capital One's record is two exits from home lending.
Caveats: Inference from balance-sheet structure; no source quantifies a warehouse-versus-deposit spread. Capital One facts come from the round-1 franchise file. Zillow's small mortgage share cuts both ways.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: The one scaled rent-rewards card lost its bank money: press reports of the Wall Street Journal say Wells Fargo lost as much as $10 million a month on the Bilt card, saw about 35% non-rent spend against a 65% projection, and decided to exit about three years before its 2029 end date; Wells Fargo's filings do not mention Bilt.
Evidence: PYMNTS (16 June 2024), relaying the WSJ citing current and former employees: Wells Fargo losing as much as $10 million a month; contract scheduled to end in 2029; both companies denied the relationship was in doubt. | Payments Dive (29 July 2025), relaying the WSJ: the bank predicted about 65% of Bilt card spend would be non-rent but only about 35% was; Wells Fargo decided to quit three years before 2029; rent carried a 30-day free float for cardholders who did not carry a balance; landlords absorb or pass on interchange when accepting card rent. | SEC EDGAR full-text search for 'Bilt' in Wells Fargo (CIK 0000072971) filings 2024-06-01 to 2026-10-01 returned zero hits (re-run in this pass).
Implication: A rewards-on-rent card starts from a negative unit-economics prior, worst for Debit-Primary renters who carry little non-rent card spend.
Caveats: Trade press kept only as the primary record of the renegotiation and exit because no filing exists; the empty EDGAR result is the evidence that none exists. Both pieces relay anonymous-source WSJ reporting; the WSJ was not fetched (paywall). The 65/35 split appears only in Payments Dive. Wells Fargo and Bilt denied trouble in June 2024. Confidence set Low because the loss and spend figures are unconfirmed by either party.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: Bilt raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025 and rebuilt its card on Column N.A. (with Cardless and Fidem Financial) so that fee-free rent points scale from 0.5x to 1.25x with everyday spend, while saying more than 85% of members use the platform without the card.
Evidence: Bilt newsroom (10 July 2025): $250 million primary round at $10.75 billion, led by General Catalyst and GID; United Wholesale Mortgage invested $100 million; network signed in 1 in 4 US apartment buildings; over 40,000 merchants; projects over $100 billion of annual housing spend by end-2025 and over $1 billion revenue by Q1 2026; more than 85% of members use the platform without the Bilt card. | Bilt newsroom (14 Jan 2026): Bilt Card 2.0 (Blue no fee, Obsidian $95, Palladium $495) powered with Cardless, Fidem Financial and Column N.A.; no transaction fee on rent; free opt-in rent reporting to major bureaus; 5.5 million homes; 'millions of Americans' (no member count). | Bilt letter (Jan 2026): fee-free housing option earns 0.5x to 1.25x points by everyday spend as a share of monthly rent, with 250 points a month below the minimum; BiltProtect required; alternative option earns 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spend; old Wells Fargo cards stop working for Bilt after 7 February 2026.
Implication: Property managers and renters will route rent through a rewards platform at scale, but the rebuild ties rent rewards to non-rent spend and most volume runs off the card, pointing T15 at high-spend renters, not Debit-Primary ones.
Caveats: A valuation is investor belief, not revenue; the $100 billion and $1 billion figures are projections; no audited volume, member count or loss data. Bilt is private and these are marketing claims. Property-manager-side economics not found.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: The consumer-scale rent product sells timing, not rewards: Flex says it has processed more than $40 billion of rent for more than 3.2 million renters since 2019 and on 24 July 2026 applied for a Utah industrial bank charter.
Evidence: Flex release (24 July 2026): more than $40 billion of rent processed for more than 3.2 million renters since 2019; more than $780 million in late rent fees avoided; applied to charter Flex Bank, a Utah industrial bank; Flex does not operate as a bank and loans and payment transmission are provided by Lead Bank or Column N.A. | Banking Dive (28 July 2026): same figures; application to the FDIC and Utah Department of Financial Institutions; proposed CEO Jeff Berkson, formerly chief risk officer at WebBank; sponsor banks Lead Bank and Column Bank; no decision reported.
Implication: Debit-Primary renters' rent problem is liquidity and someone already serves it at millions of renters, which shows rent can anchor a lending relationship but also means the renter cash-gate is not white space and the leading player is trying to become a bank.
Caveats: Company-reported cumulative figures with no definition of 'served' or split of advanced versus passed-through rent. No funding, loss or revenue data. The charter application is pending and may be denied. Banking Dive is trade press relaying the company announcement.

Claim: Where a rent platform publishes its card fee the renter pays it (RentCafe: 2.95% of the payment against ACH that is free or $0.95), and none of the platform pages fetched names Discover or publishes a Discover rent rate.
Evidence: RentCafe (Yardi) help page, fetched 2026-10-26: card rent payments carry a convenience fee of 2.95% of the transaction; the page's example is $44.25 on a $1,500 rent; ACH is free in most cases, with some properties charging $0.95; no card network is named. | AppFolio resident-payments blog, fetched 2026-10-26: lists eCheck, credit and debit cards among online rent options and tells managers to educate residents on additional card charges upfront; names no network and gives no amount. AppFolio's 10-K books electronic-payment fees as a percentage of the transaction [domicile-11]. | No Discover or PULSE rent or property-management rate card was found; the RentPayment help page returned 403 and Entrata's fee document returned 410, so Discover acceptance on Yardi, RealPage and Entrata portals is unconfirmed. | Bilt's rebuilt card charges no transaction fee on rent [domicile-09]; Wells Fargo's earlier Bilt card lost money [domicile-08].
Implication: No landlord-acceptance edge is visible because the renter, not the landlord, usually bears the card fee (about 2.95% against near-zero ACH), so pricing an owned network below Visa and Mastercard would not change what the platform charges; Debit-Primary Spenders are least able to carry such a fee.
Caveats: Edge: none (the landlord-cost edge claimed for an owned network is not where the fee is set). Help and blog pages are undated support or marketing content and fees vary by property. Discover acceptance on platforms is a gap, not a negative finding.

Claim: On 29 July 2026 the Colorado Attorney General announced a settlement with a rent payment processor (Domuso, per the linked documents) over a 3.25% certified-funds fee on card rent payments, capping the fee at 2% and requiring a cost-free payment option.
Evidence: Orrick InfoBytes summary dated 31 July 2026: the AG announced the settlement on 29 July 2026 after an investigation begun in October 2024; the fee was 3.25% on credit and debit card rent payments; the company denied liability. | Terms: certified-funds fees capped at 2% of the rent or related payment; $100,000 to reimburse investigative costs in lieu of penalties, plus disgorgement and restitution; a cost-free, reasonably accessible payment option; continued support for paper-check acceptance; officer-certified annual compliance reports for two years. | Legal theory: Colorado's surcharge and junk-fee statutes, the Uniform Consumer Credit Code and the Colorado Consumer Protection Act. | Compiler arithmetic: at 2% a $1,500 rent costs $30 by card against $0.96 at the Regulation II debit cap [domicile-13].
Implication: The state rule that bites is on the fee the renter pays, not on network pricing, so a card-rent product that relies on passing a percentage fee to renters carries junk-fee exposure and a no-fee rent card must absorb the cost itself (the Bilt model).
Caveats: Edge: none (a surcharge limit constrains whoever collects the card fee). Law-firm summary of a consent judgment; the judgment itself was not opened, so this is a pointer to the primary. One state and one processor; the 2% cap is a settlement term, not a statute. Secondary lists of other states' surcharge rules (Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey A2627) were not fetched and are not relied on.

Claim: An owned three-party network is valuable to the issuer because merchants pay more than the debit cap, not less, so it cannot be both the low-cost acceptor for landlords and the revenue source the hypothesis needs; and Flex, the scaled rent-timing product, pays landlords through sponsor banks with its own Utah industrial bank application pending and opposed by ICBA and BPI.
Evidence: The Fed's per-network table shows Discover debit at $0.83 interchange, 1.22% of value on a $68.57 ticket, all exempt [independence-103]; the Regulation II cap on a $1,500 payment is $0.96 [domicile-13]. Compiler arithmetic: 1.22% of $1,500 is $18.30, about 19 times the cap; this applies a debit average to a rent ticket and is illustrative only. | The cap exit exists only because the three-party network is exempt [independence-109, independence-110]; credit has no cap to exit, so on a credit rent charge the landlord, the renter or the issuer (Bilt, Wells Fargo) still pays [domicile-08, domicile-09]. | Banking Dive (28 July 2026, primary record of the event): Flex has processed more than $40 billion of rent for more than 3.2 million users since 2019, uses Lead Bank and Column as sponsor banks, and applied to Utah and the FDIC for an industrial loan company charter; no decision reported [domicile-10]. | ICBA page dated 30 August 2026: ICBA and BPI jointly asked the FDIC to deny Flexible Finance's deposit-insurance application for Flex Bank (letter dated 28 August 2026 per its file name). Fannie Mae already reads rent from bank-statement data [domicile-12].
Implication: P07 has no cost edge as worded: the owned network gives the issuer a revenue spread rather than the landlord a discount, rent timing is delivered without card acceptance, and what survives is an ordinary deposit-funded rent-timing or rewards card rather than a network position.
Caveats: Edge: none (the cap-exit edge is real for the issuer but is paid by the merchant; it is not a landlord-cost edge). Flex and Bilt figures are company-reported. The ICBA letter content is from the summary page, not the PDF. Charter outcome unknown. The 19x figure is illustrative arithmetic, not a rent rate.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: Landlord software already sits on the rent flow and takes a percentage cut: AppFolio's Value Added Services (electronic payments, screening, risk mitigation) were $721.5 million of $950.8 million FY2025 revenue across 9.4 million units, and Zillow's rentals tools include rental payments.
Evidence: AppFolio 10-K FY2025: total revenue $950,822 thousand; Value Added Services $721,549 thousand (2024: $605,011 thousand; 2023: $454,098 thousand); Subscription Services $211,457 thousand; 9.4 million units under management (8.7 million a year earlier); some electronic payment fees are charged as a percentage of the transaction and recorded gross of interchange; rent, security deposits and application fees can be collected through the platform. | Compiler arithmetic: Value Added Services is about 76% of AppFolio revenue, covering payments, screening and risk mitigation together. | Zillow 10-K FY2025: Rentals revenue $630 million, up 39%, 24% of revenue; renters can make secure rental payments on participating listings; new partnership with Esusu for rent reporting; no rent payment volume disclosed.
Implication: A bank that wants the rent flow must win it from the property manager's default portal, which already monetises payments and now bundles reporting, weakening T15 for every segment.
Caveats: AppFolio does not break out payments revenue or rent volume. RealPage (private since 2021) and Entrata (private) file no 10-K, so landlord-rail volume is unknown. Proves the rails exist, not how much rent they carry.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: Rent history already enters mortgage underwriting from the borrower's own bank-account data: Fannie Mae's Desktop Underwriter has read recurring rent from bank statements since 18 September 2021, Freddie Mac's LPA can upgrade a loan to Accept on positive rent history, and FHFA approved newer scores on 22 April 2026.
Evidence: Fannie Mae (Aug 2021): from 18 September 2021 DU identifies recurring rent in applicants' bank-statement data with permission; in a sample of recent non-owners without a favourable DU result, 17% could have received Approve/Eligible had rent been considered. DU page: more than 21,000 borrowers have benefited. FAQ: rent of $300 or more a month from 12 months of transaction data; no impact on credit score and data not disclosed to bureaus. | Freddie Mac LPA feedback messages (updated 3 Feb 2025): message FCL0438, positive rent history resulted in a Risk Class of Accept; applies only to sellers with Freddie Mac's written approval; document under Guide 5201.1; November 2025 release notes revise a rent-history message. Freddie Mac and Esusu (Multifamily Executive, 5 Apr 2023): 27,393 new credit scores, offered to over 240,000 units. | FHFA (22 April 2026): Fannie and Freddie implementing VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T, accepting Vantage-scored loans immediately. CFPB (reviewed Dec 2024): all three bureaus use rental payment information; on-time rent helps if the landlord reports, often through a payment app. | TransUnion (10 Sept 2025): consumers with rent reported 13% in 2025 (11% in 2024); property managers participating fell to 44% from 48%; online survey of 2,006 adults (5-10 March 2025) and 141 property managers.
Implication: A bank that already holds a renter's checking account supplies the credit-history leg of T15 as a feature at no rail cost, which undercuts the case for a separate rent rail but is a real, cheap edge for renters heading toward a mortgage.
Caveats: Fannie Mae pages fetched in this pass (domicile-B recorded 403s; domicile-A used a browser-header download). The 21,000 count is undated and cumulative. The Freddie/Esusu figure is trade press relaying a Freddie release that was blocked. Esusu and TransUnion sell rent reporting. TransUnion's 13% is an unweighted online survey and sits above the Fed SHED's 8%; neither is administrative. Whether rent history moves approvals at scale is not shown.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail
Claim: Debit interchange cannot fund rent rewards at a large bank: Regulation II caps interchange for issuers with $10 billion or more in assets at 21 cents plus 5 basis points (plus a 1-cent fraud adjustment), the Fed's 2023 proposal would cut it to 14.4 cents plus 4.0 basis points, and a 2025 vacatur of the rule is stayed pending appeal.
Evidence: Fed proposed rule (25 Oct 2023): current cap 21 cents base, 5 basis points ad valorem, 1-cent fraud-prevention adjustment; proposal 14.4 cents, 4.0 basis points and 1.3 cents, updated every other year from issuer cost surveys. | Fed Reg II FAQs: the small-issuer exemption turns on $10 billion in consolidated assets; Capital One is far above it (round-1 franchise file). | Cooley (15 Aug 2025): on 6 August 2025 the D.N.D. in Corner Post v. Board of Governors vacated Regulation II and stayed its own vacatur pending appeal. ABA Banking Journal (Feb 2026): ABA amicus filed 29 Dec 2025 urging the Eighth Circuit to reverse. | Compiler arithmetic: on a $1,500 rent payment the current cap is $0.21 + 0.0005 x $1,500 = $0.96, about 0.06% of the payment, before the fraud adjustment.
Implication: Debit rent earns about a dollar a payment at Capital One's size, so T15 economics must come from credit, float or the eventual loan, which pushes it away from the Debit-Primary segment.
Caveats: Court status rests on a law-firm alert and a trade-association item; the court order and docket were not opened and no Eighth Circuit decision was found as of October 2026. The 2023 proposal was not final in the sources found. If the vacatur is affirmed the cap lapses until rewritten. Capital One's ownership of Discover and PULSE does not change the issuer cap; no source on internal treatment.

Claim: Regulators police renter-data accuracy case by case while the CFPB's written guidance is gone: the FTC and CFPB obtained a $15 million TransUnion tenant-screening order in October 2023, the FTC a $2.25 million RentGrow order in July 2026, and the CFPB withdrew its 2021 rental-reporting bulletin and 2024 background-screening opinion on 12 May 2025.
Evidence: FTC/CFPB (12 Oct 2023): TransUnion Rental Screening Solutions and Trans Union to pay $15 million ($11 million redress, $4 million civil penalty); alleged multiple entries for one eviction case, filings reported without later dismissals, landlord claims labelled 'Judgment Amount', sealed records reported, and vendors not disclosed. | FTC (9 July 2026): RentGrow to pay a $2.25 million penalty under a proposed order; alleged duplicate criminal and eviction entries, undisclosed use of LexisNexis Accurint for address and name matching, disputes marked 'invalid' without action, and telling consumers property managers were notified when they were told there was no change; Commission vote 2-0; order needs DC district court approval. | CFPB withdrawn-guidance page: Bulletin 2021-03 Consumer Reporting of Rental Information (86 FR 35595), the Background Screening advisory opinion (89 FR 4171) and Name-Only Matching (86 FR 62468) all withdrawn 12 May 2025. 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 still bars furnishing information a furnisher has reasonable cause to believe is inaccurate and imposes dispute duties. | FTC advance notice (12 March 2026) on rental housing fees asks about application fees and security deposits and cites Invitation Homes ($48 million) and Greystar ($23 million) settlements.
Implication: The screening-error harm behind the portable renter record is on the regulatory record, but whoever compiles a record that landlords rely on likely takes on consumer-reporting-agency duties, a poor fit for a bank that wants to stay out of eviction data; reporting the bank's own rent payments carries only furnisher duties.
Caveats: Both orders are settlements; allegations are not adjudicated, and court entry was not verified. The FTC pages returned 404 to a plain HTTP client and were read through WebFetch. The consumer-reporting-agency point is the researcher's reading of the FCRA, not a quoted holding. The CFPB's reasons for withdrawal were not read. No rule had been proposed under the FTC rental-fee notice. Cornell LII mirrors the U.S. Code. Bears on T15's credit leg as well as the candidate.

Claim: Deposit law already shrinks or reprices the renter cash gate in places: New York caps any residential deposit or advance at one month's rent, and Cincinnati's January 2020 ordinance makes landlords offer a six-month instalment plan, a deposit of at most half a month's rent, or deposit insurance.
Evidence: NY General Obligations Law 7-108(1-a)(a) (nysenate.gov, current text): no deposit or advance shall exceed one month's rent, except for seasonal-use units and owner-occupied cooperative apartments under later subdivisions. | NBC News (25 Jan 2020): Cincinnati's Renter's Choice law, effective in 90 days, requires landlords to offer alternatives: instalments over at least six months, a deposit of no more than 50% of first month's rent, or rental security insurance for a nominal non-refundable monthly fee; Rhino's co-founder helped shape it, and the piece cites as little as $5 a month on a $1,000 rental. | Only the third option needs an insurer; the first two are payment terms a lender or landlord could offer.
Implication: Where deposits are capped or alternatives mandated, the entry-cash gate is smaller or already priced by insurers, so a bank's role in the cash-gate candidate is financing instalments or hardship gaps for Debit-Primary renters, not deposit insurance.
Caveats: One state statute and one city ordinance; no multi-state survey. The NY page blocked a plain client and was read through WebFetch; it does not state the effective date. Cincinnati ordinance text and 2026 status not fetched; NBC is a news report and notes a deposit-insurance company's role in drafting. Rhino sells the insurance option.

Claim: The consumer home-insurance layer is held by licensed insurers that have not reached stable underwriting profit: Hippo reported $1.1 billion gross written premium and a 113% combined ratio in 2025 after pausing new HO3 business in 2023, and Lemonade reported 2,984,513 customers and a $165.5 million net loss.
Evidence: Hippo 10-K FY2025: gross written premium $1,108.6 million (2024: $892.4 million); total revenue $468.6 million; net income attributable $57.7 million including a $95.0 million gain on sale of business (2024: $(40.5) million); net loss ratio 60% (77%, 169%); combined ratio 113% (138%, 361%); Q2 2023 catastrophe losses led to a nationwide pause on new HO3 premiums; no longer reports Total Generated Premium. | Lemonade 10-K FY2025: 2,984,513 customers (2024: 2,430,056); in force premium $1,236.5 million ($943.7 million); gross earned premium $1,050.8 million; gross loss ratio 64% (73%); net loss $165.5 million ($202.2 million); placed premium about 4% of in force premium.
Implication: If venture-backed insurers struggle to underwrite homes profitably, a bank's T22 role sits around insurance (escrow, bridge, resilience loans), and nothing here shows demand for that role.
Caveats: Company filings with non-GAAP metrics; Hippo's 2025 profit depends on a one-off gain; Lemonade's customers span renters, home, auto and pet. State exits not isolated. Kin is private and unfiled.

Claim: The insurance-withdrawal pain is a state-by-state, regulator-driven story: California's FAIR Plan held 696,562 policies (up 157% since September 2022) and $768 billion exposure in June 2026, while Florida's Citizens fell from 1,407,805 policies in September 2023 to 254,351 on 16 October 2026 after state reforms.
Evidence: California FAIR Plan (June 2026): 696,562 dwelling and commercial policies in force, up 8% since September 2025 and 157% since September 2022; exposure $768 billion, up 11% and 250%. | California Department of Insurance (March 2026): State Farm settlement keeps a +17.0% interim homeowners rate, cuts rental dwelling to +32.8%, sets renters about +15.65%, and extends the non-renewal moratorium for at least one more year. CDI (18 Sept 2026): State Farm filed to resume new homeowners business for the first time since May 2023 for homes meeting IBHS Wildfire Prepared standards, and Allstate filed on 31 August; 12 insurance groups have filed or been approved under the Sustainable Insurance Strategy; all filings remain under Prop. 103 rate review. | Citizens policies-in-force page: 254,351 as of 16 October 2026; monthly table shows 1,407,805 at 30 Sept 2023. Florida OIR (1 July 2026): pooled combined ratio 83% in 2025, lowest in more than a decade; 21 new companies approved since the reforms; Citizens at 293,465 on 5 June 2026, the lowest in 25 years. | Florida Trend (24 Sept 2026): Citizens' president said the market is working; the commissioner said 48 companies filed rate decreases since January 2024 and 53 requested no change or an increase.
Implication: The withdrawal pain behind T22 is real in California and has receded in Florida within three years on state action, so any bank case is state by state and the most exposed owners sit in markets where the regulator, not a bank, sets terms.
Caveats: FAIR Plan counts mix dwelling and commercial. Citizens' monthly high and OIR's 'approaching 1.2M at year-end 2022' are different dates. Florida officials have an interest in presenting the market as healthy, and two quiet hurricane years are not a trend; Florida Trend is trade press relaying a board meeting. California filings are not approvals. No insurer-by-insurer exit list from a regulator.

Claim: The levers a bank could pull in T22 are bounded by law: national banks may not underwrite insurance as principal beyond products authorised by 1 January 1999, disaster-finance rails are federal or insurer-funded (NFIP, Alabama's FORTIFIED grants), PACE is now regulated as mortgage-like credit, and federal climate-risk principles for large banks were rescinded in October 2025.
Evidence: 15 U.S.C. 6712: a national bank and its subsidiaries may not provide insurance as principal except authorised products (OCC determination or lawful practice as of 1 January 1999), excluding title insurance and certain annuities. | CRS Insight (updated 6 Feb 2026): NFIP has nearly 4.6 million policies and almost $1.3 trillion of coverage; 35 short-term reauthorisations since end-FY2017. NAR (Oct 2026): NFIP authority expires 11 December 2026; during a lapse NFIP cannot issue new or renewal policies and most federal lending regulators suspend the purchase requirement. Out of the Storm tracker: lapses 1 Oct to 12 Nov 2025 and 1 to 3 Feb 2026; Public Law 119-103 extended authority to 11 Dec 2026. FEMA: Risk Rating 2.0 applied to new policies from 1 Oct 2021 and renewals from 1 April 2022; most rates may not rise more than 18% a year. | Strengthen Alabama Homes: $10,000 grants to FORTIFY roofs of owner-occupied single-family homes, funded by Alabama's insurance industry, not the state budget. | CFPB PACE rule (Consumer Finance Monitor, Dec 2024): ability-to-repay applies, no qualified-mortgage status, about 35% of transactions would hit the points-and-fees trigger; effective 1 March 2026; M.D. Fla. granted the CFPB summary judgment on 12 February 2026 (Orrick via JD Supra). OCC Bulletin 2025-34 (16 Oct 2025): OCC, Fed and FDIC rescinded climate-risk principles for institutions over $100 billion; the OCC had withdrawn on 31 March 2025.
Implication: A bank can lend, escrow and bridge but not insure, and Capital One has no mortgage servicing or escrow seat since 2017, so T22's escrow leg is unavailable to it today and resilience lending is a niche between insurer grants, a lapsing federal flood program and a PACE category now regulated like a mortgage.
Caveats: The statute covers national banks as principal; agency sales and state-bank rules were not checked. NAR and Out of the Storm are a trade group and a news tracker used for the December 2026 date; the CRS Insight predates that extension. The 35% PACE estimate and the court ruling come from law-firm summaries, not the rule or order. The FEMA page blocked a plain client and was read through WebFetch. No source sizes bank resilience lending or claims bridging; those legs are untested, not refuted. Capital One facts are from the round-1 franchise file.

Claim: In 2023, 49.7% of the 42.5 million US renter households spent more than 30% of income on housing, with higher rates for Black (56.2%) and Hispanic (53.2%) renters than for White (46.7%) or Asian (43.4%) renters.
Evidence: 49.7% of 42.5 million renter households paid more than 30% of income for housing in 2023 (ACS one-year). | Black 56.2% (4.6 million households), Hispanic 53.2%, White 46.7%, Asian 43.4%. | About 2.5 million Black renter households (30.6%) paid more than 50% of income. | Median inflation-adjusted renter housing cost rose from $1,354 to $1,406 between 2022 and 2023.
Implication: The rent flow is large and near-universal, but a majority-burdened population has little margin to value rewards, so T15 fits a narrower, better-off renter slice than the Debit-Primary segment.
Caveats: Corpus row verified 2026-09; single-source ACS row; spot-checked in this pass (49.7% and 42.5 million confirmed). Direction Mixed: large flow supports, thin margin cuts against.

Opportunity: Rent as a Rewards and Credit Rail

Claim: NAR's 2025 Profile reports 26% of all buyers paid all cash, roughly 3 in 10 repeat buyers paid all cash, and over half of repeat buyers funded the down payment from a prior home sale.
Evidence: 26% of all buyers paid all cash, versus fewer than 1 in 10 in 2003-2010. | Financed-purchase share fell from 88% (2020) to 74% (2024-2025). | About 3 in 10 repeat buyers paid all cash versus 8% of first-time buyers. | Repeat-buyer median down payment 23% in 2025, the highest since 2003.

Caveats: Corpus row verified 2026-09; NAR survey (3.5% adjusted response rate) with a trade-association interest; no income or liquid-asset cut published.

Claim: A 2024 Treasury FIO report on 2018-2022 data found homeowners premiums rose 8.7 percent faster than inflation, the highest climate-risk ZIP codes paid 82% more than the lowest ($2,321 average), and nonrenewal rates there ran about 80% higher.
Evidence: FIO 2024 report (NAIC and state data call; 330+ insurers; about 50 million policies a year; 2018-2022): premiums rose 8.7 percent faster than inflation. | Top-quintile climate-risk ZIP codes paid $2,321 average annual premium, 82% more than the lowest quintile. | Nonrenewal rates about 80% higher in the highest-risk ZIP codes. | Average claim severity about $24,000 in high-risk versus $19,000 in low-risk ZIP codes.
Implication: The pain is regulator-measured, but it is a price and availability problem set by insurers and state regulation, so the bank role (financing, claim bridging, escrow) is not answered by this row.
Caveats: Corpus row verified 2026-09; spot-checked in this pass (8.7 percent, $2,321 and 82 percent confirmed). Cuts are by ZIP-code climate-risk quintile, not home value; excludes flood and earthquake.

Claim: Territory Candidate (renter cash-gate): Debit-Primary renters lose money and housing options at the point of entry (application fees, screening errors, repeat rent shortfalls) and would switch to a bank that removes the entry gate and the within-month rent timing gap, which no incumbent bank addresses at scale.
Evidence: 68% of renters pay application fees and the CFPB counted more than 16,000 complaints about incorrect screening information (CFPB 2022). | 23% of renters were behind on rent in the prior year, 33% of those under $25,000 (SHED 2025). | Nearly one-third of 2014 eviction filings were repeat filings against the same household and address, each adding about $180 in fees (Eviction Lab). | The corpus records no authoritative public source for deposit and total move-in dollar amounts, so the entry gate itself is unmeasured.
Implication: The pain is documented for Debit-Primary renters but unsized, and research rows show Flex already serves rent timing at millions of renters and deposit law reprices the gate in places, so this is a narrower form of T15 or T16, not separate white space.
Caveats: Corpus row verified 2026-09; joins three corpus findings the corpus never tied together; SHED is self-report; the Eviction Lab figure comes from a dev subdomain (primary returned 403). See domicile-10 and domicile-15 for supply and law.

Claim: Territory Candidate (renter-owned portable record): renters, with positive payment history on file for only 1.7% to 2.3% of them while errors and negative entries persist, would use a bank that holds a verified record of their payments and screening file and lets them carry it from landlord to landlord and to a mortgage lender, and no bank does this at scale today.
Evidence: Industry estimates put rental payment history coverage at 1.7% to 2.3% of US renters while inaccurate eviction and criminal entries are retained (CFPB 2022). | FHFA approved VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T on 22 April 2026; only 8% of renters had payments reported in 2025 (SHED). | GAO found no comprehensive current national eviction dataset; court data often omit outcomes. | Section 1033 rule finalised October 2024 and enjoined from October 2025 per a law-firm summary, so no enforceable right compels data sharing.
Implication: The payment-history half is the part of T15 a deposit bank can already supply from its own account data (domicile-12), but the screening-file half would pull a bank into consumer-reporting duties (domicile-14), so the candidate survives only as a payment-record feature for mortgage-bound renters.
Caveats: Corpus row verified 2026-09; corpus Direction was Supports; set to Mixed here because research rows show GSEs already read rent from bank data and screening records carry FCRA exposure. Corpus holds no row showing renters or landlords would pay for or value such a record. The 1033 bullet rests on a law-firm summary.

Evidence: Bilt announced a $250M round at a $10.75B valuation, reported 10 July 2025 (Fast Company via Yahoo Finance) | Same article: CEO Ankur Jain said about 15% of rewards members are cardholders; the Wells Fargo card launched March 2022 and reached 1 million activated accounts within 18 months; the partnership slated to run to 2029 is ending early after the WSJ reported Wells Fargo lost money on it; Bilt Card 2.0 with Cardless was due February 2026 with no-fee, $95 and $495 tiers | Coverager (undated page) records an earlier $200M round at a $3.1B valuation led by General Catalyst, $413M raised in total, and a company claim of EBITDA profitability in 2023

Fast Company is secondary, republished on Yahoo; the primary announcement and the Fintech Futures page returned 403 in round 1. The Wells Fargo loss is a WSJ report relayed secondhand, not a filing. Claim: In 2025, 6% of US homeowners had no homeowners insurance (43% of them because they could not afford it) and 14% of adults were financially affected by a natural disaster, while 2024-2025 venture money for disaster-exposed homeowners went to insurers, not to banks or lenders.
Evidence: SHED 2025: 6% of homeowners went without homeowners insurance (3% with a mortgage, 13% owning free and clear); of those without, 43% said they couldn't afford it and 8% said no insurer would cover the home (PDF pp. 78-79) | SHED 2025: 20% of insured owners would prefer more coverage but can't afford it and 14% struggle to afford premiums (33% and nearly 30% among insured owners under $50,000); more than 6 in 10 insured owners said costs rose more than expected; 14% of adults were financially affected by disasters or severe weather, 8% through property damage, against 21% in 2024, a fall the Fed links partly to no continental hurricane landfall in 2025 (PDF pp. 78-79) | Venture: Stand, a wildfire-zone insurer, announced a $30M round on 16 December 2024; its CEO said inbound demand rose about 5-10x overnight after the January 2025 Los Angeles fires while it had insured only a few properties (CNBC via NBC Miami, 19 January 2025). Implication: The pain is documented and price-driven; the funded players are insurers, so a bank-side T22 product (resilience lending, claim bridging, escrow) is untested by any funded entrant and Capital One has no mortgage or escrow business to hold it.

Disaster exposure swings year to year (21% to 14%). The Stand demand quote is a founder statement after one disaster, a spike not a trend; CNBC is read through an NBC affiliate mirror. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: In 2024 HMDA, depository lenders' conventional first-lien purchase loans above 90 CLTV carried a median rate spread of 0.25 points against 0.51 for independent lenders and a median total loan cost of $4,224 against $6,101, and 2025 shows the same pattern.
Evidence: 2024 conventional CLTV>90, first-lien owner-occupied one-unit site-built purchase originations: depository n=183,488 (median rate spread 0.252; total loan cost $4,224), independent n=361,036 (0.508; $6,101); CLTV>97 cell 0.23 vs 0.66 points and $4,418 vs $5,544 | Cell-adjusted gap (loan type x LTV band x five loan-amount bands x 30-year or not, depository-weighted, 20 cells): -0.30 points and -$1,992; adding DTI band: -0.28 points and -$1,749 | 2025: depository n=182,688 vs independent n=341,466; 0.21 vs 0.45 points; $4,339 vs $5,939; adjusted -0.27 points and -$1,744
Implication: The T01 kill criterion's condition (depositories show no lower rate spread or total loan cost) is not met, so the claim that no depository price edge exists is retired; T01 itself stays Out on Capital One's exits and the nonbank share, with the cause of the gap unproven.
Caveats: Lender type is inferred from institution names because the 2024 and 2025 HMDA Reporter Panel (agency and other-lender codes) is unavailable; bank- and insurer-affiliated mortgage subsidiaries are classed as nonbank by hand list and some lenders may be misplaced. The public LAR carries no credit score, so the kill criterion's credit-score control cannot be applied and the gap mixes price with borrower quality. Computed by the researcher from Data Browser files; the compiler re-ran the script (python -I) and reproduced the saved tables exactly. Total loan costs include points, so a lower figure can come with a different rate.

Claim: Published research finds the US unit cost of financial intermediation stayed near 2% of intermediated assets for about 130 years and reads that persistent cost as the reason new entrants appear, a cost-structure origin that none of Frameworks A, B or C names.
Evidence: Philippon (NBER WP 22476, August 2016, prepared for the 2016 BIS Annual Conference): the unit cost of US intermediation has stayed around 2% for the past 130 years; Bazot (2013) finds similar unit costs in Germany, the UK and France; data range 1886-2015. | Same paper: IT improvements have not been passed through to end users, and finance remaining expensive explains the emergence of new entrants; updated post-crisis US data show the unit cost declined only marginally since the crisis. | Same paper, model result (not an observed price): agents would pay 8.7% of consumption to bring the unit cost down to 1%. | Philippon, BIS WP 841 (12 February 2020): the unit cost of intermediation has fallen since the Great Financial Crisis; no basis-point series was read, so only the direction is cited.
Implication: Adds a fourth frame the seeded set lacks: ask where the intermediation margin or cost to serve is fattest, since that is where entrants have come from; relevant to Debit-Primary Spenders, who pay the most per dollar intermediated.
Caveats: Aggregate US finance sector (finance income over intermediated assets), not consumer banking alone. NBER working paper, not peer reviewed at that date. The NBER PDF returns binary through WebFetch; figures verified against the local extract output/framework/_pdf/nber22476.txt. WP 655 (7 August 2017) and WP 841 resolve to abstract pages; WP 655's abstract carries only the new-entrants point, not the 2% figure. No known sponsor interest. Does not show a cost-led consumer business was built; see framework-09 to framework-12 for that.

Claim: A peer-reviewed study of US mortgage origination attributes roughly 60% of shadow-bank growth in 2007-2015 to regulatory differences and roughly 30% to technology, so regulatory position is a documented origin of a large category that Frameworks A, B and C do not capture.
Evidence: Buchak, Matvos, Piskorski and Seru (NBER WP 23288; Journal of Financial Economics, 2018): shadow-bank market share of US residential mortgage origination nearly doubled from 2007 to 2015. | Their quantitative model: regulation accounts for roughly 60% of shadow-bank growth and technology for roughly 30%. | Fintech lenders appear to offer a higher-quality product and charge a premium of 14-16 basis points.
Implication: A frame asking which incumbents are regulatorily constrained, and where, would have predicted this entry; it also flags that any opportunity built on a regulatory gap can close when the rules change, and a bank is usually the constrained party, not the arbitrageur.
Caveats: Mortgages only; does not generalise to deposits, payments or wealth without further evidence. The 60/30 split is model output, not an observed count. Only the NBER abstract page was fetched; data sources were not read. Data end 2015.

Claim: The BIS 2019 Annual Economic Report describes big tech entry into finance as starting with payments and following an established customer base and brand, often as a distribution channel for third-party products, a distribution-led origin the seeded frames do not name.
Evidence: BIS Annual Economic Report 2019, Chapter III: payments were the first financial service big techs offered, mainly to build trust between buyers and sellers on e-commerce platforms. | Big techs move into finance after securing a large customer base and brand recognition, and often act as a distribution channel for third-party providers such as wealth management and insurance. | Financial services are about 11% of big tech revenue; big tech payment volume in China is about 16% of GDP; Yu'ebao exceeded CNY 1 trillion in assets with about 350 million customers; end-2018 big-tech-linked money-market balances were CNY 2.4 trillion, about 1% of bank customer deposits.
Implication: A distribution frame (who already owns the customer touchpoint and data) is supported as a fourth lens, and it is the lens on which a bank with an existing deposit base actually holds an asset.
Caveats: Heavily China-weighted; US big tech finance is not shown at this scale. A central-bank policy chapter, not an empirical test of outcomes. Pre-2024, so context only on agents. Some figures carry no year in the chapter and are recorded as stated.

Claim: A Federal Reserve Governor's 2026 speech on agentic payments names card networks, AI firms, retailers, e-commerce platforms and payment providers as the builders of the agent payment stack and liability as the open question, without discussing banks, which backs Framework B's disintermediation question.
Evidence: Christopher Waller (Fed Board of Governors), 'Payments in the age of AI agents', Sibos 2026, Miami; body text gives 29 September 2026, the BIS page's date-delivered field gives 5 October 2026. | Card networks are publishing technical specifications that let agents pay on a payer's behalf, covering agent registration and logged cardholder approvals; AI firms offer general-purpose agents; some retailers share catalogue data with AI firms. | Central question: who is responsible if an agent makes the wrong purchase; existing liability frameworks could potentially be adapted. Banks are not mentioned; no market size or volume figures are given.
Implication: Framework B's question (who sits between the customer and the account when agents transact) is live, and the stack as one regulator describes it places the relationship with networks and AI platforms, not the bank.
Caveats: A speech, not research; silence on banks is an observation about this text, not a Fed position. Covers merchant and B2B flows as well as consumer. Backs B as a stress lens; it is not evidence that B generates opportunities. BIS WP 1310 (wholesale agent cash management) was not fetched.

Claim: The canonical jobs-to-be-done exemplar is a non-financial case built on observation and interviews, and the only bank life-event evidence found is a consultancy survey with partial disclosure, so Framework A has no independent published validation as an opportunity-generation method in consumer finance.
Evidence: HBS Working Knowledge (14 February 2011): in the milkshake case a researcher spent a day recording who bought milkshakes and when, then interviewed buyers; about 40% of milkshakes were bought first thing in the morning. Examples are FedEx, Disney, OnStar, IKEA, Kodak, Milwaukee Electric Tool and P&G; no financial-services case appears. | Christensen, Hall, Dillon and Duncan, 'Know Your Customers' Jobs to Be Done', HBR September 2016: paywalled; only the preview was readable and none of its claims are cited. | Capgemini 'signature moments' (page undated, assets dated late 2024): just under 1,000 banking customers and 100 executives in the US, UK and Canada; over 52% dissatisfied with communication, nearly 48% with service, nearly 44% with digital experience. Field dates and fielding firm not stated; these are service-experience results, not demand for moment-specific products.
Implication: Treat Framework A (and the life-territory master frame that supersedes it) as a generative prompt, not an evidenced selector: demand and willingness to pay at each moment must come from the territory corpus and slices, not from the frame.
Caveats: Researcher rated Low and this stands. Capgemini sells banking consulting and has an interest in life-event programmes; sample disclosed, field dates not. HBR 2016 full text not read. No peer-reviewed critique of JTBD found; only practitioner blogs surfaced and none are cited. Absence of a finance case in one article does not show none exists. Corrected: the 40% refers to milkshake purchases, not total sales.

Claim: The main published sources for the value-chain frame (CB Insights' 2016 unbundling map, a16z's 2020 'every company will be a fintech company', and 2024 vendor embedded-finance sizing) disclose little or no method, so Framework B is a plausible argument rather than a tested one.
Evidence: CB Insights (23 May 2016): asks whether startups could inflict a 'death by a thousand cuts' on banks by attacking verticals; map first made May 2015, over 50 companies added in 2016, US startups only, no inclusion criteria stated. | a16z, Angela Strange (21 January 2020, from a November 2019 talk): Shopify and Mindbody make nearly 50 percent of revenue through financial services; no method or source given; author is a fintech investor. | MarketsandMarkets via Research and Markets: embedded finance USD 112.6 billion in 2024, USD 237.4 billion by 2029, 16.1% CAGR; method is executive interviews plus top-down, bottom-up and demand-side triangulation, with no assumptions or definition shown.
Implication: Use Framework B as a stress question (who has read-write access, who owns the flow), not as a source of size or of inevitability; its generative case rests on the outcomes in framework-13, not on this literature.
