Caveats: Sponsor interests: CB Insights sells market intelligence; a16z invests in the thesis; Research and Markets sells reports. CB Insights map is a 2016 US snapshot; no current version verified. A conflicting Grand View figure (USD 588.49B by 2030) surfaced in search but returned 403 and is not cited; vendor estimates differ by multiples. The embedded-finance figure is global, the other two sources US.

Claim: The main published critique of the three-horizons model argues that horizons are not bound by time and that incumbents fail at Horizon 3 through legacy, culture and process, while the 70/20/10 portfolio split attached to such frames could not be confirmed in its primary source.
Evidence: Steve Blank, 'The Fatal Flaw of the Three Horizons Model' (8 January 2019): Horizon 3 ideas can be delivered as fast as Horizon 1 ideas; the horizons are not bound by time; disruption usually comes from challengers rather than leaders; incumbents are burdened with legacy; matching disruptors is as much a culture and process problem as a technology one. | Nagji and Tuff, 'Managing Your Innovation Portfolio', HBR May 2012: only the intro was readable; executives suspect returns on total innovation investment are too low and describe innovation as haphazard and episodic. The 70/20/10 split is not visible and is not asserted. | McKinsey's 'Enduring Ideas: the three horizons of growth' and its incumbent new-business survey timed out on every attempt and are not cited.
Implication: Framework C is a portfolio-governance and risk-labelling device with no tested ability to pick winners; use rings 1-3 to classify risk only, and keep the brief's warning that ring 2 is adjacency.
Caveats: Rated Low because the substantive critique rests on practitioner opinion (Blank, an educator and practitioner), not research; Evidence type 'Research' is the closest controlled value and overstates it. The model's originator (McKinsey) sells the frame and its page could not be fetched. The 70/20/10 HBR text is paywalled and was not read. No peer-reviewed critique of the horizons model was found. The Blank URL is a monthly archive page containing the post.

Claim: The two main US financial-health frames (Financial Health Network's four-pillar FinHealth Score, refreshed 2026, and Aspen's three-pillar financial security framework, 2020) define household outcome states rather than moments, value-chain positions or distance from core, and both were funded by the Citi Foundation.
Evidence: Financial Health Network, 'From Insight to Impact' (11 March 2026): pillars Spend, Save, Borrow and Plan and Protect (fourth pillar renamed from 'Plan'); the approach was first outlined in 2015; a literature review and expert consultation reaffirmed the validity of core components; the report states the work was supported by the Citi Foundation. | Aspen Institute Financial Security Program, 'The State of Financial Security 2020': pillars routinely positive cash flow, personal resources, and public and private benefits; informed by eight months of research, four expert focus groups, two consumer focus groups and an expert survey (n=164, June 2020); Citi Foundation acknowledged for support. | Neither frame assigns market size or willingness to pay to any pillar.
Implication: An outcome-state frame (which pillar is unserved and measurable) is useful for pain evidence and as a success metric for any opportunity, but it is a diagnostic and does not say where a business model can be built.
Caveats: Industry-funded: Citi Foundation (a competitor's foundation); FHN members include financial institutions. Methods disclosed at process level. The Citi Foundation credit and the pillar rename are in the FHN PDF, not visible on the HTML page fetched; the FHN and Aspen PDFs return binary through WebFetch and were verified against local extracts output/framework/_pdf/fhn2026.txt and aspen2020.txt. Treating a measurement tool as a carving frame is the researcher's reading, not the authors' claim.

Claim: Chime's 2025 S-1 says it earns the substantial majority of its revenue from interchange, depends in part on its two partner banks staying under the $10 billion small-issuer exemption from debit interchange caps, and targets everyday Americans earning up to $100,000 rather than a money moment.
Evidence: Incorporated 2012 as 1debit, Inc., renamed 2019; 2024 revenue about $1.67 billion, net loss about $25.3 million; 8.6 million Active Members at 31 March 2025. | Primary focus is everyday Americans earning up to $100,000 a year; SpotMe lets eligible members overdraft up to $200 without fees. | Risk factors: Regulation II exempts issuers under $10 billion in assets from debit interchange limits; Chime depends in part on The Bancorp Bank and Stride Bank keeping that exemption and can offer no assurance they will.
Implication: The largest US neobank rests on a cost-structure and regulatory-position edge (Durbin-exempt interchange) that a bank of Capital One's size cannot use, so its success is not evidence that a money moment generates opportunities for this bank; for Debit-Primary Spenders, the edge was price, not a moment.
Caveats: Company disclosure written for investors. No interchange percentage of revenue is given in the text read (first ~300,000 of ~403,000 characters). The founding product is not stated. Corrected: the researcher's 'industry's first fee-free overdraft' wording was not found in the text read; replaced with the verified description. SpotMe targets one pain (overdraft fees), a partial fit to a moment.

Claim: Block's FY2021 10-K and Nu Holdings' FY2021 20-F show two mass consumer bases built on distribution, free P2P transfer as Cash App's primary acquisition channel and unpaid referral at Nubank, monetised through card interchange and card interest, with no money-moment origin documented.
Evidence: Block FY2021 10-K: peer-to-peer transactions are the primary acquisition channel for Cash App, offered free as a marketing tool; more than 44 million monthly transacting actives in December 2021; Square earns interchange on Cash Card purchases; the Square ecosystem began in February 2009 as card acceptance for sellers. | Nu Holdings FY2021 20-F (risk factors): founded 2013, began operations in Brazil in 2014, Mexico 2019, Colombia 2020; relied primarily on low-touch organic acquisition including an unpaid direct referral method. | Same 20-F: interchange fees and credit-card interest were 27.8% and 22.1% of 2021 revenue (34.5% and 29.5% in 2020).
Implication: Distribution engines (a free viral product, referrals) built two of the largest consumer bases without a life-event thesis; a bank should ask of each opportunity what makes it spread, since an existing deposit base is a distribution asset others lack.
Caveats: Company disclosures. Cash App grew out of a merchant-side business, a distance-from-core move inside Block (partial Framework C fit). Nubank: Brazil is not the US; the founding product, first customers, incumbent concentration and cost-to-serve (Item 4) were not read, so the founding rationale is undocumented; Nubank alone would rate Low. Later Cash App user counts (FY2024-25) came from search only and are not used. Block's sponsor-bank and Durbin language not read.

Claim: Robinhood's and Coinbase's 2021 registration statements show two large consumer outcomes whose revenue came from a pricing choice (zero commission funded by payment for order flow) and from crypto trading volume tied to a market cycle, with only a loose fit to a first-investing moment.
Evidence: Robinhood S-1/A (8 October 2021): started 2013, pioneered commission-free trading with no account minimums; more than half of customers funding accounts January 2015 to June 2021 said it was their first brokerage account; PFOF $691.3 million (72% of 2020 revenue) and $547.8 million (50%) in H1 2021; 22.5 million Net Cumulative Funded Accounts at 30 June 2021. | Coinbase S-1 (25 February 2021): started 2012; transaction revenue over 96% of 2020 net revenue; Verified Users 43 million in 2020, up from 32 million in 2019; revenue substantially dependent on crypto prices and trading volume; the 2018 price decline adversely affected results.
Implication: Pricing and market cycles produced two of the largest consumer-finance listings of the period, which a moment-based territory list will not generate; for Young Consumers, the first-investing moment was reached by a price, not a moment-designed product.
Caveats: Company disclosures from a retail-trading and crypto boom window; PFOF share fell from 72% to 50% in eighteen months. Later 10-Ks (2023-2025) were not read. Robinhood's first-account statistic is customer self-report in the filing.

Claim: Revolut's 2024 annual report says it began in 2015 with faster and cheaper transfers and FX than legacy banks and that card payments and interest income are now its largest revenue streams, a price-led entry on one narrow pain followed by breadth, rates and a crypto cycle.
Evidence: Revolut Annual Report 2024: founded 2015 in the UK; early product offered faster and cheaper transfers and FX so customers could spend like a local abroad from multi-currency accounts. | Same report: 2024 revenue GBP 3.1 billion (+72%), profit before tax GBP 1,089 million, retail customers 52.5 million (38.0 million in 2023); card payments and interest income remained the largest revenue streams (+43% and +58%); wealth revenue +298% on crypto trading; UK banking licence with restrictions in 2024. | Monzo FY25 year in review: 2.4 million new customers to 12 million+; revenue GBP 1.2 billion (+48%); adjusted profit before tax GBP 113.9 million; customer deposits GBP 16.6 billion. No origin story given.
Implication: A narrow pain plus a price advantage opened the door and breadth plus rates and interchange built the business; each opportunity should record which of the two it offers, since a moment can be the door but not the engine.
Caveats: UK, not US; UK interchange is capped under different rules, so not a Durbin case. Revolut PDF returns binary through WebFetch; figures verified against local extract output/framework/_pdf/revolut.txt. Monzo: only the summary page read (full PDF exceeded fetch limit); the page says FY25, not a stated year-end date. Adjusted profit excludes a share-sale cost. Travel FX can be read as a moment, but the filing frames it as a cheaper product.

Claim: Affirm's 2021 S-1/A and Klarna's 2025 F-1 show two large consumer-credit outcomes that began at the merchant checkout, a value-chain position, each funded through a bank (Cross River for Affirm, Klarna's own EEA licence), which backs Framework B as a generator and not only a stress lens.
Evidence: Affirm S-1/A (11 January 2021): started with its core pay-over-time solution at checkout; operating business dates to 2012; revenue about $509.5 million in FY2020 vs $264.4 million in FY2019; Peloton about 28% of FY2020 revenue; Cross River Bank originated the substantial majority of loans under a non-exclusive, short-term agreement; no late fees and no deferred or compounding interest. | Klarna F-1 (March 2025): began operations in Sweden in 2005; licensed bank in the EEA since 2017; deposits funded 94% of financing products in 2024; about 93 million active consumers and over 675,000 merchants at 31 December 2024; 2024 revenue $2,811 million and net profit $21 million after a $244 million loss in 2023.
Implication: Claiming a position inside someone else's flow produced two of the largest consumer-credit companies, and both needed a bank balance sheet; a bank's realistic B role is the funded position in another firm's flow, with merchant concentration as the risk.
Caveats: Company disclosures. Merchant concentration risk (Peloton 28%). Affirm's Amazon share and Klarna's US share not read. Klarna's 2024 profit is thin. Affirm's no-hidden-fees stance is also a pricing edge, so the origin is position plus price.

Claim: SoFi's FY2021 10-K says the company started with private student loans, mainly refinancing, under a gain-on-sale model, and became a bank holding company in 2022 by buying Golden Pacific for $22.3 million cash, the closest fit in the sample to a money-moment origin.
Evidence: Founded 2011; started with an approach to the private student loan market and primarily operates in student loan refinance; lending is primarily a gain-on-sale model (FY2021 10-K). | March 2021 agreement to acquire Golden Pacific Bancorp for a total cash price of $22.3 million; January 2022 regulatory approval to become a bank holding company; bank merger closed February 2022. | About 600,000 members became multi-product members in 2021.
Implication: The one large US outcome with a moment-shaped origin (student debt, a Framework A moment) also needed a capital-markets funding model and later a charter to scale, so the moment opened the door but did not carry the business; relevant to Young Consumers.
Caveats: Company disclosure; the 10-K web version is mostly XBRL and the narrative was read in parts. Whether low rates and secondary-market demand drove the refinance opportunity is the researcher's inference, not stated. Member counts and lending share of revenue not captured. Refinancing at origin was also a pricing play (a rate advantage for high earners).

Claim: Rocket Companies' FY2024 10-K reports Rocket Money, a subscription-cancellation and budgeting app, at 4.1 million paying subscribers and about $0.3 billion of 2024 revenue, a found-money product that reached scale only as a line inside a larger parent.
Evidence: Item 1: Rocket Money is the company's personal finance app that helps clients manage their financial lives, earning revenue from paying subscribers and service-based fees. | KPI table: Rocket Money paying subscribers at period end 4,116.5 thousand (2024), 3,017.5 thousand (2023), 2,263.5 thousand (2022); Rocket Money gross revenue $321,180 thousand in 2024. | Other income table: Rocket Money revenue $297.2 million (2024), $198.7 million (2023), $141.6 million (2022); total Rocket revenue, net, $5,100,798 thousand in 2024 (so Rocket Money is about 6% of the parent, compiler's arithmetic on the $297.2 million line).
Implication: The only pure found-money product in the sample sits as an owned product line (Framework C ring 2 for its parent), which supports C as a classifier and the 'feature not a company' worry for a bank.
Caveats: Company disclosure. The $321.2 million figure is a gross revenue KPI and the $297.2 million figure is a reported revenue line; both are in the filing and were not reconciled. Truebill acquisition date and price not in the text read, so the acquisition origin is undocumented here.

Claim: In the failures sampled, big-tech and incumbent entries without an owned customer relationship (Google Plex, Diem, Goldman's consumer push) and better-account neobanks without scale or a committed parent (Simple, N26 US, Varo) failed or stalled for execution, parent priority, entry cost or a thin interchange base, not for a missing money moment.
Evidence: Google Plex: cancelled after delays, missed deadlines and the March 2021 departure of project lead Caesar Sengupta (WSJ report confirmed by Google to Banking Dive, 4 October 2021); 11 institutions signed by November 2020 including Citi, Stanford FCU, BM Technologies and BBVA USA; Google will focus on digital enablement for banks instead. | Diem: Silvergate bought Diem's IP and technology assets on 31 January 2022 for $201,150,000 ($50,000,000 cash plus $151,150,000 in stock; $182 million at the closing price); sellers were in a pre-launch phase (Silvergate 8-K). Goldman: CFO letter to SEC staff of 24 June 2024 responds to a staff comment citing the 10-K's 'narrowing of our consumer business', listing Marcus and Apple Card deposits; no losses stated. | Simple: BBVA USA announced 7 January 2021, reassessing goals ahead of the PNC merger, that it was closing Simple, founded 2009 as BankSimple, bought by BBVA 2014, run through bank partners (American Banker). N26: about 500,000 US accounts closed 11 January 2022 after about 2.5 years, to focus on Europe; co-CEO said it had to build the bank from scratch with different licences, agreements and payment rails (Banking Dive, 18 November 2021). | Varo, the first neobank with a national charter: Q1 2022 equity $263 million, quarterly burn $84 million, possible run-out of funds by year-end; analyst Jason Mikula put about 98% of income in interchange and fees (Banking Dive, 2022). Q4 2025 call report as read by American Banker: net loss $20.8 million vs $17.9 million a year earlier; capital $94.7 million after a $123.9 million Series G announced 2 February 2026.
Implication: Entering a ring-2 category or a new network position without an owned customer relationship, or selling a better account on a thin interchange base, has a poor record even for firms with large balance sheets; Plex and Diem are failed Framework B moves and Goldman a failed Framework C ring-2 move.
Caveats: Trade press (Banking Dive, American Banker) is the primary record of the Plex, Simple, N26 and Varo events; Google's reason is its official line. The Goldman 'narrowing' point rests on SEC correspondence only (Goldman's CORRESP quoting the staff comment), not the 10-K; Apple Card exit terms are undocumented because Goldman IR returned 403 and the 10-K web version was unreadable XBRL. Varo call reports were not retrieved from FFIEC; the Q4 2025 figures are American Banker's reading, and the 98% figure is one analyst's 2022 estimate. The Silvergate 8-K does not name Meta or Novi; Meta filings not opened. Sample excludes Wise, Acorns and Moven, for which no primary record was fetched. Corrected: Goldman letter is dated June 2024 (not August); SlashGear mirror dropped.

Claim: As of October 2026 the Capital One consumer bank storefront offers five deposit products (360 Checking, MONEY Teen Checking, 360 Performance Savings, Kids Savings Account, 360 CDs) and lists no investing, mortgage, home equity, insurance, HSA, student loan or international account product; the enterprise does run card businesses in the UK and Canada.
Evidence: capitalone.com/bank (fetched 2026-10-26): lists 360 Checking, MONEY Teen Checking, 360 Performance Savings, Kids Savings Account and 360 CDs; links out to separate Canada and UK sites rather than offering an international account | capitalone.com/bank/checking-accounts: only 360 Checking and MONEY Teen Checking; no HSA, investing, mortgage, insurance or international-account product | 360 Checking page: no monthly fees, no minimum balance, 70,000+ fee-free Capital One, MoneyPass and Allpoint ATMs, Zelle, early direct deposit up to 2 days early depending on the payer | 10-K FY2025 segment definitions: the Credit Card segment includes international card businesses in the U.K. and Canada; OCC merger letter (2025-04-18) notes CONA has a branch in Canada
Implication: The sponsor's 'does not offer' list holds for the consumer bank, and the short, no-fee line-up backs the 'simple products' posture the sponsor lists as a possible weakness; 'international' is absent for consumer deposits but not for the enterprise.
Caveats: Direction: Supports the sponsor's Section 4 product list and 'simple products' description. Absence of insurance, HSA, student loans and international accounts rests on non-mention on the pages fetched, not a full site crawl or a company statement. Money market accounts are referenced on the savings page but not listed on the landing page. UK and Canada card businesses sit in the enterprise card segment, outside the consumer bank.

Claim: Capital One held $475.8 billion of deposits at 2025-12-31 ($484.3 billion at 2026-06-30), 80% in Consumer Banking, which the Federal Reserve projected would make it the sixth-largest US institution by deposits; about $106.9 billion of that came with Discover.
Evidence: 10-K FY2025: total deposits $475,771M vs $362,707M a year earlier; Consumer Banking deposits $423,932M (80%); Discover added $106.9B at the 2025-05-18 closing; estimated uninsured deposits $71.9B; brokered deposits $19.2B; average Consumer Banking deposit rate 3.02% in 2025 (3.23% in 2024) | 10-Q Q2 2026: total deposits $484.3B at 2026-06-30, up $8.5B from year-end | Fed Order 2025-10 (2025-04-18): the combined firm would be the sixth-largest US financial institution by deposits with 2.6% of US deposits; Capital One is well capitalized and well managed | Morningstar DBRS (2024-02-20): $348B deposits with minimal brokered deposits; 82% insured (84% pro forma with Discover); deposit base viewed as higher quality because a retail branch network anchors it; rating A (low), Stable
Implication: The 'large deposit base' asset holds on size and stability, but about a fifth of the 2025-end total was bought with Discover, so a deposit-led territory should not read the total as organic pull.
Caveats: Direction: Supports the sponsor's 'large deposit base'. 10-K and 10-Q figures verified against local extracts (output/franchise/_pdf/cof10k.txt, q2.txt); the Fed order PDF did not parse through WebFetch and was extracted locally with PyMuPDF. DBRS is an issuer-paid rating opinion from before the Discover close and the 360 Savings settlement; it measures stability, not loyalty or rate sensitivity. No source found measures Capital One deposit beta or switching. The 'about a fifth' share is my arithmetic ($106.9B / $475.8B).

Claim: The Consumer Banking segment earned $1.225 billion after tax on $10.433 billion of net revenue in 2025, down from $1.460 billion in 2024 and $2.258 billion in 2023, and its loan book is $83.6 billion of auto loans against $1.19 billion of retail banking loans.
Evidence: 10-K FY2025 Consumer Banking table: net interest income $8,758M; non-interest income $1,675M (up on the acquired Global Payment Network); total net revenue $10,433M; income from continuing operations net of tax $1,225M (2024 $1,460M; 2023 $2,258M) | Period-end Consumer Banking loans $84,790M: auto $83,600M, retail banking $1,190M | Segment defined as deposit gathering and lending for consumers and small businesses, national auto lending, and Global Payment Network services | 10-Q Q2 2026: H1 2026 segment net revenue $6,121M and income from continuing operations $784M
Implication: A new deposit-linked business is judged against a segment that earned about 0.3% after tax on its deposits in 2025 (my arithmetic: $1,225M / $423,932M) and whose profit fell two years running.
Caveats: Company disclosure. Figures verified against the local 10-K and 10-Q extracts. The segment blends consumer and small-business deposits, auto and network revenue; 2025 includes Discover integration costs. The 0.3% ratio is my arithmetic from two sourced figures and is indicative only.

Claim: Capital One has left real-estate and retail investing twice: it stopped mortgage and home equity origination in November 2017 and sold its online brokerage and home loan portfolio in 2018, then sold the Discover home loan business it acquired within about six months, on 2025-11-24, for $8.8 billion.
Evidence: 10-K FY2017: announced 2017-11-07 it would cease new residential mortgage and home equity originations; decision informed in part by the competitive landscape for those products | 10-K FY2018: online retail brokerage sold in Q1 2018 with about $1.4B of customer deposits transferred to the buyer; all consumer home loan portfolio sold in 2018 | OCC merger letter (2025-04-18): CONA stated its decision to largely exit mortgage lending was based on its inability to compete with nonbank mortgage lenders despite significant investment | 10-K FY2025: Discover Home Loan portfolio (refinance and home equity) sold 2025-11-24 for $8.8B cash with a $483M pre-tax gain, reported as discontinued operations; Discover sold its student loan portfolio in 2024 and a CFPB order on its student loan servicing runs to December 2030
Implication: Any opportunity that re-enters mortgage, home equity, brokerage or student lending (T01, T05, T20) must explain why the bank's own stated reason, that it could not compete with nonbanks, no longer applies.
Caveats: Direction: Supports the sponsor's 'does not offer mortgage, home equity, brokerage' list as a deliberate choice. The 2017-2018 filings do not name the brokerage buyer or price (E*TRADE is unconfirmed from a primary record). The 2025 10-K gives no reason for the home loan sale; the OCC letter's reason is the company's own statement to its regulator. The FY2017 and FY2018 EDGAR pages exceed the fetch limit, so text was verified against local extracts.

Claim: Regulators approved the Discover deal on 2025-04-18 with conditions tied to Discover's record, and the deal closed 2025-05-18, adding personal loans and the Discover, PULSE and Diners Club networks, which carried $401.8 billion of volume in 2025 after closing.
Evidence: Fed Order 2025-10 and press release (2025-04-18): approval, with a $100M fine on Discover for overcharging interchange fees from 2007 to 2023, coordinated with the FDIC; Capital One committed to comply with the action against Discover including remediation | OCC conditional approval letter (2025-04-18): within 120 days of consummation CONA must submit a plan for corrective action on the root causes of outstanding enforcement actions against Discover Bank and remediation of harm, enforceable under 12 USC 1818; OCC found CONA's financial and managerial resources consistent with approval | 10-K FY2025: closing 2025-05-18 at 1.0192 Capital One shares per Discover share; acquired personal loans, the Discover Network, PULSE, Diners Club International and Network Partners; reissuance of legacy Capital One debit cards onto the Global Payment Network substantially complete; Global Payment Network volume $401,775M | PaymentsJournal (2026-03-03): the debit portfolio is about 25 million cards; existing credit cardholders move at card expiry; a Javelin analyst expects the full shift to take five years
Implication: Owning a payment network is an asset the sponsor's list omits and it bears on agent-money and payments opportunities (T08), but the inherited remediation plan and a multi-year credit migration compete for the same management attention.
Caveats: Direction: Supports 'capital, regulatory licenses' and extends the asset list (network ownership, personal loans); Contradicts any reading of the bank as unconstrained, since remediation obligations attach. Both regulator PDFs did not parse via WebFetch and were extracted locally with PyMuPDF on retry. No source states whether the Discover remediation conditions are satisfied as of October 2026. Personal loans sit in the Credit Card segment. The PaymentsJournal analyst view is trade press.

Claim: Capital One offers small-business banking (business checking, savings and banker-led lending, plus small-business cards) and on 2026-04-07 closed its acquisition of Brex, a corporate card and spend-management company, for about $4.5 billion of consideration at close against $5.15 billion stated at signing.
Evidence: 10-K FY2025: Consumer Banking covers deposit gathering and lending for consumers and small businesses; the Credit Card segment includes domestic small business card lending | capitalone.com/small-business (fetched 2026-10-26): Business Checking Account and Business Savings Account; a business banker for treasury management and lending options | 10-K FY2025 subsequent event: Brex merger agreement 2026-01-22 at $5.15B aggregate consideration, about $2.58B cash and about 10.6M Capital One shares | 10-Q Q2 2026: closed 2026-04-07; consideration paid about $4.5B ($2.6B cash plus 10.6M shares at $1.9B fair value; purchase consideration table $4,521M); Brex debt of $1.1B repaid at close; Capital One newsroom confirms the 2026-04-07 completion as a stock-and-cash deal with no price
Implication: Small-business banking cannot appear on the 'does not offer' list, and the bank's largest 2026 deal went to business payments rather than a consumer category.
Caveats: Direction: Contradicts the sponsor brief's open item listing small-business banking as possibly absent. Brex price: $5.15B is the 10-K figure at signing, $4.5B (precisely $4,521M) is the 10-Q figure at close. They reconcile on the stock leg: cash and share count are the same, and the 10.6M shares were valued at about $2.57B at signing versus $1.891B at close (my arithmetic: $5.15B less $2.58B; about $242 versus $178 per share). Small business is outside the consumer scope except as a boundary fact.

Claim: Capital One already runs a free found-money tool (Capital One Shopping) and a travel booking service (Capital One Travel), and Travel is open only to holders of eligible Capital One or Discover credit cards.
Evidence: 2026 proxy: Capital One Auto Navigator, Capital One Travel, Capital One Shopping and CreditWise named among digital experiences expanded in 2025 | 10-K FY2025: Capital One Shopping revenue sits in the 'Other' non-interest income line with treasury income, auto industry services and other investment income; no figure given | capitalone.com/shopping: checks for deals and coupons when shopping online; described as 100% free; no statement on whether a Capital One account is needed | capitalone.com/travel: available with a US-issued eligible Capital One or Discover credit card; no debit or deposit-only route named; claims a 15% average flight saving from price prediction
Implication: T04 Found Money fails part of the additive screen because a free deal-finding product already exists at the enterprise, and debit-only customers appear shut out of Travel.
Caveats: Company marketing; the 15% saving is a company claim. The 2018 Wikibuy origin of Shopping is not named in the filings searched and remains unconfirmed from a primary record. Shopping's account requirement is not stated.

Claim: Capital One's stated interest in economic mobility rests on a $265 billion five-year Community Benefits Plan announced 2024-07-17 in connection with the Discover deal and an Outstanding CRA rating from the OCC dated 2023-08-28.
Evidence: 2026 proxy: $265 billion five-year Community Benefits Plan expanding lending, investment and services for economic opportunity and financial well-being; company calls it the largest acquisition-related community plan in US banking; Capital One serves over 100 million customers | OCC merger letter (2025-04-18): CONA announced the plan on 2024-07-17 as $265B of lending, investing and philanthropy over five years; most recent large-bank CRA evaluation (2023-08-28) rated Outstanding on lending, investment and service tests | Fed Order 2025-10: commenters argued Capital One did not fully meet a prior community benefits plan tied to the ING acquisition and questioned subprime lending inside the new plan; Capital One has an Outstanding CRA rating | capitalone.com/about/our-commitments lists socioeconomic mobility themes but no dollar targets
Implication: Economic mobility is a documented commitment the regulators weighed, which helps T07-type opportunities, but it is a merger-tied lending and investment pledge, not a product line.
Caveats: Direction: Supports 'a stated interest in economic mobility'. The plan's composition and any consumer-deposit share are not in the pages read. The proxy and the OCC letter describe the components differently (services versus philanthropy). The 100 million customer figure is enterprise-wide with no method and is not a deposit-customer count. Commenter objections in the Fed order are allegations the Board recorded, not findings. Proxy text verified against the local extract.

Claim: Capital One's 360 Savings pricing drew a CFPB suit (dropped February 2025), a New York AG suit, and a $425 million class settlement given final approval in April 2026 that was still unpaid in October 2026 because of a pending appeal.
Evidence: CFPB sued 2025-01-14 (E.D. Va. 1:25-cv-00061) under the CFPA and Truth in Savings Act, alleging more than $2B in lost interest; voluntary dismissal 2025-02-27 acknowledged with prejudice after the Acting Director halted filings (Clearinghouse; Banking Dive 2025-05-15) | NY AG suit 2025-05-14: 360 Savings held at 0.3% while 360 Performance Savings rose to as high as 4.35%, at one point more than 14 times higher; staff told not to mention the new product unless asked; $10,000 from September 2019 earned $186 over five years versus $1,090 | NY AG 2025-09-24: 18 AGs said the first class deal gave the average consumer under $54 against over $717 lost; NY AG 2026-01-12: revised deal of $425M restitution (about $34M for New Yorkers) plus matching 360 Savings to Performance Savings rates | Beinsure (2026-10-03): court rejected the first deal in November 2025; final approval 2026-04-20; class member appeal 2026-06-18 (4th Cir. No. 26-1807); no cash payments being processed; Capital One raised the legacy rate on 2026-08-04
Implication: The 'trust that comes with holding assets' claim has a documented counter-record on deposit pricing itself, so any opportunity that asks customers to let the bank move their money for yield (T03) starts behind.
Caveats: Direction: Contradicts 'the trust that comes with holding assets'. The complaints are allegations; Capital One did not admit liability. The CFPB dismissal reflects a policy change, not a merits ruling. The November 2025 rejection month and the appeal and payment status come from one press article citing the settlement administrator; the Fourth Circuit docket was not opened. The NY AG January 2026 release confirms the rejection but gives no month.

Claim: The OCC fined Capital One $80 million in August 2020 for failing to assess risk before its cloud migration around 2015 and for weak audit and board oversight; the OCC and Federal Reserve consent orders were terminated in August 2022 and July 2023.
Evidence: OCC Consent Order AA-EC-20-51 (bank directors signed 2020-07-30/31; OCC signature dated 2020-08-01): around 2015 the bank failed to establish effective risk assessment before migrating IT to the cloud; gaps in network security controls, data loss prevention and alert handling; internal audit missed numerous weaknesses; the Board failed to hold management accountable; a pattern of misconduct; $80,000,000 penalty; the bank had begun corrective action | Fed Order 2025-10: the OCC and Board consent orders on technology risk governance (entered August 2020) were terminated in August 2022 and July 2023; Capital One says it has invested to strengthen risk and compliance; a January 2025 service interruption traced to a third-party provider was restored for all customers by 2025-01-19 | DOJ W.D. Wash.: intrusion through a misconfigured web application firewall; Capital One determined the intrusion on 2019-07-19 | Banking Dive (2022-09-19): OCC termination order dated Aug. 31 (2022); breach affected roughly 106 million accounts; OCC positively considered notification and remediation
Implication: Risk capability can be claimed as an asset only with the record that the bank's largest data incident was a control failure regulators tied to its cloud move, closed out in 2022-2023.
Caveats: Direction: Contradicts 'decades of fraud and risk capability' on technology risk governance; card fraud-loss capability was not tested. OCC order text read from the local PyMuPDF extract (output/franchise/_pdf/ea2020-036.pdf); the order carries AA-EC-20-51 in the caption and AA-EC-20-49 in the wire instructions. The termination is now confirmed by month from the Fed order; the Aug. 31 day rests on Banking Dive. The OCC termination notice itself and the EASearch record were not reachable. 2019-2022 events do not describe current control state.

Claim: Capital One's claim to an advanced technology platform rests in the open record on company statements: the 'all-in on public cloud' and 2020 data-center exit come from its own executive, and no independent technical assessment of the cloud estate or a 'modern core' was found.
Evidence: Data Center Knowledge (2019-12-11): plan to close the last three data centers in 2020; 'all-in on the public cloud' attributed to technology executive George Brady; no outside analyst quoted | CIO Dive (2019-09-12): Forrester's Lauren Nelson called the 2015 public-cloud shift a 'bold claim in the market' and said the few firms migrating that way were not financial services companies; the reporter notes the breach vulnerability would also have existed in a data center | The only regulator finding on the cloud environment is critical (OCC 2020 consent order, see franchise-10)
Implication: Treat 'a modern core and the ability to integrate agentic layers' as unverified for the right-to-win screen until an outside assessment or a filing describes the platform.
Caveats: Direction: Mixed on 'a modern core'; the cloud move is real but only self-described. Both sources are 2019 trade press relaying executive statements and predate any 2025-2026 platform change. A cloud-hosted application estate is not a core banking platform, and no source addresses the core. The data-center point is the reporter's statement, not a quote from CFO Blackley.

Claim: In early 2026 Capital One was running the Discover integration and the Brex acquisition at once, with Q4 2025 non-interest expense up 53% and analysts trimming price targets over integration complexity.
Evidence: 24/7 Wall St. via Yahoo Finance (2026-03-24): Brex at $5.15B announced 2026-01-22, stock fell more than 5% that day and was about 24% down year to date near $184; Q4 2025 non-interest expense up 53% to $9.34B including $352M of Discover integration charges; EPS $3.86 vs $4.14 expected | Same piece: Truist and Barclays kept Buy-equivalent ratings but cut targets; of 23 analysts, 3 Strong Buy, 14 Buy, 6 Hold, 0 Sell | 10-Q Q2 2026: $2.1B of Discover integration expenses incurred through 2026-06-30 | PaymentsJournal (2026-03-03): credit card network migration expected to take five years (Javelin)
Implication: Management bandwidth is committed to two integrations into 2027 or later, which counts against Feasibility for any new zero-to-one build, even though the deals show the bank will take large bets.
Caveats: Direction: Supports the sponsor's 'speed, layers' weakness on bandwidth; Contradicts the 'risk appetite' part, since two large acquisitions in 15 months show high appetite for scale bets. Market commentary, not an analyst report; analyst views are secondhand. Execution to date is not shown to have failed. Brex is business payments, outside consumer scope.

Claim: Before the Discover deal, 67% of Capital One's domestic card balances were tied to FICO scores of 660 or higher versus 81% at Discover, with higher delinquency and charge-offs, per Morningstar DBRS in February 2024.
Evidence: DBRS (2024-02-20): Capital One domestic card 67% FICO 660 or higher vs Discover 81%; 30+ day delinquency 4.61% vs 3.87%; 2023 net charge-off rate 4.56% vs 3.90% | Same note: 2023 return on common equity 9.10% for Capital One vs 22% for Discover; revenue concentration in cards will increase after the deal | No debit customer count, income mix or deposit-customer profile in the note; the 10-K and proxy searched give none either
Implication: The card book's lower-score skew is consistent with an economic-mobility customer base (T07), but it is not evidence that the deposit base skews toward debit spenders.
Caveats: Direction: Mixed on 'a customer base skewed toward debit spenders': it describes card credit quality, not debit behaviour, which remains untested. Issuer-paid rating opinion restating company data; figures predate the Discover close. Evidence type relabelled from Regulatory/Standards (a rating agency is not a regulator) to market data. One-third below 660 does not by itself establish a subprime share.

Claim: J.D. Power's 2025 U.S. National Banking Satisfaction Study ranked Capital One first among large national banks for a sixth straight year, with 702 on a 1,000-point scale.
Evidence: MBA NewsLink (2025-12-15) summary: Capital One first for a sixth consecutive year, score 702; seven dimensions including trust, digital channels, account offerings and problem resolution | Comparison set: holding companies with over $250B of domestic deposits and at least 200 branches, so digital banks and neobanks are excluded | Sample size, field dates and weighting not given on the readable page
Implication: Large-bank customers rate the brand well, consistent with the 'national brand' claim, but the survey does not test trust after the 360 Savings record or compare against digital banks.
Caveats: Direction: Supports 'a national brand'. J.D. Power sells research and award licensing to the banks it ranks; commercial survey with unverified method. J.D. Power's press page returned 403 again on this pass, so rank and score come from the MBA summary only. Fieldwork largely predates the 2026 settlement approvals.

Claim: Capital One's FY2025 10-K reports Consumer Banking net interest income of $8,758M on average deposits of $379,915M, about 230 bps per deposit dollar, and a consolidated 3.21% average rate on interest-bearing deposits.
Evidence: Table 9 Consumer Banking: net interest income $8,758M (2024 $8,023M; 2023 $8,713M); average deposits $379,915M (2024 $303,873M); average deposits interest rate 3.02% (2024 3.23%); period-end Consumer Banking deposits $423,932M | Researcher arithmetic: 8,758 / 379,915 = 2.31%, about 230 bps (2024: 2.64%); implied deposit interest expense about $11.5B | Consolidated: saving deposits $274,130M at 3.10% ($8,501M expense); time deposits $92,135M at 4.33%; total interest-bearing deposits $402,209M at 3.21% (2024 3.54%) | Segment net interest income also carries average consumer banking loans of $81,225M (auto $80,009M) at a 9.36% average yield
Implication: The 230 bps figure is a ceiling on the deposit spread, not the spread itself, so the 60 to 122 bps program-bank prices in crosscut-92 are the better benchmark for the sweep test; both exceed any sweep fee.
Caveats: Not an internal funds-transfer-price spread, which the kill criterion names and which is not public. Segment net interest income includes auto-loan income and Discover-transaction effects; 2025 average deposits rose 25% with Discover. Verified against the local 10-K extract (output/franchise/_pdf/cof10k.txt); the live URL resolves. The 9.36% yield is for all consumer banking loans, not auto alone (corrected). The researcher's 360 Performance Savings 3.20% APY and the 282 bps gap to the FDIC national savings average were removed because the capitalone.com page rendered no rate to the compiler's fetch.

Claim: Variable income is broad but strictly defined gig work is narrow: in October 2025, 30% of US adults said their income varied at least occasionally and 11% struggled to pay bills because of it, while gig or contingent work as a main job is a low single-digit to 7% share depending on definition.
Evidence: Fed SHED 2025 (fielded October 2025): 30% of adults had income that varied at least occasionally, similar to 2024 and up from 28% in 2023; 11% struggled to pay bills because of the variation; self-employed 58% and 22%; working for someone else 28% and 10%; retirees 17% versus non-retirees 34% | SHED 2025 Appendix A: the hardship item (I12, 'Because your income varies, have you ... struggled to pay your bills') is asked only of those who said income varies occasionally or quite often | BLS Contingent Worker Supplement (July 2023, released 8 November 2024): contingent workers 4.3% of employed (6.9 million), up from 3.8% in May 2017; independent contractors 11.9 million (7.4%); 80.3% of independent contractors preferred their arrangement and 44.8% of contingent workers would have preferred a permanent job | Pew (10,348 adults, 23-29 August 2021): 16% ever earned on an online gig platform; 31% of current or recent gig workers (3% of all adults) call it their main job; 23% say the income was essential and 35% important for basic needs; 52% cite covering gaps or changes in income as a major reason | JPMorgan Chase Institute (February 2016, Chase accounts October 2012-September 2015): 4.2% of adults (about 10.3 million) earned platform income at some point; in any given month roughly 1% (about 2.5 million), 0.4% from labor platforms
Implication: The pain pool for smoothing is the SHED variable-income population (mostly wage earners whose hours move, Debit-Primary Spenders), not gig workers, so a product built only for platform earners addresses a 3-9% slice.
Caveats: Merges T02-A findings 1 and 3. SHED is self-reported and 'occasionally' is self-defined; SHED has no gig item; the income-level hardship breakdown is chart-only and not cited. BLS, Pew and JPMCI use different questions and are not additive; Pew 2021 and JPMCI 2015 predate post-2021 platform growth. Compiler correction: the JPMCI URL is named 'volatility-2' but serves the February 2016 'Paychecks, Paydays, and the Online Platform Economy' report; figures were verified against that PDF. The slice's '82% of labor-platform participants relied on it for under 25% of income' figure was not found in the extract and was removed. Overlaps corpus income-19/20 (JPMCI 2022, SHED 2024).

Claim: The scaled, profitable market for cash-flow liquidity sells speed on already-earned or near-term pay, not smoothing: Dave earned $554.2M in 2025 on advances averaging $205, Chime's MyPay added $212.5M of revenue in 2025, MoneyLion's Instacash drove $318.3M of 2024 banking revenue, and employer-partnered EWA users paid about $69 a year in fees.
Evidence: Dave FY2025 10-K: operating revenue $554.2M (2024 $347.1M); processing and overdraft service fees $466.8M (2024 $218.8M), 84% of revenue (compiler arithmetic); ExtraCash up to $500 via bank partner Evolve, originations about $7.6B (2024 $5.1B), average advance $205 (2024 $170); provision for credit losses $91.0M; net income $195.9M; underwritten by CashAI on real-time cash flow | Chime FY2025 10-K: 9.5M Active Members; revenue $2,186.8M (2024 $1,673.3M); platform-related revenue $686.2M (2024 $396.7M), the increase driven primarily by a $212.5M year-over-year gain from the full launch of MyPay in July 2024; MyPay is free within 24 hours or instant for a low fee; MyPay at Work launched 2025; provision for credit losses $77.7M (2024 $33.5M) | MoneyLion FY2024 10-K: revenue $545.9M; banking revenue $318.3M (up $80.9M, 34.1%) driven by Instacash instant-transfer fees and tips; 20.4M Total Customers; provision $86.1M plus $40.3M loss on sale of Instacash receivables; merger agreement with Gen Digital signed 10 December 2024 | CFPB Data Spotlight (July 2024; 8 employer-partnered providers, 2021-2022): $22.8B across 214M transactions for 7.2M workers in 2022; average advance $106; workers paid $68.88 a year in fees; 96.61% of fees were expedite fees; illustrative APR 109.5%. California DFPI 2021 data: $765M advanced, average APR 334% (tip companies) and 331% (non-tip), average repayment 10 days
Implication: Revealed demand is for timing, priced per transfer and small per user, so a bank smoothing product must show a reason to pay beyond speed; the base is Debit-Primary Spenders on paycheck cadence.
Caveats: Merges T02-B findings 1, 6 and 8 with T02-A finding 5. Company filings about their own business. Chime's $212.5M is a year-over-year increase, not total MyPay revenue. Dave's provision is an accounting charge, not a loss rate. CFPB covers about half the employer-partnered market and 2021-2022 data; DFPI APRs include tips. The DFPI host returned 403 on re-fetch this pass; figures verified against the researcher's local extract (output/income/T02/_pdf/dfpi-ewa-2021.txt). Gen Digital deal completion not verified. Overlaps corpus row 6 (CFPB EWA), which is not carried separately.

Claim: The only US startup built around guaranteed steady pay, Even, dropped its smoothing feature within about two years and became an earned-wage-access provider, and the one live paid-smoothing example found, SteadyPay in the UK, reported about 9,000 active users in 2022.
Evidence: May 2015 launch coverage: Even turned uneven hourly income into a simulated steady salary, banking surplus weeks in an Even-managed savings account and covering short weeks from savings or a no-interest credit line, for $3 a week; access planned for several thousand people by September 2015, full launch January 2016 | TechCrunch (July 2018): $40M Series B (total $50.5M); Even had announced the previous year that it stopped its Pay Protection product; it kept Instapay (earned pay in advance) and charged $2.99 a month without an employer sponsor | Banking Dive (27 January 2022, event record): Walmart-backed One merged with Even, which served about 2 million employees with Walmart its largest client and about half of employers paying; terms undisclosed; the companies declined to explain how users would transition. OnePay @Work page (2026) offers Instapay and lists 'formerly Even'; no smoothing feature | TechCrunch (4 March 2022): SteadyPay $5M Series A; top-ups when earnings fall below the monthly average, average about GBP 250, cap GBP 1,000; over 9,000 active users; defaults below 10%; lends from its own balance sheet. Companies House: SteadyPay Limited (10713752) Active, last accounts to 30 April 2025
Implication: The clearest attempt at paid smoothing in the US retreated to earned wage access, which is evidence that the smoothing promise did not find paying demand at startup scale; a bank would be re-running an experiment that failed without a stated reason.
Caveats: Merges T02-B findings 5 and 9. Trade press is the primary record because Even was private. No source states why Pay Protection ended. Compiler correction: the slice said Even had 'a few thousand beta users'; the 2015 article says access was planned for several thousand people by September 2015. TechCrunch gives SteadyPay's price inconsistently (GBP 4 a week and 'just over $5 a month'); no price is relied on. SteadyPay figures are company claims; Active registration does not show the product still sells. SteadyPay is UK.

Claim: Federal and state enforcers sued or settled with the main cash-advance and EWA providers between 2023 and 2025 over fees, tips and subscriptions, so the revenue model of the scaled players is the thing regulators attack.
Evidence: FTC (2 November 2023): Brigit to pay $18M; FTC alleged 'instant' advances up to $250 were rarely delivered, a $0.99 instant-transfer fee was added, and the $9.99/month Plus subscription was required; FTC sent more than $17M to 1,818,930 members (4 November 2024) | Dave 10-K (FY2025): FTC complaint filed 5 November 2024 in C.D. Cal.; DOJ amended complaint 30 December 2024; City of Baltimore sued 30 December 2025; unresolved at filing | NY Attorney General (14 April 2025): sued DailyPay and MoneyLion as illegal payday lenders; advances usually under $100 repaid in seven to ten days at annualized rates of 200% to 350%; DailyPay's common $20 seven-day advance for $2.99 exceeds 750%; DailyPay collects fees on about 90% of loans | DC Attorney General (November 2024): sued EarnIn; 'Lightning Speed' fees of $3.99 or $5.99, average rate over 300% against DC's 24% cap, default tips $1-$14; more than 20,000 DC consumers and more than a million transactions since 2016
Implication: A bank entering smoothing needs a pricing model that does not resemble per-transfer expedite fees and tips, since those are what enforcers have called deceptive or usurious; this also caps the fee pool a bank could inherit.
Caveats: T02-B finding 2. Allegations, not findings of liability, except the Brigit settlement. Outcomes after March 2026 (Dave), and of the NY and DC suits, were not checked. The NY AG figures are the AG's characterization. The FTC URLs returned 404 to a scripted fetch but resolved through WebFetch with the cited figures.

Claim: As of October 2026 the federal posture favors payroll-linked EWA but not underwritten smoothing: the CFPB's December 2025 advisory opinion says Covered EWA is not Regulation Z credit only where the provider does not assess individual worker credit risk, it withdrew the July 2024 proposed interpretive rule, and states split between licensed non-loan regimes and treating EWA as loans.
Evidence: CFPB advisory opinion (December 2025): Covered EWA must be capped at accrued wages from payroll data, repaid by payroll deduction, carry no recourse, collection or credit reporting, and the provider must not directly or indirectly assess the credit risk of individual workers; expedite fees and tips are not finance charges; it withdraws the July 2024 proposed interpretive rule (89 FR 61358), which was never finalized; the January 2025 rescission of the 2020 opinion was itself withdrawn (90 FR 20084, May 2025) | Same opinion, footnotes 50-51: Kansas (Kan. Stat. 9-2407), Missouri (361.749), South Carolina (39-5-860) and Utah (13-78-106) statutes, quoted in the opinion, say registered EWA is not a loan; Arizona (December 2022) and Montana (December 2023) AG opinions agree | Nevada SB 290 (2023): licensed EWA providers' services are not a loan or money transmission. California DFPI rule effective 15 February 2025 states EWAs are loans under the California Financing Law, with proposed rate caps dropped (law-firm blog; DFPI page not reached). McGuireWoods (March 2025): Kansas, Missouri, Nevada, South Carolina and Wisconsin enacted EWA laws in 2023-2024 | Section 1033: CFPB final rule released 22 October 2024; advance notice of proposed rulemaking on reconsideration issued 22 August 2025 (CFPB-2025-0037, RIN 3170-AB39); CFPB pages last modified August 2025 show no newer proposal. Pointer only: Faegre Drinker alert says H.R. 9330 was introduced 18 June 2026 and advanced 29-22 by House Financial Services on 30 June 2026; not law
Implication: A product that smooths income by underwriting the worker's earnings or credit risk falls outside the Covered EWA safe harbor and is credit under Reg Z, TILA and ECOA, so the hypothesis as written ('underwritten on earnings data') takes on the full credit regime while the timing products beside it do not.
Caveats: Merges T02-A finding 8 and T02-B findings 3 and 4. The '2024 CFPB EWA interpretive rule' in the brief was a proposal, withdrawn in December 2025; the CFPB rules page still shows only the 2024 proposal (stale). Advisory opinions do not bind courts or states. California and the state list beyond Nevada rest on law-firm summaries (pointers); the four statutes are quoted in the CFPB opinion but were not opened. The Faegre Drinker alert is a law-firm summary and is a pointer only; H.R. 9330 primary text (congress.gov) not fetched. That a bank would treat underwritten smoothing as credit is the researchers' inference. 1033 litigation and compliance-date status not verified.

Claim: Early access to a direct-deposited paycheck is already a free, table-stakes feature at Capital One, Fifth Third and Chime, and DoorDash offers earners instant deposit into its own bank-partnered account, so cash timing is not a reason to switch banks.
Evidence: Capital One early paycheck page (October 2026): paycheck up to 2 days early with 360 Checking and direct deposit, free; the 360 page footnote says certain non-payroll and tax payments are not eligible | Fifth Third (18 May 2022): Early Pay extended to gig and some benefit income; 'hundreds of thousands of accounts' received pay early since the 2021 launch; Fifth Third calls its own MyAdvance 'an expensive form of credit' | Chime FY2025 10-K: Get Paid Early gives direct-deposit members their full paycheck up to two days before the scheduled pay date | DoorDash Fast Pay costs $1.99 per cash-out; DoorDash Crimson, with banking services from Starion Bank, offers instant earnings deposits with no credit check (undated help page)
Implication: Capital One already gives away the cheapest layer of this territory, so a new product would need to deliver income insurance or underwritten smoothing, which is the part with no demonstrated demand; additive screen: early pay is already in motion at Capital One.
Caveats: T02-B finding 7. Company pages and a press release. Compiler correction: the slice's 'not guaranteed, may take two pay cycles' wording was not found in the fetched early-paycheck page text and was removed. No source measures switching caused by early pay. Capital One's uptake is undisclosed.

Claim: Payfare, the program manager behind DoorDash's DasherDirect, lost its largest program when DoorDash declined to renew in September 2024, its shares fell more than 75%, and Fiserv bought it, closing 2 March 2025 at C$4.00 a share (C$193.1M), which Fiserv's 10-K records as $95M net of $46M acquired cash.
Evidence: BetaKit (October 2024, event record; Payfare's own release unreachable): DasherDirect was Payfare's largest program and a 'substantial proportion' of revenue; TSX shares fell from C$8.35 to C$2.00, a more than 75% drop; strategic review launched | BNN Bloomberg (27 September 2024): Eight Capital estimated DoorDash at 70 to 80 per cent of Payfare revenue (analyst estimate, not company disclosure) | Fiserv closing release (syndicated): 48,287,259 shares at C$4.00, C$193,149,036 aggregate. Fiserv FY2025 10-K: acquired 2 March 2025, a Canada-based provider of program management powering instant access to earnings and banking for workforces, purchase price $95M net of $46M acquired cash; now the orchestration layer of Fiserv's embedded-finance stack | Pointer check: Lyft's FY2024 10-K contains no Payfare or Lyft Direct mention, so the brief's 'Lyft contract loss' is not supported; the loss was DoorDash
Implication: In earning-platform banking the platform holds the customer and can end the program by non-renewal, so a provider that depends on one platform carries the concentration risk; the surviving value was bought as software infrastructure, not as a consumer franchise.
Caveats: income-A finding 1. The 70-80% revenue share is one analyst's estimate; Payfare's SEDAR+ filings were not retrieved. Compiler addition: the slice said Fiserv did not separate Payfare's price; the 10-K acquisitions note does ($95M net of $46M cash). Payfare also served Lyft and Uber programs; their status after the deal is unknown. Trade press is the event record. Geography Canada for the issuer; the programs served US earners.

Claim: At the largest US earning platforms the platform brands the account and the bank sits behind it: DoorDash says it acts as a service provider to a bank for Dasher banking, DoorDash Crimson runs on Starion Bank, and the Uber Pro Card runs on Marqeta and Branch with Evolve or Lead Bank as sponsor; none discloses uptake.
Evidence: DoorDash FY2025 10-K: gives US Dashers access to certain banking services for immediate access to earnings and in that offering acts as a service provider to a bank; no account, deposit or uptake figure; the product name DasherDirect does not appear | DoorDash help page (undated): DoorDash Crimson banking services provided by Starion Bank, instant earnings deposits, no credit check; Fast Pay to other accounts costs $1.99 | Marqeta (6 October 2022): Uber, Marqeta, Mastercard and Branch launched the Uber Pro Card; up to 10% cashback on gas and 12% on EV charging at Diamond status; up to $150 Backup Balance. Branch legal page: banking services by Evolve Bank & Trust or Lead Bank as sponsor banks | Uber FY2025 10-K: no mention of the Uber Pro Card or earner-banking uptake
Implication: Platform-payout banking exists, but distribution runs through the platform and the bank is a small sponsor named in the footnotes, so a deposit bank would be selling a rail to platforms, not winning the earner.
Caveats: income-A finding 2, with the DoorDash Crimson/Starion fact added from the T02-B help page. Uptake is undisclosed everywhere. The help page carries no date, so whether Crimson replaced DasherDirect after Payfare is the compiler's reading, not stated. dasherdirect.com did not resolve and Uber's own card page returned 404 in the slice pass. Creator finance (Karat, Creative Juice) was dropped; see notes.

Claim: Synapse's 2024 collapse showed the failure mode of the silent middle layer: the trustee estimated a $60M to $90M shortfall of end-user funds, more than 100,000 customers lost access, and the FDIC's September 2024 record-keeping proposal for custodial accounts still has no final-rule date in the 2026 Unified Agenda.
Evidence: CFPB complaint against Synapse (filed 21 August 2025, Adv. No. 1:25-ap-01052-MB, C.D. Cal.): Synapse bridged fintech platforms and partner banks; filed Chapter 11 on 22 April 2024; the trustee estimated the end-user shortfall at $60M to $90M; as early as September 2023 Synapse's records did not match its first partner bank, and by then both Evolve and Synapse knew of a deficit of tens of millions of dollars; Evolve froze all end-user activity on 11 May 2024 | Same complaint: from mid-2023 a Cash Management Program moved consumer funds from platforms to more than one partner bank into an omnibus account held by a Synapse subsidiary (carried from the framework slice T13-B finding 11) | FDIC Vice Chairman Hill on the September 2024 proposal: over 100,000 customers lost access; the proposal estimated 600 to 1,100 banks could be in scope though only a few dozen are heavily engaged. FDIC FIL-64-2024: beneficial-owner records, daily reconciliation, third-party records only with continuous bank access, annual certification | Unified Agenda RIN 3064-AG07 (2026): stage Long-Term Actions; comment period extended to 16 January 2025; Final Rule date To Be Determined
Implication: A bank behind a platform's accounts carries reconciliation and pass-through insurance risk with an unsettled rule, which weighs against a separate T09 build, most heavily for omnibus or custodial designs rather than accounts opened in the earner's name.
Caveats: Merges income-B finding 1 with the framework compiler's carried-over Synapse finding (T13-B 11). Compiler correction to T13-B: its caveat said the complaint states no dollar shortfall; the complaint text (verified this pass) does state the trustee's $60M-$90M estimate. Allegations are the CFPB's; the Bureau consented to a final order. Long-Term Actions is a planning signal, not a withdrawal.

Claim: The banks that served as the silent provider for fintech programmes drew formal actions in 2024 on the same themes: the Fed ordered Evolve (June 2024) to fix fintech-partner risk management, the OCC put Blue Ridge under a January 2024 consent order (terminated 13 November 2025 after it exited BaaS), and the FDIC issued orders to Sutton, Piermont and Lineage.
Evidence: Federal Reserve (14 June 2024, with the Arkansas State Bank Department): action against Evolve for deficiencies in AML, risk management and consumer compliance, including failing to have an effective risk management framework for its fintech partnerships; requires oversight of those relationships and better record keeping | OCC: AA-ENF-2024-13 terminated Blue Ridge's August 2022 agreement because a consent order dated 24 January 2024 superseded it; AA-ENF-2025-58 terminated that consent order (AA-ENF-2023-68), signed 13 November 2025. Blue Ridge FY2024 10-K: exited its BaaS depository operations through an orderly wind-down in 2024; total assets about $2.74B | Banking Dive (event record; FDIC order text not fetched): Sutton order 1 February 2024 (verify prepaid customer identities back to July 2020, revised AML/CFT programme, third-party inventory, BSA officer); Piermont order 26 February 2024 (look-back to September 2022, third-party programme review, board strengthening); Lineage order made public end of February 2024 (enhanced risk programme, more capital, end some fintech partners). Piermont's CEO: every bank that touches BaaS is getting an enforcement action
Implication: A large bank entering as platform provider would be examined against this list (partner oversight, BSA/AML, records); Blue Ridge shows an order can be cured in about 22 months but only after the programme was shut.
Caveats: income-B finding 2. Correction carried from income-B: only Blue Ridge is an OCC order; Evolve is a Federal Reserve order; Sutton, Piermont and Lineage are FDIC orders resting on Banking Dive because orders.fdic.gov failed a certificate check; confidence mapped down to Medium for that reason. Whether the Evolve, Sutton, Piermont and Lineage orders remain in force in October 2026 was not established. The CEO quote is an affected party's opinion. These banks were small; the orders show what examiners look for, not what they would find at a $660B bank.

Claim: In IRS tax year 2020 data, 25.6 million of 28.4 million nonfarm sole-proprietor returns (90.1%) reported business receipts under $100,000 and held $421.9 billion, 26.3% of all sole-proprietor receipts; Census counts 31.99 million nonemployer establishments with $1.86 trillion of receipts in 2024, 86.7% of them in receipts classes under $100,000.
Evidence: IRS SOI Table 3, TY2020 (dollars in thousands): 28,353,367 returns and $1,605.2B receipts in total; the six size rows under $100,000 sum to 25,559,563 returns and $421.9B receipts; net income less deficit for those rows sums to $114.5B of $337.2B. Shares are compiler arithmetic from the IRS rows, re-run on the downloaded table | The IRS publishes this size table only through TY2020. The SOI Bulletin (Spring 2025) gives TY2022 headlines of 31.0 million returns with sole-proprietor activity, receipts of $2,080 billion and profits of $410.7 billion, with no size cut | Census Nonemployer Statistics 2024 national file (released 2026-09-29): 31,985,874 establishments and $1,861.4B receipts; individual proprietorships 27,644,187 and $1,124.3B. Counts under $5K 7,176,486; $5K-$9,999 4,750,572; $10K-$24,999 7,377,611; $25K-$49,999 4,805,950; $50K-$99,999 3,618,068, summing to 27,728,687 or 86.7% (compiler arithmetic). Receipts by class are suppressed in the file | Census 2022 comparison: 29.8 million nonemployer businesses with $1.7 trillion of receipts
Implication: The population is large, but the sole proprietors whose money is plausibly personal (under about $100K of receipts) hold roughly $422B of receipts in TY2020 dollars, about a quarter of the total, so the prize is much smaller than the $2,080B headline.
Caveats: Edge: none. TY2020 is a pandemic year and the size table is two years older than the TY2022 totals. Tax returns are not firms; one person can file more than one Schedule C. Receipts cover all payment types; no source gives the card share. NES is built from IRS business records, so the two series are not independent at the source. The Census press release is a tip sheet with no headline numbers; the 2024 figures were read from the downloaded zip. The researcher reported that Census changed its receipts cutoffs from 2022; the story page fetched in this pass does not say so, so year-to-year comparison is unconfirmed.

Claim: Published acceptance prices are 2.6% plus 15 cents for Square's entry tier in person, 2.9% plus 30 cents for Stripe online and 2.55% plus 15 cents for Capital One Merchant Services, while Square settles seller funds within one to four days, so the card-fee ceiling for the under-$100K sole-proprietor segment is about $11 billion a year and the float is days of flow, not balances.
Evidence: Square fees page (fetched 2026-10-26): in person 2.6% + 15 cents, 2.5% + 15 cents, 2.4% + 15 cents; online 3.3% + 30 cents, then 2.9% + 30 cents; keyed 3.5% + 15 cents. The scout's 2.6% + 10 cents does not appear on the page | Stripe pricing: 2.9% + 30 cents online; 2.7% + 5 cents in person on Terminal; Instant Payouts 1.5% of volume, minimum 50 cents; no setup or monthly fees. Capital One Merchant Services (powered by Worldpay): 2.55% + $0.15 in person, 2.90% + $0.30 online, 3.45% + $0.20 keyed, monthly minimum up to $30 | Block FY2025 10-K: settlements receivable and customers payable represent one to four days of flows; customers payable $6.8B at year-end 2025 including Cash App funds. Compiler arithmetic: Square GPV $259.6B / 365 = about $0.71B a day, so one to four days is about $0.7B to $2.8B. PayPal FY2025 10-K: funds payable and amounts due to customers $40,198M on 439M active accounts, about $92 an account (compiler arithmetic) | Card-fee ceiling, LABELLED COMPILER ARITHMETIC: 2.6% x $421.9B (income-101) = about $11.0B a year, assuming every under-$100K receipt is card-paid and acquired at Square's entry in-person rate. It is a gross-revenue ceiling before interchange and network fees, not an estimate of the prize
Implication: Acceptance revenue for the personal-money segment is a gross ceiling near $11B before interchange, and the float is thin, so any P05 economics have to come from the deposit relationship rather than from holding settlement balances.
Caveats: Edge: none. The fetch tool inferred the Free, Plus and Premium column labels on the Square page; the page's FAQ says Premium is cheapest, which fits the order. Pricing pages are company statements; the Capital One page may be stale. Processor revenue is not margin: interchange and network fees come out of these rates. PayPal and Block customer balances include consumer wallets. No source gives the card share of sole-proprietor receipts, so the true pool is below the ceiling; income-114 shows part of it already moves on Zelle with no card fee.

Claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act retroactively restored the pre-2021 Form 1099-K threshold for third-party settlement organizations, $20,000 and more than 200 transactions, while payment card transactions still carry no threshold.
Evidence: IRS IR-2025-107 (2025-10-23): the act retroactively reinstated the threshold in effect before the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021; a TPSO need not file unless gross payments to a payee exceed $20,000 and transactions exceed 200 | IRS 1099-K general FAQ A2: for payment card transactions there is no threshold amount for receiving a Form 1099-K; a state may set a lower TPSO threshold
Implication: The $600 rule would have pulled millions of small sellers into reported, account-linked receipts; its reversal removes that tailwind, so P05 has no tax-reporting why-now for the under-$100K segment.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory (removed). The statute section was not fetched; facts come from IRS guidance, and the IRS page is marked archival. That the $600 rule pushed sellers toward formal acceptance is an inference; no source measures it. The researcher saw, but did not fetch, a January 2026 backup-withholding proposal aligned to the same threshold; its status is not verified.

Claim: Block's FY2025 10-K shows Square with $259.6 billion of gross payment volume, $3.9 billion of gross profit, a wholly owned industrial bank, Square Financial Services, and more than 4.0 million loans and advances since 2014, so one incumbent already combines acceptance, a bank charter, deposits and sales-based credit.
Evidence: Block 10-K FY2025: Square GPV $259,631M in 2025, $240,812M in 2024, $227,699M in 2023; Square gross profit $3.9B, up 9%, driven by financial solutions, most notably Square Loans | Same 10-K: Square Checking earns revenue primarily through debit card interchange; Square Savings is an FDIC-insured business savings account; Square Loans has facilitated more than 4.0 million loans and advances and more than $32.8B of principal since May 2014, mostly funded by institutional third-party investors on a forward-flow basis | Compiler arithmetic: $3.9B / $259.6B = 1.5% gross profit yield; gross profit includes loans, hardware and software, so it is not a payments take rate. The 10-K gives no seller count or Checking adoption figure
Implication: The micro-seller position is already held by a firm with the combined acceptance, deposit and credit stack P05 claims for the bank, and it holds that position through software.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to Square (Block), through software distribution and its own bank charter. Block's own filing. Square is not purely sole proprietors and the 10-K does not split GPV by seller size. Square Checking is issued by Sutton Bank, not Square Financial Services (income-110).

Claim: Stripe reports $1.9 trillion of 2025 volume across more than 5 million businesses, PayPal $1.79 trillion of TPV on 439 million active accounts, Shopify $248.1 billion through Shopify Payments (65.6% of $378.4 billion GMV) and Toast $195.1 billion of GPV across about 164,000 locations.
Evidence: Stripe 2025 annual update: $1.9T total volume, up 34% from 2024; more than 5 million businesses directly or via platforms; robustly profitable | PayPal 10-K FY2025: $1.79T TPV, up 7%; 25.4B payment transactions; 439M active accounts; US merchant loans are provided by a state-chartered industrial bank and PayPal acquires the receivables; merchant loans, advances and fees receivable $1.8B net | Shopify 10-K FY2025: Shopify Payments penetration 65.6% of GMV, $248.1B of $378.4B; North America adoption 88% of merchants where available. Toast 10-K FY2025: GPV $195.1B, up 23%; about 164,000 locations | Compiler arithmetic: the four sum to about $3.7T, but the series overlap and are global, so the sum is not a US market size
Implication: Every large micro-merchant acceptance pool is attached to software or a marketplace the seller already uses, so a bank offering acceptance alone would have to displace software, not just beat a price.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to platforms (onboarding and software distribution). All self-reported, with different definitions (TPV, GPV, GMV). None splits sole proprietors. Stripe's letter has no audited segment data. Fiserv's Clover GPV was not found in the 10-K text searched.

Claim: Discover's network reaches small merchants through third-party acquirers, not directly: its FY2024 10-K describes direct relationships with large US merchants only, Capital One's FY2025 10-K says the network earns acquirer interchange primarily from merchant acquirers, and the network carries a $1.2 billion reserve for misclassifying merchants and acquirers into its highest pricing tier.
Evidence: Discover 10-K FY2024: merchant acquiring model includes direct relationships with large merchants in the US and arrangements with third-party merchant acquirers; Payment Services volume $402.5B in 2024; no merchant count disclosed | Capital One 10-K FY2025: acquirer interchange income is earned primarily from merchant acquirers on Global Payment Network transactions; Global Payment Network volume $401,775M (franchise-05). Card Product Misclassification: Discover and DFS Services entered a Federal Reserve consent order on 2025-04-18; Discover reserved $1.2B, with the class settlement (preliminary approval 2025-07-30) the primary means of restitution to merchants, acquirers and other intermediaries | Stripe's Discover guide (vendor page): Discover is accepted at 99% of credit-card-accepting US locations, holds a significantly smaller share of cards in circulation, and is enabled by default on all Stripe-hosted payment options | Compiler arithmetic: $401.8B / ($6.51T US credit + $4.99T US debit card value, Fed Payments Study 2024) = about 3.5%, indicative only because the network volume includes PULSE and international Diners
Implication: The premise that Discover's direct merchant relationships give the bank micro-merchant acceptance fails: the direct book is large merchants, small sellers already accept Discover through facilitators, and the network's standing with acquirers carries a live remediation.
Caveats: Edge: none. Company filings; 'direct relationships with large merchants' is a description, not a quantified share. The Discover filing is pre-merger. The misclassification concerned card-product pricing tiers, not small merchants specifically. Stripe's acceptance claim has no method. The 3.5% share mixes definitions and years; it is kept only as context and is not a finding on its own (researcher B rated it Low).

Claim: Large banks and the one long-standing three-party network have stepped back from owning small-merchant acquiring: Wells Fargo let its Fiserv merchant joint venture lapse on 2025-04-01, Bank of America and First Data ended theirs in June 2020, and American Express acquires small merchants through OptBlue, where third-party processors hold the contract and set the price.
Evidence: Fiserv 10-K FY2025: Wells Fargo gave notice of non-renewal of Wells Fargo Merchant Services; on expiry on 2025-04-01 Fiserv received an initial $453 million cash payment; a $595 million non-cash impairment of the WFMS investment was booked in 2024; Fiserv signed a multi-year agreement to process for Wells Fargo's merchant clients | Payments Dive (2019-07-30, trade press as the primary record of the event): Bank of America and First Data would end Banc of America Merchant Services when the contract ended in June 2020, with uninterrupted service through at least 2023; First Data held 51% | American Express 10-K FY2017: Amex works with third parties to acquire small and medium-sized merchants; through OptBlue, third-party processors contract directly with small merchants and determine merchant pricing; US network could accommodate nearly 95 percent of general-purpose card spend at end-2017; Amex expected its discount rate to keep falling partly from a shift of merchants into OptBlue | Counter-case: JPMorgan 10-K FY2025 still runs Merchant Services in CIB Payments for merchants of all sizes, with no micro-merchant volume disclosed
Implication: No record found shows a bank or an owned network scaling micro-merchant acquiring on its own; the precedents run the other way, toward processors and facilitators owning the small merchant.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to acquirers and payment facilitators (merchant contract and pricing). The filings do not say why Wells Fargo or Bank of America left, so this is not proof the product fails. BAMS rests on trade press only (the press-release host returned 403 to the researcher). The Amex filing is 2017 and no later OptBlue volume was found; its motive was coverage and cost, not a deposit account.

Claim: Visa's Payment Facilitator model says the model exists to cut the cost of signing long-tail merchants including individuals and professionals, lets the facilitator hold the merchant contract and makes the acquirer responsible for both, and Discover's facilitator roadmap applies the same structure on its network.
Evidence: Visa Payment Facilitator model (2024): acquirer benefits include reducing the cost of signing and supporting long-tail merchants; eligible merchants include individuals/professionals and community events; acquirers are responsible for the acts of both PFs and sponsored merchants | Visa Core Rules and Product and Service Rules (edition April 2026), rule 5.3.1.4: an acquirer must enter a direct Merchant Agreement with a sponsored merchant exceeding USD 1 million of annual transaction volume | Discover Global Network facilitator roadmap: a facilitator must register with an acquiring bank; the acquiring bank ultimately assumes the risks; the facilitator sets its own processing terms, costs and fees
Implication: Network rules route micro-merchants to the facilitator channel, where a bank's role is sponsor (risk and capital) rather than owner of the relationship; no rule found gives an owned network a cheaper way to onboard a sole proprietor.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to payment facilitators (merchant contract, pricing and onboarding). Visa's PF document is guidance marked informational. Both Visa PDFs were verified against the researcher's local extracts (output/sweep2/_pdf/p05b/vpf.txt, vrules.txt); both URLs return 200 in this pass. Mastercard's rules returned 403 and Discover's operating regulations are not public, so no sponsor-fee level was seen. No public source prices a bank acquirer against a payfac sponsor fee.
