Claim: Regulation II's interchange cap applies to business-purpose debit cards: the official commentary says 'account' includes business accounts and an issuer of a business-purpose debit card is subject to the fee limits, and 12 CFR 235.5 exempts only small issuers, government-administered programs and certain reloadable prepaid cards.
Evidence: Official commentary 2(a)-1, as reproduced in the Federal Reserve's October 2023 proposal: account includes consumer accounts and business accounts; the limits apply whether the card is issued for personal, family or household purposes or for business purposes; an issuer of a business-purpose debit card is subject to the interchange fee restrictions | 12 CFR 235.2(a): account means a transaction, savings or other asset account established for any purpose and located in the US. 235.5: exemptions for issuers under $10 billion of assets with affiliates, government-administered programs and certain reloadable prepaid cards; no business or commercial card exemption | Fed report on 2023 debit data (published 2025-12-19): 100.70B transactions worth $4,658.42B; split is covered versus exempt and prepaid versus non-prepaid, with no consumer versus business split; the Fed's Regulation II FAQs have no entry on business cards | Status: the 2023 proposal (14.4 cents plus 4.0 bps) is not final; ICBA (2026-01-12) reports a North Dakota district court ruling against the rule in Corner Post, appealed to the Eighth Circuit (see also independence-112)
Implication: A sole proprietor's business debit card issued by a covered bank is capped like a consumer card, so the scout's 'Durbin exemption of small-business debit' does not exist and there is no business-debit preference to build on.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory (none in P05's favour). Corrected pointer: the scout's small-business debit exemption is not in the rule. The commentary was read from the Fed's 2023 proposal text (extracted locally) because the live eCFR supplement returned 404 to the researcher; the eCFR sections were re-fetched in this pass. The litigation status rests on ICBA, a trade group with an interest in the rule; dockets were not checked.

Claim: In 2026 the federal posture turned toward easing bank-fintech partnership oversight, but only as proposed guidance: on 15 September 2026 the OCC, Fed, FDIC and NCUA proposed to rescind and replace the 2023 third-party guidance and its supplements, including the July 2024 joint statement on deposit arrangements, citing Executive Order 14405, with comments due 16 November 2026.
Evidence: Federal Register vol. 91 no. 177 (15 September 2026), p. 58536 (OCC-2026-0793, Fed OP-1881, NCUA-2026-1684): agencies plan to rescind and replace existing third-party risk guidance and remove language that may unduly impede fintechs from entering bank partnerships; supplemental resources include the 25 July 2024 Joint Statement on Banks' Arrangements with Third Parties to Deliver Bank Deposit Products and the community-bank guide; comments by 16 November 2026 | E.O. 14405 (19 May 2026): federal financial regulators must review rules and guidance that unduly impede fintech-bank partnerships within 90 days and act within 180 days | OCC news release 2024-85: the July 2024 joint statement said it did not establish new supervisory expectations and was issued with a request for information on bank-fintech arrangements
Implication: Supervisory friction on being a platform's bank is falling on paper, a why-now for T09, but it is non-binding guidance at proposal stage that leaves the 2024 orders, the pending custodial rule, Reg E, UDAAP and BSA untouched and can be reversed.
Caveats: income-B finding 3. Proposed, not final. Calendar dates for the order's 90- and 180-day deadlines are derivations, not stated in the order. No agency output from the 90-day review was found.

Claim: Square Checking is issued by Sutton Bank ($1.74 billion of assets) and Square's savings and loans by Square Financial Services ($2.06 billion), both under Regulation II's $10 billion line, while Capital One's debit escapes the cap only on its own three-party network.
Evidence: FDIC institution data, report date 2026-06-30: Sutton Bank (Ohio, CERT 5962) assets $1,740,659 thousand; Square Financial Services, Inc. (Utah, CERT 59177) assets $2,057,172 thousand. Square Checking terms: the agreement is between the seller and Sutton Bank | Fed report on 2023 data: average interchange $0.23 for covered issuers and $0.52 for exempt issuers; covered transactions 61.67B of 100.70B (independence-102) | Capital One 10-K FY2025: Regulation II limits interchange on debit cards issued on networks not owned by the Company; Regulation II has requirements for debit cards issued on networks that are not three-party networks. The Fed approval order and Commentary 2(m)-2 treat a three-party system as outside the cap (independence-109, independence-110). 10-Q Q2 2026: Consumer Banking non-interest income rose $384M to $778M, mainly from the Global Payment Network and reissuance of legacy debit cards onto it | Compiler illustration: average 2023 ticket $4,658.42B / 100.70B = $46.26; the cap on that ticket is about $0.23; Square's 2.6% + 15 cents on the same ticket is about $1.35. The gap is everything above a covered issuer's interchange, an upper bound on what a cheaper acquirer could take, not a margin
Implication: The bank's one real regulatory edge is on the deposit side, uncapped debit on its own network, but it applies to every debit customer, not to sole proprietors, and Square already earns uncapped interchange through exempt issuers.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory for Capital One on own-network debit only; belongs to Square on exempt-issuer interchange. Exempt status depends on each issuer's consolidated assets with affiliates, which was not tested beyond the FDIC totals. The 10-K does not quantify own-network debit interchange. The $0.23 and $0.52 averages mix consumer, business and prepaid cards. If three-party debit became subject to the cap the edge would vanish (independence-111).

Claim: Regulation E covers only accounts established primarily for personal, family or household purposes, and the incumbents route sole proprietors' business money out of that category: Square Checking is for business purposes only and says commercial accounts lack the same error-resolution rights, and PayPal requires a business account for business activity even if the business is not incorporated.
Evidence: 12 CFR 1005.2(b)(1): account means a demand deposit, savings or other consumer asset account established primarily for personal, family or household purposes; 1005.2(e): consumer means a natural person | Square Checking terms (Sutton Bank): the card account can only be used for business purposes; eligible applicants include US sole proprietors with a tax ID; commercial accounts are not subject to the same legal requirements for the resolution of errors; errors to be reported within 60 days; FDIC pass-through insurance up to $250,000 | PayPal User Agreement (US): an account established primarily for business or commercial activity must be a business account, even if the business is not incorporated; PayPal is not a bank and does not take deposits
Implication: The 'sole proprietor whose money is personal' falls between definitions: once receipts are business receipts, the product is a commercial account outside Regulation E, which is small-business banking rather than a consumer product.
Caveats: Edge: none. The CFPB interpretation on mixed-use accounts was not retrieved. The PayPal agreement returned no text to WebFetch in this pass; its quotes were verified against the researcher's saved extract (output/sweep2/_pdf/p05b/ppua.txt). Whether PayPal applies Reg E-style protection to business accounts is not stated.

Claim: FinCEN's beneficial-ownership reporting now covers only foreign-formed companies, under an interim final rule of 2025-03-26 made permanent by a final rule issued 2026-08-11 and effective 2026-08-14, and the customer due diligence rule's definition of a legal entity customer does not name sole proprietorships.
Evidence: FinCEN BOI page: US companies are exempt from BOI reporting; only foreign entities registered to do business in a US state remain reporting companies; final rule issued 2026-08-11, effective 2026-08-14; interim final rule published 2025-03-26 | 31 CFR 1010.230(e)(1): legal entity customer means a corporation, LLC or other entity created by a public filing, a general partnership, and similar foreign entities; sole proprietorships are not mentioned | Researcher inference: a sole proprietor is a natural-person customer, so the account carries the same customer identification as a consumer account and no beneficial-ownership step
Implication: Compliance load is no barrier to a sole-proprietor account, but the same is true for Square and PayPal, so it creates no edge for the bank.
Caveats: Edge: none. The customer identification rule (31 CFR 1020.220) was not fetched. Facilitator AML duties for merchant acquiring were not tested. The 'no beneficial-ownership step' reading is an inference from the definition.

Claim: Capital One already sells small-business checking at $15, $35 and $99 a month (waived at $2,000, $25,000 and $100,000), refers card acceptance to Worldpay, books Brex, a spend platform for over 25,000 companies, to its card segment, and discloses no sole-proprietor segment or small-business deposit figure.
Evidence: Capital One small-business checking page and Basic Checking fee sheet: Basic $15 a month waived at a $2,000 minimum average balance, teller cash deposits free up to $5,000 a month; Enhanced $35 (waived at $25,000); Premier $99 (waived at $100,000); not intended for clients with annual sales above $10 million; the page lists no invoicing, payment acceptance or Zelle, and its required-documents list names corporations, S-corps and LLCs, not sole proprietors | Capital One Merchant Services page: partnered with Worldpay from FIS; the page does not name the acquiring bank; most funds available the next day. The FY2025 10-K says Capital One faces credit risk 'as an issuer and as a merchant acquirer' on the Global Payment Network | Brex announcement (2026-01-22): over 25,000 companies from startups to enterprises; cards, spend software, banking and payments; no mention of small merchants or sole proprietors. 10-Q Q2 2026: Brex closed 2026-04-07 (franchise-06), results in Domestic Card; goodwill preliminarily $2.4B to Credit Card and $710M to Consumer Banking; Consumer Banking covers deposit gathering and lending for consumers and small businesses; Commercial Banking clients typically have revenues of $20 million to $2 billion | No small-business customer count, small-business deposit balance or sole-proprietor figure was found in the 10-K or 10-Q
Implication: The additive screen fails: Capital One already runs small-business banking with a fee schedule that charges the segment P05 targets, its acceptance is a processor referral, and Brex's base is venture-scale and enterprise companies, not sole proprietors.
Caveats: Edge: distribution (unproven). Whether sole proprietors can be found inside the consumer base is not disclosed. Fee pages are company statements; an older Spark Business checking PDF may be discontinued. Whether Worldpay pays Capital One a referral fee or sponsor margin is unknown. The $10 million limit appears on the checking page, not in the Basic fee sheet. The goodwill split is preliminary.

Claim: Early Warning reports $357 billion of small-business payments, 647.6 million small-business transactions and 7.7 million enrolled small businesses on Zelle in 2025, and the CFPB lists Capital One among Early Warning's seven bank co-owners.
Evidence: Early Warning release (2026-02-11): $357B of small-business payments, up 26%; 647.6M small-business transactions, up 23.5%; 7.7M enrolled small businesses, up 15%; small businesses accounted for nearly 30% of dollars moved; no fee statement | CFPB company listing: Early Warning is co-owned by Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo | Researcher inference: a Zelle payment into the sole proprietor's own bank account carries no card interchange or acquirer markup, so the $11.0B ceiling in income-102 should be reduced by the unknown share of under-$100K receipts already paid this way

DailyPay and MoneyLion, DC AG v. EarnIn) [income-04]; bank small-dollar loans fall under the 2020 interagency principles [rupture-10].
Implication: A deposit bank's receiving-account advance gets no EWA exemption and is regulated as small-dollar credit, which is a known path for a bank rather than a regulatory edge; Debit-Primary Spenders are protected by lending rules, not EWA rules.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory (neutral: the bank's lending powers allow it, but no safe harbour applies). One law-firm update and a short search window; a law-firm alert is a pointer, and the bill text was not fetched. The article does not address the bill's scope, bank products or preemption. State EWA bill outcomes in 2026 are a gap.

Claim: Regulators pushed banks out of refund anticipation loans in 2010-2012 although the product was legal, and IRS e-file rules still make the preparer the gatekeeper of refund-related bank products while letting a taxpayer split a refund across up to three accounts.
Evidence: FDIC OIG report OIG-16-001 (February 2016): FDIC concern dates to January 2008; the OCC required one institution to exit RALs effective with the 2011 season; the IRS withdrew an underwriting tool; the FDIC caused all three of its supervised institutions still facilitating RALs to exit in 2011 and 2012; RALs 'were, and remain, legal'; the FDIC issued no formal RAL guidance; the report notes the absence of significant examination-based evidence of harm and records insurance-assessment increases, reputational damage and litigation costs for the banks | IRS Publication 1345 (Rev. 12-2025): the IRS is not involved in or responsible for RALs, RACs or other refund products, which are a business contract between provider and taxpayer; providers must tell taxpayers RALs are interest-bearing loans and disclose all fees, obtain written consent under Treas. Reg. 301.7216-3(a) to share return data with the lender, and the preparer must not be a related taxpayer of the lender | Same handbook: Form 8888 lets a taxpayer split a refund among up to three qualified accounts, including an IRA or HSA
Implication: A bank chasing the 'advances' half of T17 inherits a reputationally scarred product class with the preparer as control point, leaving refund receipt and splitting as the clean lever.
Caveats: income-B finding 5. The OIG report is critical of the FDIC's process and does not endorse RALs; the consumer-advocate view (CFA, NCLC) was not fetched. The OCC action rests on the OIG report. Compiler correction: the slice said Form 8888 cannot be used to collect preparer fees; that rule was not found in the fetched handbook text and was removed. Whether any bank re-entered RALs after 2012 was not verified.

Claim: Three 2025-2026 changes reshape the refund moment: refunds jumped (average $3,268, up 11%, through 24 April 2026) on unadjusted 2025 withholding, the government stepped back from filing (Direct File suspended after reaching under 0.5% of returns), and the 2026 paper-check phase-out pushed refunds into accounts while delaying unbanked filers 6 weeks or more.
Evidence: IRS filing season statistics, cumulative to 24 April 2026 versus 2025: 95.7M refunds (up 6.1%), $312.882B refunded (up 17.8%), average $3,268 versus $2,945 (up 11.0%). Tax Foundation: 2025 tax cuts were not reflected in withholding tables, leaving many over-withheld. IRS: tips deduction up to $25,000 and overtime up to $12,500 ($25,000 joint) for 2025-2028, phasing out above $150,000 ($300,000 joint); senior deduction $6,000; Child Tax Credit up to $2,200 with up to $1,700 refundable | National Taxpayer Advocate mid-year report (2026): average refund $3,275; about 65% of returns got refunds and about 98% of refunds went by direct deposit; more than 14 million returns suspended in processing; under Executive Order 14247 on electronic payments, unbanked, lower-income and some elderly taxpayers seeking paper checks met refund delays of 6 weeks or more, and the IRS issued about 4 million notices for missing or invalid direct-deposit details | Treasury (October 2025): Direct File returns were under 0.5% of about 146M tax year 2024 returns at a cost of at least $138 per accepted return; the IRS will suspend Direct File. TIGTA (19 March 2026): 32M eligible, 751,000 registered (up 78% from 423,000), 59% never filed through it; FY2025 cost $16.2M versus a $61.2M estimate. IRS Free File page (updated 21 October 2026): closed until January 2027, guided software at AGI $95,000 or less
Implication: The paper-check phase-out is the most bank-relevant change: refunds must land in an account, and the unbanked lower-income filers who cannot receive one are exactly the T17 audience a deposit bank could onboard; the refund jump itself may not repeat in 2027.
Caveats: Merges income-A finding 7 and income-B finding 7, with the EO 14247 paper-check fact added from the NTA page on verification. Cumulative IRS figures compare the same calendar point, not season totals. No Treasury, CBO or JCT estimate of the 2026 refund effect was found. Statistics are not cut by income, so the 'lower-income' wording of T17 is untested. Treasury is an interested party in the Direct File decision. Whether 2026 withholding catches up is unverified.

Claim: Capital One has no tax-filing, refund-advance or tax-partner product on record, and its early-paycheck feature excludes certain non-payroll and tax payments, so T17 passes the additive screen but starts with no filing relationship.
Evidence: Capital One 360 Checking page (fetched October 2026): early paycheck up to 2 days for direct deposits from an employer or other payer; certain non-payroll and tax payments are not eligible; no-fee overdraft requires deposits of at least $250 in two of the previous three months; the page does not mention tax filing or refunds | Capital One FY2025 10-K (full text searched by compiler): the string 'tax refund' does not appear; Capital One Shopping is the named consumer digital product in other non-interest income
Implication: T17 does not duplicate announced Capital One work, but the bank would build or buy the filing step from zero and would need to change its early-pay carve-out to make refund speed a feature.
Caveats: income-B finding 8. Absence inferred from one product page and one 10-K search; an internal project would not appear. Whether federal refunds are among the excluded payments is unclear from the wording. Card-side tax promotions were not checked.

Claim: Tax-calendar liquidity candidate: under 2026 IRS rules supplemental wages are withheld at a flat 22% up to $1M a year (37% above, regardless of Form W-4), and filers whose prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000 must pay 110% of prior-year tax to reach the estimated-tax safe harbour, so a bonus or vest can leave a predictable gap; no bank-specific rule or edge was found.
Evidence: IRS Publication 15 (2026): supplemental wage withholding remains 22% (37% on the excess over $1 million in the calendar year, applied without regard to Form W-4) because P.L. 119-21 permanently extended the 2017 individual rates; supplemental wages include bonuses and commissions | IRS Publication 505 (2026): if 2025 AGI was more than $150,000 ($75,000 married filing separately), substitute 110% for 100% in the prior-year safe-harbour test | IRS Tax Topic 306 (updated 24 September 2026): penalty generally avoided if tax owed after withholding is under $1,000 or payments reach 90% of current-year or 100% of prior-year tax, with special rules for higher-income filers | RSU and sell-to-cover mechanics are not described in the Publication 15 text read
Implication: The mechanism is current law, but it is a planning task that advisers, payroll and brokers already handle, it sits outside the Debit-Primary and Young Consumer focus, and no regulatory barrier or bank-only edge appeared.
Caveats: income-B finding 9. Mechanism only: no source sizes the affected population or measures take-up of a pre-funding product. That 22% sits below many such households' marginal rate is inference; rate schedules were not fetched. Lending, UDAAP or fiduciary issues for such a product were not researched. Direction is relative to the white-space proposition for this candidate.

Claim: JPMorgan Chase Institute account data and the Census SIPP 2021-2022 panel show that low-wage workers' monthly earnings swing mostly because employers change hours, not because workers change jobs.
Evidence: JPMCI (Chase checking and payroll records): the typical hourly worker's month-to-month earnings change is 9%, and 1 month in 4 brings a swing of at least 21% | Same source: take-home pay changes in 7 of every 10 months even within one job; employer-driven hours changes account for roughly half of earnings instability | Census SIPP 2021-2022 (Hamilton Project): coefficient of variation of monthly earnings 84% in the lowest quintile versus 41% in the highest; lowest quintile averages 5.5 zero-earnings months a year versus 1.2
Implication: The volatility a smoothing product would address is documented in administrative bank data and is employer-caused, which makes it structural for hourly Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Corpus finding 1 (corpus row 1). JPMCI covers Chase accounts and excludes the unbanked and cash-paid. SIPP earnings are self-reported. Compiler spot-check 2026-10-26: JPMCI page confirms 9%, 21%, 7 in 10 months and roughly half (pass).

Claim: In the Fed's SHED 2024 wave, 41% of adults who did any gig work reported variable income against 26% of non-gig adults, and 19% of adults earning under $25,000 struggled to pay bills because of income variation.
Evidence: SHED 2024: 29% of adults reported income that varied at least occasionally; 28% of employees, 59% of the self-employed | 41% of adults who did any gig work reported variable income versus 26% of non-gig adults | 11% struggled to pay bills because income varied; 19% under $25,000 versus 3% at $100,000 or more; 49% of gig workers wished their pay were more consistent, 61% among app-coordinated platform workers
Implication: Hardship concentrates under $25,000, pointing a smoothing offer at Debit-Primary Spenders; 'wish pay were more consistent' is a want, not a willingness to pay.
Caveats: Corpus finding 2 (corpus row 4). Self-reported survey. One wave older than SHED 2025 in income-01. Not spot-checked this pass.

Claim: For thin-file, debit-primary households the deposit account is close to the only relationship that generates data: in the 2022 SCF only 34% of the bottom half of the income distribution held any stock against 98.6% of all families holding a transaction account.
Evidence: Fed SCF 2022: 34% of the bottom half of the income distribution hold any stock; 98.6% of all families hold a transaction account | FinRegLab (July 2025): cash-flow-inclusive ML models raised approvals by roughly 4% at mainstream thresholds; data limits made effects on thin-file consumers hard to evaluate
Implication: The bank that holds the deposit account sees the only underwriting-grade signal for Debit-Primary Spenders, which supports the 'underwritten on earnings data' half of T02, though the measured lift is small and untested for thin files.
Caveats: Corpus finding 11 (corpus row 33). The link between the two sources is a corpus inference. The 4% lift is not shown for thin files. Not spot-checked this pass.

Claim: In SHED 2024, 20% of adults did some gig work in the prior month but only 21% of those called it their main job, so gig-as-primary-income is a low single-digit share of adults.
Evidence: SHED 2024: 20% of adults did gig work in the prior month; 21% of them called it their main job; 51% held a separate non-gig primary job | Activity: 13% selling items, 9% short-term tasks, 4% app-coordinated platform tasks; 26% among ages 18-29 and 24% among Hispanic adults | NBER (Garin, Jackson, Koustas and Miller, 2023, IRS records): at least 5 million individuals received platform gig information returns by 2021, nearly all from transportation platforms
Implication: A bank embedded in earning platforms reaches a wide but mostly part-time, transport-concentrated, Young Consumer-skewed base; few households depend on one platform.
Caveats: Corpus finding 3 (corpus row 6). SHED gig definition is broad and self-classified. Compiler spot-check 2026-10-26: Fed page confirms 20%, 21%, 51%, 13%, 9%, 4%, 26% and 24% (pass). Corpus finding 4 (BLS CWS) is merged into income-01.

Claim: About 104 million taxpayers (63%) of 165 million returns received a refund averaging $3,167 in FY2025, and JPMorgan Chase Institute found refund day is the peak cash-flow day of the year for 29% of refund-receiving Chase families.
Evidence: National Taxpayer Advocate 2025 Annual Report (released January 2026): of 165M returns, about 104M taxpayers (63%) received a refund averaging $3,167 | IRS SOI Data Book FY2025: 116.9M individual refunds totalling $516.4B; 22.2M included a refundable EITC and 14.0M a refundable CTC | JPMCI (March 2020, Chase accounts 2015-2017): refund day is the highest cash-flow day for 29% of refund-receiving families, averaging $3,602; spending rises 119% that day
Implication: The refund is a large, dated lump sum that reaches most filers and lands in deposit accounts, supporting the 'largest cash event' premise, especially for EITC and CTC households.
Caveats: Corpus finding 7 (corpus row 18). NTA and SOI are different series and not combined. Not cut by income, so 'lower-income' is untested. Compiler spot-check 2026-10-26: NTA page confirms 165M, 104M, 63%, $3,167 (pass).

Claim: TIGTA found that on average only 3% of eligible taxpayers use IRS Free File, and 59% of the 751,000 people who registered for Direct File in 2025 never submitted a return through it.
Evidence: TIGTA (30 September 2024), processing years 2020-2024: on average 3% of eligible taxpayers use Free File, about 3 million returns a year since 2003; paid advertising lapsed in 2015 | TIGTA Direct File report (19 March 2026): 59% of 751,000 registrants did not submit a return through it
Implication: A filing product cannot win on price, since free options go unused; the 'files' half of T17 needs a reason other than cost.
Caveats: Corpus finding 8 (corpus row 17). The 59% and 751,000 figures were re-confirmed this pass in the TIGTA 2026 PDF while verifying income-16. Does not say what the 97% use instead.

Claim: A Columbia analysis of the 2021 hybrid Child Tax Credit found monthly payments cut food insufficiency by at least 2.4 points with no effect on rent arrears, while the lump sum cut the chance of being behind on rent by at least 1.2 points with no effect on food insufficiency.
Evidence: Columbia CPSP, Census Household Pulse data on the 2021 CTC (six monthly advances then a lump sum at 2022 filing), AEA Papers and Proceedings | Monthly: food insufficiency down at least 2.4 points (about 20%), no effect on rent arrears | Lump sum: behind-on-rent down at least 1.2 points (about 10%), no effect on food insufficiency
Implication: Lump-sum and monthly delivery solve different problems, so refund planning has a use for lumpy debts but not recurring costs; the audience skews to Young Consumers with children.
Caveats: Corpus finding 9 (corpus row 14). Self-reported hardship; one non-repeated natural experiment. Not spot-checked this pass.

Claim: Territory Candidate (tax-calendar liquidity for equity- and bonus-paid earners above $150,000 AGI): households with prior-year AGI above $150,000 paid in bonuses, RSUs or K-1 distributions face a forecastable underwithholding gap at each vest or payout, and fewer than half would use a bank product that pre-funds or schedules the tax liability if one were offered.
Evidence: IRS Publication 15 (2026): supplemental wages withheld at a flat 22% up to $1M while top marginal rates are 32-37% before state tax; no independently sourced estimate of the affected population or dollars (corpus row 31) | National Taxpayer Advocate Purple Book (December 2024): quarterly estimated payment dates; safe harbour rises to 110% of prior-year tax above $150,000 AGI (corpus row 44) | BLS Employee Benefits (March 2025): 58% of management and professional workers have access to a nonproduction bonus versus 37% of service workers; NCEO estimates 11.8M employees hold equity compensation outside ESOPs (advocacy source) (corpus row 43) | Counter: SHED 2024 shows 75% of adults at $100,000 or more hold a three-month cushion (corpus row 46)
Implication: A mechanism with a dated statutory basis but an unmeasured population, outside the Debit-Primary and Young Consumer focus; a candidate to test, not to rank.
Caveats: Corpus finding 13. Mechanism is current law (re-confirmed in income-18); prevalence is unsourced and the willingness-to-use threshold is unmeasured. NCEO is an advocacy body. Wealth advisers already serve the gap. Verdict in income-notes.md.

Claim: The tax refund is a large annual cash event (the IRS issued 99.1 million refunds totalling $324.757 billion, average $3,276, in the 2026 season through 8 May), and venture money is building embedded filing (april, $38M round reported July 2025) sold through partners rather than direct to consumers.
Evidence: IRS filing-season statistics, cumulative to 8 May 2026 against the same point in 2025: refunds 99,138,000 (up 6.0% from 93,569,000); amount refunded $324.757B (up 18.1% from $274.979B); average refund $3,276 (up 11.5% from $2,939); current-year returns only | JPMorgan Chase Institute, Tax Refunds and Household Spending (March 2020, data 2015-2017): 78% of the sample received a refund, average $3,602 (about six weeks of take-home pay); for 29% of refund recipients the refund day was the year's largest positive cash-flow day | JPMorgan Chase Institute, Tax Time FY22 (February 2022): before the pandemic a refund was the single largest cash infusion of the year for 40% of families; earliest filers had cash balances 61% lower and incomes 28% lower than later filers. The two JPMC shares (29% and 40%) differ and the pages do not reconcile them | april: headline says $30M Series A, body says $38M Series B led by QED Investors, $78M total (FinancialIT, 23 July 2025); company claims 50+ partners, hundreds of thousands of 2024 returns, median 22 minutes to file, over 98% refund deposit rate at partners; named partners Carry and Gusto
Implication: The refund flow is large and lands hardest on low-balance early filers (Debit-Primary Spenders), supporting the size half of T17; the venture model is B2B2C embedding, so the bank may be a partner channel rather than the owner of the tax moment.
Caveats: Merged from T14-A finding 5 and T14-B finding 6. The IRS dollar figure is a transfer of the customer's own money, not a revenue pool; the 18.1% rise reflects 2025 tax-law changes not researched here. JPMC figures are pre-pandemic and pre-TCJA; the 29% and 40% shares conflict and are kept with their URLs. april's numbers are company claims in a funding article, with a series and amount conflict between headline and body. Seasonal, once-a-year event. Refund-advance products and prices of Intuit, H&R Block and banks were not verified, so neither white space nor saturation is established.

Claim: Robinhood, SoFi and Cash App already run zero-commission investing on-ramps at mass scale inside multi-product apps: Robinhood reported 27.0 million Funded Customers at December 31, 2025 with an IRA match, and SoFi counted 3.24 million Invest products among 13.6 million members.
Evidence: Robinhood FY2025 10-K key metrics: Funded Customers 25.2M (2024) to 27.0M (2025); Total Platform Assets $192.9B to $322.1B; Net Deposits $68.1B; ARPU $171; Gold Subscribers 2.64M to 4.18M (+58%). Roll-forward: 2.5M new, 0.4M resurrected, 0.6M acquired, 1.7M churned in 2025 | Robinhood Item 1: IRA contributions earn a company match subject to a five-year holding period, 3% for Gold; instant IRA deposits up to $1,000; Robinhood Strategies at 0.25% capped at $250 a year for Gold; the company says millions of its customers entered the financial markets for the first time on Robinhood (no count given) | SoFi FY2025 10-K: over 13.6 million members (+35%); Invest products 3,244,143 (2024: 2,525,059; +28%); Money products 6,791,108 | Block FY2025 10-K: Cash App had 59 million monthly transacting actives in the US in December 2025; Cash App Investing LLC is an SEC-registered, FINRA-member broker-dealer; no investing customer count disclosed
Implication: The saver-to-investor step is not unserved for the mass market; a bank entering T05 faces free, scaled on-ramps that are adding retirement, managed accounts and banking, so for Young Consumers the bank route is a feature inside its own account (adjacency), not a new category.
Caveats: Company disclosures written for investors. A Funded Customer meets a balance or activity test and is not an investor with a meaningful balance; no median balance is disclosed. SoFi product counts are not unique people and SoFi skews prime. Cash App investing users are not disclosed, so reach into Debit-Primary Spenders is unshown. Robinhood retirement match dollars and retirement assets were not in the 10-K text; the earnings release returned 403 to the researcher. Merged from independence-A findings 1 and 2. Stats verified in local extracts of the filings (output/independence/_pdf/); URLs re-fetched and confirmed live this pass.

Claim: Wealthfront's first 10-K (fiscal year to January 31, 2026) reports $94.1 billion of platform assets and 1.417 million funded clients, with cash management supplying about 74% of revenue through sweeps to program banks, and states that Wealthfront is not a bank.
Evidence: Key business metrics FY2026 vs FY2025: platform assets $94,106M vs $80,175M (+17%), of which cash management $45,361M and investment advisory $48,745M; net deposits $6,659M vs $17,714M (-62%); funded clients 1,417 thousand vs 1,212 thousand (+17%). Platform assets per funded client is about $66,000 (compiler arithmetic: $94,106M / 1.417M) | Cash management was approximately 74% (FY2026) and 75% (FY2025) of total revenue; annualised cash management fee rate fell from 0.64% to 0.62% | Founded 2008, automated investing launched 2011; the platform targets digital natives born after 1980; Wealthfront says it is not a bank and relies on program banks for deposits
Implication: The one robo-advisor at scale monetises mainly through deposits swept to banks, which suggests save-then-invest is a deposit-franchise business a bank could run itself, but its clients hold far more than a first-wealth Debit-Primary Spender.
Caveats: Company disclosure from a newly public company. Net deposits fell 62% in the year, so asset growth leaned on markets; the cash share is rate-sensitive. The 10-K text searched gives no Form ADV AUM, so the earlier corpus comparison of platform assets with advisory AUM is not resolved. Betterment, the other large robo-advisor, has no primary AUM record (see gaps). Stats verified in the local extract; URL live.

Claim: The downmarket micro-investing subscription models failed to reach a venture-scale exit: Stash fell from 2 million subscribers in 2022 to over 1.3 million in 2024 and agreed in February 2026 to a Grab deal at a US$425 million enterprise value against a $1.4 billion 2021 valuation, and Acorns' SPAC merger at about $2.2 billion was mutually terminated in January 2022.
Evidence: Fortune (Dec 4, 2024): Stash cut 40% of about 220 staff in October 2024 after 25% (about 80 people) in March 2024; more than 1.3 million subscribers, down from 2 million in 2022; last valuation $1.4 billion (2021); an eToro offer reportedly below that valuation was rejected | Stash press page: May 12, 2025 headline announces a $146M Series H with $4.3B under management. Fintech News Singapore (Feb 12, 2026): Grab takes an initial 50.1% stake at a US$425M enterprise value, over one million US subscribers, more than US$5B assets, adjusted-EBITDA and cash-flow positive; close expected Q3 2026 | Acorns: Pioneer Merger Corp. 8-K exhibit (May 2021) cites 4+ million subscribers, an expected 10 million by 2025, and about $2.2 billion fully diluted equity value; Pioneer's 8-K (event date January 15, 2022) reports a Termination Fee Agreement dated January 3, 2022 under which Acorns pays $17.5 million monthly through December 15, 2022 plus $15 million if Pioneer redeems its public shares; no reason stated | Acorns pricing page: $4, $8 and $12 monthly tiers; 1% (Silver) or 3% (Gold) first-year IRA match; over 16 million all-time customers and over $33 billion invested since inception as of 8/26/2026; no paying-subscriber count
Implication: A small-balance subscription on-ramp for Debit-Primary Spenders has not produced a venture-scale company on its own, which weakens T05 as a standalone business while leaving it open as a retention feature inside a bank.
Caveats: Stash facts are trade press (Fortune, Fintech News Singapore) used as the primary record of the layoffs and the Grab deal, plus the company's own press headline; no filing for the Grab deal was read. $425M is enterprise value for an initial 50.1% stake. Acorns is private; the 2021-2022 SPAC filings are the last filed disclosure; the 10 million target was a projection and no current subscriber count exists, so a miss is inferred from absence. Correction this pass: the $450M figure in the SPAC exhibit is projected cash at closing, not the PIPE size; it was removed.

Claim: Bank attempts at a retail investing on-ramp were sold or are undisclosed: Capital One sold its online retail brokerage in 2018, Goldman moved Marcus Invest accounts to Betterment in 2024 after the product never gained much traction, and Bank of America's FY2025 10-K does not mention Merrill Edge.
Evidence: Capital One FY2018 10-K: restructuring included the decision to sell the online retail brokerage business in the first quarter of 2018; on sale it transferred about $1.4 billion of customer deposits and an equal cash amount to the purchaser; no reason given | Financial Planning (April 22, 2024): Marcus Invest clients and assets (not technology or staff) move to Betterment; price undisclosed and expected to be immaterial; more than 10,000 accounts opened in the first months after the 2021 launch, mostly existing Goldman clients; Goldman's president said it was a lot harder than expected | Goldman 8-K (January 2026): the Apple Card program moves to an unnamed new issuer over about 24 months, with a $2.48 billion reserve release offset by a $2.26 billion net-revenue reduction (+$0.46 EPS); Goldman says it continues to narrow its consumer focus | Bank of America FY2025 10-K: no occurrence of 'Merrill Edge' or 'self-directed'; Merrill appears only as Merrill Wealth Management, which serves clients with over $250,000 investable
Implication: No bank offers a proof point for a mass-market investing on-ramp, and Capital One's own exit means T05 would need a partner, a new broker-dealer or a non-securities model.
Caveats: Pointer correction carried from independence-A: Marcus Invest was sold to Betterment (accounts transferred), not shut; the Goldman side rests on trade press (Financial Planning) as the primary record of the event, and Betterment's notice returned 404. Absence of Merrill Edge from one 10-K is not evidence it is small. Apple Card is a card programme, included only for the pattern of consumer retreat. The Capital One 2018 and Bank of America 10-K pages exceed the fetch tool's 10MB limit; both were verified against the local extracts saved by the researcher (fiscal years confirmed on the cover).

Claim: As of October 2026 a national bank cannot run a mass-market retail investing on-ramp that is not a brokerage through a collective fund: 12 CFR 9.18 limits bank collective funds to fiduciary accounts and tax-exempt employee-benefit trusts and bars advertising them, and Regulation R excuses broker registration only for trust and fiduciary, sweep, custody and nominal-fee referral activity.
Evidence: 12 CFR 9.18(a)(1): a fund maintained exclusively for money held as trustee, executor, administrator, guardian or custodian under a uniform gifts to minors act; (a)(2): funds of tax-exempt retirement and similar trusts; (b)(7): the bank may not advertise or publicize an (a)(1) fund except in advertising its general fiduciary services; (c)(2) mini-funds capped at $1,500,000 total assets and 100 participating accounts (eCFR as of 2026-10-20) | SEC Regulation R small entity compliance guide: trust and fiduciary exception requires the bank to be chiefly compensated by relationship compensation; networking exception allows unregistered employees only a nominal one-time referral fee (one standard is a flat $25 adjusted for inflation); sweep exception covers deposit funds invested in money market funds; custody exception allows order-taking for IRAs and employee-benefit plans as an accommodation
Implication: The 'not a brokerage' model in T05 has no wide legal route at a national bank; it survives only as custodial or fiduciary accounts (minors, IRAs), money-fund sweeps, or referral to a partner or affiliate broker-dealer, so a Debit-Primary on-ramp needs a registered broker-dealer or a partner.
Caveats: The SEC guide is a 2008-era compliance guide, not the current text of 17 CFR Part 247. State charters, other collective vehicles (401(k) collective investment trusts) and insurance-wrapper models were not examined. No OCC statement on retail use of 9.18 funds was found. Capital One's 2018 brokerage sale is in the bank-attempts row.

Claim: Under IRC 530A as implemented by IRS Notice 2025-68 and an April 6, 2026 Treasury release, every initial child 'Trump account' is opened by a Treasury-selected trustee (BNY as financial agent, Robinhood as brokerage and initial trustee), and any other bank can only become trustee of a later whole-balance rollover account.
Evidence: Notice 2025-68 A-3: the trustee must be a bank under section 408(n) or an IRS-approved nonbank trustee; Treasury will select one or more financial institutions as financial agent to serve as trustee of the initial accounts; rollover-account trustees are not subject to that selection. A-4: a rollover account can be set up only after Treasury or its agent creates the initial account, funded by a trustee-to-trustee transfer of the entire balance | Treasury release (April 6, 2026): BNY designated financial agent for the program; Robinhood will serve as brokerage and initial trustee | Account terms (Notice 2025-68): a $1,000 federal pilot contribution for U.S.-citizen children with an SSN born after December 31, 2024 and before January 1, 2029; other contributions capped at $5,000 a year for 2026 and 2027, indexed after; no contributions before July 4, 2026; growth-period investments limited to unleveraged index mutual funds or ETFs with fees at or below 0.1%; growth period ends January 1 of the year the child turns 18
Implication: A bank cannot originate the child account at the start of the first-wealth moment; its entry points are the competitive rollover-trustee role into a cheap index-fund menu and the parent's savings relationship around it, which is thin ground for a bank-owned T05 product for Young Consumers.
Caveats: The Notice PDF resolves but does not parse through the fetch tool; figures were verified against the local extract (output/independence/_pdf/n-25-68.txt). The statute text was not fetched (uscode.house.gov returned 404 to the researcher). Proposed or final regulations and post-launch status after July 4, 2026 were not read (trumpaccounts.gov returned 403). An unverified claim about trustee reporting on Form 5498-TA was removed this pass.

Claim: IRS Notice 2026-48 (August 7, 2026) sets a federal Saver's Match of up to 50% of $2,000 of qualified 2027 retirement contributions for filers under $35,500 (single) or $71,000 (joint) of MAGI, paid in 2028 into a registered non-Roth IRA or workplace plan, while 12 state auto-IRA programs held $2.90 billion across 1,194,337 funded accounts at February 28, 2026.
Evidence: Notice 2026-48: maximum MAGI for 2027 is $35,500 single, $53,250 head of household, $71,000 joint; the match is the applicable percentage of up to $2,000 of qualified contributions; it is claimed on Form 8880-A and paid to a traditional (non-Roth) IRA whose provider has registered with Treasury and the IRS for an IRA tracking number, or to a workplace plan; matches under $100 can be taken as a refundable credit; comments were due October 5, 2026 | IRS release IR-2026-89 (Aug 7, 2026): payments in 2028 for 2027 contributions; Executive Order 14403 (April 30, 2026) establishes TrumpIRA.gov, which Treasury plans to launch January 1, 2027, focused on workers without an employer plan | Georgetown CRI deck (12 reporting states, as of 2/28/2026): $2.90 billion assets, 1,194,337 funded accounts, 381,807 registered employers; the deck says about 70% of workers stay enrolled. About $2,430 per funded account (compiler arithmetic)
Implication: The match gives a deposit bank a concrete reason to offer an IRA to Debit-Primary Spenders under about $35,500, but the rail is open to any registered provider, worth at most $1,000 a year (compiler arithmetic) and paid a year late, and state programs show default enrolment, not a new bank model, is what moves small balances.
Caveats: Notice 2026-48 is a notice of intent to issue regulations, not a rule. The Notice and CRI PDFs resolve but do not parse through the fetch tool; figures verified against local extracts. Georgetown CRI advocates for state programs (interest flagged); its 70% figure is its own statement. Correction this pass: the researcher's '47% of private-sector workers lacked an employer plan in 2024' does not appear in the deck's extracted text and was removed. Whether a deposit (non-securities) IRA will be listed on TrumpIRA.gov is untested.

Claim: Consumer-facing cash-flow underwriting has been sold, repriced or turned into a vendor product: Petal was agreed to be sold to Empower in April 2024 after never getting the traction it needed, Nova Credit raised at $200 million in 2023 after $300 million in 2020, Prism Data raised a $20 million Series A in October 2026 selling to lenders, and FICO made a Plaid-fed cash-flow UltraFICO score generally available on May 20, 2026.
Evidence: Petal: Coverager reports Empower agreeing to acquire Petal (price not stated); nearly 400,000 consumers approved since 2018 for a WebBank-issued card, most with thin or no files, underwritten on open-banking cash-flow data. Fintech Nexus (April 9, 2024): the card never received the traction it needed; reported struggling and seeking a buyer in November 2023; Prism Data spun off in May 2023 | Nova Credit (Forbes Colombia reprint, Feb 2025): $50M at a $300M valuation in 2020, $45M at $200M in 2023 (a down round); revenue about $2M pre-pandemic, about $500K after banks cut Credit Passport use, about $25M in 2024 with Credit Passport about half of sales | Prism Data (FF News, October 19, 2026): $20M Series A led by Story Ventures; over $25M raised in total; monthly API volume up more than 100x in two years; claims three of the five largest US fintech lenders and six of the ten largest digital banks as clients | FICO release (May 20, 2026, via Seeking Alpha mirror): UltraFICO uses consumer-permissioned cash-flow data from Plaid's network of more than 12,000 institutions on the FICO scale, sold through Plaid Check; FICO reports a 7% relative approval increase with no incremental risk and higher scores for 79% of non-prime applicants with positive balances. FHFA (page updated Oct 2, 2026): VantageScore 4.0 accepted from all approved lenders since September 9, 2026; FICO 10T not currently eligible for delivery; the page does not mention cash-flow data
Implication: The value in cash-flow underwriting has moved to a B2B and score-vendor layer any lender can buy, so a bank's T07 edge for thin-file Debit-Primary Spenders would have to come from its own deposit data and credit box, not from the method.
Caveats: Merged from independence-A finding 6 and independence-B finding 7. Petal and Prism facts are trade press used as the primary record of the deal and round; Nova Credit figures come from one Forbes profile (Spanish reprint) and are unaudited; FICO performance figures are the company's own analyses, and the release was read through a Seeking Alpha mirror because investors.fico.com returned 403 to the researcher. FHFA decisions concern mortgage delivery, not card underwriting. Funding rounds show investor belief, not demand.

Claim: Upstart's FY2025 10-K reports $11.0 billion of transaction volume across 1,497,149 loans in 2025, up from $4.6 billion across 437,659 loans in 2023, through more than 100 lending partners whose own hard credit criteria are applied before Upstart's model and cause the majority of denials.
Evidence: Key metrics: transaction volume $4,645,669K (2023), $5,930,029K (2024), $11,003,995K (2025); loans 437,659 / 697,092 / 1,497,149; conversion rate 9.8% / 15.1% / 19.4%; 91% of 2025 loans fully automated; adjusted EBITDA -$17.2M (2023) to $230.5M (2025) | Item 1: personal-loan model grew from 23 variables (2014) to over 2,500 (2025), including bank account transactions, trained on nearly 104 million repayment events; more than 100 lending partners at December 31, 2025 | Upstart applies lenders' hard criteria (minimum credit scores, loan amounts, maximum debt-to-income) before its model, and the majority of denials are due to those criteria; no figure is given for approvals a bureau model would have declined
Implication: Behavioural underwriting already runs at consumer scale, but lender-set score cut-offs gate who reaches the model, so T07's 'open credit to the excluded' is narrower than written: the gate is the credit box, not the data.
Caveats: Company disclosure. Conversion rate was redefined in Q4 2025 with prior periods recast. 2022 performance and the 2022-2023 volume collapse are not in the FY2025 table (see gaps). Upstart serves mostly prime and near-prime borrowers; thin-file share not disclosed. Stats verified in local extract; URL live.

Claim: Chime's FY2025 10-K reports 9.5 million Active Members served with fee-free secured credit cards and deposit-based loan pre-approval, while the OCC's Project REACh (launched July 10, 2020) claimed in May 2024 only that more than 100,000 credit invisibles had gained access to credit, with no cash-flow underwriting results published.
Evidence: Chime 10-K: 9.5 million Active Members at December 31, 2025, the majority using Chime as primary financial relationship; Chime Card and Credit Builder are secured Visa cards with no annual, late or application fees and no interest on missed payments; members receiving direct deposit may be pre-approved for Instant Loans; FICO Score tracking via Experian | OCC release 2020-89 (July 10, 2020): Project REACh launched; Acting Comptroller Brooks said almost 50 million Americans have no credit score; no mention of cash-flow underwriting | OCC release 2024-55 (May 29, 2024): Acting Comptroller Hsu said more than 100,000 credit invisibles now have access to credit through Project REACh; no mention of cash-flow underwriting; no results report found
Implication: The thin-file Debit-Primary segment is already served at scale with secured cards and deposit-linked pre-approval, so T07's white space shrinks to unsecured credit for people with deposit history and no score, where the public programme evidence is one headline count.
Caveats: Chime does not disclose Credit Builder cardholder counts or loss data in the text read. The OCC 100,000 figure has no definition or method. Secured cards build a file but do not extend unsecured credit. Stats verified in local extract (Chime) and live pages (OCC).

Claim: In 2023 the 13 card networks that processed US debit and general-use prepaid transactions collected $12.95 billion in network fees, an average of $0.129 a transaction, of which acquirers and merchants paid $8.40 billion and issuers $4.54 billion.
Evidence: Fed Regulation II report on 2023 data, published December 2025: 100.70 billion debit and general-use prepaid transactions worth $4,658.42 billion; network fees to all parties $12.95 billion (from $11.49 billion in 2021); average $0.129 a transaction ($0.125 in 2021, $0.098 in 2011), about 0.28 percent of value | By payer: acquirers and merchants $8.40 billion ($0.083 a transaction), issuers $4.54 billion ($0.045). By network type: dual-message $10.95 billion ($0.152 a transaction), single-message $2.00 billion ($0.069) | Networks paid back incentives of $1.98 billion to issuers and $3.71 billion to acquirers and merchants. Compiler arithmetic: net of incentives issuers paid $2.56 billion and acquirers $4.69 billion, total $7.25 billion, about $0.072 a transaction | The report names no network and does not say whether three-party transactions are inside the totals
Implication: The network-fee pool the hypothesis names is real (about 13 cents a transaction gross, about 7 cents net of incentives) but an issuer that owns its network saves only the issuer-side share and earns the acquirer-side share from merchants, so the prize is a merchant-paid revenue line, not a consumer benefit.
Caveats: Edge: none (sizes the pool). The report is the December 2025 release on 2023 data, not a 2023 publication; the October 2023 release covered 2021 data. Net-of-incentive figures are compiler arithmetic. Three-party systems are not payment card networks under Reg II Commentary 2(m)-2 (independence-109), so Discover's own-issued debit may sit outside these totals. Averages mix point-of-sale debit and prepaid.

Claim: In 2023 issuers covered by the Regulation II cap received an average $0.23 interchange per debit transaction and paid $0.016 in network fees, while exempt issuers received $0.52 and paid $0.096.
Evidence: Fed report on 2023 data: covered transactions 61.67 billion, interchange $14.02 billion, average $0.23; exempt transactions 39.02 billion, interchange $20.10 billion, average $0.52; total interchange $34.12 billion. The exempt average rose from $0.43 at the 2011 start to $0.52 by 2021 and held in 2023 | Network fees paid by issuers: covered $0.99 billion ($0.016 a transaction); exempt $3.55 billion ($0.096). The cap allowed $0.245 (dual-message) and $0.243 (single-message) on the average covered transaction including the 1 cent fraud adjustment | Compiler arithmetic: gross gap 0.52 - 0.23 = about 29 cents; net of issuer network fees 0.424 - 0.214 = about 21 cents. The covered issuer's $0.016 network fee on the report's $48.59 average covered ticket is about 3.3 bps, the most a covered issuer saves by not paying Visa or Mastercard
Implication: The value in owning the network is mostly the uncapped issuer rate, worth tens of cents a transaction, not the 1.6 cents of issuer-side network fee avoided; that reframes P01 from fee capture to cap exit.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Exempt issuers are institutions under $10 billion of assets on Visa and Mastercard exempt rate cards, so the $0.52 shows what four-party rails pay small issuers, not what a three-party operator can charge. Incentives are bilateral and not allocated here. Gap figures are compiler arithmetic.

Claim: The Federal Reserve's per-network table labelled 2024 shows debit on the Discover network averaging $0.83 interchange a transaction (1.22 percent of value, $68.57 average ticket), with all of it in the exempt column, against $0.23 (0.47 percent) for covered issuers across all networks.
Evidence: Fed average interchange by network, 2024 (data revised as of 2025-06-10): Discover exempt 100.0 percent of transactions, $68.57 average value, $0.83 fee, 1.22 percent; all networks covered $48.95 average value, $0.23, 0.47 percent; Visa covered $0.22 (0.44 percent); Mastercard covered $0.24 (0.49 percent); PULSE all issuers $0.27 (0.63 percent); all networks exempt $0.51 (1.21 percent) | Compiler arithmetic, unlike tickets: 0.83 - 0.23 = 60 cents; 1.22 - 0.47 = 75 bps | Compiler arithmetic, like-for-like at Discover's $68.57 ticket: the current cap allows 21 cents + 5 bps x $68.57 + 1 cent = about 25.4 cents (0.37 percent), so the gap is about 58 cents or about 85 bps a transaction
Implication: The only primary per-network figure puts the three-party debit edge at roughly 58 to 60 cents, or 75 to 85 bps, a transaction above the capped rate, which is the size of the prize Capital One moved its debit base to reach.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. The $0.83 and $68.57 are printed on the Fed page; only the 60 cent, 75 bps and 85 bps gaps are compiler arithmetic. The Discover rate reflects Discover Bank's own debit mix before the migration, not Capital One's reissued base, and Capital One told the OCC it did not intend to raise network fees (independence-110). The page does not explain why Discover is wholly exempt; the three-party exemption is the likely reason but the page does not say so. The Discover covered row has 0.0 percent share and is immaterial.

Claim: Visa and Mastercard do not disclose US debit revenue or fee per transaction; the nearest figure is the Justice Department's allegation that Visa charges over $7 billion a year in network fees on US debit, earning $5.6 billion net, on 57.6 billion debit transactions worth $2.8 trillion in 2023.
Evidence: DOJ v. Visa complaint (S.D.N.Y., filed 2024-09-24): Visa runs more than 60 percent of US debit transactions, is front-of-card on over 70 percent of debit payment volume (Mastercard around 25 percent), charges over $7 billion in network fees on US debit annually earning $5.6 billion net revenue, and routed 57.6 billion debit transactions worth $2.8 trillion in 2023 | Compiler arithmetic: $7 billion / 57.6 billion = about 12 cents a transaction gross; $5.6 billion / 57.6 billion = about 9.7 cents net, close to the Fed's all-network 12.9 cent average (independence-101) | Visa FY2025 10-K: US consumer debit volume $3,213 billion (12 months to 2025-06-30, includes prepaid and Interlink); net revenue $40,000 million after $15,751 million of client incentives; no US debit revenue line. The 10-K records that on 2025-06-23 the court denied Visa's motion to dismiss | Mastercard FY2025 10-K: net revenue $32,791 million; payment network revenue $19,476 million; global consumer debit and prepaid volume $5,349 billion; no US debit revenue or volume
Implication: The Visa debit pool a bank could displace on its own cards is estimable at about 10 to 12 cents a transaction but is not disclosed, and it is Visa's revenue, so moving off Visa saves the issuer only its own fee share and shifts the rest to the bank's network.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Visa. The $7 billion and $5.6 billion are allegations in a pending case, not findings; DOJ is a party. Per-transaction figures are compiler arithmetic. Visa and Mastercard have an interest in keeping debit unit economics private while the case runs. The complaint was fetched from justice.gov in this pass; the researcher's Courthouse News mirror was dropped.

Claim: Debit outside Visa and Mastercard has stayed small: the other networks together carry about 11 percent of US debit transactions, Discover carried 6 percent of debit and prepaid purchase volume in 2023 after 18 years owning PULSE, and American Express issued its first proprietary debit card only in 2021.
Evidence: DOJ complaint (2024): PIN networks collectively represent approximately 11 percent of all debit transactions and about 5 percent of card-not-present debit; Visa's merchant and acquirer contracts cover over 75 percent of its debit volume | Capital One merger prospectus (424B3, 2025-01-06), citing Nilson Report data: Visa and Mastercard 85 percent of 2023 US debit and prepaid general-purpose purchase volume; Discover 6 percent | Fed approval order (2025-04-18) footnote 46: Capital One's post-merger share of debit-card network purchase volume no more than 6.9 percent. OCC letter: Capital One represented the combined bank at 6.5 percent of US debit transaction volume | Discover 2007 information statement: PULSE acquired 2005; PULSE transactions 1.9 billion in fiscal 2006. American Express FY2021 10-K: introduced its first-ever proprietary debit card in 2021 with a business checking product
Implication: Two decades of Discover ownership of PULSE and a debit stack produced a single-digit share, so the owned network's position in debit rests on Capital One's own migrated base, not on winning other issuers.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Visa and Mastercard (scale and contracts). The 11 percent figure is a DOJ allegation; the 6 percent is Capital One's use of Nilson data in a deal document. The Amex line shows only that its first proprietary debit card exists, not that earlier attempts failed. No Fed series gives routing shares by network.

Claim: Capital One announced in February 2024 network synergies of $1.2 billion in 2027 from moving its debit and selected credit purchase volume, about $175 billion, to the Discover network, and said the significant majority of the modelled synergies are on the debit side.
Evidence: Deal press release (2024-02-20): network synergies of $1.2 billion in 2027, driven by adding Capital One debit purchase volume and selected credit card purchase volume to the Discover network, alongside $1.5 billion of expense synergies | Deal call (2024-02-20): migration to drive $175 billion of purchase volume to the Discover network by 2027, resulting in $1.2 billion of synergies; Capital One will move its entire debit card business; the significant majority of the modelled network synergies are on the debit side; the deal adds the vertical integration benefits of the debit network to Consumer Banking | Compiler arithmetic: $1.2 billion / $175 billion = about 69 bps on mixed credit and debit volume, in the same range as the 75 to 85 bps Fed-table gap (independence-103)
Implication: The bank's own plan figure confirms the edge is worth on the order of a billion dollars a year at Capital One's scale, but it mixes debit and credit and no filing splits them.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. A modelled target by the party that wanted the deal seen as valuable; gross of any lost Visa or Mastercard incentives and of network investment. The 69 bps is compiler arithmetic on a figure that mixes credit and debit, so it cannot be read as a debit rate.

Claim: By Q3 2026 Capital One had substantially completed reissuing its debit cards onto the Global Payment Network, network volume reached $554.9 billion in nine months of 2026, and Consumer Banking non-interest income rose to $769 million a quarter from $695 million for all of 2024, but no filing isolates the debit or network component.
Evidence: FY2025 10-K: reissuance of legacy Capital One customer debit cards onto the Global Payment Network substantially completed; Global Payment Network volume $401,775 million for 2025 (from the 2025-05-18 close) | Quarterly Global Payment Network volume: $174,332 million (Q1 2026), $189,612 million (Q2 2026), $190,934 million (Q3 2026); $554,878 million for nine months of 2026 | Consumer Banking non-interest income: $695 million (2024), $1,675 million (2025); quarterly $475 million (Q3 2025), $623 million (Q4 2025), $683 million (Q1 2026), $778 million (Q2 2026), $769 million (Q3 2026). The Q1 and Q2 2026 10-Qs attribute the rise to the addition of the Global Payment Network and the reissuance of legacy debit cards, not split | Consumer Banking discount and interchange fees, net: $1,035 million (2025); $538 million (Q2 2026)
Implication: The uplift is visible at segment level and is consistent with the plan, but it bundles acquired Discover network revenue with debit economics, so the debit edge is shown to be in motion inside Capital One without being measurable from outside.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Q3 2026 figures are from the earnings financial supplement (Exhibit 99.2), preliminary; WebFetch showed only part of it and the figures were verified against the local extract. Segment composition changed with the acquisition. The 25 million migrated debit card count is trade press (PaymentsJournal, 2026-07-22) and is not cited. The Q1 and Q2 2026 call transcripts, which secondary summaries say put debit synergies fully in run-rate, were not obtained from a primary source.

Claim: In 2024 PULSE carried 9.6 billion transactions and $328.3 billion of volume and earned $345 million of transaction processing revenue, about 3.6 cents a transaction, and Discover's whole Payment Services segment earned $517 million before tax.
Evidence: Discover FY2024 10-K: PULSE network volume $328,295 million (2023 $285,616 million); PULSE transactions 9,609 million (2023 7,705 million); PULSE transaction processing revenue $345 million (2023 $303 million); Payment Services other income $712 million and pre-tax income $517 million (2023 $450 million and $256 million) | Compiler arithmetic: $345 million / 9,609 million = about 3.6 cents a transaction, which includes ATM and non-purchase activity | The 10-K says Visa and Mastercard arrangements with some merchants and acquirers have the effect of discouraging routing of debit to PULSE; the largest merchant was about 16 percent of PULSE volume | Discover FY2013 10-K: PULSE transaction processing revenue $180 million (FY2011), $218 million (FY2012), $192 million (CY2013), with Reg II-era merchant rerouting and lower rates cited
Implication: PULSE's own economics are a few cents a transaction on a PIN rail, so any large value in P01 comes from the cap-exempt Discover front-of-card issuer rate on Capital One's own cards, not from the network Capital One bought.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Discover's own filings; PULSE revenue per transaction mixes ATM, PIN and other activity. The 2023 and 2024 Payment Services income includes a legal settlement the 10-K does not quantify, so the run-rate is lower.

Claim: Under Regulation II the cap of 21 cents plus 5 bps plus a 1 cent fraud adjustment applies only to an interchange fee set by a payment card network, and the Official Commentary says a three-party system whose operator is also the issuer is not a payment card network for those transactions.
Evidence: 12 CFR 235.3(b): cap of 21 cents plus 5 bps of value; 235.4 adds up to 1 cent for fraud prevention (eCFR, current text) | Commentary 2(m)-2: in a three-party system the system operator is also the issuer, holds the cardholder's funds and authorizes and settles itself; because it does not network multiple issuers or route, it is not a payment card network for those transactions | Commentary 2(j)-2: fees a network charges issuers and acquirers for its own services are not interchange transaction fees, so four-party network fees sit outside the cap | 235.7(a): issuers and networks may not restrict a debit transaction to fewer than two unaffiliated networks; Commentary 7(a)-7 allows two affiliated networks on a card if at least two networks for each transaction are unaffiliated
Implication: The first kill limb fails on the current text: the owned network's issuer-side and network-side fees are not folded into a capped interchange, because the cap never attaches to a three-party transaction.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Whether Capital One debit on the Discover network is three-party when the issuing bank (CONA) and the network operator are separate subsidiaries is not addressed in the rule text; the Fed order and the 10-K treat it as exempt (independence-110, independence-111). Whether 235.7(a) requires a second unaffiliated network on Capital One's own Discover-network cards is unresolved in the record: the 10-K says the routing and exclusivity rules apply to the Global Payment Network when third-party issuers issue on it, implying they do not reach own-issued three-party cards, but no source says which, if any, second network Capital One's cards carry.

Claim: As of October 2026, Regulation B (12 CFR 1002.9) still requires specific principal reasons for any adverse action, including model-based declines, while a CFPB final rule effective July 21, 2026 removes the disparate-impact ('effects test') language from Regulation B.
Evidence: 12 CFR 1002.9 (eCFR as of 2026-10-20): notice within 30 days of a completed application; reasons must be specific and indicate the principal reason(s); 'internal standards or policies' and 'failed to achieve a qualifying score' are insufficient | CFPB Circular 2022-03 (May 26, 2022): creditors using complex algorithms must still give specific, accurate reasons; the CFPB page shows no withdrawal notice, but NCLC lists it among documents withdrawn by the May 12, 2025 notice (90 FR 20084) | CFPB final rule on Regulation B (issued and published April 22, 2026, FR doc 2026-07804; effective July 21, 2026) amends provisions on disparate impact, discouragement and special purpose credit programs; KPMG's summary says it removes the effects-test language, states ECOA does not recognise disparate-impact liability, and keeps disparate-treatment prohibitions
Implication: Federal disparate-impact exposure for a cash-flow model fell in 2026, which helps feasibility, but the duty to give a declined Debit-Primary applicant readable, specific reasons binds whatever the model.
Caveats: The final rule text and the Federal Register notices were not fetched (federalregister.gov blocked); the effects-test description rests on KPMG, a professional-services summary, used as a pointer to a primary the CFPB page partly confirms. Circular 2022-03 status rests on NCLC (consumer advocate) and conflicts with the CFPB page. State fair-lending law and the Fair Housing Act were not tested; a future administration could reverse the rule.

Claim: The Federal Reserve and OCC approvals of 2025-04-18 accepted that Regulation II does not apply to three-party systems and imposed no condition on debit network pricing, routing, migration or acceptance; Capital One's statement that it does not intend to raise network fees is a representation, not a condition.
Evidence: Fed order, footnote 45: Regulation II does not apply to three-party systems in which the processor is also the issuer (citing Commentary 2(m)-2), and Discover relies on this exemption for most debit transactions on its debit network; commenters had argued the migration would escape the cap and raise merchant fees | Fed order, footnote 46: Capital One's post-merger share of debit-card network purchase volume no more than 6.9 percent; the Board found fee-schedule changes would not substantially increase market power | OCC letter: the single condition is a plan within 120 days of consummation addressing Discover Bank's outstanding enforcement actions; the appendix records Capital One's representations that it does not intend to increase fees on the affiliated debit or credit networks and that in a three-party system there is no interchange fee to regulate
Implication: Regulators looked directly at the debit migration and left the three-party position open, so the edge is held by Capital One today with only a soft, unenforced pricing pledge as a constraint.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. The orders describe Capital One's statements as the applicant's, not findings. Whether the OCC accepted the 120-day plan is not in either document. Both PDFs would not parse through WebFetch; they were fetched, saved and text-extracted with PyMuPDF in this pass.

Claim: Capital One states in its FY2025 10-K that if debit on three-party networks became subject to the Regulation II cap it might not realise a significant majority of the network revenue synergies, and SEC staff asked it in July 2024 to quantify that exposure.
Evidence: FY2025 10-K: for cards issued on the Global Payment Network, a three-party network, the Bank earns an issuer rate instead of interchange fees, and a portion of what merchants pay the network passes through to the Bank; Regulation II applies to the Bank's debit cards on networks not owned by the Company; a change subjecting three-party debit to the cap could mean not recognising a significant majority of the network revenue synergies | Merger prospectus (424B3, 2025-01-06): the revenue synergies assume three-party transactions continue not to be subject to the debit interchange limits | SEC staff comment letter to Richard Fairbank, 2024-07-15, Comment 2: asks Capital One to clarify the reasonably likely impact on revenue synergies if the Discover Global Network's exemption were eliminated; the company's response was not located | Deal call (2024-02-20): Fairbank said the Durbin debit rules were written to explicitly exclude networks like Discover and American Express
Implication: The edge exists only while the three-party exemption stands, and the bank's own filing says losing it would remove most of the synergy, so P01 is a regulatory-contingent position rather than a structural one.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Risk-factor language is conditional and the company has an interest in describing both the advantage and its fragility. The SEC letter pre-dates the close.

Claim: As of October 2026 the Fed's 2023 proposal to cut the cap to 14.4 cents plus 4.0 bps plus 1.3 cents was not finalised, a North Dakota court's August 2025 vacatur of Regulation II was stayed pending appeal while a Kentucky court upheld it, and the only pending network-routing bill, S.3623, is credit-only and exempts three-party systems.
Evidence: Federal Register 2023-11-14 proposal: base 14.4 cents, ad valorem 4.0 bps, fraud adjustment 1.3 cents, recalculated every two years; comments due 2024-02-12. Compiler arithmetic at the $48.59 average covered ticket: about 24.4 cents now against about 17.6 cents proposed | Capital One FY2025 10-K (filed February 2026): the proposal has not been finalised; a North Dakota district court held in August 2025 that the Fed exceeded its authority in 2011, vacated Regulation II, stayed the vacatur pending appeal and allowed the 2023 proposal to take effect if finalised; a Kentucky district court upheld the rule. Mastercard FY2025 10-K: the cap remains in effect while the litigation continues | Fed Regulation II page (last updated 2024-05-17): lists the proposal and no final rule after 2022 | S.3623, Credit Card Competition Act of 2026 (introduced 2026-01-13 by Marshall with Durbin and Welch): network choice for credit cards at issuers above $100 billion of assets; the rules shall not apply to a credit card issued in a 3-party payment system model
Implication: A lower cap would widen the gap the owned network escapes and a final vacatur would erase it by uncapping everyone, so P01's value rides on unfinished litigation and rulemaking, while Congress has not moved against three-party debit.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Appellate status (Eighth and Sixth Circuits) came only from unfetched trade and advocacy pages and is not cited. Absence of a final rule rests on the 10-K date, a Fed page last updated May 2024 and no contrary result found; it is inferred, not confirmed for October 2026. Absence of a debit bill is from search, not a legislative database. Proposal was announced 2023-10-25 and published 2023-11-14.

Claim: Discover's FY2024 10-K claims near parity with competing cards in US merchant acceptance, but no filing gives a Discover or PULSE debit acceptance count, and Capital One's own risk factors name large-merchant acceptance and pricing as risks.
Evidence: Discover FY2024 10-K: merchant acceptance of the Discover card has reached near parity with competing cards in the US by merchants enabled and actively accepting, while the legacy perception of lower acceptance limits attracting cardholders and debit issuers; largest merchant about 6 percent of Discover network volume | Deal call (2024-02-20): Fairbank said actual acceptance is nearly universal but there is a gap between perception and reality | Capital One FY2025 10-K: a reduction in the number of large merchants that accept cards on the Discover or PULSE networks, or in the rates they pay, could materially hurt results; top merchants could condition participation on pricing | OCC appendix: opposing commenters said merchants would likely be unable to reject the bank's cards and that Discover Bank debit fees are higher than four-party debit. Stripe merchant guidance (undated, 2026): migrated cards are no longer subject to interchange caps, fees likely higher, and some cards may fail outside Discover country coverage
Implication: Acceptance is probably not binding in the US, but the only evidence is the network owners' own claims; because the cards cannot be rerouted, the real check on the edge is large-merchant refusal or renegotiation, which no source measures.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: merchants (acceptance and pricing leverage). Near parity is undefined by any number and is asserted by the party selling the network. No Nilson or independent acceptance count was obtained. Commenter positions are regulator summaries. Stripe is an acquirer describing its own processing; no figures. No merchant trade-group statement or complaint about the migration was found.

Claim: No filing, order or announcement found describes a consumer debit product whose terms are better because of the owned network; the only link is Capital One's representation to the OCC that avoided network fees could fund no-fee checking or cash bonuses.
Evidence: OCC appendix: Capital One said that, no longer paying a third-party network fee, it could lower per-transaction costs and invest in no-fee, no-minimum-balance checking or cash bonuses to new checking customers; supporting commenters said a three-party model could fund debit rewards and free checking for lower-income customers. Neither is a condition | Deal call (2024-02-20): the network adds vertical integration benefits to Consumer Banking; the FY2025 10-K and Q2 2026 10-Q describe reissuance and higher non-interest income but no debit rewards or pricing product | Capital One's no-overdraft-fee policy pre-dates and is unrelated to the network
Implication: Under the sponsor's Section 5 screen P01 today is infrastructure margin, not a consumer product; it enters scope only as a debit product for Debit-Primary Spenders funded by the cap-exempt spread, and no such product is disclosed.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Absence of disclosure is not absence of a product; Capital One's own 360 Checking pages were not read, and third-party listings of time-limited debit spend bonuses were not cited. The cap-exempt rate is paid by merchants, so a bank keeping the spread transfers value from merchants to itself without any consumer gain unless it is passed through.

Claim: The CFPB's October 2024 Section 1033 personal financial data rights rule is enjoined from enforcement by the E.D. Kentucky (October 29, 2025) pending a reconsideration that began with an August 22, 2025 advance notice, so cash-flow underwriting on data from other institutions has no settled federal portability right as of October 2026.
Evidence: CFPB rule page: issued October 22, 2024; published November 18, 2024 (89 FR 90838); effective January 17, 2025; no later status update on the page | CFPB reconsideration page: ANPR of August 22, 2025 (90 FR 40986, docket CFPB-2025-0037) on who counts as a representative, fees for access, data security and privacy; no later proposed rule listed | Moore & Van Allen summary: Forcht Bank, N.A., et al. v. CFPB, No. 5:24-cv-00304-DCR (E.D. Ky.), Doc. 90, October 29, 2025, enjoins enforcement until reconsideration is complete; Kentucky Bankers Association and Bank Policy Institute are co-plaintiffs.
