Cozen O'Connor (April 9, 2026): the first compliance date of April 1, 2026 arrived but not as a binding enforcement trigger
Implication: With portability frozen, a bank underwriting its own depositors holds data outside underwriters cannot count on, which favours T07 built on a bank's own Debit-Primary customers rather than on data pulled from elsewhere.
Caveats: The injunction and compliance-date status come from law-firm summaries; the court order itself was not fetched (Low-grade pointers corroborated in part by the CFPB pages). Correction this pass: the researcher's 'compliance dates beginning 2026-06-30, schedule effectively suspended' was not on the Cozen page, which gives April 1, 2026 as the first compliance date; corrected. Any 2026 replacement rule was not found.

Claim: Affirm facilitated $50.2B of GMV in the year to 30 June 2026, 70% of it interest-bearing instalment loans, earning merchant network revenue of 2.29% of GMV against a provision for credit losses of 1.59% of GMV.
Evidence: Affirm FY2026 10-K: GMV $50.2B; about 571 thousand active merchants and about 7.0 transactions per active consumer at 30 June 2026; GMV mix Pay-in-X 16%, 0% APR monthly instalments 14%, interest-bearing instalments 70% (72% FY2025, 74% FY2024) | Statement of operations: total revenue $4,261.1M (FY2025 $3,224.4M); merchant network revenue $1,149.9M; card network revenue $294.0M; provision for credit losses $796.7M (FY2025 $616.7M); funding costs $454.0M | Compiler arithmetic: merchant revenue / GMV = 2.29%; provision / GMV = 1.59%; funding costs / GMV = 0.90%; revenue / GMV = 8.5%
Implication: The contested pool is large and mostly interest-bearing credit rather than free pay-in-4, which supports the size of P02, but funding is the smallest of the three big cost lines (0.9% of GMV against 1.6% losses), so a funding edge moves the least important number.
Caveats: Edge: none. Affirm's own filing. GMV includes Canada and the UK (Affirm is mostly US). FY2026 net income is inflated by a one-off tax valuation-allowance release and is not used here. Verified against the local extract output/sweep2/_pdf/afrm10k.txt and the live EDGAR URL.

Claim: Affirm funds the loans it holds through warehouses and securitisations at a principal-weighted stated rate of about 4.95% at 30 June 2026 (securitisation notes 4.85%, US warehouses 5.27%), and sold $21.9B of loans to third parties in FY2026, so most of its volume is funded by loan buyers, not by its own debt.
Evidence: Affirm FY2026 10-K Note 8 debt table (rates weighted by outstanding principal at 30 June 2026): US warehouse facilities 5.27% on $2,410.6M; international warehouses 4.49% on $586.7M; variable funding notes 5.12% on $356.9M; sale and repurchase 6.90% on $4.7M; notes issued by securitisation trusts 4.85% on $5,350.0M; total secured borrowing capacity $14.0B with $8.7B outstanding | Compiler arithmetic: principal-weighted stated rate across secured debt = 4.95% (4.99% excluding international facilities) | Same filing: funding costs $454.0M (FY2025 $425.5M); average funding debt from warehouses and securitisations $7.5B (FY2025 $5.9B); loans sold with unpaid principal $21.9B (FY2025 $15.8B), 86% interest-bearing; gain on sales of loans $596.6M; loans held for investment $9,466M; risk factors say some forward-flow counterparties have faced redemption pressure | American Banker ABS Report (trade press as record of the deal): Affirm Asset Securitization Trust 2026-X1, $548.9M, weighted-average collateral APR 28.3%, 627,108 loans, average balance $1,110, weighted-average credit score 681, class A credit enhancement 30.24%; no coupon given
Implication: The position P02 attacks is a capital-markets funding stack whose disclosed coupon is about 5%, and the larger part of Affirm's volume is not on its balance sheet at all, so a bank's deposit cost competes with loan buyers' required returns, which are not disclosed.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Corrects the researchers' gap: the weighted rates are disclosed in Note 8 of the 10-K (local extract), though per-deal ABS coupons are not. Stated rates are point-in-time at 30 June 2026 and exclude fee amortisation and unused-commitment fees (0.15%-0.95%). The buyers' return on the $21.9B sold sits inside gain on sale and is not disclosed. ABS deal data are trade press; Fitch and DBRS presales were paywalled.

Claim: On like-dated disclosures, Affirm's stated secured funding rate (about 4.95% at June 2026) exceeds Capital One's average interest-bearing deposit cost (2.91% in Q2 2026) by about 2.0 points, worth roughly 0.3% to 0.5% of Affirm's GMV, but the gap is about 1.1 points against Capital One's time-deposit cost and about 0.4 points against Capital One's own securitised debt.
Evidence: Capital One Q2 2026 10-Q average balance table (three months to 30 June 2026): interest-bearing deposits $458.1B at 2.91%; savings 2.81%; time deposits 3.89%; interest-bearing checking 1.17%; securitised debt obligations 4.59%; six-month interest-bearing deposit rate 2.96% | Capital One FY2025 10-K: interest-bearing deposits $402.2B average at 3.21% (3.54% in 2024); securitised debt obligations 5.04%; average Consumer Banking deposit rate 3.02% (franchise-02) | Compiler arithmetic, stated-rate basis (Affirm 4.95%, from independence-122): gap 2.04 points vs 2.91%; 1.06 vs time deposits 3.89%; 0.36 vs Capital One securitised debt 4.59%. Applied to Affirm's average funding liabilities of $7,560.6M ((8,664.5 + 6,456.7)/2), a 2.04-point gap saves about $155M, 0.31% of GMV | Compiler arithmetic, all-in basis (researcher method): $454.0M / $7,560.6M = 6.0% including fee amortisation; gap 2.8 points vs 3.21% (P02-B) or 3.0 vs 3.02% (P02-A); saving about $211M, 0.42% of GMV. Either way the saving is below merchant revenue (2.29% of GMV) and provision (1.59%)
Implication: The deposit-funding edge over Affirm is real at average deposit cost but is about a point at the margin (time deposits) and is a deposits-versus-securitisation edge, not a bank-versus-Affirm edge, since Capital One's own securitised debt costs within half a point of Affirm's; it cannot carry a share-taking position alone.
Caveats: Edge: cost. All gaps are compiler arithmetic on mixed bases: Affirm stated rates are point-in-time and exclude fees; Capital One rates are period averages across all deposit products, not the marginal cost of funding a new book; Capital One would also carry capital, FDIC premium and liquidity costs not in a deposit rate. Only the held book (about $9.5B) bears Affirm's funding cost; the cost of the $21.9B sold is not visible. The P02-A (605 bps) and P02-B (about 600 bps) figures are the all-in ratio and overstate the coupon by about one point. Capital One 10-K and 10-Q verified from local extracts (output/franchise/_pdf/cof10k.txt, output/sweep2/_pdf/cof_q2_2026.txt).

Claim: Affirm's FY2026 10-K names Celtic Bank (a Utah industrial bank) and Lead Bank (a Missouri state bank) as originators of substantially all its US platform loans, with Affirm directly originating about 19% ($9.5B) under its own state licences, and lets those banks allow rates up to 36%.
Evidence: Affirm FY2026 10-K: substantially all US loans facilitated through the platform are originated through Celtic Bank and Lead Bank; Celtic and Lead generally allow borrowers to agree to rates up to 36%, Cross River up to 30%; Cross River is the partner for the Affirm Money Account | Same filing: Affirm directly originated about $9.5B, or 19%, of loans in FY2026 ($6.3B, 17% in FY2025); the originating bank retains an interest through a loan performance fee payable by Affirm on principal repaid, carried as a fair-value liability (Note 12) | Compiler arithmetic: the partner-bank share of FY2026 originations is roughly the remaining 81%, an inference from the 19% figure | Pointer correction: framework-13 records Cross River as the originating bank from the 2021 S-1; that is stale for FY2026
Implication: Affirm does rent charters, as P02 says, but it has moved from one partner to two and grown its own licensed origination without disruption, so the rented-charter structure is a cost line, not evidence of fragility.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Affirm's own filing, verified in the local extract. The fee paid to the banks is not quantified in the extract read; the loss on loan purchase commitment ($311.9M) is not equated with bank fees. The 81% is inference.

Claim: Klarna already holds the deposit-funded position P02 attributes to a bank: customer deposits of $11.7B were 88% of its funding at 30 June 2026, and its Q2 2026 interest cost on funding annualises to about 3.7% of deposits plus borrowings, within a point of Capital One's 2.91%.
Evidence: Klarna Q2 2026 earnings release (SEC 6-K): total GMV $36.6B (+18%); US GMV $7.9B (+27%); take rate 2.84%; provisions $192M, 0.52% of GMV; funding costs $171M, 0.47% of GMV, of which interest costs on funding $125M; customer deposits $11,673M at 30 June 2026 vs $13,003M at 31 December 2025, 88% of funding; notes payable and other borrowings $1,687M | Compiler arithmetic: $125M x 4 / ($11,673M + $1,687M) = 3.74% annualised; gap to Capital One Q2 2026 interest-bearing deposits (2.91%, independence-123) = 0.83 points | Klarna Holding AB 2025 annual report: deposits from the public SEK 121,797m vs loans to the public SEK 102,438m; interest expenses SEK 4,038m; credit losses 0.63% of GMV (0.49% in 2024), the rise attributed to the growing US share (18% to 20% of GMV); compiler arithmetic on average 2024-25 interest-bearing funding about 3.3% | Klarna F-1 (2025): deposits funded 94% of lending in 2024 ($9.5B); WebBank originates Klarna's US Fair Financing loans, which Klarna buys and services for a volume-based and fixed fee. KBRA (29 May 2026): Pagaya sued Klarna on 13 May 2026 over trade secrets; Pagaya's POSH 2025-1 and 2025-2 revolving ABS are backed by Klarna BNPL loans
Implication: Against Klarna the kill criterion's funding arm is met: its funding already costs within about a point of Capital One's average deposit rate, so deposit funding gives no decisive edge against the second named incumbent.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Klarna (cost). Klarna's deposits are mostly Swedish and German savings in lower-rate currencies; the US funding split (deposits vs forward flow vs ABS) is not disclosed, so Klarna's US book may cost more than the group figure. The 3.74% is period-end and blended. Correction: P02-A said the Q2 release aims to diversify funding with forward flow; the release describes forward flows as committed, pre-priced loan sales and does not frame them as diversification. WebBank originates Fair Financing (longer loans), not all US loans. Annual report verified from local extract.

Claim: Three of the four large US BNPL incumbents hold or are seeking their own deposit-taking bank: Block originates Cash App Borrow through its Utah industrial loan company since Q2 2025, PayPal applied for a Utah ILC in December 2025, and Affirm applied for a Nevada ILC in January 2026.
Evidence: Block FY2025 10-K: Square Financial Services is a Utah-chartered ILC; from Q2 2025 Cash App Borrow is originated through it and held for investment; consumer receivable losses (Afterpay BNPL) $314.4M vs $273.2M, up 15% with BNPL growth, loss rates stable; loan losses $820.8M vs $323.0M | Block Q4 2025 shareholder letter: Cash App consumer lending origination volume (Borrow and Afterpay together) $18.5B, up 69%; an estimated 60% of Afterpay users have household income above $70K | PayPal FY2025 10-K: December 2025 applications to the Utah DFI and FDIC for PayPal Bank, an ILC, with no assurance of approval; certain US instalment products are provided by a state-chartered industrial bank. PayPal release (24 September 2025): Blue Owl funds to buy about $7B of US Pay in 4 loans over two years, PayPal keeping underwriting and servicing; PayPal BNPL volume over $33B globally in 2024, up about 21% | Affirm FY2026 10-K: January 2026 applications to the Nevada Financial Institutions Division and the FDIC to establish Affirm Bank, a proposed ILC, with no assurance of approval
Implication: The deposit-funding edge P02 rests on is being acquired by the incumbents themselves through ILC charters, so whatever edge exists today narrows as those applications are decided, and it never applied to Block.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Block, and pending for PayPal and Affirm (regulatory and cost). Company filings about themselves. Approval status of the PayPal and Affirm applications in October 2026 was not checked (FDIC application listings would answer it). Block does not disclose Afterpay US GMV or a numeric BNPL loss rate; the $18.5B mixes Borrow and BNPL. PayPal's $33B is global.

Claim: The CFPB's December 2025 Data Spotlight reports that six large lenders originated 335.8M pay-in-4 loans worth $45.2B in 2023 (average $135), with 1.83% of loans charged off, and estimates the six held about 40% of the overall point-of-sale financing market.
Evidence: CFPB Data Spotlight (December 2025), six firms including Affirm, Afterpay, Klarna and PayPal: 2023 originations 335.8M loans and $45.2B, inflation-adjusted (2022: 273.8M and $35.8B) | Charge-offs: 1.83% of loans in 2023 (2.63% in 2022); charged-off dollars 0.92% of GMV in 2023 | The six firms were about 40% of the overall POS financing market in 2023, which includes pay-in-4 and other short-term financing; longer POS instalment loans are outside the pay-in-4 data
Implication: Pay-in-4 is a small-ticket, low-loss, interest-free product funded by merchant fees, so any funding edge matters mainly for the longer interest-bearing loans outside this dataset.
Caveats: Edge: none. Data are 2023. Dollar values inflation-adjusted. The 40% share and the $45.2B cover different scopes, so no market total is derived. Verified from local extract output/sweep2/_pdf/cfpb_bnpl_2025-12.txt; the PDF URL resolves.

Claim: Deposit-funded POS lending already operates at scale: Synchrony funds 84% of its balance sheet with deposits at a 4.10% average cost, sells Pay in 4 and pay-monthly products, and names Affirm, Afterpay and Klarna as rivals with lighter capital rules, while Truist bought Service Finance in 2021 to hold most of its POS loans on balance sheet.
Evidence: Synchrony FY2025 10-K: deposits $81.1B, 84% of funding; interest-bearing deposits averaged $81,228M with interest expense $3,330M, 4.10% (4.63% in 2024); securitisation borrowings 5.23%; net interest margin 15.24%; net charge-off rate 5.65% | Same filing: Synchrony Pay Later comes as a pay-monthly product and an interest-free Pay in 4 product; non-bank pay-over-time providers such as Affirm, Afterpay and Klarna do not face the same capital and regulatory requirements, which could place Synchrony at a competitive disadvantage; no Pay Later volume disclosed | Truist (10 August 2021): $2B for Service Finance, more than 14,000 home-improvement dealers, 2021 originations expected above $2.5B, about 30% annual growth; the vast majority of loans to be held on Truist's balance sheet | Compiler arithmetic: Synchrony's 2025 deposit cost is 0.89 points above Capital One's 3.21% (independence-123)
Implication: A deposit-funded bank already holds the POS position and treats the nonbanks' lighter capital load as its own handicap, which says deposit funding is not a decisive edge in this market and that the edge varies with how a bank gathers deposits.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Synchrony's deposits are mostly online savings and CDs; definitions differ from Capital One's. Truist's deal is home-improvement POS, not checkout instalments, and dates from 2021. Fifth Third and Dividend Finance appeared in search only and are not cited. Synchrony 10-K verified by direct EDGAR download.

Claim: Capital One barred card payments of BNPL debt in December 2020 and announced a BNPL beta with existing customers at select merchants in September 2021, but no later launch appears in its filings or site, and its only current Pay Over Time product is an invitation-only revolving feature; separately, Apple's Pay Later, lent by Apple, ended in June 2024.
Evidence: Banking Dive (14 September 2021, trade press as record of the event): Capital One stopped customers using its cards to pay BNPL debt the previous December; CEO Richard Fairbank said it would beta-test BNPL with some existing customers at a limited group of existing merchants, not linked to private-label cards, and called the sustainability of the merchant subsidy the elephant in the room, warning competitors could bid down the merchant discount | Capital One Pay Over Time page: available by invitation on cards with no preset spending limit; carries part of the statement balance at a Pay Over Time APR; no instalments at checkout. Capital One learn-and-grow article (7 May 2026) names Affirm, Klarna and Afterpay and no Capital One instalment product | Compiler search of local extracts: no hits for buy now, pay later, BNPL, Klarna, instalment loan or pay over time in the FY2025 10-K, the Q1 and Q2 2026 10-Qs, or the Q3 2026 earnings exhibits. Affirm's FY2026 10-K names Capital One among card issuers it competes with | 9to5Mac (17 June 2024): Apple will no longer offer Apple Pay Later in the US; Apple backed the loans and Goldman issued the Mastercard credential; Apple moved to card instalments from Citi, Synchrony and Fiserv-served issuers, and Affirm at Apple Pay checkout
Implication: P02 passes the additive screen (Capital One has no checkout instalment product in motion), but the bank's own last public view was that merchant-subsidy economics, not funding, was the constraint, and the one big-brand exit at checkout was Apple's, so the hypothesis needs a reason that view no longer holds.
Caveats: Edge: distribution. The two events rest on trade press; no filing records the 2021 beta outcome. The December ban year (2020) is inferred from the article date. Earnings-call transcripts 2022-2026 were not read, so an unfiled statement could exist. Pointer correction: the scout's Goldman Apple Pay Later shutdown is wrong; Apple lent, Goldman only issued the credential.

Claim: Capital One's FY2025 10-K says it made the strategic choice to originate and service subprime credit card and auto loans, reports 27% of domestic card loans at refreshed FICO 660 or below at December 31, 2025, describes card underwriting as generally based on credit bureau information including FICO scores and applicant income, and contains no text on alternative-data or cash-flow underwriting.
Evidence: Risk factors: the company made the strategic choice to originate and service subprime credit card and auto loans, which typically have higher delinquencies and charge-offs than prime accounts | Credit score distribution: domestic card 73% above 660 and 27% at 660 or below at 2025-12-31 (69% / 31% at 2024-12-31), with balances lacking a valid score counted in the 660-or-below group; personal loans 94% above 660; auto at origination 51% above 660, 19% at 621-660, 30% at 620 or below | Card underwriting generally based on credit bureau information including FICO scores and other factors such as income; auto adds collateral and LTV. A text search found no 'alternative data' or 'cash-flow'; 'machine learning' appears only in AI and compliance risk factors | FinRegLab's research page on ML and cash-flow data in underwriting (bureau plus aggregator bank-account data, accounts opened 2018-2019; bureau-plus-cash-flow model most predictive overall and across subgroups) lists JPMorgan Chase and Capital One as supporters
Implication: T07 largely fails the additive screen: the enterprise already serves a large sub-660 population through Card and Auto, so a cash-flow model belongs inside Card's credit box using deposit data Capital One already holds; the open question is whether deposit signals extend credit to Debit-Primary customers Card now declines.
Caveats: Absence of a disclosure is not evidence of non-use; earnings calls and investor decks were not searched. The 660 line is not a subprime definition by itself, and no-score balances are included in the 660-or-below share, which inflates it slightly as a measure of subprime. FinRegLab support does not show Capital One uses the method; FinRegLab is part-funded by industry. The 10-K page resolves but is too long to read whole through the fetch tool; quoted text was verified in the local extract (output/independence/_pdf/cof10k.txt, identical to output/franchise/_pdf/cof10k.txt).

Claim: A national bank lending in its own name holds the same rate-exportation power Affirm's state-bank partners use, so it gains no rate headroom, but it avoids two risks the partner model carries: no federal true-lender safe harbour since Congress voided the OCC's 2020 rule in June 2021, and state DIDMCA opt-outs, which the Tenth Circuit held in November 2025 reach out-of-state state banks but not national banks.
Evidence: 12 CFR 7.4001 (eCFR as of 2026-10-20): a national bank may charge the maximum rate permitted to any state-chartered or licensed lender in its state (paragraph b); permissible interest is not affected by sale, assignment or transfer of the loan (paragraph e; amended 85 FR 33536, 2 June 2020) | Public Law 117-24 (approved 30 June 2021): Congress disapproved the OCC rule National Banks and Federal Savings Associations as Lenders (85 FR 68742), which has no force or effect | Affirm FY2026 10-K: relies on Celtic's and Lead's federal rate authority and the FDIC Federal Interest Rate Authority rule; if the partner structure were successfully challenged it could violate state licensing and rate laws and need new banks, state licences or a federal charter | Consumer Finance Monitor (Ballard Spahr, law-firm pointer): Tenth Circuit, NAIB v. Weiser, 10 November 2025, held a loan is made in an opt-out state if the lender or borrower is there, so Colorado caps apply to out-of-state state banks; national banks keep full exportation; an en banc petition was to be filed 9 December 2025
Implication: The regulatory edge is real but narrow: it removes structure risk on interest-bearing loans priced above state caps, a product a bank brand may not want to price at 36%, and gives nothing on pay-in-4.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. The Weiser holding rests on a law-firm blog; the opinion and the en banc outcome were not fetched, so that point is Low on its own. Statute 12 U.S.C. 85 not fetched; the regulation states the operative rule. No state has been shown to have succeeded against Affirm's structure. Public Law text verified from local extract.

Claim: The CFPB withdrew its 2024 BNPL interpretive rule on 12 May 2025, and New York's BNPL law exempts national banks from the licence that nonbank BNPL lenders will need once the Department of Financial Services finalises its July 2026 proposed rule.
Evidence: CFPB BNPL resource page: on 12 May 2025 the CFPB withdrew several guidance documents including the 2024 BNPL Interpretive Rule; no reissuance noted | NY Banking Law section 736: a BNPL loan is closed-end credit for a consumer's particular purchase; a BNPL lender includes a person operating a platform with which a consumer interacts; exempt organization includes any national bank licensed by the Comptroller to do business in New York | DFS proposed 3 NYCRR Part 423: other than an exempt organization or authorised lender, no person may act as a BNPL lender without a licence, and non-exempt lenders need a category permission | Mayer Brown (August 2026, law-firm pointer): proposed rule issued 15 July 2026; final rules take effect 180 days after State Register publication; non-exempt lenders apply within 45 days of that date. No final rule found as of 2026-10-26
Implication: State BNPL licensing costs fall on Affirm, Klarna and their platforms rather than on a national bank, a small compliance-cost edge that does not change product economics.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Part 423 is proposed, not final. Illinois Public Act 104-475, reported by the researcher as exempting banks of any charter, is dropped: the local extract is an ILGA access-denied page and the claim rests on search summaries. UDAAP and TILA still apply to finance-charged loans. Other states not surveyed. NY 423 verified from local extract.

Claim: Affirm's checkout position is concentrated and contract-based (top five partners 44% of FY2026 GMV, Amazon 22%), extended through wallets such as Apple Pay, and Klarna claims more than 960k retailers plus Apple Pay and Google Pay, which a bank without merchant contracts cannot replicate.
Evidence: Affirm FY2026 10-K: top five partners 44% of GMV (47% in FY2025 and FY2024); Amazon 22% (22%, 21%); 25% of transactions began in Affirm's app, website or Affirm Card; Amazon, Shopify and Apple Pay named as key relationships; many partner agreements are non-exclusive, some had exclusivity periods | Same filing: merchant network revenue $1,149.9M, 2.29% of GMV (compiler arithmetic); in November 2025, with an amended Amazon commercial agreement, Affirm cut the exercise price of Amazon warrants vesting from February 2026 from $100 to $63.06 per share, a distribution cost paid in equity | Klarna Holding AB 2025 annual report: consumers can pay with Klarna online, in store and through Apple Pay and Google Pay; more than 960k retailers; about 118m active consumers across 26 markets
Implication: Distribution, not funding, is where Affirm and Klarna hold the position, so a bank play is bounded by its own customers unless it buys merchant placement at a cost Affirm already pays in equity and fees.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Affirm and Klarna (distribution). Company filings about themselves. Exclusivity terms are undisclosed. Affirm 10-K verified from local extract; Klarna annual report from local extract.

Claim: Visa's instalment service needs issuer, acquirer and merchant participation and a merchant checkout upgrade, while Mastercard's lets issuers present instalment offers on an existing credit line at checkout or after purchase through wallets, merchants and browsers, and Affirm already converts eligible debit-card purchases into loans after the fact.
Evidence: Visa Developer, Installment Transaction Service: plans are for eligible Visa cardholders and require participation of issuers, acquirers and merchants; merchants sign up and upgrade checkout; issuers define plans and update their own apps; debit eligibility not addressed | Mastercard Developers, Installments: issuers present offers to cardholders with an existing line of credit during or after purchase; distribution via wallets, merchants or PSPs, browsers and gateways; benefits list Credit/Debit Cards enabled without detail | Affirm FY2026 10-K: Affirm Card users can apply for an instalment loan on any eligible debit transaction after purchase
Implication: A bank can give its own cardholders instalments without merchant contracts, post-purchase or through Mastercard distribution, which is a feature on an owned card rather than a checkout position; whether Discover-network debit has an equivalent was not found.
Caveats: Edge: distribution. Developer pages describe technical flows, not US adoption or volumes. Debit coverage under both programmes is unclear. The reading that a bank could replicate Affirm's post-purchase conversion is inference.

Claim: Bureau BNPL data are still hidden from lenders (Affirm furnishes to TransUnion from May 2025 but lenders cannot see it, and FICO's BNPL scores wait on bureau data at scale), so a bank's own deposit and card data is a genuine information edge on its own customers, but cash-flow underwriting is a vendor commodity and its lift for instalments is untested.
Evidence: PYMNTS (22 April 2025, trade press reporting Affirm's announcement): Affirm reports all pay-over-time loans including Pay in 4 to TransUnion from loans issued 1 May 2025; consumers see them, lenders cannot, and they are not in traditional scores | FICO blog (12 March 2026): BNPL scores will be offered at the bureaus concurrently with BNPL data at scale; lenders choose when to activate; BNPL furnishing adoption has been gradual and uneven, limiting lender access; validation used Affirm data on over 500,000 consumers | Sweep-1 rows: independence-08 (cash-flow underwriting sold or turned into vendor products, FICO UltraFICO generally available 2026); independence-13 (Capital One FY2025 10-K: 27% of domestic card loans at refreshed FICO 660 or below, no alternative-data text); rupture-06 (Chime transaction and risk losses up 85% to $407.3M in 2025 as deposit-based advances scaled)
Implication: The underwriting half of P02 is plausible only as a proprietary-data edge on the bank's own base, unproven by any published test, and for Debit-Primary Spenders the loss cost it must beat is larger than the funding saving.
Caveats: Edge: none (underwriting data, own base only). Trade press and a company blog. Furnishing status beyond Affirm-TransUnion is unconfirmed: the Experian start date and TransUnion October 2026 attributes rest on search snippets and are not cited. No deposit-data lift study for instalments exists in the sources reached. Sweep-1 rows cited by ID, not re-fetched.

Claim: New Direct PLUS loans to graduate and professional students ended July 1, 2026 and Parent PLUS is capped at $20,000 a year and $65,000 per dependent, while student-loan refinancing is concentrated in prime lenders: SoFi's student-loan originations rose 170% in Q2 2026 year on year, mainly on rate-driven refinancing, and Navient's Earnest doubled refinance originations to $2,076 million in 2025 at a 773 average FICO.
Evidence: 34 CFR 685.200(b)(2) (eCFR as of 2026-10-20): beginning July 1, 2026 a graduate or professional student may not borrow a Direct PLUS loan, except during the expected time to credential for students enrolled as of June 30, 2026 with a Direct Loan made before July 1, 2026. 685.203(f)(2) and (g)(2): Parent PLUS limited to $20,000 a year and $65,000 aggregate per dependent for periods from July 1, 2026 | SoFi Q2 2026 10-Q: student loan origination volume up 170% (quarter) and 143% (six months) year on year as borrowers refinanced at lower rates; focus on prime and super-prime borrowers; student loans held for investment $16.9 billion at June 30, 2026 versus $13.7 billion at December 31, 2025 (fair value incl. accrued interest); total deposits $45.5 billion; SoFi says the OBBB changes could lead to changes in demand and outcomes are highly uncertain | SoFi FY2025 10-K: student loans $12,875,440K unpaid principal at December 31, 2025; student-loan products 644,225 (2024: 568,612) | Navient Q4 2025 presentation: Earnest refi originations $1,034M (2024) to $2,076M (2025); rate-check volume $6.5B to $17.3B; refi average FICO 750 to 773; in-school originations $366M to $401M; over $24 billion refinanced since 2014. Navient 10-K: Earnest refinances education loans for high-quality borrowers
Implication: The caps open a real private-credit gap for graduate and parent borrowers, but it is being filled by prime refinancing and in-school lenders, one of which (SoFi) already holds a bank charter and $45.5 billion of deposits, so T20 reads as a rate business for prime Young Consumers rather than choreography for Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Merged from independence-A finding 9 (refinance half) and independence-B finding 8. The graduate annual and aggregate dollar caps and RAP terms are NOT asserted: ed.gov and the Federal Register were blocked and the eCFR 685.203 text carries an editorial note that a May 1, 2026 amendment could not be applied. SoFi's growth reason is management's attribution and SoFi is a competitor. Earnest figures come from an investor presentation (PDF resolves, does not parse; verified in local extract). The Navient 10-K page exceeds the fetch tool's 10MB limit; verified in the local extract.

Claim: The employer student-loan match sits with plan sponsors and small, consolidating vendors and federal servicing is moving to Treasury: IRS Notice 2024-63 lets 401(k), 403(b), SIMPLE IRA and governmental 457(b) plans match qualified student-loan payments, Candidly reports $73 million of employer contributions in 2025, Summer bought Vault's assets in 2024, and a March 19, 2026 agreement moves defaulted federal loans to Treasury servicing.
Evidence: Notice 2024-63: SECURE 2.0 section 110 matches on qualified student loan payments for plan years beginning after December 31, 2023; the employee certifies payment annually; a plan cannot limit matches to certain loans (A-4); all employees eligible for elective-deferral matches must be eligible; proposed regulations anticipated | Candidly 2025 impact report: $73 million of employer student-loan contributions in 2025; new employers up 121% and student-loan retirement match clients up 111% (no base counts); notes the OBBB made the $5,250 Section 127 tax-free employer contribution permanent. Plan Adviser (Aug 5, 2024): Summer bought Vault assets, IP and select contracts in an all-cash deal; Vault had served more than 3,000 employers; Vault products to be phased out; price undisclosed | CRS R48962 (updated June 9, 2026): ED and Treasury signed an agreement on March 19, 2026; Phase 1 moves defaulted federally held loans to Treasury's Cross-Servicing Program; Phase 2 would move non-defaulted servicing to Treasury to the extent practicable; about 7.8 million borrowers (about 18%) owed about $179 billion in default at December 31, 2025
Implication: The employer-match lever belongs to employers and recordkeepers and servicing is consolidating in government, so a bank holds no natural position in the navigation layer for borrowers with federal loans; what is left is refinancing, which is a prime rate play.
Caveats: Merged from independence-A finding 9 (employer platforms) and independence-B finding 9. Candidly's report is a vendor document about its own category (interest flagged) with no employer or borrower totals. The Notice PDF resolves but does not parse through the fetch tool; verified in the local extract. CRS is a background report hosted on a mirror (everycrsreport.com). The advocacy claim that the CFPB has deprioritised student-loan supervision was dropped (no primary).

Claim: In 2022, 50.4% of US households with a head under 35 held no retirement account (DC plan or IRA), so the median under-35 household had $0 in retirement savings.
Evidence: CRS IF12928 (Feb 2025) and R48143 (Jul 2024) on the 2022 SCF: 49.6% of under-35 households hold any retirement account, so 50.4% hold none and the population median is $0 | Among holders, the under-35 median combined balance is $18,880 (mean $49,127); DC-only median $15,000 | Fed SCF 2022: 98.6% of all families hold a transaction account
Implication: For Young Consumers the deposit account is the one reliable contact with a household that has no retirement account, which supports exploring T05, though the gap is partly a plan-default artifact that auto-enrollment is closing.
Caveats: Corpus row 82 (independence corpus finding 1). SCF 2022 is four years old and omits crypto; the wave-3 shortlist calls the $0 median a melting fact as SECURE 2.0 defaults spread. Spot-check this pass: the 98.6% transaction-account figure was confirmed on the Fed page.

Claim: In a January 2025 Philadelphia Fed survey module, 44.9% of US adults who do not own stock cited insufficient financial resources, the most-cited of eight reasons, while 5.0% cited a negative past experience.
Evidence: Philadelphia Fed CFI (fielded Jan 2025, N=5,089; 2,912 non-owners): 44.9% insufficient resources, 38.6% do not understand the market, 20.3% too volatile, 19.5% not a priority, 5.0% negative past experience | Correct diversification answers: 31.9% without a degree versus 57.4% with one | Resource constraint is cited at similar or higher rates by White (47.8%) than Black (36.4%) non-owners; the knowledge barrier is higher among underrepresented groups
Implication: The stated barrier is too little money, which points away from an on-ramp product as the missing piece for Debit-Primary Spenders and toward income and cash-flow constraints.
Caveats: Corpus row 79 (independence corpus finding 3); originally Self-Reported (Flagged); stated reasons, multi-select. Not re-fetched this pass.

Claim: US retirement assets reached $49.1 trillion at year-end 2025 and most IRA inflows are rollovers from employer DC plans, so retirement wealth is intermediated by employers and recordkeepers rather than the primary bank.
Evidence: ICI 2026 Fact Book: $49.1 trillion at year-end 2025, up 11%; IRAs ($19.2T) and DC plans ($14.2T) are 68% of the total | DOL/EBSA Form 5500 abstract 2023: private pension assets $12.4 trillion; DC assets $9.4 trillion; 81.6 million active 401(k)-type participants | CRS on the 2022 SCF: most IRA inflows are rollovers from DC accounts at job change or retirement
Implication: Where young households accumulate, the channel is the employer plan, so a deposit-based on-ramp competes for a thin link in the chain, a counter-case for T05 across segments.
Caveats: Corpus row 84 (independence corpus finding 5). ICI is a fund-industry trade association (interest flagged) corroborated by DOL; rollover mechanism is qualitative; $49.1T is a stock, not a flow. Not re-fetched this pass.

Claim: CFPB's June 2025 correction puts the December 2020 credit-invisible share at 2.7% of adults (7.0 million), down from a revised 5.8% (13.5 million) in 2010, though about 64% to 67% of 18-19-year-olds were invisible in the 2016 report.
Evidence: CFPB June 2025 technical correction: December 2010 revised to 5.8% (13.5 million) from 11.0% (25.9 million); December 2020 2.7% (7.0 million) | CFPB 2016: 64% to 67% of consumers aged 18-19 credit invisible | CFPB Becoming Credit Visible: almost 80% of transitions out of invisibility occur before age 25
Implication: The excluded-by-absence population is small and mostly a timing problem before age 25, which limits T07's scale in the strict thin-file sense.
Caveats: Corpus row 53 (independence corpus finding 8). Two point-in-time panels; demographic cuts are 2010-vintage. Credit-invisible is not the same as poorly scored. Not re-fetched this pass (PDFs do not parse through the fetch tool).

Claim: A July 2025 FinRegLab study found the two strongest ML models combining bureau and cash-flow data raised approvals about 4% over simpler models at mainstream thresholds, about two million card accounts and 152,000 mortgages a year at 2023 volumes, and could not evaluate consumers with little or no credit history.
Evidence: FinRegLab press release (Jul 2025): about 4% approval increase at mainstream risk cut-offs | Applied to 2023 volumes: roughly two million additional card accounts and 152,000 additional mortgages | Data limits made effects on thin- or no-history consumers hard to evaluate
Implication: The measured lift from cash-flow data is modest and sits among applicants who already have files, so T07 for Debit-Primary Spenders remains untested rather than refuted.
Caveats: Corpus row 56 (independence corpus finding 9). FinRegLab is part-funded by industry sponsors including Capital One and JPMorgan (see the Capital One additive-screen row). Simulation, not observed lending. Spot-check this pass: 4%, two million and 152,000 confirmed on the page.

Claim: In 2022, 37.1% of consumers aged 18-24 with a credit record used BNPL against 21.2% of all record holders, and 61% of 2021-2022 BNPL originations went to subprime or deep-subprime scores.
Evidence: CFPB Jan 2025 (matched origination data from six lenders): 37.1% of 18-24s with a record used BNPL in 2022; BNPL about 28% of their average unsecured debt | 61% of 2021-2022 originations to subprime or deep-subprime consumers; 78% of those applications approved in 2022 | CFPB Dec 2025 spotlight: 53.6 million BNPL consumers in 2023, up 12%
Implication: Young and subprime consumers already get credit-like products outside the bureau and the bank, which supports T07 for Young Consumers if a bank can see and price that behaviour in its own account data.
Caveats: Corpus row 45 (independence corpus finding 10). Six lenders only; a later corpus row finds BNPL growth shifting to existing borrowers. Not re-fetched this pass.

Claim: Parents who give young adults recurring support or down-payment gifts move the money through ordinary accounts with no product category built around the flow, and a bank holding both ends could own that category.
Evidence: Brandsaas (FEDS 2025-094): without parental transfers, first homeownership is delayed about 2.5 years (model counterfactual); about 30% of first-time buyers received a parental down-payment gift in the 2015-2016 SHED wave | Social Forces (HRS 1992-2018, 39,626 dyads): money transfers are 3-5x likelier in the most advantaged families | Add Health: 46% of youth partially independent (living apart, receiving parental funds) at Wave 3
Implication: The flow is documented and class-sorted but has no demand or willingness-to-pay evidence, and it benefits advantaged Young Consumers more than Debit-Primary Spenders, so it is a lead, not an opportunity.
Caveats: Corpus rows 98-100 (independence corpus finding 15). Model output and 2001-2009 data; overlaps transfer and domicile. No supply check was made by Slice A. Kill criterion: an existing product at scale, or no revealed demand. Not re-fetched this pass.

Claim: Young adults hit several fixed-age separation dates (CARD Act age 21, bank fee cutoffs at 25, loss of parental health coverage at 26) that act as predictable cohort-wide events with no bank product built around them.
Evidence: KFF on CPS ASEC 2024: dependent coverage falls from 93% at 18-19 to 50% at 24-25; employer-plan dependents drop from 1.2 million 25-year-olds to 300,000 26-year-olds | Census ACS 2019: uninsured rate rises from 14.7% at 25 to 18.3% at 26 | CFPB Dec 2024 college banking report: partner banks waive fees only under 25; with the CARD Act and IRS dependency tests, four uncoordinated regimes and no single separation milestone
Implication: The cliffs are real and dated, but the evidence shows dates and a coverage drop, not a banking pain or a price, so for Young Consumers it is at most a feature of a transition product (T10).
Caveats: Corpus rows 58-59 (independence corpus finding 16). Policy-dependent; Census single-age data is 2019. Kill criterion: no cash-flow stress or switching at these ages beyond the insurance bill. Not re-fetched this pass.

Claim: Non-prime and underserved consumer lending drew new early-stage entrants in 2025 (Karoo in YC Winter 2025; Ava's October 2025 seed for one-click loan origination), adding to T07's player list.
Evidence: Karoo, YC Winter 2025, team of 3, describes itself as an AI-native consumer lending platform for underserved Americans; its CEO was previously Head of US Loans at Lendable (YC company page) | Ava's $15.5M seed (reported 27 October 2025) funds one-click loan origination alongside credit-profile improvement for a $10 monthly fee (FinTech Global) | A $50M Series B for Yendo (vehicle-secured card for non-prime borrowers, October 2025) surfaced in search but its pages returned 403, so it is not cited
Implication: T07 has fresh seed-stage entrants, but two small companies do not make it crowded; the T07 compiler should weigh at-scale players from independence slice A.
Caveats: Two early-stage entrants are a thin basis for crowding. Funding is investor belief, not demand or repayment performance. Ava evidence also appears in rupture-81; here it bears on underwriting, there on the subscription model.

Claim: In 2025, 16% of US adults had student loans and 23% of borrowers reported recent payment difficulty, mostly on affordability, and student loans had the highest serious-delinquency flow of major consumer debts in Q2 2026 (7.83%), but terms are set by federal policy.
Evidence: SHED 2025: 16% of adults had outstanding student loans (21% of those with some college); 23% of borrowers had recent payment difficulty and slightly more than three-quarters of those cited affordability; 45% of borrowers were not currently required to make payments (PDF pp. 8, 72-73) | SHED 2024: 20% of borrowers were behind or in collections (16% in 2023); 3 in 10 borrowers with some college or an associate degree and 27% of borrowers earning under $25,000 were behind; of everyone who ever borrowed for education, 8% were behind and 59% had repaid in full (2024 report, PDF pp. 78-79) | NY Fed Q2 2026: student-loan balance $1.65 trillion; annualized flow into 90+ day delinquency 7.83%, against 6.97% for cards and 3.00% for auto
Implication: Pain is real and rising for non-completers and low earners, but it is an affordability and federal-repayment problem a bank cannot change; refinancing federal loans strips federal protections, so T20 survives only as navigation or employer-match administration, not lending.
Caveats: Caused by policy and income: difficulty falls steeply with income and completion. The 2025 budget act's loan caps and repayment changes effective 2026 were not researched in round 1. Whether Capital One originates student loans was not checked. Self-reported. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Couples-specific money apps of 2019-2025 stayed small and were sold or sunset: Acorns bought Zeta's assets on 24 June 2025 with terms undisclosed, Ivella (YC Summer 2021) is inactive with its team at EarnIn, and HoneyFi was acquired by a debt-relief firm by June 2021.
Evidence: Acorns release dated 24 June 2025 (page header shows a later date): asset acquisition of Zeta, financial terms not disclosed, co-founders Kevin Hopkins and Aditi Shekar join Acorns; no Zeta user count given (Acorns cites 16 million people served for itself). | Y Combinator lists Ivella (banking and savings products for couples, Summer 2021) as Inactive; CB Insights shows $3.63 million raised, last a $3.5 million seed about four years ago, products sunset and team joined EarnIn. | CB Insights shows HoneyFi at $1.31 million raised and quotes a 4 June 2021 American Banker item saying it was recently acquired by debt-relief firm Strategic Financial Solutions. | Honeydue's joint-banking page (copyright 2024) is a pre-launch waitlist; Honeydue Cash Visa cards issued by Sutton Bank and powered by Marqeta; automatic bill pay 'coming soon'; no user count.
Implication: No couples-money product has reached visible consumer scale or a priced exit, so T23's merge-money half looks like a feature inside a larger bank or platform rather than a standalone business, for Young Consumers above all.
Caveats: Venture-database statuses are undated snapshots (CB Insights lists Ivella as Alive while saying products are sunset); Zeta price and users unknown and an asset sale may be an acqui-hire, not a failure; a CB Insights snippet giving Zeta funding of about $1.5 million was never fetched and is not used; HoneyFi's acquisition rests on a trade-press reference quoted by CB Insights.

Claim: As of October 2026, federal deposit-insurance rules set no relationship test for joint owners, while Capital One's 360 Checking agreement lets any one joint owner withdraw, transfer or close the account without the other's consent.
Evidence: 12 CFR 330.9 (eCFR current): a qualifying joint account needs natural-person co-owners, each with a signature card or equivalent record and equal withdrawal rights; no relationship between co-owners is required (spouses appear only for community property); interests are aggregated per co-owner up to the standard maximum ($250,000 in the rule's example); amendments listed include 84 FR 35027 (2019). | Capital One 360 Checking agreement (page dated 10/14/2026): deposits belong to all owners; any owner may withdraw, transfer or close without the others' consent; joint tenancy with survivorship; if one owner asks the bank not to pay another's items, the bank may (not must) restrict the account and lifts that only on all owners' written agreement; if it does not restrict, all owners stay responsible for items paid; no relationship requirement or divorce provision found. | 12 CFR 1005.6 (Reg E unauthorized-transfer liability) refers only to 'the consumer' and has no joint-holder provision, so the allocation of loss between joint owners is not settled by the section text.
Implication: Federal deposit law does not block shared accounts for unmarried partners or non-couple co-residents, but the standard joint-tenancy contract gives each owner unilateral control, which is the breakup exposure itself, so a formation product needs a different ownership structure; relevant to Young Consumers and Debit-Primary Spenders and to both Territory Candidates.
Caveats: Capital One's agreement is company disclosure and was read in part (about 100,000 of 130,000 characters). The FDIC rule governs insurance, not state ownership or survivorship law, which was not surveyed. Bank practice on unrelated co-owners (denials, friction) is unmeasured. Reg E commentary on joint holders was not fetched, so the loss-allocation question is open, not answered.

Claim: Regulation B as of October 2026 counts single, divorced and widowed people as 'unmarried', bars requiring a spouse's or other person's signature from a creditworthy applicant, and the CFPB's 22 April 2026 final rule (effective 21 July 2026) amended disparate impact, discouragement and special purpose credit program provisions.
Evidence: 12 CFR 1002.2: marital status means unmarried, married or separated as defined by state law; 'unmarried' includes single, divorced or widowed persons; 'applicant' covers anyone who is or may become contractually liable. | 12 CFR 1002.7(d)(1): a creditor shall not require the signature of an applicant's spouse or other person, other than a joint applicant, if the applicant qualifies; 1002.7(c)(1) bars requiring reapplication, changing terms or terminating an account on the basis of a change in marital status. | 12 CFR 1002.5(d)(1): no marital-status inquiry on individual unsecured credit outside community-property situations; otherwise only the terms married, unmarried and separated may be used. | 12 CFR 1026.12(b): credit-card unauthorized use is use without actual, implied or apparent authority and no benefit to the cardholder; liability capped at the lesser of $50 or the value obtained before notice. Federal Register 2026-07804 (91 FR 21620): Reg B final rule published 22 April 2026, effective 21 July 2026, abstract names disparate impact, discouragement and special purpose credit programs.
Implication: Credit rules treat a cohabiting partner as an ordinary applicant and give a bank no legal reason to require marriage, so shared credit for unmarried partners or co-residents faces no federal bar of its own; this is a legal floor, not evidence of demand.
Caveats: eCFR renderer output carried no 'current as of' stamp. The April 2026 rule text itself (federalregister.gov HTML blocked) was not read, so whether its special-purpose-program changes affect programs defined by relationship status is untested; law-firm summaries of removal of the disparate-impact effects test are pointers only. Reg Z authorised-user and joint-obligor commentary not fetched.

Claim: Progyny, the scaled fertility-benefits manager, reported 2025 revenue of $1.289 billion from more than 590 employer clients covering about 7.2 million lives, and collects members' deductibles and coinsurance itself.
Evidence: 10-K filed 27 February 2026: revenue $1,288,661 thousand (2025), $1,167,221 thousand (2024), $1,088,598 thousand (2023); 2025 net income $58,520 thousand. | More than 590 employer clients each with at least 1,000 covered lives; about 7.2 million employees and dependents under contract; over 70 new clients in 2025; no client above 10% of 2025 revenue, versus one at 12% in 2024 that terminated effective 1 January 2025. | Progyny assumes full responsibility for collecting members' deductibles and coinsurance, removing that collection burden and bad debt from provider clinics.
Implication: Fertility finance at scale is employer-paid through a benefits manager that already handles the member's out-of-pocket share, so a consumer bank's reachable pool is the uncovered patient, mainly better-off employed couples rather than Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Company-reported. Revenue is employer billing, not consumer spend; member out-of-pocket totals were not found in the filing text read.

Claim: Fertility coverage is set by employers and state mandates, not lenders: 27% of large employers covered IVF in KFF's 2024 survey, state mandates (25 states plus DC by one count) do not reach self-insured plans, and the October 2025 White House IVF announcement created no mandate, subsidy or tax incentive.
Evidence: KFF fertility-access brief: 27% of large firms offering health benefits covered IVF (2024 KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey); state coverage laws do not apply to self-insured plans, where most people with employer coverage sit; Medicaid rarely covers fertility; a 'upwards of $25,000 per IVF cycle' figure is attributed to a clinic blog. | KFF (27 October 2025) on the 16 October 2025 announcement: TrumpRx discounts on three IVF drugs (CMS estimate of up to $2,200 per cycle); employers may offer fertility benefits as excepted benefits, with excepted-benefit HRA contributions capped at $2,150; no mandate, federal subsidy or new tax incentive; 27% of employers with 200+ workers and 53% with 5,000+ workers offer IVF coverage. | MultiState (1 April 2026): 25 states plus DC require private-insurance fertility coverage with varying scope; Virginia's enrolled HB 328 would add up to three lifetime ART cycles to the 2028 benchmark plan; Medicaid coverage only in New York, Utah and DC, each limited.
Implication: Roughly three in four large employers leave IVF uncovered, which leaves an out-of-pocket gap a lender could fill, but the coverage and cost levers sit with employers, insurers and states, so a bank's role is narrow and skews to upmarket couples.
Caveats: Merged from partnerships-A finding 5 and partnerships-B finding 8. KFF is independent research but its employer figures cover firms offering benefits (large firms), not the share of couples covered. MultiState is a government-relations consultancy that does not name its dataset; mandate counts vary by definition. The $25,000 cycle cost is a clinic-blog figure, context only. The 2025 KFF employer figure and a WTW survey (67%) seen in search were not fetched.

Claim: Consumer fertility lending exists at small scale through specialist non-bank lenders: Future Family reports more than 10,000 families, over $200 million of credit extended and 600-plus partner clinics, and Sunfish reported hundreds of customers in 32 states at its January 2023 $4 million round.
Evidence: Future Family site: loans up to $50,000, APR 9.74% to 23.74%, +$200 million credit extended, +10,000 families, +600 partner clinics; loans originated by Future Family Inc. or an affiliate (NMLS 1813777); 'Baby or Money Back' insurance via an affiliate. | TechCrunch (4 April 2022): Future Family $25 million Series B led by Munich Re Ventures; $150 million total funding including a $100 million credit facility from 2018; 60-month plans of $300-$475 a month; gross transaction volume up 300% in 2021. | TechCrunch (24 January 2023): Sunfish raised $4 million led by Walkabout Ventures; it connects families to lenders rather than lending; over $20 million in loan requests from hundreds of applicants in 32 states; credit lines $12,000-$100,000. | Carrot Fertility blog (21 July 2022): $75 million Series C led by Tiger Global; about 450 customers and nearly 1 million covered lives expected that year (an employer benefit, not consumer finance).
Implication: Fertility credit for consumers is a niche specialty-lending category, so a bank would enter as adjacency with cheaper funding and underwriting, not as zero-to-one, and the buyer is mainly upmarket couples.
Caveats: All figures are company claims; Future Family's are cumulative and undated (vintage set to the fetch year of the page). Funding rounds are investor belief, not demand. Gaia, CapexMD and Kindbody financing could not be verified and are not used.

Claim: The CFPB's May 2023 report found consumers paid about $1 billion of deferred interest on almost $23 billion of medical purchases on deferred-interest cards and loans in 2018-2020, and named fertility treatment among procedures that installment lenders target.
Evidence: Over 17 million medical purchases on deferred-interest terms in 2018-2020; purchase volume peaked at about $8.2 billion in 2019 (CFPB, read from a local PyMuPDF extract). | Medical credit cards are primarily offered by CareCredit (Synchrony), Wells Fargo and Comenity (Bread Financial). | Some installment lenders target low-score patients and others target specific procedures such as fertility treatments; fertility is also listed among services insurance may not cover.
Implication: The proven procedure-finance profit pool is the deferred-interest card regulators have criticised, so a bank entering fertility lending inherits that reputational record, with exposure heaviest for lower-score Debit-Primary borrowers.
Caveats: Data are 2018-2020, published 2023, before the 2025 change in CFPB priorities; current enforcement posture not re-checked. The report is about medical credit generally; fertility appears as an example. The PDF does not parse through WebFetch; verified against output/partnerships/_pdf/cfpb-medical-credit-2023-05.txt.

Claim: Hello Divorce, a leading US online divorce service, raised a $3.25 million seed in October 2022 and sells flat-fee help at $400-$2,000 plus filing fees with hourly divorce financial analysts and a mortgage specialist, but offers no banking or credit product.
Evidence: LawNext (19 October 2022): $3.25 million oversubscribed seed led by The Artemis Fund; then in CA, CO, NY, TX and UT with Florida planned; funds for a 'Hello Next Chapter' module on credit repair, retirement planning, insurance and real estate; no customer count. | Hello Divorce site (fetched 2026): attorney-led plans in 16 states; 'thousands of successful divorces'; $400-$2,000 for an uncontested divorce excluding filing fees versus $15,000-$20,000+ for a lawyer; hourly CDFA services; a divorce mortgage specialist on refinance and assumption; states it is not a law firm; no accounts, loans or credit products listed. | Institute for Divorce Financial Analysts (founded 1993) says it has certified more than 5,000 CDFAs in the US and Canada. | SecureSplit, a divorce financial-modelling tool founded 2024, is self-funded and aimed mainly at professionals (Legal Technology, 6 March 2026).
Implication: Divorce services are legal and advice businesses run by lawyers and a few thousand analysts, and the banking-side steps (mortgage release, joint-credit separation) are referred out, which leaves them open but unpriced, mainly for older asset-holding households.
Caveats: Trade press (LawNext) is the primary record of the round. Customer counts are vague company claims. A company FAQ claim that about half of customers are high net worth was not verified and is not used. The brief's pointer 'SplitReady' did not resolve to any company; Divorce.com yielded no primary page. FINRA's CDFA facts sit in the regulatory row.

Claim: Divorce financial analysis carries no licence of its own (the CDFA is a private designation FINRA does not endorse), while legal document help is bounded by state unauthorised-practice rules, as in Arizona where certified preparers may give general legal information but not legal advice.
Evidence: FINRA: the CDFA is issued by the Institute for Divorce Financial Analysts; requires a bachelor's degree plus three years' experience (or five years without a degree) and a proctored exam; 30 divorce-related CE hours every two years; FINRA does not approve or endorse any designation; fiduciary status not addressed. | Arizona Supreme Court certified legal document preparer page (undated): preparers may help unrepresented people with documents and give general legal information but may not give legal advice; links to family law without naming divorce. | Harvard Center on the Legal Profession (July/August 2018): Arizona preparers certified since 2003 for factual legal information only; Utah was approving licensed paralegal practitioners with family law among their services; California legal document assistants must post a bond of at least $25,000.
Implication: A bank could offer divorce financial planning without a special licence, but the decree and document work that drives outcomes is lawyer or licensed-preparer territory by state, so a bank service would sit beside legal help rather than bundle it.
Caveats: Merged the FINRA CDFA support from partnerships-A finding 7. Investment advice to a divorcing client would trigger adviser rules (not examined); Capital One offers no brokerage or wealth service. State UPL sampled through Arizona only, plus a 2018 article; Utah and Washington programme status not verified from primary pages.

Claim: A divorce transfer is exempt from due-on-sale under federal rule and Fannie Mae policy, but the departing borrower is released only if the servicer finds the remaining spouse creditworthy and, where there is mortgage insurance, the insurer agrees; otherwise release is denied and the transfer proceeds.
Evidence: 12 CFR 191.5(b)(1)(v): a lender may not exercise due-on-sale on a transfer from a decree of dissolution of marriage, legal separation agreement or incidental property settlement by which the spouse becomes an owner and occupies. | Fannie Mae Servicing Guide D1-4.1-02 (dated 13 August 2025): transfer to a spouse under a divorce decree is exempt and processed without review unless the previous borrower requests release, when the servicer must find the transferee's credit and financial capacity acceptable; occupancy is not required for loans acquired on or after 1 June 2016. | Guide F-1-28 (dated 11 March 2026): review follows Selling Guide credit rules, via DU as a limited cash-out refinance for unmodified loans; with MI the insurer must agree, and the servicer must deny release if it does not; transfer may proceed without release. Selling Guide B3-6-06 (dated 2 September 2026): a non-released departing borrower's contingent liability can be excluded from debts once title transfer is documented. | CFPB (17 December 2024), complaints December 2021-August 2024: servicers told successors to refinance at higher rates when assumption was available; VA expects decisions within 45 calendar days, and one Missouri widow reported 156 days; CFPB asked investors to stop servicer policies that unnecessarily push refinancing.
Implication: The best-documented divorce pain is decided by investor rules and the mortgage servicer, and Capital One has not originated mortgages since 2017, so a Capital One transition service would stand outside the decision that matters; its possible edge is the remaining spouse's deposit and income record as evidence of capacity.
Caveats: Freddie Mac Guide pages were JavaScript-rendered and unread; FHA and VA assumption rules and 2025-2026 assumption fees could not be read (HUD pages 404 or binary), so those halves are gaps. No 2025-2026 CFPB successor-in-interest enforcement found. The Capital One mortgage facts come from the round-1 franchise slice, not re-fetched here.

Claim: The Federal Register through October 2026 holds no proposed or final CFPB coerced-debt rule: the only coerced-debt documents are the 13 December 2024 notice and a 7 March 2025 comment-period extension.
Evidence: Federal Register API query (CFPB, 'coerced debt identity theft Regulation V', newest first): 'Identity Theft and Coerced Debt' (2024-12-13, listed as Proposed Rule category) and its 'Extension of Comment Period' (2025-03-07) are the only coerced-debt entries; the other eight results are unrelated Reg V, F, E and Z rules. | The corpus records the prevalence figures in the December 2024 notice as CFPB's characterisation of advocacy research (corpus row 4, Low).
Implication: A protective dissolution service cannot rely on a federal coerced-debt rule as of October 2026; any such service would be voluntary bank policy for thin-file Debit-Primary customers with no regulatory edge.
Caveats: Absence rests on one API query and shows no later document, not a withdrawal. The December 2024 document was an advance notice (ANPRM), filed under the Federal Register's proposed-rule category. A search-summary claim of a May 2026 agenda step was not confirmed and is not used.

Claim: No US bank programme or US regulator statement on inferring divorce or marriage from transaction data was found, while the UK FCA's FG21/1 lists relationship breakdown as a life-event driver of vulnerability that calls for care.
Evidence: FCA FG21/1 (published 23 February 2021, page updated 22 July 2026): four key drivers of vulnerability; the life-events driver reads 'bereavement, job loss or relationship breakdown'; paragraph 2.10 says a relationship breakdown may lead to further vulnerability such as mental ill-health or low resilience (verified in a local PyMuPDF extract; the HTML landing page's summary gives only 'new caring responsibilities' as its example). | 12 CFR 1016.13 (GLBA privacy) covers disclosure to nonaffiliated service providers and joint marketing and does not address a bank's own internal use of transaction data; no CFPB or OCC statement on inferring marriage or divorce was found.
Implication: Detecting a breakup from transactions is untested in US law and framed by the nearest regulator as a moment for restraint, so the safer form is customer-initiated ('we are separating') rather than inferred.
Caveats: UK guidance is not US law and addresses vulnerable-customer treatment, not data inference. US absence is a gap in what was found (patents, a European 60-million-transaction study and vendor content were seen only in search and not fetched). Regulation P scope and state privacy laws were not read. The PDF does not parse via WebFetch; verified against output/partnerships/_pdf/fg21-1.txt.

Claim: Capital One offers joint 360 Checking accounts added online with a one-time passcode, says (3 March 2026) it does not offer joint credit cards, and its only divorce content found is an October 2018 education article whose sole product reference is CreditWise.
Evidence: Help centre: a joint holder is added online via account services if the invitee can receive a one-time passcode, or at a branch for branch accounts; the page does not cover removing a joint holder. | Capital One article (3 March 2026): 'Capital One doesn't offer joint credit cards'; authorised users can be added without additional applications or credit checks; no mention of divorce. | 'Managing Money During a Divorce' (18 October 2018): ten steps (credit reports, closing joint accounts by certified letter, utilities, own credit, one-income budget, dividing debt, taxes, health coverage, beneficiaries, legal documents); CreditWise is the only product named; balances remain the holder's responsibility. | A site search surfaced no divorce or life-event team or product.
Implication: A formation or transition product would be additive, not a duplicate of a Capital One programme, but it is also far from current capability: the card side cannot hold two obligors and the deposit side has no removal or life-event flow.
Caveats: Supports refers to additivity only, not demand. Absence is inferred from three pages and one site search, not an internal inventory; unpublished work may exist.

Claim: Braid, the only funded US shared account for pooling money with friends, roommates and family, shut in September 2023 after about $10 million of venture funding, with its founder blaming sponsor-bank and third-party dependency rather than lack of users.
Evidence: TechCrunch (9 October 2023): founded January 2019; about $10 million over multiple rounds from Index Ventures, Accel and others; a sponsor-bank problem left it 'effectively in a coma' from July 2022 to January 2023, processing $0 in payment volume; a new sponsor bank was found but the company continued to struggle. | The founder wrote that every added partner could break key parts of the stack and that building mostly in-house was the only way unit economics worked; she bought the IP at auction and said every customer dollar was cashed out. | TechCrunch (15 October 2023) describes Braid as a shared wallet for friends and family, backed by Index and Accel, and gives sponsor-bank and third-party software problems as causes.
Implication: The co-resident shared-account candidate has no surviving scaled example, and the stated failure cause (dependency on a sponsor bank) is exactly what a regulated deposit bank removes, so the death neither proves nor disproves demand among Debit-Primary and Young Consumer households.
Caveats: Trade press is the primary record of the shutdown; the founder's blog was not fetched. Cause is the founder's own account. Direction changed from Contradicts to Mixed because the failure was on cost structure, which cuts against fintechs and for a bank, not against the white-space proposition.

Claim: Splitwise, the only scaled multi-person money app found, reported tens of millions of registered users and about $90 billion of expenses shared since 2011 at its April 2021 $20 million Series A, and earns from a $3-a-month Pro tier, not from holding funds.
Evidence: TechCrunch (28 April 2021): $20 million Series A led by Insight Partners after about $9 million raised; tens of millions of registered users; active users undisclosed. | Same article: about $90 billion of expenses shared since 2011 (company calculation); no transaction fees or stored consumer funds; Pro at $3 a month. | Splitwise site (2026): free app, no user count or Pro price shown; footer links to Splitwise Pay, Splitwise Card and a Coastal Community Bank privacy policy without describing them.
Implication: Multi-adult households coordinate money at scale through an IOU ledger over separate accounts, the coordination form the corpus says survives, and no bank owns it; relevant to both candidates for Debit-Primary Spenders and Young Consumers.
Caveats: Registered, not active, users; figures five years old and company-reported. The Coastal Community Bank link suggests a sponsor-bank product, but its role is undescribed. A vendor revenue estimate seen in search was not verified and is not used.

Claim: Cohabiting adults aged 18-64 grew from 15.2 million in 2012 to 18.4 million in 2022, with the highest rate (19.0%) at ages 25-29.
Evidence: Cohabiting adults 18-64: 15.2 million (7.75%) in 2012 to 18.4 million (9.06%) in 2022; ages 25-29 from 15.5% to 19.0% (BGSU NCFMR, CPS/IPUMS). | Ever-cohabited women 19-44: one-third in 1987, 64% in 2013, 56% in 2022; highest (66%) for women without a high school diploma (BGSU NCFMR, NSFG). | In 2018, 9% of 18-24-year-olds lived with an unmarried partner versus 7% with a spouse (Census CPS).
Implication: A large, growing population forms households with no legal act, which supports a formation product that does not depend on marriage, skewing to Young Consumers and, by education, Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Corpus notes: the 2022 NSFG moved to mixed-mode interviewing, so part of the 2013-2022 decline may be measurement. Spot-checked 2026-10-26: 15,222,203 and 18,404,227 and 19.0% confirmed on the BGSU page.

Claim: Married couples with no joint bank account rose from 15% in 1996 to 23% in 2023, and only 16% of unmarried cohabiting couples hold a joint account.
Evidence: Married couples with no joint account: 15% (1996) to 23% (2023); all-joint structures fell from 53% to 40%; mixed joint-plus-separate rose from 9% to 17% (Census SIPP). | Cohabiting couples hold joint accounts at 16%, 25% with minor children (Census SIPP). | 47% of women who married at 20-24 hold all-joint accounts versus 29% of those who married at 30-34.
Implication: Couples are merging money less, so a viable T23 form is a coordination layer over separate accounts rather than a merged account, strongest for later-marrying and cohabiting couples.
Caveats: Corpus notes: SIPP account type is respondent-reported. Spot-checked 2026-10-26: 15%, 23% and 16% confirmed on the Census story.

Claim: In CFPB's credit panel, 37.5% of consumers with a credit record were credit-linked in June 2024, while 54% of a linked survey sample say they share finances with a partner against 44.9% identifiable as linked.
Evidence: 37.5% credit-linked in June 2024, stable at 36-38% since 2009 (CFPB Consumer Credit Information Panel). | About a third of nominally individual auto, mortgage and student loans and nearly half of individual card accounts belong to a credit-linked consumer; CFPB calls this likely an undercount. | Joint deposit accounts largely do not appear in credit data; sharing rent, food or childcare from separate accounts is generally not detectable in credit data (CFPB).
Implication: Household exposure is invisible to bureau underwriting, but a deposit bank that sees both partners' flows holds data the bureaus lack, which bears on T23 formation and T10 unwinding for both segments.
Caveats: Corpus notes: single regulator source; restrictive linked definition; the 54% figure is survey self-report inside an administrative report. Not re-fetched in this pass.

Claim: The crude US divorce rate fell from 4.0 per 1,000 in 2000 to 2.4 in 2023, while divorce among women 55-64 rose from 4 to 11 per 1,000 married women between 1990 and 2017.
Evidence: Women 55-64: 4 to 11 per 1,000 married women 1990-2017; women 65+ from 1 to 6; the 15-24 rate fell from 47 to 27 (BGSU NCFMR). | First-divorce rates in 2023 highest at 18-29 (17.6 men, 19.3 women per 1,000 married) and declining in every age band since 2008 (BGSU NCFMR). | Crude divorce rate 4.0 per 1,000 (2000) to 2.4 (2023) (CDC/NCHS); refined rate 22.6 (1980 peak) to 14.6 per 1,000 married women (2022).
Implication: Fewer divorces weaken a volume play while the shift to older, asset-holding divorcees raises value per event, but those customers sit outside the Young Consumer and Debit-Primary core.
Caveats: Corpus notes: compositional shift in a shrinking pool; NCHS 2023 excludes CA, HI, IN, MN and NM; age series ends 2017. Not re-fetched in this pass.

Claim: CFPB's review of complaints from December 2021 to August 2024 found homeowners waiting months to years for release, successor status or assumption after divorce or death, against federal timeframes of about 45 calendar days.
Evidence: 2021 ACS homeownership: 80% of married, 59% of divorced and 48% of never-married adults (BGSU NCFMR). | Complaints show servicers insisting on refinance at higher rates rather than assumption, and refusing to release original borrowers after successors had paid for long periods (CFPB). | CFPB April 2026: about 52% of consumers with a mortgage share it; over two-thirds of those also share at least one credit card.
Implication: The best-evidenced divorce pain is mortgage and joint-credit unwinding, a servicing problem a lender could address, though homeowning divorcing couples skew away from Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Corpus notes: complaint narratives show severity, not frequency; homeownership by marital status is a 2021 cross-section. The 45-day figure is the VA assumption timeline (confirmed on the CFPB page in this pass while verifying partnerships-10).

Claim: Dissolution of cohabiting unions among women who formed a union at 18-25 rose from 27.6% (1960-1964 birth cohort) to 45.2% (1985-1989 cohort), while marital dissolution fell from 22.0% to 17.5%.
Evidence: Four NSFG waves: cohabitation dissolution 27.6% to 45.2% across those cohorts; marital dissolution 22.0% to 17.5% (Eickmeyer, Journal of Marriage and Family, 2018, Table 1). | Overall union instability rose from 31.4% to 44.4%, entirely on the cohabitation side. | CFPB's successor-in-interest and assumption protections run to divorce and death; unmarried partners who split have no decree and no equivalent servicing protection.
Implication: The majority dissolution mode for Young Consumers has no legal or servicing framework, which widens T10's divorce half to unmarried breakups whose financial mechanics are unmeasured.
Caveats: Corpus notes: cohorts end 1985-1989; the no-framework half rests on CFPB protection scope, not a measurement. Spot-checked 2026-10-26: 27.6%, 45.2%, 22.0% and 17.5% confirmed; the two rates use different bases (ever-cohabited vs ever-married women), so they are not shares of one group.

Claim: Territory Candidate (financial infrastructure for unmarried partners, from joint start to unwind): unmarried cohabiting partners, who hold joint accounts at 16% and whose unions dissolve at 45.2% for the 1985-1989 cohort, would use a bank that offers a shared-money structure at formation and a defined unwinding path at breakup.
Evidence: Cohabiting adults 18-64 reached 18.4 million in 2022, and cohabiting couples hold joint accounts at 16% (25% with minor children) (BGSU NCFMR; Census SIPP). | Cohabitation dissolution reached 45.2% for the 1985-1989 cohort, with no decree or servicing protection for unmarried partners (Eickmeyer 2018; CFPB 2024). | An unmarried partner named as a retirement-plan beneficiary has no statutory consent protection, unlike a spouse; and a partnered household looks financially single to bureau data (DOL EBSA; CFPB 2026).
Implication: This reframes T23 formation and T10 dissolution around unmarried partners, the larger and younger population, and fits Young Consumers; research rows partnerships-02 and partnerships-03 show no federal bar, but nothing shows these partners want a structure or would pay for it.
Caveats: The combined proposition is the corpus miner's inference; no source measures unmarried partners' financial unwinding. Three of the cited figures were spot-checked in this pass (BGSU, Census, PMC). Confidence Low because demand is untested.

Claim: Territory Candidate (shared accounts and credit for co-residents who are not couples): unrelated adults sharing a home, including roommates, siblings and chosen family, would use a bank that provides shared accounts and shared credit, because the regulatory floor allows it and current practice does not.
Evidence: Adults 50-74 living with a sibling or roommate rose from 1.2 million (1990) to 3.2 million (2016); single young adults living with a sibling or roommate rose from about 5.0 million to about 6.5 million (1990-2022) (BGSU NCFMR). | FDIC joint-account insurance (12 CFR 330.9) has no relationship test, and NCUA's 1999 opinion defines a household by shared residence and a single economic unit. | Among adults 50-74 sharing housing, poverty is 31% for women living with a roommate versus 8% for women living with a sibling (BGSU NCFMR).
Implication: The regulatory floor is verified (re-confirmed in partnerships-02 and partnerships-03) and the population is large, but the only funded attempt (Braid, partnerships-14) died and the scaled behaviour is an IOU ledger (Splitwise, partnerships-15), so this is a hypothesis for Debit-Primary households, not a finding.
Caveats: The 'current practice does not' half is inference with no data on denials or product availability. Roommate arrangements may be short and transactional, weakening the pooling need. ACS dropped its roomer/boarder category in 2019.

Claim: Fertility-finance startups raised Series A rounds in January 2025 (Sunfish $10M; Gaia $14M, later a $100M debt facility) for outcome-contingent IVF financing sold through clinics.
