Evidence: Sunfish: $10M Series A led by Haymaker Ventures, reported 29 January 2025 (Femtech Insider); membership with financial tools and cost prediction, partial refunds if treatment fails or predictions are wrong; the success programme is at 14 US clinic locations and lending reaches nearly 100 | Gaia: $14M Series A led by Valar Ventures in January 2025, $37M equity in total, and a $100M debt facility from Viola Credit (Coverager, facility undated); covers the next IVF cycle at no extra cost if the first fails
Implication: Investors back outcome-contingent fertility credit distributed through clinics, so the fertility half of T23 already has specialist players and is medical financing (T12-adjacent) rather than household money merging.
Caveats: Investor interest, not demand; no customer counts. Femtech Insider cost-per-cycle figures are unsourced and not used. Gaia's US scale and the facility date were not confirmed. Axios Pro original returned 403 in round 1. Medical credit is reputationally sensitive for a bank. Nothing here tests the merge-and-unwind half of T23.

Claim: Checking-or-savings complaint narratives naming a joint account together with a separation term numbered 8 in 2023, 12 in 2024, 21 in 2025 and 2 to mid-August 2026, 43 in all, far below the stress test's low-hundreds-a-year benchmark.
Evidence: Counts by year 8 / 12 / 21 / 2; a looser joint-account pattern (also joint checking, joint savings, joint bank account) gives 10 / 14 / 29 / 6 | Joint account appears in 230 / 258 / 330 / 138 checking-or-savings narratives in those years, so a separation term appears in about 4 to 6% of them; normalised, 2.9, 4.1, 4.1 and 1.1 per 10,000 narratives (researcher arithmetic) | Issues among the 43: managing an account 24, closing an account 12; terms: my ex 25, divorce 19, ex-husband 15, ex-wife 8, separated 8, ex-partner 2 | Paraphrased cases: banks refusing to close or remove a name from a joint account without the ex-spouse; an ex draining an account; a payroll deposit taken for an ex-partner's debts on a shared account
Implication: On the stress test's own terms (a count in the low hundreds a year shows no deposit-side pain at scale), 8 to 21 a year confirms the kill on the complaint leg of the joint-account exit test; the conversion-rate and remaining-owner attrition legs need Capital One data and stay open.
Caveats: Same archive provenance and opt-in limits as transfer-92 (56 to 61% of checking-or-savings complaints in 2023 and 2025 carry a narrative), so true complaint counts are somewhat higher, and many people would complain to the bank or a state regulator instead. The regex is narrow and some matches are unrelated to separation, so 43 is an upper bound on the strict reading. The cases show the pain is real where it occurs.

Claim: Synchrony's Health & Wellness platform (CareCredit plus partners such as Walgreens) held $15.5B of loan receivables and 7.75M average active accounts in 2025, earned $3.8B or 17% of Synchrony's interest and fees on loans, sold through more than 290,000 locations and funded by a bank that draws 84% of its funding from deposits, so deposit-funded medical financing at consumer scale is already owned by a regulated bank.
Evidence: Synchrony FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-02-06): Health & Wellness purchase volume $15,654M (2024: $15,678M); period-end loan receivables $15,545M (2024: $15,436M); average active accounts 7,750 thousand; interest and fees on loans $3,783M, described as $3.8B or 17% of total interest and fees on loans. | Same filing: network exceeded 290,000 provider and retail locations at 2025-12-31; excluding Walgreens no single partner exceeded 0.7% of total interest and fees; dental-originated accounts were 49% of Health & Wellness interest and fees; about 62% of CareCredit network purchase volume in 2025 came from repeat use. | Same filing: deferred-interest promotions cover 17.7% of total loan receivables (all platforms); about 80% of deferred-interest customer transactions are typically paid off before interest is assessed; Health & Wellness interest and fees rose $112M or 3.1%, driven by receivables yield, not volume; the platform is described as more susceptible to health-related regulation. | Same filing: deposits $81.1B, 84% of total funding sources, at 2025-12-31.
Implication: A bank entering T12 as a financier competes with a deposit-funded incumbent holding 290,000 points of care, so the funding edge is already taken and any opening sits in the unfinanced or provider-unreached slice, for Debit-Primary Spenders as much as anyone.
Caveats: Company filing; merged from rupture-A 1 and rupture-B 3. Verified against a local copy of the filing whose byte size matches the live EDGAR document. Receivables include Walgreens and pet care, not only medical bills. No Health & Wellness loss rate, and no share of volume from thin-file patients, is disclosed. The 17.7% deferred-interest share is company-wide, not platform-specific.

Claim: The funded medical-bill companies found sell to providers, health plans or employers, and the consumer-paid or consumer-side services found are small (Resolve claims $55.2M of savings to date on success fees) or donor-funded (Dollar For), so the bill-resolution channel is owned provider-side and consumer willingness to pay is unproven.
Evidence: Cedar site (fetched 2026-10-26): customers are health systems, hospitals and clinician groups; products include Cedar Pay, Cedar Cover and Cedar Support; claims $13.6B in patient payments processed and both 58M+ and 50M patients served (not reconciled on the page). | PayZen site (fetched 2026-10-26): sold to hospitals and health systems; 'always interest-free, always fee-free' patient plans; integrations with Epic and Cerner; claims about 30% average collection lift and a 78% enrollment success rate. Goodbill site: serves self-funded plans, employers and TPAs (claims 13K+ employers, 600K+ members) with claim review, 501(r) and hospital bill advocacy. | Resolve site (fetched 2026-10-26): $250 deposit plus 25% success fee (bills $5K-$15K) or $499 plus 10% (larger bills), minimum total fee $1,000 ($2,500 above $200K); counter shows $55,235,678 total savings to date; says it does not sell loans or consolidation. | Dollar For site (fetched 2026-10-26): nonprofit, '100% funded by generous donors', free to patients, prepares hospital charity-care applications; no aggregate results on the page.
Implication: A consumer bank offering to negotiate, finance and plan bills would sell to a patient whose bill the provider already routes through Cedar, PayZen or CareCredit, and the only consumer-side services are small or charitable, which points to low willingness to pay among Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Merged from rupture-A 2 and 3. All figures are self-reported marketing claims with no method or audit; Resolve's total has no date. Provider-pays is the revealed business model; it does not prove patients would not pay. Dollar For is also a benefits non-take-up (T04-type) service. PayZen and Cedar funding rounds were seen only in search snippets (403) and are not cited.

Claim: HealthEquity administered 10.6M HSAs holding $36.5B at 31 January 2026, reaching consumers through employers and health plans and placing HSA cash with insurer and depository partners, so pre-funded health-cost saving is an established custodial category in which banks supply deposits rather than own the relationship.
Evidence: HealthEquity FY2026 10-K (filed 2026-03-17): 10.6M HSAs and $36.5B HSA Assets (HSA cash $17,982M, investments $18,482M; total $36,464M vs $32,111M, up 14%), plus 7.2M other consumer-directed benefit accounts, 17.8M total accounts. | Same filing: share of HSA Assets grew from 4% in December 2010 to 20% as of June 2025 (company citing Devenir). | Same filing: consumers reached mainly through employer Clients and health-plan Network Partners; HSA cash held with insurance company partners and federally insured bank and credit union 'Depository Partners'.
Implication: The planning side of T12 already has a scaled custodian with employer distribution that bypasses the consumer bank, whose role in the chain is depository partner, not relationship owner.
Caveats: Company filing, verified against a local copy matching the live EDGAR document. HSAs are saving, not shock finance, and only HDHP-eligible people can open one, a narrower group than households hit by a bill. The Devenir share is relayed by HealthEquity.

Claim: The CFPB's January 2025 rule barring most medical debt from credit reports was vacated on 11 July 2025 by the E.D. Texas in Cornerstone Credit Union League v. CFPB on a joint request from the Bureau and the plaintiffs, so no federal rule removes medical collections from credit files as of October 2026.
Evidence: CFPB rule page (fetched 2026-10-26): issued 2025-01-07; Federal Register 2025-01-14 (correction 2025-01-27); effective date 2025-03-17, stayed to 2025-06-15; status vacated. | Same page: vacated 2025-07-11 by the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Texas; the Bureau and plaintiffs jointly requested vacatur; the court held the rule exceeded the Bureau's authority and conflicted with the FCRA, which allows coded medical information, and that the Bureau could not limit report contents based on state law. | The page does not mention an appeal.
Implication: Medical marks stay on credit files, which keeps the T12 and T18 problem alive but gives a bank no federal hook and no federal clean-up to ride, so T12 must stand on its own economics for Debit-Primary Spenders with medical collections.
Caveats: Single primary page; appeal status beyond what the page shows not confirmed. The vacatur reflects the 2025 change in Bureau policy as much as the merits. State medical-debt reporting laws exist separately (corpus) and were not re-verified. A related ACA International case seen in an NCLC snippet was not fetched.

Claim: The CFPB ordered CareCredit's bank to refund up to $34.1 million in December 2013 for deceptive deferred-interest health-card enrollment and in May 2023 reported that patients paid about $1 billion in deferred interest on medical cards and loans in 2018-2020, and state reforms now target provider conduct because preemption shields federally chartered banks.
Evidence: CFPB press release, 2013-12-10: GE Capital Retail Bank and CareCredit to refund up to $34.1M to potentially more than 1 million consumers; providers misled some consumers on deferred-interest terms, many never received agreements, office staff had little or no CareCredit training; 26.99% interest charged. CFPB order terminating the consent order (September 2021): at least $34.1M in redress provided. | CFPB press release, 2023-05-04: in 2018-2020 patients used medical credit cards and installment loans for almost $23B of care across more than 17M purchases and paid about $1B in deferred interest; typical rates about 26.99% (cards) and 16% (installment loans). | NCLC guide (advocacy; file dated 2026.06): California, Connecticut, Illinois and New York have enacted reforms; some lender-side solutions will not apply to federally chartered banks because of federal preemption, so a second set targets provider conduct.
Implication: The proven bank profit pool in medical financing is the deferred-interest mechanism regulators have attacked twice, so a bank entering T12 as a financier inherits that record and the thesis should not be read as 'finance medical bills' for any segment.
Caveats: 2013 order entered by consent; the 2023 figures rest on the CFPB press release because the report PDF was not fetched. NCLC is an advocacy source and the preemption point is its summary, not a court holding; enacted state text was not read; NCLC PDF verified from a local extract matching the live file. No 2025-2026 federal action on medical cards was found.

Claim: Chime's transaction and risk losses rose 85% to $407.3M in 2025 as it scaled MyPay, SpotMe and Instant Loans for direct-deposit members, and Varo Bank's October 2026 agreement routinely offers advances up to $700, so pre-approved shock liquidity from deposit data is already sold at neobank scale and carries a heavy loss cost.
Evidence: Chime FY2025 10-K (filed 2026-03-06): transaction and risk losses $407.3M (2024: $219.7M; 2023: $152.4M) on revenue of $2,186.8M (losses about 18.6% of revenue, compiler arithmetic); transaction margin 69% vs 74% in 2024. | Same filing: the increase included $121.5M from MyPay (full launch July 2024), $29.3M from SpotMe and other negative balances 'due to higher SpotMe volume and isolated fraud incidents', and $24.7M from Instant Loans (fully launched March 2025); SpotMe is monetized partly by voluntary tips. | Same filing: SpotMe, MyPay, Instant Loans and related products are available only to members with qualifying direct deposits; MyPay and Instant Loans are not yet in all 50 states; Chime expects transaction margin to remain flat or decrease further as liquidity products scale. | Varo Advance Account Agreement effective 2026-10-06: open-end line of credit from Varo Bank, N.A., repaid within 30 days; routinely up to $250 without and up to $700 with Qualifying Deposits; Varo may test up to $1,000.
Implication: Deposit-data shock liquidity is not white space; a bank's opening is price, loss rate and trust for Debit-Primary Spenders, and any entrant must be funded to carry a loss cost that Chime says is compressing its margin.
Caveats: Company filing and contract, verified against local copies matching the live documents. Losses combine MyPay, SpotMe, overdrawn accounts and disputes; no SpotMe usage count or product-level loss rate is disclosed. No Varo volume or loss data. Possible Finance (marketing claims only) was dropped.

Claim: Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Wells Fargo all sell flat-fee small-dollar loans to checking customers, but in Fed credit-bureau data banks held only about $319 million of a $1.4 billion small-dollar loan stock at 2023Q4, and Bank of America's reported 1.6 million Balance Assist loans of more than $700 million since 2020 went about 80% to repeat borrowers.
Evidence: Fed FEDS Note (2024-07-19; 5% NY Fed CCP/Equifax sample, 2010-2023; loans with a limit of $1,000 or less opened in the prior two quarters): about $1.4B across 2.7M accounts at 2023Q4; banks about 22% ($319M), up from about 6% before 2019; about 12% of balances delinquent, 8.4% at depository institutions; median $507; not all such loans are reported to bureaus. | Bank of America release (2023-09-13): Balance Assist topped 1 million loans since its March 2021 national launch, new originations up more than 10% on the prior year, up to $500 in $100 increments for a $5 flat fee. American Banker (2024-10-15): 1.6M loans for more than $700M since launch, about 80% repeat borrowers, effective APR 5.99%-29.76%. | Wells Fargo release (2022-11-16): Flex Loan $250 for $12 or $500 for $20, four monthly payments, digital only, no usage figure; American Banker relays more than 350,000 loans per Wells Fargo's 2023 annual report. U.S. Bank blog (2022-09-21): Simple Loan up to $1,000 over three months at $6 per $100 after a 50% cut in 2021, needs six months of account history and three months of recurring direct deposits; bank estimates more than $25M saved versus payday; 58% of borrowers used it for unexpected expenses. | Scale contrast (compiler arithmetic from sourced numbers): $700M over about four years at Bank of America versus the CFPB's $9.1B 2022 overdraft revenue estimate (finding rupture-08).
Implication: A bank-owned below-overdraft shock loan is not zero-to-one: large banks already offer it and it has stayed a feature rather than a line of business, so T16 needs an approach that reaches people these products miss without the repeat-borrowing pattern, for Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Merged from rupture-A 6 and rupture-B 6. The Fed note is administrative; bank volumes are company statements, two of them relayed by American Banker (secondary, no filing found). The Fed stock excludes unreported loans, EWA and BNPL and is not comparable to cumulative loan counts. No bank discloses loss rates. Huntington Standby Cash (403) and Truist not verified; Flex Loan availability in 2026 not confirmed.

Claim: The CFPB's December 2024 overdraft rule for institutions above $10 billion in assets was disapproved by a joint resolution signed 12 May 2025 and has no force or effect, leaving a pool the CFPB estimated at $9.1 billion in 2022, of which $6.16 billion went to institutions above $10 billion.
Evidence: CFPB overdraft resource page (fetched 2026-10-26): the President signed a joint resolution disapproving the final rule on 2025-05-12; the rule 'has no force or effect'; the rest of Regulations E and Z is unchanged. CFPB final-rule page: issued 2024-12-12, Federal Register 2024-12-30 (89 FR 106768), effective date 2025-10-01. | Final rule text: marketwide overdraft revenue an estimated $9.1B in 2022 ($7.9B in 2019 dollars, a 37% real drop); $6.16B, 68%, earned by institutions above $10B; most charge $30 to $37 per overdraft and more than half charge $35; nearly two-thirds of banks above $10B had eliminated NSF fees (CFPB October 2023 data spotlight).
Implication: With no cap, pricing shock liquidity below overdraft is a competitive choice, not a compliance one, and the pool being undercut is fee income at the largest banks, mostly paid by Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: The 2022 figures are CFPB estimates from Call Reports; the corpus carries an NCLC (advocacy) estimate of $12.4B for 2025 by a different method, not re-verified here. The final-rule page itself shows no disapproval note; the signing date rests on the CFPB resource page because congress.gov returned 403. Rule PDF verified from a local extract matching the live file.

Claim: Capital One states it has eliminated all overdraft fees for consumer banking customers, but its no-fee overdraft requires at least $250 of deposits in two of the previous three calendar months and other overdrawing transactions are generally declined, and no small-dollar loan or line of credit appears on its checking pages.
Evidence: capitalone.com overdraft options page (fetched 2026-10-26): 'Capital One has completely eliminated all overdraft fees for its consumer banking customers'; options are no-fee overdraft, auto-decline and free transfer; no-fee overdraft needs at least $250 deposited in two of the previous three calendar months; new accounts qualify at the earliest in the third calendar month; internal Capital One transfers do not count; if the requirement is not met the bank will 'generally decline' overdrawing transactions; debit and ATM coverage on request. No date for the change. | 360 Checking page (fetched 2026-10-26): no overdraft fees; early direct deposit up to 2 days earlier; no small-dollar loan, line of credit or cash advance mentioned. | Capital One emergency-loans explainer (fetched 2026-10-26): names no Capital One emergency loan; says such loans 'might be available from banks, credit unions, online lenders and more' and points readers to Capital One credit cards.
Implication: T16's 'priced below overdraft' claim has nothing to undercut at Capital One, which narrows the opportunity to households the $250-deposit rule declines or that need more than an overdraft; cannibalization risk is low and only a new credit product would add revenue.
Caveats: Company statements, not tested against customer experience; the fee-elimination date was not found on a dated primary page. Absence of a small-dollar product is inferred from non-mention on three pages, not a company statement; Discover personal loans and card cash advances were not checked.

Claim: The OCC, Fed, FDIC and NCUA issued interagency principles for responsible small-dollar loans on 20 May 2020, the FDIC exam manual says compliant programs generally face no criticism but flags high charge-off and reborrowing as signs of harm, and the FDIC's 2008-2009 pilot found interest and fees not always sufficient for robust short-term profit.
Evidence: FDIC FIL-58-2020 (2020-05-20): FDIC, Federal Reserve, OCC and NCUA issued the 'Interagency Lending Principles for Responsible Small-Dollar Loans'. | FDIC Consumer Compliance Examination Manual V-17 (fetched 2026-10-26): programs consistent with the guidelines 'will generally not be subject to examination criticism, if appropriately managed'; high charge-off or default rates or high refinancing or reborrowing may suggest elevated consumer harm; unaffordable payments, no limits on extensions or renewals, and simultaneous loans are risk factors; UDAP, UDAAP or ECOA violations may warrant a CRA downgrade. | FDIC FIL-31-2010 (2010-06-24) and FDIC Quarterly 2010 vol. 4 no. 2: 28 banks made more than 34,400 small-dollar loans with $40.2M principal; default rates were in line with similar unsecured loans; the cumulative charge-off ratio on loans up to $1,000 was 6.2% at 2009Q4; interest and fees 'are not always sufficient to achieve robust short-term profitability', and about three-quarters of pilot bankers used the loans to build or retain relationships.
Implication: Regulation does not block a bank from T16 and mildly supports it, but the only regulator-recorded economics are relationship and retention value, not standalone profit, and Bank of America's 80% repeat share is the pattern examiners watch, for Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: The 2020 principles' content (scope exclusions) was not on the fetched FIL page and is not asserted. The pilot is 2008-2009, community-bank-heavy, with a 36% APR template and loans up to $2,500. The pilot PDF's two-column layout made the unsecured-loan comparator ratio ambiguous, so it is omitted; verified from a local extract matching the live file. Tying the 80% repeat share to the exam-manual signal is the researcher's reading.

Claim: In Q2 2026 US consumers owed about $281 billion on unsecured personal loans (TransUnion) against $1.263 trillion of card balances (NY Fed), so the personal-loan market that would carry consolidation is roughly a fifth the size of the card balances it could refinance.
Evidence: TransUnion Q2 2026 Credit Industry Insights (released 2026-08-06): unsecured personal loan balances $281B; 26.9M consumers; 33.3M accounts; originations 6.4M in the prior quarter, up 19.5% year on year; borrower-level 60+ days past due 3.81% vs 3.37% a year earlier; subprime originations +29%, super prime +9%; personal loans called 'a key tool for debt consolidation and refinancing'; bankcard balances $1.14T | Reconciliation (compiler and researcher arithmetic): the release gives $281B 'up 9.6%' and a prior-year $246B, which do not agree ($281B / $246B = +14.2%; 9.6% implies a base near $256B). The level is used; the growth pair is not | NY Fed Household Debt and Credit Q2 2026 (released 2026-08-11): card balances $1.263T, per sweep-1 row rupture-81. $281B / $1,263B = 22% (compiler arithmetic; different sources and definitions)
Implication: P03 is a claim on a slice of a $281B, fast-growing market, not on the $1.263T card pool; relevant to prime and near-prime revolvers.
Caveats: Edge: none. TransUnion sells bureau data to the lenders in this market; its headline growth and prior-year figures are internally inconsistent, so no growth rate is cited. The TransUnion PDF returned 403; figures verified on the newsroom release page. The NY Fed figure is cited through rupture-81 (verified in round 1), not re-fetched. TransUnion's bankcard figure ($1.14T) and the NY Fed card figure ($1.263T) use different definitions.

Claim: Card payoff is the main use of personal loans on the platforms that disclose purpose (at least 80% of LendingClub loans each year; 66% of Prosper loans to borrowers under $25,000 income in early 2023), but no filing, Fed or CFPB series gives a national share.
Evidence: Philadelphia Fed WP 18-15 (LendingClub data), note 7: at least 80% of LendingClub consumer loans each year were used to pay off card balances or consolidate debt; about 90% as of 2015. Philadelphia Fed WP 21-17 states that more than 80% of personal instalment loans have been used to pay off card balances (citing earlier work) | NY Fed brief, The Role of Fintech in Unsecured Consumer Lending to LMI Individuals (November 2023, Prosper loan data): in early 2023 the share of unsecured personal loans used for debt consolidation by borrowers below $25,000 income rose to 66%; higher card rates made consolidation more attractive | Lender filings: LendingClub FY2025 10-K says a 'significant portion' of loan customers use its personal loan to refinance higher-rate card debt and offers a balance-transfer feature that pays card debts directly; Discover FY2024 10-K says its personal loans are 'primarily intended to help customers consolidate existing debt'; SoFi FY2025 10-K lists debt consolidation first among uses; Upstart FY2025 10-K says personal loans 'often serve as a replacement for credit cards'. None gives a percentage
Implication: Consolidation demand is real and is the core use of the product, but the addressable share of the $281B cannot be stated from public data; a bank would have to measure it on its own applicants.
Caveats: Edge: none. Platform shares come from self-selected LendingClub and Prosper borrowers, not the market; the WP 21-17 figure is secondhand. Lenders have an interest in describing their product as a card refinance; LendingClub's statement sits in a risk factor on a proposed 10% card-rate cap. Philadelphia Fed and NY Fed figures verified against local extracts in output/sweep2/_pdf/; URLs re-resolved 2026-10-26.

Claim: Deposits cost 156 to 191 bps less than wholesale funding at both a chartered fintech and Capital One: SoFi paid 3.07% on deposits against 4.63% on warehouse lines in Q2 2026 (3.40% vs 5.31% in 2025), and Capital One paid 2.96% against 4.55% on securitised debt in H1 2026 (3.21% vs 5.04% in 2025).
Evidence: SoFi Q2 2026 10-Q and earnings release: interest-bearing deposits 3.07% vs warehouse facilities 4.63% (a year earlier 3.36% vs 5.23%); the release says the deposit rate was 156 bps below warehouse, worth about $712.6M of annualised interest savings; deposits $45.5B at 2026-06-30; personal-loan warehouse lines carry stated rates of 4.28% to 4.88% | SoFi FY2025 10-K: interest-bearing deposits 3.40% on $29.9B average; warehouse 5.31%; securitisation debt 3.45% on only $62.7M average; gap 191 bps (researcher arithmetic). The 10-K says deposits 'generally' cost less than warehouse and securitisation financing | Capital One Q2 2026 10-Q: six-month average interest-bearing deposits $455.1B at 2.96%; securitised debt 4.55%; senior and subordinated notes 5.66%; Q2 alone 2.91% vs 4.59%. FY2025 10-K: 3.21% vs 5.04% securitised and 6.39% senior notes. Gaps 159 and 183 bps (researcher arithmetic, checked) | SoFi personal loans: $27.5B originated in 2025 ($17.6B in 2024), including $11.0B for third parties through its Loan Platform Business ($575.9M of platform fees); weighted average rate earned 13.00%; $12.8B of personal loans sold; Q2 2026 originations $10.7B ($3.1B for third parties), annualised net charge-off 2.62%
Implication: The deposit-versus-wholesale gap of about 1.6 to 1.9 points is real, but SoFi already earns it as a bank, so the gap separates deposit-funded lenders from capital-markets lenders, not Capital One from the leading fintech consolidator.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Average balance-sheet rates, not marginal funding costs; warehouse lines are floating-rate facility costs, not term ABS pricing, and no 2025-2026 personal-loan ABS class coupons were found. SoFi's securitisation balance is too small to read as a market price. Rates are not split by product. All figures verified against EDGAR documents downloaded 2026-10-26 and the Capital One local extracts.

Claim: Against each class of incumbent, Capital One's 2025 deposit cost (3.21% interest-bearing) is 19 bps below SoFi (3.40%), 62 bps below LendingClub (3.83%) and about 257 bps below securitisation- and note-funded OneMain (about 5.78%); in Q2 2026 the gap to SoFi was 16 bps (2.91% vs 3.07%).
Evidence: Capital One FY2025 10-K average balances: interest-bearing deposits $402,209M, interest $12,925M, 3.21% (2024: 3.54%); total interest-bearing liabilities 3.50%; average total deposits $429,620M, so interest over all deposits is 3.01% (researcher arithmetic) | LendingClub FY2025 10-K: interest-bearing deposits $8,770M average at 3.83% ($335.7M; 2024: 4.65%); noninterest-bearing $301.5M; all-deposit cost 3.70% (researcher arithmetic). Gap to Capital One 62 bps interest-bearing, 69 bps all-deposit. Total deposits $9.8B at 2025-12-31, about 88% FDIC-insured; $10.8B at 2026-06-30 (Q2 2026 10-Q, registrant renamed Happen, Inc.) | SoFi FY2025 10-K: interest-bearing deposits 3.40%; Q2 2026 3.07%. Capital One Q2 2026 2.91%. Gaps 19 bps (2025) and 16 bps (Q2 2026), researcher arithmetic | OneMain FY2025 10-K: interest expense $1,272M on average daily debt $22,013M, about 5.78% (researcher arithmetic); gap to Capital One 257 bps (228 bps against Capital One's 3.50% all-liability rate). OneMain consumer loans yield 22.61% with a 7.30% net charge-off ratio
Implication: The funding edge is 0.2 to 0.7 points against the deposit-funded fintech banks that compete for prime consolidation and about 2.3 to 2.6 points only against finance companies that serve a lower credit tier than Capital One's 94%-above-660 book, so it is a tailwind, not a reason to enter.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Company disclosures with slightly different average definitions; all-deposit rates are arithmetic. Deposit mixes differ (LendingClub and SoFi are online high-yield savings; Capital One includes branch and checking balances). The gap is narrowing: Capital One's rate fell 33 bps in 2025 and LendingClub's 82 bps. OneMain is the comparator for capital-markets funding, not for pricing. Franchise-02 gives Capital One's Consumer Banking deposit rate on a different perimeter.

Claim: LendingClub's 2021 bank charter lifted its net interest margin from 3.0% in 2020 to 5.6% in 2021 and 5.6% to 7.0% through 2025, but return on equity was only 3.2% in 2023 and 4.0% in 2024 before 9.6% in 2025, and it still sold 74% of 2025 originations.
Evidence: LendingClub FY2021 10-K: net interest margin 5.6% (2021), 3.0% (2020), 3.6% (2019); total interest-bearing liabilities cost 2.36% in 2021 vs 10.95% in 2020 and 11.97% in 2019, the earlier figures being mostly retail notes that pass borrower returns to investors | LendingClub FY2025 10-K: net interest margin 6.07% (2025), 5.62% (2024), 6.97% (2023); return on average equity 9.6%, 4.0%, 3.2%; net charge-off ratio 3.6% (2025), 5.8% (2024); marketing 1.56% of originations; originations $9.59B (+33%), of which 74% held for sale and 26% held for investment | Unsecured personal loans held for investment yielded 13.42% on $3.2B average in 2025. Yield less 3.6% loss less 3.83% deposit cost leaves about 6.0 points before operating cost; at Capital One's 3.21% about 6.6 (researcher arithmetic)
Implication: The one natural experiment shows deposits widened margin once the lender kept loans, but returns stayed in single digits for three years and the lender still sells three-quarters of its volume, so cheap funding alone did not make consolidation lending a standout business.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Confounded by the 2020 pandemic trough, the zero-rate year 2021 and the shift from marketplace fees to balance-sheet interest, which changes what margin means; the 2020 liability cost is not a like-for-like funding cost. Company disclosure by a seller of the product. Verified against local extracts lc20211231.txt and lc20251231.txt.

Claim: Upstart's 'capital-markets-funded' platform is largely bank-funded: its top three lending partners (banks and credit unions) originated 83% of its 2025 loans and more than 50% of platform funding came through committed capital and co-investment arrangements.
Evidence: Upstart FY2025 10-K: top three lending partners originated 83% of marketplace loans and their fees were 61% of revenue; the company calls partners largely interchangeable; lending partners are defined as banks and credit unions; more than 50% of loan funding is through committed capital and other co-investment with institutional investors and lending partners | Same filing: transaction volume $11.0B on 1,497,149 loans in 2025 ($5.93B in 2024; $4.65B in 2023); conversion rate 19.4%; contribution margin 56% (63% in 2023); 66% of loans held on its own balance sheet at year-end were R&D loans (mainly auto refinance) | Upstart says personal loans 'often serve as a replacement for credit cards' and names banks, credit unions and fintech platforms as competitors
Implication: Much of the fintech consolidation volume the bank would take share from already runs on deposit-funded charters, so the funding edge over the field is smaller than the hypothesis assumes.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Upstart's bank and credit-union lending partners and chartered fintechs (SoFi, LendingClub). Partners are not named in the text read and their funding cost is not disclosed, so the edge over Upstart-originated loans cannot be sized. Upstart sells the platform and has an interest in showing bank adoption. Verified against local extract upst2025.txt.

Claim: Capital One's personal-loan book, inherited from Discover, fell from $10.3B at end-2024 to $7.98B at 30 September 2026, down 17% in a year and four straight quarters, and no filing read states a plan to grow it.
Evidence: Discover FY2024 10-K: personal loans $10,314M at 2024-12-31; average $10,281M at 13.64% yield; net charge-offs $418M or 4.06% (2023: 2.60%); 30+ day delinquency 1.69%; marketed primarily through direct mail, digital channels and email; competitors named include SoFi and LendingClub | Capital One Q3 2026 financial supplement (Exhibit 99.2): personal loans held for investment $7,984M (Q3 2026), $8,619M (Q2), $9,070M (Q1), $9,499M (Q4 2025), $9,646M (Q3 2025); down 7% on the quarter and 17% on the year; net charge-off rate 3.41% in Q3 2026 (3.83% for 2025 per the FY2025 10-K); 30+ day delinquency 1.84%. Decline since end-2024 22.6% (researcher arithmetic) | Capital One FY2025 10-K and Q2 2026 10-Q: 94% of the personal-loan book at refreshed FICO above 660 (3% at 621-660, 3% at 620 or below); reported inside the Credit Card segment; nonperforming 0.12%. $8.0B is about 3% of the $281B market and 3.1% of domestic card loans (researcher arithmetic, mixed dates) | Discover personal-loan page (fetched 2026-10-26): $2,500 to $40,000, 36 to 84 months, no fees, APR 6.99% to 24.99%, option to pay creditors directly
Implication: The bank already owns the product and is running it down, so P03 is a line extension or restart of an owned prime book, not a new position; why it is shrinking is the question to put to the Discover personal-loan team.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. The reason for the decline is not stated in any primary document read; runoff, tighter credit or an integration pause all fit. The OCC's 120-day plan for Discover's open enforcement actions [franchise-05] may bear on growth. Discover's pre-acquisition balance and Capital One's post-18 May 2025 reporting are mixed in the end-2024 comparison. A MarketBeat summary of the April 2026 call (a 'brownout' in Discover personal loans) was not used: aggregator summary, not a transcript.

Claim: Capital One's own terms remove its card balances from consolidation: its balance-transfer page bars transfers between Capital One cards and affiliates, and the Discover personal loan cannot be used to pay any Capital One or Discover account.
Evidence: Capital One balance-transfer page (fetched 2026-10-26): balances cannot move from one Capital One card to another, including affiliates or subsidiaries; other issuers' card balances, personal loans, student loans and auto loans can be transferred; transfer plus fees cannot exceed the credit limit | Discover personal-loan page (fetched 2026-10-26): the loan 'cannot be used to directly pay any Capital One account (including any Discover or Capital One credit card)' | Discover FY2024 10-K: issuers compete through low-priced balance transfer programmes; card interest income included $425M of amortised balance transfer fees in 2024 ($468M in 2023) | TransUnion study (released 2023-08-17, data April 2021 to September 2022): card balances of consolidators fell 57% on average; median card utilisation 59% before, 14% just after and 42% after 18 months; consolidators skewed prime or above
Implication: The bank's own policy bar already confines its consolidation offers to other issuers' debt, which is the form P03 names, and card balances partly return within 18 months, so the cannibalisation risk is real only if that bar is relaxed or the offer reaches its own revolvers indirectly.
Caveats: Edge: none. A product exclusion on a web page is not evidence of demand. The bar stops direct payoff only; a Capital One cardholder can still take the loan and pay down another issuer while keeping the Capital One revolve, or vice versa (not documented). TransUnion is a bureau with a commercial interest and states no sample size. Capital One balance-transfer fee and intro APR were not on the pages fetched.

Claim: Capital One's $260.3B of domestic card loans is about 21% of the $1.263T national card total, and moving a dollar of its own revolve into a personal loan gives up roughly 3 points of margin (credit-card loan yield 17.95% and domestic card charge-offs 5.12% vs personal-loan yield 13.64% and charge-offs 3.83%).
Evidence: Capital One Q3 2026 supplement: domestic card loans $260,252M at 30 September 2026. NY Fed Q2 2026 card balances $1.263T [rupture-81]. Own share 260.3 / 1,263 = 20.6% (researcher arithmetic; bank book includes small-business cards, two dates) | Capital One FY2025 10-K: Credit Card segment average loan yield 17.95% (2024: 19.09%); domestic card net charge-off rate 5.12%; personal-loan net charge-off rate 3.83%; 27% of domestic card loans at refreshed FICO 660 or below [independence-13] | Discover FY2024 10-K: personal loans yielded 13.64% on $10,281M average. Yield down 4.3 points, charge-offs down 1.3 points, about 3.0 points of margin lost per dollar before funding and capital (researcher arithmetic, mixed years)
Implication: At market level most consolidation demand is other issuers' debt (about four-fifths by proportional share), but every own-revolve dollar the bank refinances costs it about 3 points, so the offer must be fenced to other issuers' balances.
Caveats: Edge: none. Proportional-share logic assumes consolidators hold cards in line with issuer share; Capital One is revolve-heavy and holds more sub-660 balances than prime peers, so its share of the consolidation-prone pool is probably above 21% (direction known, size not). Correction: the 17.95% is the whole Credit Card segment loan yield (domestic, personal loans and international), not a domestic-only yield as P03-B stated. The 3-point loss ignores the lower capital cost of an instalment loan.

Claim: Tally, a consumer app that paid down card balances with its own lower-rate credit line, shut down on 12 August 2024 after failing to raise funding, having raised about $172M and been last valued at $855M per PitchBook.
Evidence: TechCrunch, 2024-08-12: CEO Jason Brown said Tally was 'unable to secure the necessary funding to continue our operations'; about $172M raised, including an a16z-led $50M Series C (2019) and an $80M Series D led by Sway Ventures (October 2022); PitchBook: last valued at $855M with 183 employees. | TechCrunch and Banking Dive (2024-08-14): in April 2024 Tally said it would sunset its consumer app and shift to a white-label B2B card-debt product with a public consumer company of more than 50 million users due to launch in July 2024, which was never announced; Tally ended its direct-to-consumer loan portfolio in April; its credit lines were issued by Cross River Bank; Tally says it helped pay down more than $2B of debt since 2015. | Neither article gives user counts, loss rates or unit economics.
Implication: The best-funded consumer attempt to manage and consolidate card debt could not stay fundable as an app, which counts against T18 as a consumer business and raises a funding-cost question a deposit bank would answer differently.
Caveats: Trade press used as the primary record of a private-company shutdown; no filing exists. Funding and valuation are investor figures. The stated reason is funding, which does not say whether economics, credit losses or demand was the cause. Corrects the brief's pointer: the shutdown was 2024, not 2023.

Claim: Fintech consolidation borrowers relever within months, and the balance transfer, a no-new-underwriting substitute for prime revolvers, moved $59.5B in 2024 at an average 4.3% fee at the 25 largest issuers.
Evidence: Di Maggio and Yao, NBER Working Paper 28021: fintech personal-loan borrowers' indebtedness and revolving balances rise more than matched bank borrowers'; 'even when borrowers use the personal loan to consolidate their credit card debt' revolving balances increase again a few months after origination; fintech borrowers are more likely to default | CFPB Consumer Credit Card Market Report 2025: balance transfers $59.5B in 2024, down slightly from 2023 but above the 2019 nominal peak of $55.4B; average fee 4.3% at the 25 largest issuers in H2 2024 (3.9% in 2022); transfers are typically at a lower, often zero, rate; balance transfer fees were $2.1B of $5.6B of other card fees in 2024
Implication: A bank marketing consolidation to other issuers' revolvers inherits a product whose borrowers relever, and for prime customers it competes with the balance transfer, which issuers already offer.
Caveats: Edge: none. The NBER sample covers earlier fintech vintages and compares fintech with bank borrowers, not a bank's own screened consolidation product. CFPB balance-transfer volume covers general-purpose cards at Y-14 reporters, not all issuers. Verified against local extracts nber_w28021.txt and cfpb_cc2025.txt.

Claim: Fintech consolidation lenders pay 1.6% to 2.3% of principal to acquire a borrower (LendingClub marketing 1.56% of originations; Upstart borrower acquisition $256.2M or 2.33% of volume, about $171 a loan, in 2025), more than the bank's lifetime funding edge of about 1.4% of principal over LendingClub.
Evidence: Upstart FY2025 10-K: borrower acquisition costs $90.5M (2023), $125.0M (2024), $256.2M (2025) on volume of $4.65B, $5.93B, $11.0B: 1.95%, 2.11%, 2.33% (researcher arithmetic, checked), $171 a loan in 2025; channels include third-party referral partnerships, direct mail and digital advertising; 'a significant amount' of originations comes from Credit Karma traffic | LendingClub FY2025 10-K: marketing 1.56% of originations (1.39% 2024, 1.26% 2023); repeat members return 'at a very low acquisition cost' | Lifetime funding edge: 0.62 point a year over LendingClub x 4 years x 55% average balance of a level-pay loan = about 1.4% of principal (researcher arithmetic and assumption). Credit Karma's personal-loan revenue growth (+$235M in Intuit FY2026) shows the paid comparison channel [rupture-12]; Philadelphia Fed WP 21-17 finds about 80% of solicitations in its sample were direct mail | Capital One serves over 100 million customers [franchise-08] and runs CreditWise [franchise-07]
Implication: The bank avoids most acquisition cost only on customers it already knows, who mostly revolve on its own cards; for other issuers' customers it carries the fintechs' acquisition cost with a funding edge smaller than that cost.
Caveats: Edge: distribution. Acquisition-cost definitions differ (Upstart borrower acquisition cost vs LendingClub marketing expense) and neither is fully loaded. The 55% average-balance factor and four-year term are assumptions. CreditWise user counts and whether it shows other issuers' balances usably were not found. The Philadelphia Fed sample is 2010s solicitations.

Claim: The one large bank that ran a branded consumer personal-loan line at scale sold it: Goldman sold substantially all of its Marcus loan portfolio in 2023 and narrowed its consumer activities, while Prosper, after $30.5B of originations since 2006, originated $2.7B in 2025 and still reported operating losses.
Evidence: Goldman Sachs FY2025 10-K: sale of substantially all of the Marcus loan portfolio in 2023 with net revenues of about -$370M; GreenSky portfolio transferred to held for sale and sold in 2024; since 2023 the firm has narrowed its focus on consumer-related activities | Prosper FY2025 10-K: $2.7B of personal loan originations in 2025 and $30.5B since 2006; operating losses in prior years, including 2025; 2019 SEC settlement with a $3.0M penalty over a platform error | Tally, which paid down card balances with its own credit line, shut on 2024-08-12 after raising about $172M [rupture-11]
Implication: A deposit base alone did not make Marcus earn its cost, and the survivors needed marketplace volume and loan-platform fees, which weakens the claim that cheap funding is the decisive edge.
Caveats: Edge: none. Goldman does not state why it sold; the loss reflects a discounted sale and a broader strategy change, not a proven personal-loan P&L. Prosper's size is not by itself a failure signal. Verified against EDGAR documents downloaded 2026-10-26.

Claim: No law bars a bank from offering unsecured consolidation loans to other issuers' cardholders: the limits are general UDAAP and Regulation Z advertising rules, the closest lender case is the FTC's $18M 2021 LendingClub settlement, and banks are outside the Credit Repair Organizations Act.
Evidence: 12 U.S.C. 5531: unfairness requires substantial injury not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by benefits; abusive acts include taking unreasonable advantage of consumers' lack of understanding, inability to protect their interests or reasonable reliance | 12 CFR 1026.24: a closed-end ad stating a payment amount, number of payments, repayment period or finance charge must also state repayment terms and the APR; the ban on misleading claims that a product will eliminate debt (paragraph (i)(5)) applies only to dwelling-secured credit | FTC press release 2021-07-14: LendingClub paid $18M and must disclose up-front fees and the net amount received; the FTC alleged 'no hidden fees' claims while deducting fees, false approval messages and unauthorised withdrawals; vote 4-0-1 | Sweep 1: the FTC Telemarketing Sales Rule advance-fee bar and a $106.8M default judgment on 2026-10-14 target debt settlers [rupture-14]; CROA excludes depository institutions and affiliates [rupture-15]. Two targeted searches found no 2023-2026 FTC or CFPB order against a personal-loan lender for consolidation claims
Implication: Legal exposure is ordinary advertising accuracy and UDAAP that a large issuer can meet; it is neither a barrier nor a regulatory edge.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory. Absence of recent actions in two searches does not prove none exist; state attorney general and private actions were not searched. FTC monetary powers narrowed after AMG Capital (2021). Statute and rule text read from Cornell LII copies, not GPO or eCFR (eCFR redirected to a block page in this pass).

Claim: Federal fair-lending guidance on model-driven offers has been withdrawn (CFPB Circulars 2022-03 and 2024-01, among 67 documents withdrawn on 12 May 2025) and the Regulation B final rule effective 21 July 2026 amends the disparate-impact provisions, but adverse-action notices with specific principal reasons are still required.
Evidence: NCLC list of the 67 CFPB guidance documents withdrawn by notice at 90 Fed. Reg. 20,084 (12 May 2025) includes Circular 2024-01 (preferencing and steering by digital intermediaries) and Circular 2022-03 (adverse action based on complex algorithms); the CFPB Circular 2024-01 page still resolves | CFPB Regulation B page: final rule issued and published 22 April 2026, effective 21 July 2026, amending provisions on disparate impact, discouragement and special purpose credit programmes | 12 CFR 1002.9: a creditor gives the reasons for adverse action or discloses the right to request them; reasons must be specific and indicate the principal reasons. Sweep 1 [independence-11] summarises the rule as removing the effects-test language while keeping disparate-treatment bans | A model choosing who gets a consolidation offer (prescreened mail, an in-app offer) is an eligibility and pricing decision under ECOA; the bank's own conflict runs toward steering a revolver away from a lower-yield loan, not toward it (researcher inference)
Implication: The federal burden on a model-driven consolidation offer is lighter than in 2024 and does not block the product; disparate-treatment, adverse-action, state-law and reputational risk remain, the last heightened by Discover's open enforcement actions [franchise-05].
Caveats: Edge: none. The withdrawal rests on NCLC (a consumer advocate), not the Federal Register notice, which was not fetched (federalregister.gov blocked). The substance of the Regulation B amendments rests on sweep 1's secondary summary. 1002.9 read from Cornell LII because eCFR redirected to a block page. State fair-lending exposure not researched.

Claim: Credit Karma earned $2.64B in Intuit fiscal 2026, mainly from cost-per-action fees on cards issued and loans funded, and Rocket Money had 4.58M paying subscribers and $390M revenue in 2025, so consumer credit-health and money-management services reach scale by selling credit and by subscription cancellation and budgeting, not by managing or negotiating debt.
Evidence: Intuit FY2026 10-K (FYE 2026-07-31): Credit Karma revenue $2,641M (FY2025 $2,200M; FY2024 $1,645M); growth from personal loans +$235M, credit cards +$101M, insurance +$85M; revenue recognized mainly from cost-per-action transactions. | Rocket Companies FY2025 10-K: Rocket Money paying subscribers 4,583 thousand at period end (2024: 4,117; 2023: 3,017); Rocket Money revenue $390M (2024: $297M; 2023: $199M); described as a personal finance app. | Neither filing reports debt consolidation, settlement or negotiation as a revenue line in the text read.
Implication: Free credit-health tools and a paid budgeting subscription work at scale, but the money comes from selling more credit and cancelling subscriptions, so a debt-management subscription is not shown to be a paid category and Credit Karma's incentives cut against a debt-relief position.
Caveats: Company filings, verified against local copies matching the live EDGAR documents. Credit Karma user counts and Rocket Money churn not extracted. Rocket Money's functions (cancellation, budgeting, credit score) are company description; it also touches T04.

Claim: In fiscal 2025 the Bureau of the Fiscal Service issued more than 1.32 billion payments worth more than $6.01 trillion, 97.0% of them electronic, and Treasury still printed 40.9 million checks at an average cost of $3.07 each.
Evidence: Fiscal Service Federal Disbursement Services page: FY2025 more than 1.32B payments totalling more than $6.01T, 97.0% electronic; no breakdown by programme and no check count on the page | Proposed rule 2026-08278 (Federal Register, 29 April 2026), background: in FY2025 Treasury still printed 40.9M checks; Treasury checks are 16 times more likely than electronic payments to be reported lost or stolen, returned undeliverable or altered; printing averages $3.07 a check, 20 times an ACH payment | Arithmetic (researcher): 40.9M / 1.32B = about 3.1% of payments by count. Checks are payments, not people; one recipient can receive many | Refund side, from income-16 and rupture-123: about 98% of 2026 refunds went by direct deposit
Implication: The federal flow is huge but the paper residual a bank could convert is about 3% of payments, spread across vendors, one-off payments and individuals; no source sizes the Debit-Primary Spender share of it in people.
Caveats: Edge: none. Government figures. The 40.9M is an all-programme check count; no per-programme split was found on any Fiscal Service page, and ssa.gov and cbo.gov returned 403 throughout, so beneficiary counts are missing. The scout logged 40.9M as a search snippet only; it is now verified in the proposed rule's text. Researcher A's Monthly Treasury Statement outlay figures were dropped: the API response does not label the unit or table.

Claim: Treasury's 29 April 2026 proposed rule under EO 14247 counts bank accounts, certain prepaid debit cards and digital wallets alike as eligible destinations, names no preferred provider, would drop Treasury's power to redirect a payment to a Treasury-sponsored account without the payee's consent, and was still a proposal with no final rule as of 26 October 2026.
Evidence: Proposed rule 2026-08278 (91 FR 23039, comments due 15 June 2026): eligible accounts may include bank accounts and certain prepaid debit cards and digital wallets; proposed 208.7 adds payment to a prepaid account designated by the recipient that meets 31 CFR part 210; the text names no fintech or provider type | Same proposal: Treasury would delete the sentence allowing payment to a Treasury-sponsored account where a recipient designates none, because it does not view unilaterally redirecting certified payments without payee consent or statutory authority as feasible | Same proposal: the age waiver (born before 1 May 1921 and paid by check on 1 March 2013) would go; individual hardship waivers would remain for mental impairment or lack of electronic infrastructure where the payee lives; Treasury's RFI drew 248 comments | EO 14247 (28 March 2025): sec. 3(a) ends paper checks from 30 September 2025 for benefits, vendor payments and tax refunds to the extent permitted by law; sec. 3(e) names digital wallets and real-time payment systems; sec. 5(c) asks Treasury to work on access for unbanked and underbanked people. Federal Register search (26 October 2026): newest Fiscal Service item under this title is the 2026-04-29 proposed rule; the last final rules are 2024-02-21 and 2020-05-01
Implication: The mandate creates no forced demand for a bank account and gives a national bank no regulatory edge over prepaid, a wallet or a sponsor-bank fintech; a holdout who names no account keeps a waiver rather than being routed into any bank.
Caveats: Edge: regulatory (Slice A) / none (Slice B); merged verdict none. Merges A-2 and B-1. Proposed text can change in a final rule; a final rule filed under another title would not appear in the search. The fetch tool summarises long documents; quoted phrases were confirmed against the local extract in output/sweep2/_pdf/P04/fr.txt.

Claim: Paper-check tax refunds fell from 8.4 million to 2.2 million between the 2025 and 2026 filing seasons (1 January to 26 May), with about 98% of refunds by direct deposit, while the current 31 CFR 208.3 mandate does not apply to Internal Revenue Code payments, so the refund phase-out rests on the executive order.
Evidence: National Taxpayer Advocate filing season review: paper-check refunds 2.2M from 1 January to 26 May 2026, against 8.4M in the same period of 2025; direct-deposit share about 98%, up from 94% | NTA mid-year report (IR-2026-79, 24 June 2026): about 4M notices for missing or incorrect direct-deposit details as of 27 April; notices pointed to online accounts or a paper-check waiver; unbanked and underbanked taxpayers cannot take direct deposit, and delays ran 6 weeks or more (also income-16) | 31 CFR 208.3 (eCFR as of 2026-10-20): all federal payments by EFT, but the requirement does not apply to payments under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986; EO 14247 sec. 3(a) names tax refunds (rupture-122) | Arithmetic (researcher): 8.4M less 2.2M is about 6.2M refunds moved off paper in one season. Who received them is owned by preparers and platforms (income-13, income-14)
Implication: The refund half of the why-now was spent in a single season and the destination was chosen inside filing software, so a bank arriving now bids for a 2.2M residual of waiver holders and unreached filers.
Caveats: Edge: none. The 8.4M and 2.2M are the Advocate's text; no matching IRS table was found. No source splits the 6.2M former paper filers by destination account type (open gap from the income stress test). This corrects the stress test's estimate of about 1.9M remaining, which combined unlike series.

Claim: The government's own receiving account for benefit recipients without a bank account is Direct Express, a prepaid card run by one bank under a five-year financial-agency agreement: Comerica held it from 2008, BNY was announced in November 2024 but never took over, and Fifth Third was designated on 9 September 2025 for about 3.4 to 3.5 million cardholders.
Evidence: Fiscal Service (7 January 2020): Comerica re-selected for five years from January 2020, about 4.5M Americans on the card, most without a bank account. Fiscal Service (21 November 2024): BNY selected after a competitive process, five years from 3 January 2025, about 3.4M users, about 95% of SSI payments electronic against 53% in 2008 | Reconciliation: Comerica's FY2024 10-K says Treasury extended Comerica's contract up to three years past 2 January 2025 for transition; a BNY spokesperson told PaymentsJournal (30 September 2025, trade press as record of the event) that Fiscal Service discontinued the agreement over readiness challenges at one provider; Fifth Third's release (9 September 2025) announces its designation under a five-year agreement starting that day, Money Network as programme manager, Mastercard as network, Comerica servicing existing cards until reissue, about 3.4M Americans; it does not mention BNY. The Fiscal Service Direct Express page (updated 1 September 2026) names Fifth Third as issuer. No Treasury page explaining the change was found | Fifth Third 2025 annual report: Treasury selected it as the exclusive Financial Agent and Issuing Bank; more than 3.5M participants; it claims the scale of the second-largest US neobank, similar revenue per customer and significantly better profitability. 10-Q Q2 2026: commercial payments revenue up $102M (quarter) and $167M (six months), partly from Direct Express; card and processing expense up $44M and $101M, primarily from the programme | 31 CFR 208.5: Treasury may designate a Financial Agent to run Treasury-sponsored accounts at reasonable cost with the same consumer protections as other account holders; the 2020 Comerica cardholder count to the 2024 count is a 24% fall (researcher arithmetic)
Implication: The one receiving position the government assigns is a tendered contract, now held by Fifth Third to about 2030 and shrinking, so a consumer bank would be bidding for a contract on Treasury's terms, not acquiring primary-account customers on its own.
Caveats: Edge: belongs to: Fifth Third (contracted financial agent) (Slice A said regulatory; Slice B said none). Merges A-3 and B-3. Fifth Third's profitability and neobank claims are its own and unquantified. '3.5M participants' (annual report) and '3.4M Americans' (its own release, Treasury) may not count the same thing. 'Exclusive' is Fifth Third's word; no agreement text was read, and 208.5 does not bar other Treasury-sponsored accounts. The BNY reason rests on a BNY statement in trade press. Fifth Third SEC numbers were verified against local extracts in output/sweep2/_pdf/P04/; the 2030 end date is compiler arithmetic from the five-year term.

Claim: In 2024, the last year Comerica disclosed, Direct Express produced $121 million of card fee income against $119 million of programme expense and an average of $3.4 billion of noninterest-bearing deposits, while Treasury paid the bank a fee for every enrolled beneficiary.
Evidence: Comerica FY2024 10-K: average Direct Express deposits $3.4B in 2024 ($3.1B in 2023), all noninterest-bearing; card fee income $121M ($137M); noninterest expense $119M ($138M), mostly outside processing; told in July 2024 it was not selected to continue | CFPB complaint v. Comerica (6 December 2024, N.D. Tex.) para. 17-18: Fiscal Service pays Comerica a fee for every beneficiary who enrols; around $3B in benefits a year to about 4.5M cardholders | Arithmetic (researcher, mixing the 10-K with Treasury's 3.4M count): about $1,000 of average deposit and about $36 of fee income per card; fee income less expense is $2M in 2024 and minus $1M in 2023 | Franchise anchor (franchise-03, sweep2-brief): Consumer Banking earned $1,225M after tax in 2025, about 0.3% after tax on deposits; applied to $3.4B that is roughly $10M a year after tax (compiler illustration; the segment includes auto and network revenue)
Implication: The only disclosed economics of a government-benefit receiving account show a break-even fee line and value in free deposits of about $1,000 a card, which at Capital One's deposit returns is a small business; the case would rest on these Debit-Primary Spenders later becoming broader customers, which no source measures.
Caveats: Edge: cost. Company filing; expenses may exclude allocated overhead and the deposit value depends on a rate the 10-K does not state. The $3B benefits figure is a CFPB allegation and looks low for 4.5M cards. Per-card figures divide a 2024 average balance by a November 2024 count from another source. The 10-K figures were verified against the local extract output/sweep2/_pdf/P04/cma.htm (the live SEC page loads but the fetch tool returned only the cover). The $423.9B segment-deposit and 3.02% rate figures in Slice A were not re-verified and were removed; the 0.3% comes from franchise-03 as stated in the sweep-2 brief.

Claim: Servicing the benefit-prepaid population has broken incumbents: the CFPB alleged in December 2024 that Comerica's vendors dropped almost 25 million cardholder calls and charged more than 1 million cardholders ATM fees they did not owe, the case was dismissed without prejudice in April 2025, and the named successor BNY never took the programme over.
Evidence: CFPB complaint (6 December 2024, N.D. Tex. 3:24-cv-03054): a vendor's 'Heavy Queue' function intentionally ended almost 25M calls from cardholders on hold; more than 1M cardholders were charged ATM fees on withdrawals that should have been free; claims also covered fraud-enrolment denials and Regulation E failures | CFPB newsroom archive: the Bureau filed a notice of dismissal without prejudice on 11 April 2025 and the court closed the case the same day; no merits ruling | Comerica FY2024 10-K: notified in July 2024 it was not selected; BNY announced November 2024, discontinued before taking over (rupture-124)
Implication: Serving benefit recipients at scale is operationally unforgiving (call volumes, enrolment fraud, Regulation E), which warns a new entrant and also shows the government slot is contestable when the holder fails.
Caveats: Edge: none. Allegations only, dismissed without prejudice. The BNY reason is a BNY statement relayed by trade press. Complaint figures verified in the local extract output/sweep2/_pdf/P04/comerica.txt; the newsroom page carries no figures.

Claim: The people still outside the banking system are few and mostly do not want an account: in 2023 4.2% of US households (about 5.6 million) were unbanked and 70.9% of them were not interested in an account, 21.6% of unbanked households used prepaid cards and 66.2% were cash-only, and in 2025 6% of adults were unbanked.
Evidence: FDIC 2023 National Survey (published November 2024): unbanked 4.2% of households, about 5.6M; underbanked 14.2%, about 19.0M; prepaid use 5.9% of households (6.9% in 2021), 21.6% of unbanked against 5.2% of banked; 59.0% of unbanked prepaid users used the card to receive income | Same survey: 29.1% of unbanked households very or somewhat interested in an account, 70.9% not; not enough money for minimum balance cited by 42.3% (main reason 23.3%); a fee or minimum-balance reason was the main reason for 33.4%; 66.2% of unbanked households were cash-only | Fed SHED 2025 (published May 2026): 6% of adults unbanked, 21% of those with income under $25,000; 28% of unbanked and 11% of banked adults used nonbank check cashing or money orders | Arithmetic (researcher): 29.1% of 5.6M is about 1.6M unbanked households interested in an account
Implication: Fees and minimum balances are what a no-fee account answers, but only about 1.6M unbanked households want an account at all, so the addressable Debit-Primary Spender pool is low single-digit millions before overlap with Direct Express and prepaid users.
Caveats: Edge: distribution (Slice A) / none (Slice B). Merges A-6 and B-7 (survey part). Household-level, self-reported, fielded June 2023 before the phase-out; it does not identify benefit or refund recipients. Multiple reasons were allowed for the 42.3%. SHED is adult-level and not comparable with FDIC household rates. FDIC figures verified on the live report PDF and the local extract.

Claim: No public source measures whether an account opened to receive a federal benefit or refund becomes the holder's primary account, and the one linkage study found most self-reported unbanked Social Security recipients already took payment electronically.
Evidence: Anderson, Strand and Collins (September 2012, FDIC-hosted, Social Security Administration co-author, authors' views): in January 2009, 69.1% of self-reported unbanked Social Security recipients already received direct deposit, against nearly 92% of banked recipients; the authors read this as misreporting rather than missing access | Researcher B searched Fed, FDIC and bank disclosures for a 12-month primary-account rate on refund- or benefit-opened accounts and found none; SHED's banking page has no primary-account measure | Green Dot processed 12.02M refunds in 2025 while its consumer active accounts fell 20.7% (rupture-129), the only public signal on refund conversion, and it is inference
Implication: A receiving deposit is not evidence of a primary relationship, and the kill criterion's first limb has no external proxy; only a Capital One cohort cut (accounts whose first credit is an IRS or Treasury ACH, against payroll-opened accounts) can settle it.
Caveats: Edge: none. 2009 data on one programme; recent recipients not studied. Rated Low because the claim rests on an absence and one old study. Figures verified on the live PDF (parsed locally) and output/sweep2/_pdf/P04B-fdic2012-ss.txt.

Claim: The public players built on prepaid and refund money for the underserved show no winning model: Green Dot's consumer segment lost 20.7% of active accounts in 2025 to 1.49 million while it processed 12.02 million refunds and agreed in November 2025 to split its bank from its payments business, and Cash App and Chime disclose no benefit or paper-check conversion figures.
Evidence: Green Dot FY2025 10-K: refunds processed 12.02M (13.82M in 2024, down 13.0%); Consumer Services active accounts 1.49M (1.88M), direct-deposit active accounts 0.39M (0.43M), segment revenue $364.3M (down 9.5%), segment profit $130.7M; total active accounts 3.42M (down 6.8%); tax division processes about 13M refunds a year; markets to never-banked through fully-banked consumers | Same 10-K: pending transactions with CommerceOne Financial (bank merger) and a $690M sale of the payments business to a Smith Ventures affiliate | Block FY2025 10-K: direct deposit lets customers receive a paycheck, tax refund or government disbursement into Cash App; no count of benefit or refund converts. Chime FY2025 10-K: 9.5M active members (8.0M), revenue per active member $257, sales and marketing $635.4M including $53.2M stock-based pay; no government-benefit deposit line | Arithmetic (researcher): Green Dot consumer revenue about $244 per year-end active account; Chime ($635.4M less $53.2M) / 1.5M net additions is at most about $388 per net member. Preparer-linked side held by H&R Block and Pathward (income-13, income-14)
Implication: The incumbent that most resembles a receiving account for refund and benefit money is shrinking and breaking up, and nobody discloses acquisition cost or retention for a government-money account, so there is no benchmark that says the pool is worth chasing.
Caveats: Edge: none. Company filings; active accounts are accounts, not households; Green Dot segment profit is before allocated corporate cost. Green Dot does not split refunds by prior paper status. The Chime figure is an upper bound mixing gross acquisition and retention spend. Numbers verified against local extracts in output/sweep2/_pdf/P04/ (gdot.txt, chime.txt, block.htm).

Claim: The largest debt-settlement firm claimed $7B settled for 300,000+ consumers on 18% to 25% fees when the CFPB sued it in November 2017, while Ava, the one subscription credit-health startup found with a round, raised a $15.5M seed in October 2025 for a $10-a-month app and discloses no member count.
Evidence: CFPB press release, 2017-11-08: CFPB sued Freedom Debt Relief and co-CEO Andrew Housser, alleging it misled consumers about creditor negotiation, its services and fees and failed to disclose rights to their funds, under Dodd-Frank and the TSR; fees 18% to 25% of enrolled debt; Freedom claims more than $7B settled for more than 300,000 consumers (not verified by the CFPB); the page reports no outcome. | fintech.global, 2025-10-27: Ava raised a $15.5M seed (Greylock, Transform VC, Firebolt and others, plus angels from Meta, Credit Karma and Plaid) for a $10-per-month AI app that works on credit profiles and one-click loan applications; no member count.
Implication: Paid debt help at scale exists only as debt settlement, a litigated model, while the subscription model is at seed stage with no disclosed traction, so T18 as a subscription is close to new-to-world but unproven and carries reputational risk for a bank.
Caveats: The 2017 complaint is an allegation; the outcome was not fetched. Freedom's figures are company claims eight years old. The Ava item is a funding report derived from a press release; a funded startup is investor belief, not demand. Karoo, Achieve and Beyond Finance had no primary record (EDGAR full-text search returned 403 for rupture-A).

Claim: The account the hypothesis would sell already exists and is already Capital One's: more than 23 million Bank On-certified accounts were open at 45 reporting institutions in 2024, 360 Checking appears on Oregon's 2025 Bank On list and is described by Capital One as fully certified, and the bank's July 2024 Community Benefits Plan commits to grow Bank On accounts by at least 50% and enable about 100,000 ITIN holders, with no target for benefit or refund recipients.
Evidence: St. Louis Fed Bank On data release (20 November 2025, 2024 data): over 23M certified accounts open, up 19%, at 45 reporting institutions holding over two-thirds of national deposit share; 39% of holders use direct deposit; average monthly balance $1,273; over $260B deposited in 2024 | CFE Fund Bank On National Account Standards 2025-2026: monthly fee $5 or less if not waivable ($10 or less if waivable), opening deposit $25 or less, no overdraft or NSF fees; checking or prepaid accounts both qualify. Oregon Bank On brochure (PDF modified September 2025) lists Capital One 360 Checking Account | Capital One Community Benefits Plan (17 July 2024): more than $265B over five years, $200B consumer lending ($125B cards, $75B auto); grow Bank On certified checking accounts by at least 50% (no baseline stated); about 100,000 ITIN holders via digital acceptance; 360 Checking 'fully Bank On certified'; over 16,000 cash deposit locations; Discover customers to get 'tens of thousands' of cash-load locations; no target for government-benefit or refund recipients. NCRC (11 August 2024, merger opponent) puts new money under $5B | Corpus: franchise-08 (the plan and the OCC Outstanding CRA rating), franchise-01 (five deposit products, no prepaid or benefit product)
Implication: Because the no-fee account and the commitment to grow it already exist inside Capital One, P04 adds only a government-money acquisition channel, so it fails the additive test as a new position and belongs with the Bank On and ITIN owners.
Caveats: Edge: none. Merges A-8 and B-6. The Bank On data are reported voluntarily by participating banks; the CFE Fund sets the standard and runs certification; 23M includes any holder of a certified product, not only the formerly unbanked. The Oregon PDF carries no printed date (date from file metadata). Certification of 360 Checking is the bank's claim plus a state list; Capital One's 360 product page does not mention Bank On. Plan progress reporting was not located.

Claim: Treasury wound down myRA, its government-sponsored starter retirement account, in July 2017 because demand was extremely low and the roughly $70 million spent since 2014 could not be justified when private no-fee options existed.
Evidence: Treasury press release sm0135 (28 July 2017): review found myRA not cost effective; demand for and investment in it was extremely low; taxpayers paid about $70M to manage it since 2014; private accounts with no fees or minimums available; the Treasurer said the cost could not be justified by the assets | No participant or asset totals in the release | Related: IRS Direct File was suspended after reaching under 0.5% of returns (income-16)
Implication: A free, government-prompted account for lower-income savers did not draw demand when private no-fee options existed, which warns against assuming that a free account plus the federal phase-out moves the Debit-Primary Spender.
Caveats: Edge: none. A retirement account, not a receiving account, and a different decade. CRS participant and asset figures seen in a search excerpt were not verified (congress.gov 403) and are not used.

Claim: Treasury endorses no financial institution for receiving federal money: its direct-deposit page names no bank and sends unbanked people to the FDIC's #GetBanked site, Go Direct is a Treasury and Federal Reserve enrolment programme, and the federal statute on misuse of federal names (18 U.S.C. 709) does not list the word Treasury.
Evidence: Fiscal Service direct-deposit page: payments go to an account at the recipient's financial institution, a Treasury-sponsored account, or a waiver under part 208; no bank is named or recommended; unbanked recipients are pointed to the FDIC #GetBanked site and the Electronic Payment Solution Center for direct deposit or Direct Express enrolment | Fiscal Service Go Direct page (5 December 2023, updated 12 December 2023): a Treasury and Federal Reserve partnership since 2005 to move benefit recipients from checks to direct deposit; announces the eleven millionth enrolment; no bank channel described | 18 U.S.C. 709 (Cornell LII copy): bars misleading use of words such as national, Federal, United States, reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance; Treasury appears only in an editorial note | The Direct Express page names Fifth Third only as issuer and endorses no bank (rupture-124)
Implication: Whatever the advertising law says, there is no Treasury endorsement for a bank to borrow, so the receiving position stays the recipient's own choice and offers no distribution edge.
Caveats: Edge: none. Pointer corrected: the brief said a bank cannot market itself as Treasury-endorsed; no rule saying so was found, and deceptive-advertising law (FTC, OCC) was not retrieved. Cornell is a mirror of the U.S. Code, not govinfo. Go Direct campaign status beyond the 2023 page is unconfirmed (godirect.gov returned no text).

Claim: The Community Reinvestment Act gives no reason to chase benefit- or refund-opened accounts: the 2023 rule that would have credited Bank On-type deposit products was enjoined on 29 March 2024 and never applied, and the OCC and FDIC proposed on 12 August 2026 to limit the retail-services test to credit services, excluding deposit services.
Evidence: OCC and FDIC proposed rule (91 FR 52114, 12 August 2026, comments to 13 October 2026): the 2023 rules were preliminarily enjoined on 29 March 2024 and the agencies apply rules largely based on the 1995 rules; the Fifth Circuit dismissed the agencies' appeal on 9 July 2026 | Same proposal: evaluation of retail banking services would cover credit services and exclude deposit services, superseding the Interagency Questions and Answers to the extent they treat deposit products as retail services | 2023 final rule (Federal Reserve copy): deposit products responsive to low- and moderate-income needs could include accounts certified to the Bank On National Account standard and second-chance accounts; nothing treats benefit or refund recipients as a category
Implication: The regulatory framework in force does not reward these accounts and the pending proposal would stop counting deposit services at all, so there is no CRA reason for Capital One, an OCC-supervised bank (franchise-08), to build this position.
Caveats: Edge: none. Only the first 100,000 of about 670,000 characters of the 2026 proposal were read; later text could mention deposit products. The Federal Reserve is not a party to the 2026 proposal. The 2023 text is a Fed-hosted copy; the Bank On passage was verified in the local extract output/sweep2/_pdf/P04B-cra2023.txt.

Claim: On price 360 Checking beats commercial prepaid cards but not Direct Express, which is almost free with no credit check, and 360's application asks for an SSN or ITIN, citizenship, employment and income and warns applicants may be denied, so it cannot take every holdout that prepaid serves.
Evidence: Direct Express terms page (Comerica schedule; terms differ by issuer): no monthly or overdraft fee listed, first ATM withdrawal free per federal deposit, $0.85 per further US withdrawal, $1.50 per transfer to a personal bank account, $4.00 card replacement after one free a year, $0.75 paper statement; Fiscal Service page: no sign-up cost, no monthly or overdraft fee | Green Dot product page: $7.95 monthly fee, waived with $500 direct deposit in the prior month; $5.95 flat fee to deposit up to $500 at retail and a retail service fee up to $4.95; $3 out-of-network ATM. Netspend's own blog (fees as of 5 July 2025): $9.95 monthly, $5.00 with $500 direct deposit, or $1.95 per purchase; reload up to $3.95; ATM $2.95 | Capital One 360 Checking page: no monthly fee, no minimum balance, no overdraft fees; cash deposits at Walgreens, CVS, Kroger, Dollar General, 7-Eleven and others up to $999 a transaction, $1,500 a day, $5,000 a month, 10 times a month, with no fee stated; 70,000+ fee-free ATMs; applicants give SSN or ITIN, citizenship, employment and income; 'you may be denied'; certain non-payroll and tax payments are excluded from early paycheck (income-17) | Capital One's ChexSystems explainer (7 July 2022) does not say the bank uses ChexSystems or offers a second-chance account; the Bank On standard lists denial only for past actual fraud as strongly recommended, not core
Implication: The cost edge is real only against Green Dot and Netspend; against Direct Express it is nil, and identity and denial gates leave the account best suited to banked-but-unaccounted refund filers, whom ordinary acquisition already reaches.
Caveats: Edge: cost (B-8) / none (B-9). Merges B-8 and B-9. Company pages, flagged; the Direct Express table is Comerica's and Fifth Third's may differ. The Netspend table is a promotional blog. A missing cash-deposit fee on the 360 page is not a confirmed zero. Whether 360 screens on ChexSystems, approval rates and ITIN acceptance are not disclosed.
