Claim: The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule bars debt-relief sellers from collecting any fee before at least one debt is settled or altered and the customer has paid under it, and enforcement continued into 2026 with a $106.8M default judgment entered on 14 October 2026 and a pending CFPB-and-seven-state suit alleging at least $100M of advance fees.
Evidence: 16 CFR 310.4(a)(5)(i) (Cornell LII eCFR copy): no fee until the seller has renegotiated, settled, reduced or otherwise altered at least one debt under a valid agreement, the customer has made at least one payment under it, and the fee is proportional to that debt or a fixed percentage of the amount saved. | FTC business guide (July 2010): covers for-profit sellers and their telemarketers, inbound and outbound calls, and unsecured debts including medical debt; 'substantial assistance' such as processing payments or offering dedicated accounts creates liability; the guide does not address banks. | FTC press release, 2026-10-22: $106.8M default judgment entered 2026-10-14 against Accelerated Debt Settlement and related companies, with corporate and individual defendants banned from debt relief; alleged posing as banks and government agencies, promising reductions of 75% or more and collecting illegal advance fees. | CFPB enforcement page: CFPB and seven state AGs sued StratFS in W.D.N.Y. on 2024-01-10, alleging at least $100M collected before debts were settled; TRO 2024-01-11; preliminary injunction 2024-03-04; status pending (page updated 2024-04-03).
Implication: A subscription that bundles negotiation with an upfront or monthly fee collides with the advance-fee ban, and the category's enforcement record makes negotiated settlement reputationally toxic for a bank, leaving management and coaching of Debit-Primary Spenders' own accounts as the defensible scope.
Caveats: Allegations in the StratFS case are not findings and its status is as of April 2024. The ADS judgment is a default against absent defendants. Whether the TSR reaches a bank or an in-app flow was not resolved; the 2010 guide predates app delivery and FTC Act limits on bank jurisdiction were not researched.

Claim: Synchrony's FY2025 10-K shows deposits of $81.1 billion funding 84% of the company and says most CareCredit provider agreements are not exclusive and typically terminable at will on 15 days' notice, so the incumbent is already deposit-funded and its provider network is not locked by contract.
Evidence: Synchrony FY2025 10-K: most CareCredit provider agreements are not exclusive and typically may be terminated at will upon 15 days' notice; multi-year agreements cover larger multi-location relationships; over 215,000 provider and retail locations processed a CareCredit application or sale in 2025; deposits $81.1B ($75.2B direct, $5.9B brokered), 84% of total funding at 31 December 2025. | Deferred-interest promotions cover 17.7% of Synchrony's total loan receivables (all platforms); Health & Wellness held $15.5B of receivables and earned $3.8B, 17% of interest and fees on loans [rupture-01]. | Capital One holds $475.8B of deposits [franchise-02]; patients paid about $1B of deferred interest on medical cards and loans in 2018 to 2020 [rupture-05].
Implication: Deposit funding is not an edge against an 84% deposit-funded incumbent, though non-exclusive, short-notice provider contracts mean entry is not blocked by contract; the moat is CareCredit's enrolled account-holder base, and reputational exposure for patients with high out-of-pocket costs is high.
Caveats: Edge: none (deposit funding is shared with the incumbent). Verified against the local 10-K extract at output/rupture/_pdf/syf.txt. Non-exclusivity is risk-disclosure language; actual provider switching is not measured. The 17.7% deferred-interest share is company-wide, not Health & Wellness only.

Claim: PayZen says it underwrites patient plans on a non-recourse basis and assumes the repayment risk itself, names a bank only as issuer of its card (Patriot Bank, N.A.), and does not state its fees or capital sources.
Evidence: PayZen platform page, fetched 2026-10-26: non-recourse, ability-to-pay underwriting; PayZen assumes the repayment risk and gives providers accelerated cash; plans described as interest-free in the FAQ; Balance Sheet Boost moves a provider's existing plan book to PayZen; the PayZen Care Card is issued by Patriot Bank, N.A.; PayZen is not a bank; claims a 30% increase in patient payments (baseline undefined) and 78% enrollment success; no fees or capital sources stated. | Cedar sells to health systems and processes patient payments [rupture-02]; no lender or bank partner for Cedar was found.
Implication: Provider-side vendors hold the provider relationship and keep the risk, leaving a possible balance-sheet role behind them, but that is the silent-funder position Section 5 rules out and its economics are undisclosed; the segment is provider-referred patients, not the deposit base.
Caveats: Edge: none. Vendor marketing page with self-reported performance claims; a PayZen sales PDF would not parse. Cedar's financing sources are undisclosed. The bank's role behind PayZen beyond card issuance is unknown.

Claim: California will require hospitals from 1 July 2027 to screen uninsured, certain Medi-Cal and Covered California patients for charity care with presumptive eligibility, shrinking the balance a patient-instalment product could finance, while no Discover disclosure of patient-pay acceptance at providers was found.
Evidence: California Health and Safety Code 127406 (FindLaw text, fetched 2026-10-26): from 1 July 2027 hospitals must screen uninsured patients, Medi-Cal enrollees with cost sharing or HPE eligibility, and Covered California enrollees; presumptive eligibility can rest on enrolment in CalFresh, CalWORKs, WIC and similar programmes, approval within the prior six months, or self-attested homelessness; hospitals must adopt and publish a written screening process. | A search found only a 2005 health-account card pilot, a First Data processing certification and a 2022 B2B hospital-supplier arrangement for Discover in healthcare; none was fetched and no current provider acceptance count exists in the sources found. | The CFPB medical-debt reporting rule was vacated on 11 July 2025 [rupture-04]; the first-order cause of burden is price and coverage [rupture-20].
Implication: Network acceptance is not a bottleneck because a provider already takes any card and the instalment is a credit product, so the owned network adds nothing, while presumptive charity-care screening reduces the financeable balance in states that require it.
Caveats: Edge: none. Statute text via FindLaw, not the legislature site. The Discover healthcare result is a search-only negative and is not cited by URL. The count of states with automatic screening was not verified.

Claim: The Credit Repair Organizations Act covers paid services intended to improve a consumer's credit record, history or rating and bars covered firms from charging before the service is fully performed, but excludes any depository institution, federal or state credit union and their affiliates and subsidiaries.
Evidence: 15 U.S.C. 1679a(3) (Cornell LII, fetched 2026-10-26): a credit repair organization uses interstate commerce or the mails to sell, provide or perform, for payment, a service to improve a consumer's credit record, history or rating, or to advise or assist with that; subparagraph (B) excludes 501(c)(3) nonprofits, creditors restructuring debt owed to that creditor, and in (B)(iii) 'any depository institution (as that term is defined in section 1813 of title 12) or any Federal or State credit union ... or any affiliate or subsidiary' of one. | 15 U.S.C. 1679b (Cornell LII, fetched): no credit repair organization may charge or receive money 'before such service is fully performed'; untrue or misleading statements about creditworthiness are barred. | Reading (researcher's, not a regulator's): a fintech credit-health subscription promising score improvement is covered and must wait to be paid; a depository institution is outside CROA but remains subject to UDAAP and state law.
Implication: The law that makes a paid credit-health subscription awkward for an app does not bind a bank, a genuine regulatory edge for coaching Debit-Primary Spenders, but it does not cover negotiation or settlement (TSR, rupture-14) or remove reputational and UDAAP exposure.
Caveats: Statute text read on Cornell LII (uscode.house.gov returned 404); the depository exclusion was confirmed verbatim in the compiler's fetch of 1679a(3)(B)(iii). The application to a bank-sold subscription is the researcher's reading of statute text, not a regulator's or court's; affiliate structures, case law and state credit-services laws were not reviewed.

Claim: In 2025, 63 percent of US adults said they would cover a hypothetical $400 expense using only cash, savings or a card paid off at the next statement, and 12 percent said they could not pay it by any means.
Evidence: Fed SHED 2025: 63% would cover a $400 expense with cash or equivalent, the same as 2022-2024; 68% in 2021; 50% in 2013. | SHED 2025: 12% could not pay $400 by any means (13% in 2024); in 2023 those not using cash would use a card carried as a balance (16%), friends or family (10%), selling something (7%), a bank loan or line of credit (3%), and payday, deposit advance or overdraft (2%). | SHED 2025: 55% had three months of expenses set aside, down from 59% in 2021.
Implication: A stable one-in-eight group cannot absorb a $400 shock, a real audience for T16 among Debit-Primary Spenders, and only 3% of non-cash households use a bank loan today.
Caveats: Corpus row 2. Hypothetical payment-method question, not a balance measure. Compiler spot-check: 63% and 12% confirmed on the SHED 2025 savings page, 2026-10-26.

Claim: In Chase deposit data for 2021-2023, 92 percent of households could cover a $400 shock, but only 37 percent of the lowest-income households could cover a $1,600 shock versus 97 percent of the highest-income households.
Evidence: JPMorgan Chase Institute (2024-07-30; 5.9M Chase deposit households, 2021-2023): 92% could cover a $400 shock. | Same study: 37% of the lowest-income households could cover a $1,600 shock versus 97% of the highest-income households.
Implication: The shock-liquidity audience is the lower-income, low-liquidity slice; for upmarket households a shock is a cash-flow event, so T16 should be scoped to Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: Corpus row 24. Chase account holders only; income proxies liquidity. Compiler spot-check: 92%, 37%, 97% and 5.9M confirmed on the page, 2026-10-26; the appendix gives 49% and 98% under an alternative spending assumption.

Claim: In 2022 roughly 10 million workers used earned wage products for over $31.9 billion, and the CFPB's illustrative APR for a typical employer-partnered transaction was 109.5 percent.
Evidence: CFPB Data Spotlight (2024-07-18): employer-partnered transactions rose from 43.2M in 2021 to 83.4M in 2022 and from $4.6B to $8.9B. | Across employer-partnered and direct-to-consumer channels, about 10M workers used earned wage products for over $31.9B in 2022. | About 90% of workers paid at least one fee, averaging $68.88 a year; illustrative APR 109.5%, with examples up to 580.4%.
Implication: A fee-bearing shock-liquidity market at 100%-plus APR exists for hourly Debit-Primary Spenders, which leaves price room for a cheaper bank alternative.
Caveats: Corpus row 14. Provider data runs only to 2022. Regulatory status moved after the corpus: the project brief records the 2024 proposal withdrawn in December 2025 and replaced by an advisory opinion excluding underwritten products; not re-verified here.

Claim: KFF analysis of the 2020 SIPP found about 9 percent of adults, roughly 23 million people, owe medical debt, with 11 million owing more than $2,000 and 3 million more than $10,000.
Evidence: KFF analysis of the 2020 SIPP (debts for 2019 bills): 9% of adults, about 23M people, owe medical debt; 11M owe more than $2,000; 3M more than $10,000. | KFF analysis of the 2021 SIPP: at least $220B owed; state prevalence from 2.3% (Hawaii) to 17.7% (South Dakota).
Implication: Medical debt is a mass stock with a concentrated tail, so T12 has to show it addresses the flow of new bills, not only the legacy stock.
Caveats: Corpus row 4. Different SIPP waves and thresholds; debts from 2019-2020, stale against the horizon; counts of people, not a revenue pool. Compiler spot-check: 9%, 23M, 11M and 3M confirmed on the KFF page, 2026-10-26.

Claim: KFF's 2022 survey found 26 percent of adults in households with income of $90,000 or more had health care debt versus 57 percent under $40,000, while the 2026 ACA out-of-pocket maximum is $10,600 individual and $21,200 family.
Evidence: KFF Health Care Debt Survey (fielded 2022-02-25 to 2022-03-20, n=2,375): 26% of adults at $90,000+ had health care debt versus 57% under $40,000. | Georgetown CCF yearly guidelines: 2026 ACA out-of-pocket maximum $10,600 individual and $21,200 family. | CMS: from 2022-01-01 the No Surprises Act bans most balance billing for emergency and certain out-of-network care.
Implication: Statutory caps narrow insured exposure but debt persists across income bands, so T12 is a product for lower-income and underinsured households, not the mass affluent.
Caveats: Corpus row 29. Self-reported survey (corpus type), 2022 field period; caps apply by plan type, not income.

Claim: On 5 May 2025 the Department of Education restarted Treasury Offset for defaulted federal student loans, stating that more than 5 million borrowers had not paid in over 360 days and that almost 10 million could be in default within months.
Evidence: Dept. of Education release: Treasury Offset restarted 2025-05-05; more than 5M borrowers in default; almost 10M could be in default within a few months (almost 25% of the portfolio); only 38% in repayment and current; administrative wage garnishment notices to follow later that summer. | NY Fed Household Debt and Credit Report (2026-08-11): flow into 90+ day student-loan delinquency moved from 12.88% (Q2 2025) to 7.83% (Q2 2026), attributed to re-reporting distortions.
Implication: A large defaulting population facing offsets and garnishment is a why-now for debt-management services, though it overlaps T20 and offers no bankruptcy off-ramp.
Caveats: Corpus row 8. The near-10M figure is a forward projection; 2020-2026 delinquency series are distorted by the pause.

Claim: Among US non-retirees in SHED 2025, adults with a major unexpected expense borrowed from, cashed out or cut contributions to a retirement account at roughly twice the rate of others, and a bank offering pre-approved shock liquidity secured by retirement balances would reduce cash-outs among its customers.
Evidence: Fed SHED 2025: 14% of non-retirees borrowed from, cashed out or reduced contributions to a retirement account in the prior 12 months. | Rates roughly double after a major unexpected expense (7% borrowed vs 3%, 5% cashed out vs 2%, 10% reduced contributions vs 4%) and rise further after a layoff. | Corpus row 2: only 3% of non-cash households use a bank loan or line of credit for a $400 shock.
Implication: A T16 variant for households holding retirement balances; it dies if few shock-exposed households hold balances or if a bank cannot take security over recordkeeper-held plan assets.
Caveats: Corpus row 21 plus row 2. Low because the security mechanism is untested. Compiler spot-check confirmed the 14% composite figure; the page's overall component shares (5%, 4%, 8%) sum above 14% because of overlap.

Claim: Bankruptcy filers recover their risk score within about a year but face total credit limits of 10 to 15 percent of the prior peak for at least six quarters, and a bank lending on recovered scores and deposit behaviour would find a population other lenders decline despite the score.
Evidence: Philadelphia Fed WP 14-25 (about 600,000 filers, 2002-2013): scores return to pre-filing levels within about a year; total limits bottom at 10% to 15% of the peak and stay flat at least six quarters; reduced lending persists more than six years for Chapter 13 filers. | Administrative Office of the US Courts (year to 2025-06-30): 542,529 bankruptcy filings, up 11.5%, 519,486 non-business.
Implication: The unserved step after distress is credit re-extension, a lending decision a bank can make and a T18 subscription cannot; it may belong to T07 as its distress-side segment.
Caveats: Corpus rows 6, 7 and 20. The key study ends in 2013 and post-filing default rates are unmeasured; post-bankruptcy cards exist, so this may be adjacency.

Claim: In October 2025, 59% of US adults had at least one major unexpected expense in the prior 12 months and 37% would not cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent, a share unchanged for four years.
Evidence: SHED 2025 (fielded 17-28 October 2025, Ipsos KnowledgePanel, nearly 13,000 adults), new questions drawn from the CFPB Making Ends Meet survey: 59% had at least one major unexpected expense; vehicle repair or replacement 30%, house or appliance repair 22%, unexpected major medical 21%; median cost for these three in the $1,000 to $1,999 band among those who knew the amount (PDF pp. 7, 45-46) | SHED 2025: 63% would cover a hypothetical $400 expense exclusively with cash, savings or a card paid off at the next statement, unchanged from the prior three years and down from 68% in 2021; the report itself refers to the other 37% (PDF pp. 7, 49) | SHED 2025: among adults with income under $50,000, 4 in 10 could not cover even a $100 emergency expense with only their savings (PDF p. 8) | SHED 2025: 7% used a payday, pawn, auto title or tax refund anticipation loan in the prior year, up 1 point (PDF p. 66)
Implication: The shock-liquidity pain is large and stable, which supports the size half of T16; whether a bank's pre-approved line beats existing overdraft, card and advance products is untested here; most relevant to Debit-Primary Spenders.
Caveats: The SHED notes low-income and young adults were LESS likely to have a major unexpected expense, while homeowners (63%) and adults with a car (60%) were more likely, so shock frequency and lack of buffer fall on partly different households; the $400 gap is concentrated in lower income, pointing to income rather than a missing product. Credit for shocks already exists (overdraft, cards, BNPL 16%, small-dollar loans 7%). Self-reported; 'unexpected' is respondent-defined. CFPB Fulford and Low work and the Aspen expense-shock page (403) were not used. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Revolving debt is widespread and served at scale (45% of card owners carried a balance in 2025; card balances were $1.263 trillion in Q2 2026 with 6.97% flowing into serious delinquency), while venture interest in a debt-management subscription is a single $15.5M seed (Ava, October 2025).
Evidence: SHED 2025: 45% of credit-card owners carried a balance at least once in the prior 12 months, down 12 points over a decade; BNPL use 16% of adults, and 11% of BNPL users had a payment trigger an overdraft or NSF fee; using merged bureau data, average card balances rose more than 35% since 2023 among those finding it difficult to get by (PDF pp. 8, 67) | NY Fed Household Debt and Credit, Q2 2026 (released 11 August 2026): credit-card balances $1.26 trillion; annualized flow into 90+ day delinquency 6.97%; total household debt $18.771 trillion | Ava raised a $15.5M seed reported 27 October 2025 (FinTech Global; Greylock, Transform VC and others, angels from Meta, Credit Karma and Plaid); product is a $10-per-month app pitched as a 'CFO in your pocket' that improves credit profiles, finds lending options and offers one-click loan origination; a Transform VC founder called it a $100B market, unsourced
Implication: The T18 audience exists in size, but the credit it carries is already served by card issuers including Capital One's enterprise, and the paid-subscription model has one seed-stage entrant and no demand data, so T18 survives only as a narrower debt-resolution service if at all.
Caveats: Merged from T14-A finding 2 and T14-B finding 9. Ava evidence is investor interest only: no customers or revenue; the $100B figure comes from an investor in the round (rated Low); the Axios Pro report returned 403 in round 1 and is not cited. 'Saturated' is inferred from SHED usage and the sponsor brief naming the card business, not from a product map. Debt-management features overlap the sponsor's out-of-scope money-assistant list and T07. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: In 2025, 26% of US adults skipped medical care because of cost, 18% carried medical debt and 21% had an unexpected major medical expense, with the uninsured nearly twice as likely as the insured to skip care.
Evidence: SHED 2025: 26% skipped medical care because of cost in the prior 12 months, down from 28% in 2024; 45% of the uninsured skipped care against 24% of the insured (PDF pp. 7, 45) | SHED 2025: 18% had debt from their own or a family member's medical care (not necessarily from the past year), a share that has ranged from 15% to 18% since 2019; a prevalence, not a dollar total (PDF p. 45) | SHED 2025: 21% had an unexpected major medical expense in the prior 12 months, median in the $1,000 to $1,999 band (PDF pp. 7, 45-46)
Implication: Supports the pain half of T12; the gap by insurance status says the barrier is coverage and price, which a bank's negotiation or financing does not change, so the T12 slices should test that counter-argument directly.
Caveats: Supports the prevalence claim only. Pain is caused by coverage and pricing (45% versus 24% skipped by insurance status), the counter-evidence the T12 brief already flags. Self-reported. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Unpromoted candidate, auto total cost of ownership: vehicle repair is the most common major unexpected expense (30% of adults in 2025) and auto-loan balances were $1.713 trillion in Q2 2026, but no total-cost-of-ownership pain figure was found and Capital One's enterprise already owns auto lending.
Evidence: SHED 2025: 30% of adults had a major vehicle repair or replacement in the prior 12 months, the most common major unexpected expense; 60% of adults with access to a car had some major unexpected expense (PDF pp. 45-46) | NY Fed Q2 2026: auto-loan balance $1.713 trillion; annualized flow into 90+ day delinquency 3.00% for auto loans, against 6.97% for cards and 7.83% for student loans | T14-A found no qualifying 2024-2026 consumer venture round for auto total cost of ownership (Caribou auto refinance is 2022)
Implication: Not promoted: fails the Additive screen because auto lending is enterprise-owned, and the only data measure shocks and loan stress, not all-in vehicle cost; the repair-shock pain is better carried inside T16.
Caveats: No dataset on all-in household vehicle cost was found; shock frequency and loan stress are proxies. Auto delinquency is driven by loan size, rates and incomes. Absence of venture rounds rests on a limited search. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Empathy, a bereavement-logistics and estate-support company, raised a $72M Series C in May 2025 (total $162M) and reaches families at no cost through life insurers and employers, with Citi Impact Fund the only bank among its ten Empathy Alliance investors.
Evidence: Series C announced 2025-05-29: $72M led by Adams Street Partners, total raised $162M; Empathy Alliance members are Aflac, Allianz Life, MassMutual, Munich Re, MetLife, New York Life, Securian, Sumitomo and TIAA venture arms plus Citi Impact Fund (company blog) | Company blog: covers 45M+ lives in North America; works with 8 of the 10 top US life insurers; reaches 1 in 5 insurance claimants in the US and Canada | Calcalist (trade press quoting the company): 1,000+ employers offer it as a benefit; tens of millions of dollars in revenue; revenue up more than 300% since the round a year earlier; 130 staff; 50M+ covered lives | Series B 2024-03-12: $47M led by Index Ventures, $90M total; families pay nothing, the insurance benefit or the employer pays (Index Ventures)
Implication: An executor-side support product already operates at scale and is paid for by insurers and employers, so a bank entering T06 on bereavement logistics meets an incumbent holding that channel; the open question is the account-and-asset half of settlement that Empathy does not own.
Caveats: All metrics are company statements or trade press repeating them; unaudited. Covered lives differ by source (45M company blog, 50M Calcalist). Compiler correction: the slice file said revenue rose 10x in two years; Calcalist says more than 300% (tripled) since the prior round. BMO and TD logos appear on empathy.com unlabelled, so no bank partnership is claimed. Insurer investors fund Empathy to serve their own claimants (sponsor interest). No Form D located (EDGAR full-text search does not index Form D), so rounds rest on company disclosure. Funding is investor belief, not demand.

Claim: Fifth Third Bank has given all customers free wills through Trust & Will since May 2025 and by June 2026 reported more than 39,000 wills and 3,000 trusts created; Navy Federal has offered members a discounted version since October 2023.
Evidence: Trust & Will release 2026-06-11: 39,000+ wills redeemed (subtitle says 42,000+ estate plans), 3,000+ trusts, 64.8% registration-to-completed-will conversion, $12.6M estimated customer savings, $10B+ customer-reported estate value; benefit to extend to Comerica customers after the acquisition | Banking Dive 2025-05-19 (primary record of the launch): Fifth Third is an investor in Trust & Will, partnership about six years with discounted service since 2020; the bank framed it as a way to deepen relationships amid intense competition for customers and deposits and declined to say what it pays | Navy Federal release 2023-10-16: special-rated discount for members; Navy Federal serves 13M members | NBC (2025-03-11): Trust & Will $25M Series C led by Moderne Ventures, $75M total, hundreds of thousands of families; sells direct and through financial-institution partners
Implication: Will and trust drafting is already a bank-distributed consumer product, so for a bank it is adjacency not zero to one; the unserved part of T06 is post-death settlement and heir retention, and Fifth Third's stated motive (deposit competition) is testable.
Caveats: Figures are the vendor's and the bank's own; the bank is also a Trust & Will investor. Release is internally inconsistent (39,000 wills vs 42,000 estate plans); no Fifth Third customer base is given so penetration cannot be computed. NBC names Bank of America and USAA as partners too; no bank page confirms them, so they are not claimed. Planning, not settlement.

Claim: Post-death settlement and advisor-channel estate-planning firms (Alix, Wealth.com, Vanilla) raised 2024-2026 rounds with Schwab, Edward Jones, Vanguard, Citi and Nationwide as investors and sell through financial advisors rather than direct to consumers.
Evidence: Alix 2025-07-21: $20M Series A led by Acrew Capital with Charles Schwab and Edward Jones Ventures; $30.65M total; founded about two years earlier; no estates-settled figure (FinTech Global). Edward Jones Ventures portfolio note 2026-02-06: AI plus human settlement specialists who coordinate with financial advisors (Pulse 2.0) | Wealth.com 2026-04-16: $65M Series B; existing investors include Schwab, GV, Citi Ventures; approved by the three largest US broker-dealers giving access to 50,000+ advisors; client firms oversee $15T+; no bank named (Pulse 2.0) | Vanilla news page: $35M round 2024-10-16 led by Insight Partners with Vanguard, Edward Jones Ventures, Nationwide and Allianz; Vanguard pilot with advised clients announced 2024-01-18; all 700+ Mariner advisors from 2025-04-18; $99/month starter plan for small RIAs from 2025-09-30
Implication: Capital is flowing to the executor and heir problem but into advisor-distributed B2B2C tools, so a consumer bank would compete with brokerages for the estate-assets relationship; mass-market Debit-Primary households sit outside the advisor channel and none of these serve them.
Caveats: Trade press (FinTech Global, Pulse 2.0) is the primary record of the rounds because no Form D was located; both largely repeat company releases (BusinessWire returned 403). Wealth.com's $15T and growth figures are company claims. Strategic investors have a sponsor interest. Alix scale is unreported, not shown to be small.

Claim: Consumer estate and end-of-life organizer startups Willing (2019), Everplans (2021 and 2024) and Cake (2024) were each bought by an insurer or funeral operator rather than scaling as standalone consumer brands, with terms undisclosed.
Evidence: Refresh Miami 2019-11-20 (trade press as primary record of the deal): MetLife agreed to buy Willing, a YC-backed will startup with at least $7.1M raised and more than half a million families helped, to offer to group-benefits customers alongside Hyatt Legal | Everplans' own posts: National Guardian Life Insurance acquired Everplans 2021-01-25; Precoa, an end-of-life planning company with 1M+ households, acquired it 2024-10-16 | PrivSource deal record (aggregator, pointer only): Foundation Partners Group, a funeral operator, acquired Cake, listed 2024-10-02
Implication: The consumer-direct estate-organizer category exited into insurers and funeral groups, which lowers the odds of standalone consumer demand and names the rivals who value the heir relationship.
Caveats: Acquisitions, not shutdowns; no prices disclosed, so distress cannot be inferred. Willing's $7.1M raised is Crunchbase via trade press. The Cake deal rests on an aggregator that does not cite a filing; no Cake or Foundation Partners primary was fetched. No verified 2024-2026 shutdown of a US estate startup was found.

Claim: In Vanguard's 2025 recordkeeping data on participants who left their employer, 58% of assets stayed in the plan, 36% rolled over and 5% were cashed out, while installment payments took under 0.5% of participants and of assets.
Evidence: Vanguard How America Saves 2026, Figure 115 (2025 terminations): by participants, remain in plan 46%, rollover 25%, cash lump sum 28%, installments under 0.5%; by assets, remain 58%, rollover 36%, lump sum 5%, installments under 0.5% | Same report: 68% of sponsors allowed installment payments and 43% of plans permitted partial ad hoc distributions in 2025, up from 35% in 2020 | Figure 117: participants in their 70s chose installments 10% of the time but installments held 1% of their assets; 55% of their assets were rolled over
Implication: At the retirement-exit moment the balance stays with a recordkeeper or moves to an IRA custodian, not to a bank deposit relationship, so T19 is a distribution fight against recordkeepers; structured income is almost unused, which may reflect weak demand as much as missing supply.
Caveats: Vanguard is a recordkeeper with an interest in retaining assets; its plan base skews large. Compiler correction: the slice cited 27% in 2018 for ad hoc partial distributions; the page reviewed states 35% in 2020, so that figure replaces it. Text says 94% of assets preserved (Figure 116). PDF does not parse through WebFetch; verified against a local PyMuPDF extract of the fetched file (output/transfer/_pdf/vanguard-has2026.txt).

Claim: US annuity sales set a first-half record of $223.0B in 2025, but single-premium immediate and deferred income annuities were only $6.5B and $2.1B; the digital income-annuity platforms were bought by an insurer (Blueprint Income, MassMutual) or sell to advisors (DPL).
Evidence: LIMRA release 2025-07-29: H1 2025 total annuity sales $223.0B (+3%); SPIA $6.5B (-8%); DIA $2.1B (-14%). Compiler arithmetic from those two LIMRA figures: SPIA plus DIA is about 3.9% of the total | Coverager (trade press as primary record of the deal): MassMutual acquired Blueprint Income from Stone Ridge; 1.5M+ users visited Blueprint in 2020; price undisclosed | Pulse 2.0 2024-12-03: DPL Financial Partners $23M Series C led by Eos Ventures with TIAA Ventures; $3.7B on platform; serves RIAs | Blueprint Income news page (updated 2026-06-18) names no recordkeeper or bank partner
Implication: Insurers sell annuities at very large scale, so a bank selling them is adjacency; the guaranteed-income niche is small, which means either white space or weak demand, and the consumer digital attempts were absorbed by an insurer or turned to advisors.
Caveats: LIMRA is an insurance trade body (sponsor interest); figures are preliminary and dominated by accumulation products. The Coverager article carries no date (it says last month); the acquisition is dated early 2021 from the slice's other reading, not confirmed on the page. MassMutual's own page timed out.

Claim: Retirable, a retirement-income app for middle-income households, says it has helped more than 50,000 people and delivers income and advice as an SEC-registered investment adviser, renting banking and its Visa debit card from Thread Bank.
Evidence: Retirable site (copyright 2026): more than 50,000 people helped; describes itself as an SEC-registered investment adviser and not an FDIC-insured bank | Thread Bank (Member FDIC) provides banking services and issues the Retirable Visa debit card; sweep program offers up to $3M of FDIC coverage | No AUM, pricing or funding figure appears on the site; reported Series A and AUM figures were seen only in search snippets and are not claimed
Implication: The nearest consumer decumulation pure play is sub-scale and borrows the bank layer from a sponsor bank, so a deposit bank already holds the ingredient the app rents; demand and willingness to pay are unshown.
Caveats: Single company self-description; people helped is not paying clients. No funding or AUM verified. Status active per its own site only.

Claim: As of 2026 a US bank's duties at a depositor's death are set by rule: FDIC coverage holds for six months, Treasury can reclaim federal benefit payments made after death with the bank liable if it fails to certify and report on time, and the CFPB sends survivors to the account agreement.
Evidence: 12 CFR 330.3(j): a deposit owner's death does not affect coverage for six months unless the account is restructured; afterwards coverage follows actual ownership. FDIC bankers' guide (updated 2024-05-29): no grace period when a beneficiary dies | 31 CFR 210.11: a bank's liability on a reclamation is capped at the lesser of the balance when it acts on the notice or the outstanding total, plus payments received within 45 days after death; it must certify when it first knew of the death and give names and addresses of co-owners, others authorized to withdraw, and anyone who withdrew after death; failing to comply on time and accurately makes it liable for the loss | CFPB Ask CFPB page (reviewed 2026-08-28): joint-account funds pass to the survivor under rights of survivorship or to heirs under tenancy in common; readers are told to check the account agreement or ask the bank
Implication: The deposit account is where a death becomes legally visible and the bank already runs freeze, reclaim and certify duties, a distribution edge an app lacks, but those duties are cost and liability, so a heir service would sit on a process the bank runs defensively; weakest fit for Young Consumers.
Caveats: Rules, not usage data: nothing here says how fast banks learn of deaths, how long freezes last, or whether heirs stay. eCFR section pages redirect to a block page; text was read through the official eCFR versioner API (as of 2026-10-01). Capital One's own deceased-customer process was not found.

Claim: A national bank can gain executor, trustee and fee-based investment-adviser capacity by OCC application, deemed approved on day 30 for an eligible bank, yet Capital One's FY2025 10-K names no fiduciary, trust, wealth-management or insurance-agency business.
Evidence: 12 CFR 9.2(e): fiduciary capacity includes trustee, executor, administrator, guardian, UGMA custodian, investment adviser where the bank takes a fee, and any capacity with investment discretion for another | 12 CFR 5.26: prior OCC approval (or notice) is needed to exercise fiduciary powers; an eligible bank on expedited review is deemed approved on the 30th day; the OCC weighs proposed senior trust management and the business plan; approval expires if activity does not start within 18 months | Compiler text search of Capital One's 10-K for fiscal 2025 (filed 2026-02-19 per EDGAR index): zero hits for trust powers, fiduciary, investment advis, wealth management, insurance agen; the only broker-dealers named are Capital One Securities, KippsDeSanto and TripleTree
Implication: The licence is a 30-day filing, not the barrier; the barrier is building and staffing a fiduciary operation Capital One shows no trace of, so it starts from zero on operations but not on permission.
Caveats: Absent keywords in a 10-K do not prove no trust powers exist; the OCC trust-powers registry was not checked (FFIEC blocked). Eligibility for expedited review was not tested. eCFR text read via the official versioner API. The 10-K is company disclosure.

Claim: Small-estate thresholds in three large states differ roughly fourfold, from $50,000 of personal property in New York to $75,000 excluding homestead in Texas to $208,850 in California, and the procedures differ (court voluntary administration, judge-approved affidavit, out-of-court affidavit).
Evidence: NY SCPA 1301: a small estate is personal property of gross value $50,000 or less, excluding property set off under EPTL 5-3.1 (NY Senate statute page) | Texas Estates Code 205.001 via a mirror (texas.public.law): estate value not above $75,000 excluding homestead and exempt property, 30 days after death, judge must approve the affidavit | Kern County Superior Court affidavit packet: $208,850 gross-value limit under Probate Code 13100-13101 for deaths on or after 2025-04-01, next adjustment 2028-04-01; California real property uses a separate route ($69,625 tier)
Implication: An executor product must be rebuilt per state and kept current, and the small-estate fast path is a state form an executor can file without a bank, which narrows T06 to navigation for larger estates or those with real property.
Caveats: Texas text comes from a mirror; the legislature's statute site returned only navigation on two attempts, so the primary was not fetched and the row is rated Low under the prune rule. California figure is from a court form, not the code (code page 403); PDF does not parse through WebFetch and was verified against a local extract of the freshly fetched file; the packet itself says values next adjust 2028, so an unverified $239,700 2026 figure is not used. Three states, not a survey; no source gives the share of estates under thresholds.

Claim: In Janson v. LegalZoom (W.D. Mo., 2011-08-02) the court denied summary judgment because whether LegalZoom went beyond selling self-help forms was a factual question, under Missouri precedent that allows forms sold without personal advice on legal remedies or consequences.
Evidence: Blog summary of the ruling (No. 2:10-CV-04018-NKL): summary judgment denied; LegalZoom's First Amendment and due process defences rejected | Missouri Supreme Court precedents cited: In re Thompson (do-it-yourself divorce kits allowed absent personal advice) and Hulse v. Criger (document preparation ancillary to a main business with no separate fee is not unauthorized practice) | No state-bar opinion on non-lawyer estate help and no bank-specific UPL ruling was found
Implication: A bank can supply forms, checklists and deadlines, but individual advice on who inherits or what a survivor owes edges into legal practice in at least one state, so T06 must be information and routing to counsel, which caps margin and any AI-executor claim.
Caveats: Pointer only: an academic's blog summary; the opinion itself was not fetched (CourtListener returned 403). Missouri-specific, 2011; UPL is state law and some states have since opened sandboxes (not researched). A settlement figure seen in a search result is not used.

Claim: A national bank's collective investment funds are limited to money held as fiduciary and to tax-exempt retirement trusts and may not be advertised, and under SEC Regulation R an unregistered bank can pay staff only a nominal fee for referrals to a broker-dealer except for institutional or high-net-worth customers.
Evidence: 12 CFR 9.18(a)(1)-(2): permitted funds are those maintained exclusively for money the bank holds as trustee, executor, administrator, guardian or custodian, and funds consisting solely of assets of tax-exempt retirement, pension and similar trusts; 9.18(b)(7): a bank may not advertise or publicize an (a)(1) fund; IRAs and Keoghs appear only in footnotes on funds registered under the Investment Company Act | SEC Reg R small-entity compliance guide: the trust and fiduciary exception uses a chiefly-compensated test applied per account (Rule 721) or bank-wide (Rule 722); networking referral pay to unregistered employees must be nominal, e.g. a flat $25 inflation-adjusted (Rule 700), with higher contingent fees only for institutional or high-net-worth referrals (Rule 701)
Implication: The not-a-broker route is a trust-department product for fiduciary and retirement-plan money, or a token-fee referral to someone else's broker-dealer, so it cannot be sold as an open consumer income product; it fits Young Consumers and Debit-Primary Spenders least.
Caveats: The Reg R guide is dated 2008 (modified stamp) and summarises the 2007 rule; current 17 CFR part 247 was not read. 9.18 read through the official eCFR versioner API. Affiliate broker-dealer or RIA routes are outside T19's not-a-broker premise.

Claim: Annuity income requires an insurance company to issue it and a state-licensed person to sell it: federal law bars states from preventing or significantly interfering with bank insurance sales but lets them require licensing for commissions and not-a-deposit disclosures, and a QLAC must be bought from an insurer.
Evidence: 15 USC 6701 (Gramm-Leach-Bliley s.104), via Cornell LII: McCarran-Ferguson remains law; anyone in the business of insurance as principal or agent must hold the state licence; bank insurance sales are judged under the Barnett standard; states may require that unlicensed persons not receive commissions, that products be disclosed as not a deposit and not FDIC-insured, separate insurance records, and limits on tying credit to insurance | IRS Form 1098-Q instructions (revised 04/2025): a QLAC is an annuity contract purchased from an insurance company; the 25% premium limit is repealed for contracts bought on or after 2022-12-29; the 2025 dollar limit is $200,000 | Capital One FY2025 10-K: no insurance agency or insurer subsidiary found; the only annuity mention is annuity contracts purchased from an independent insurance company to settle its terminated pension plan
Implication: Without being an insurer the bank can only distribute a third-party carrier's product through licensed staff, the position banks already occupy, so any edge is distribution to existing older deposit customers, not either named segment.
Caveats: The statute text is from a mirror (Cornell LII); uscode.house.gov and govinfo returned 404 in this pass, so under the prune rule the row is rated Low even though the IRS and 10-K bullets are primary. Annuity-specific statutory text beyond character 100,000 was not read. The 2026 QLAC limit is not stated on the IRS page.

Claim: The DOL's 2024 Retirement Security Rule was vacated by two Texas federal courts and the Federal Register published a notice of court vacatur on 2026-03-20, effective 2026-04-20, so the 2024 widening of fiduciary status for rollover advice is not in force.
Evidence: DOL Retirement Security Rule page: rule and related PTE amendments vacated by court order in Federation of Americans for Consumer Choice v. DOL (E.D. Tex., No. 6:24-CV-163-JDK) and American Council of Life Insurers v. DOL (N.D. Tex., No. 4:24-CV-00482-O); notice at 91 FR 13503 published 2026-03-20 | Federal Register record 2026-05492 (API metadata): notice of court vacatur, effective 2026-04-20; reflects vacatur of 2024 amendments to PTE 2020-02 and republishes its text as of 2020-12-18 | 401k Specialist 2026-03-13 (trade press): DOL stopped actively defending the rule by late 2025 and filed jointly for, or did not oppose, vacatur
Implication: Lower federal fiduciary exposure helps whoever already holds the rollover (recordkeeper, broker, insurer) and opens no path for a deposit bank to reach balances it does not hold; it removes one regulatory risk to T19 and leaves the structural one.
Caveats: Status can change; no replacement proposal confirmed. Federal Register page redirected to a block page; read through the official FR API. What governs now (the 1975 five-part test) comes from trade press and a search summary, not a fetched DOL page. SEC Reg BI and state insurance best-interest rules not researched.

Claim: Cerulli projects $84.4 trillion transferring through 2045 and, in a later vintage, $124 trillion through 2048, mostly from Baby Boomers and older generations and concentrated in wealthy households.
Evidence: Cerulli $84.4T through 2045 ($72.6T to heirs, $11.9T to charity); HNW and UHNW households, 1.5% of households, account for $35.8T (42%) | Cerulli 2024-2048 update: $124T ($105T to heirs, $18T to charity), nearly $100T (81%) from Boomers and older | In that projection Gen X inherits $14T and Millennials $8T over the next 10 years, against $46T for Millennials over 25 years, so most money lands after 2036
Implication: The headline pool is large but concentrated in wealthy estates and mostly pending past the next decade, so it cannot size a mass-market executor or heir product; the HNW slice belongs to wealth managers.
Caveats: Cerulli sells to wealth managers (sponsor interest) and its estimate moved 47% across two vintages about two years apart. Corpus Evidence Type: Market Research; corpus Medium mapped down to Low.

Claim: In Survey of Consumer Finances data 2001-2019, inheritance receipt peaks at 11.2% over five years for households aged 56-65 versus 5.0% under 26, at least half of recipients get their first transfer after 40, and the top 5% by labor income average $51,499 against $9,097 for the bottom decile.
Evidence: Penn Wharton Budget Model, median across seven SCF waves 2001-2019: five-year receipt probability 11.2% at ages 56-65 versus 5.0% under 26 (text says about 5 percent); top 5% by income 11.1% across all ages | Average unconditional inheritance (2019 dollars) is highest at 56-65 ($19,792), then 46-55 ($14,237); $3,314 under 26 | By labor income, all ages: top 5% $51,499 versus bottom decile $9,097; conditional on receipt the top 5% average about $424,000 versus $90,000-$158,000 for the bottom 90% | Richmond Fed brief using SCF: among those who ever receive a transfer, at least half get the first one after age 40
Implication: Heirs are mostly middle-aged, average sums are small, and dollars sit with higher-income households, so the heir is a one-time mid-life customer and a poor fit for Young Consumers or the Debit-Primary balance sheet, though debit households still carry the executor burden.
Caveats: Merged from corpus findings 2 and 3 (same Penn Wharton source). Compiler correction on spot-check: corpus gave under-26 receipt as 4.5% (actual 5.0%; 4.5% is the 26-35 cell) and said averages peak at 46-55 ($14,237) and 56-65 ($12,328); the page shows 56-65 at $19,792 and $12,328 is the 66-75 cell. The table has an extra header column that shifts values, which caused the misreads. SCF is respondent-recalled; households ranked by labor income only. Corpus confidence High mapped to Medium because two corpus figures failed verification. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: In 40 states with comparable data, probate and estate filings in 2022 were 3% above 2018 while total civil filings were 17% below, and probate rose from 7% to 10% of the civil caseload.
Evidence: NCSC Court Statistics Project: probate/estate was the only civil category with 2022 filings above 2018 (+3%); total civil 17% below 2018 | Probate/estate grew from 7% of tracked civil caseload in 2018/2019 to 10% in 2022; 28 of 36 states reported higher 2022 filings than 2018 | Guardianship was a further 12% of the probate/estate caseload
Implication: Court-supervised estate work is a growing observable workload, the executor's pain, but it is legal process and not yet evidence of unmet banking demand.
Caveats: Rotating 20-40 state sample; comparability imperfect. Not re-verified this pass. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: Alameda County studies find most estates settle without litigation (12.5% litigated, executor-related claims 55% of litigated claims) and that probate compensation runs about 2.9% of estate value in undisputed matters and 3.6% in disputed ones under California's statutory fee schedule.
Evidence: Horton (Iowa Law Review 2018, quoted with pincites): litigation in 12.5% of estates; 204 of 368 litigated claims (55%) concerned fiduciary breach, objection to the personal representative or removal; corpus arithmetic implies executor conflict in about 7% of estates | Horton's 571-matter Alameda study: of 70 litigated estates, 22 involved objections to appointment or removal of the personal representative | Horton: personal-representative commissions 1.0% and attorney fees 1.5% of gross estate value; average total compensation 2.9% undisputed, 3.6% disputed, attributed to California's statutory schedule (4% of first $100,000 down to 1% above $1M)
Implication: Contested estates are a minority and the professional fee pool is modest in statutory-fee states, so a cheaper executor tool must win on time and complexity, not on undercutting fees.
Caveats: Merged from corpus findings 5 and 6 (same author and county). Single county; the 7% is the corpus agent's arithmetic, not stated by either source; hourly and flat-fee states may differ; the marketed 3-10% probate cost range has no checkable source. Not re-verified this pass. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: CFPB analysis of SIPP and HRS data finds new surviving spouses with unpaid medical bills carry an average of $28,749 versus $15,785 for others with such bills, and the CFPB warned that pursuing non-liable survivors may violate the FDCPA.
Evidence: CFPB analysis of Census SIPP (2018-2022) and HRS (2004-2020): new surviving spouses with unpaid bills average $28,749 versus $15,785; 11% carry unpaid medical bills versus 10% generally | 1.7 million US adults were widowed within the prior 12 months as of 2022; two-thirds women, average age 71 | CFPB: collectors pursuing a deceased spouse's medical debt from a non-liable survivor may violate the FDCPA and state law
Implication: A concrete dated pain for an older, mostly female survivor with a bank-visible account, pointing to advocacy and triage rather than a financial product, and away from Young Consumers.
Caveats: Spot-checked this pass: $28,749, $15,785 and 1.7 million confirmed. Spousal liability is state law (doctrine of necessaries); enforcement posture reflects one CFPB era; page is in the CFPB archive. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: CFPB's December 2024 spotlight on complaints from December 2021 to August 2024 documents mortgage servicers pressing heirs and other successors in interest to refinance at higher rates and taking months to years to recognize their status.
Evidence: CFPB issue spotlight: servicers pressure successors in interest (heirs and divorced spouses) to refinance at prevailing rates, delay recognizing successor status, and refuse to release original borrowers | NY Fed Household Debt and Credit Report: HELOC balances $422B in Q3 2025, up $35B year over year
Implication: The pain sits with mortgage servicers, a line Capital One left in 2017, so an heir product here is advocacy or refinance routing rather than something a deposit bank owns.
Caveats: Complaint-driven and qualitative; no share of successors affected. Not re-verified this pass. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: Defined-benefit plan participants fell to just over 29 million in 2023 from a roughly 42 million peak while defined-contribution participation grew 4.0%, and most IRA inflows are rollovers from DC accounts, keeping the recordkeeper or brokerage in the retirement-income chain.
Evidence: DOL/EBSA Abstract of 2023 Form 5500: DB participants just over 29 million in 2023 versus roughly 42 million peak; DC participation +4.0%, 401(k)-type plan count +5.6%; 81.6 million active 401(k)-type participants | CRS on the 2022 SCF: the majority of IRA inflows are rollovers from DC plans at job change or retirement
Implication: The decumulation balance sits with recordkeepers and brokerages before retirement, so a bank would have to win assets it does not hold; weakens T19 for the upmarket segment and says nothing about Debit-Primary households.
Caveats: Rollover mechanism described qualitatively by CRS without a volume figure. Corpus segment tag upmarket. Not re-verified this pass. Corpus Evidence Type: Observed/Administrative.

Claim: Territory candidate (Heir and survivor obligation triage): a bank could help surviving spouses, adult children and successors who face a dead relative's medical bills, mortgage or HELOC, co-signed private student loan or reverse mortgage learn what is legally owed and which deadlines apply, and route them to action, keeping the survivor's deposit relationship.
Evidence: Corpus R5: new surviving spouses with unpaid medical bills average $28,749 versus $15,785; CFPB says pursuing non-liable survivors may violate the FDCPA | Corpus R8: CFPB complaint narratives 2021-2024 show servicers delaying successor status and pressing heirs to refinance | Corpus R7: more than 681,000 active HECMs with $64.3B maximum claim amount at 2025-09-30; heirs generally have 30 days after the borrower's death to buy, sell or surrender the home, extendable up to six months | Corpus R6: CFPB's review of 2,300+ private student loan complaints found contracts allowing auto-default when a co-signer dies
Implication: The pains share a pattern (a death triggers a debt or deadline the survivor does not understand) but each is owned by a different counterparty, so a bank would be advocate and router; no evidence on willingness to pay or event frequency per customer.
Caveats: Four corpus rows combined as a hypothesis; no statistic merged. HUD figure spot-checked this pass (681,000 and $64.3B confirmed). Also folds in corpus finding 9 (HECM). Information and routing only, given the UPL limit in transfer-11. Confidence Low because it is inference across rows, not a measured demand signal.

Claim: Round 1 found no 2024-2026 consumer-facing decumulation venture round, only B2B activity (Nestimate's $3M round for plan advisers and sponsors, September 2025), and no decumulation pain data, while 73% of US adults aged 55-64 held a tax-preferred retirement account in 2025.
Evidence: Nestimate closed a $3M round on 15 September 2025 led by S3 Ventures with PruVen Capital, TIAA Ventures and Invest Nebraska; customers are retirement plan advisers, consultants, sponsors, recordkeepers and insurers; product helps plan fiduciaries assess retirement income strategies (401k Specialist) | a16z essay (27 July 2023) lists 'plan for retirement' among AI autopilot use cases but names no startups | SHED 2025: 73% of adults aged 55-64 had a tax-preferred retirement account (63% of 25-54, 62% of 65+); 35% of non-retirees thought their retirement saving was on track (40% in 2021); 14% of non-retirees borrowed from, cashed out or cut contributions in the prior year (PDF pp. 7, 53-55)
Implication: Balances to decumulate exist for most near-retirees, but venture money is going to the plan sponsor and recordkeeper channel, consistent with the corpus finding that the bank is bypassed at rollover; T19 rests on demographics alone until decumulation data are found.
Caveats: Merged from T14-A finding 6 and T14-B finding 8 (decumulation half). Absence in two searches is not proof of absence. The a16z essay predates the window and is investor content. Small-round trade-press source. SHED 'on track' is self-assessed; balances and spend-down behaviour (Fed SCF, EBRI) were not opened. The retirement-adequacy data bear mainly on T05; the T05 compiler holds the corpus for it. SHED PDF verified against the local PyMuPDF extract (output/crosscut/T14-candidates/_pdf/); PDF page numbers are the file's, not the printed pages.

Claim: Seventeen months after launching free wills, Fifth Third has disclosed programme activity but no deposit, retention or account-opening effect, and no US bank, Fed or FDIC source found reports heir retention or deposit attrition after a depositor's death.
Evidence: Fifth Third June 2026 programme update (BriefGlance summary of the release): launched May 2025; over 39,000 customers created wills; 3,000 established trusts; estimated $12.6 million saved; nearly 65% completion from registration to finalised will; about $10 billion of estate value; no retention or deposit figure on the page | Banking Dive (19 May 2025): Fifth Third is an investor in Trust & Will and has partnered with it for about six years; Erin Crawford, head of consumer digital, said the benefit is building and deepening relationships and that the bank is trying to deepen and protect them; the bank declined to state the programme cost and expected thousands of initial users | Earnings calls: Q2 2025 (17 Jul 2025) has one prepared-remarks line on the free-wills initiative with no effect stated; Q3 2025 (17 Oct 2025), Q1 2026 (17 Apr 2026), Q2 2026 (17 Jul 2026) and Q3 2026 (19 Oct 2026) do not mention wills, Trust & Will or estate planning; the only retention figure in Q3 2026 is generic (about 80% of roughly $2.5 billion of monthly deposit movements on the platform retained), unrelated to deaths | Huntington's five calls Q3 2025 to Q3 2026 (caregiving-90) and two open-web searches by the researcher returned no death-related attrition or heir-retention figure
Implication: The only bank with a stated relationship motive for estate help has published no retention result, so T06's heir-retention kill test cannot be run from public records and the In-as-adjacency verdict is left where it was; the Capital One settlement-check match is the only route to the number.
Caveats: Programme figures come from BriefGlance, a self-described unverified summary of a Business Wire release that returned 403 (prune list: press-release aggregator; pointer only, hence Low); an earlier pass noted the release is internally inconsistent (39,000 vs 42,000). Fifth Third is both investor in and customer of Trust & Will. Wills created are not accounts opened. Transcripts are a third-party mirror (stockanalysis.com). Absence from calls and searches is a clean no-disclosure result, not a negative measurement; ABA Banking Journal, FDIC research and FEDS notes were not searched in full. Merges researcher findings uptake-4 and uptake-6.

Claim: Trust & Will's Navy Federal partnership page offers members 30% off and states no member count or outcome, and Fifth Third's CEO said the Comerica trust business it acquired carried a public consent order.
Evidence: Navy Federal page: all plans 30% off for members (individual will $139.30 instead of $199; individual trust $349.30 instead of $499); Trust & Will says it has served over a million families overall; no Navy Federal member count, wills created or retention | Fifth Third Q3 2025 call (17 Oct 2025): Tim Spence said Comerica had a public consent order attached to the trust business and that the first priority is putting the trust business on stable footing; the call does not mention wills or Trust & Will | June 2026 programme update (BriefGlance summary): free wills extend to Texas, Arizona and California following the September 2026 Comerica integration, with no Comerica figures
Implication: No partner bank of the leading will vendor has published an outcome, so the T06 verdict is left where it was; the trust-side consent order is a reminder that estate adjacency carries supervision risk.
Caveats: Trust & Will is the vendor and states its own reach. Trust & Will is a will-drafting vendor, not one of the post-death navigation vendors (Empathy, Atticus) named in T06's second kill test, so its distribution through Fifth Third is analogous evidence for that test, not a hit. Consent-order wording is from a third-party transcript mirror. The earlier Atticus-Comerica logo observation was not re-verified.

Claim: In 2024, 1,280 CFPB complaints with a narrative mentioning death or estate terms were filed in checking or savings, credit card, mortgage and debt collection, about 42 per 100,000 US deaths (about 33 on a strict term set).
Evidence: Narratives matching deceased, passed away, estate (not real estate), executor, surviving spouse, successor in interest or probate: 1,228 (2023), 1,280 (2024), 1,484 (2025), 678 (to 15 Aug 2026), 4,670 total; strict series without the estate term 1,013 / 1,026 / 1,179 / 571 | 2024 by product: checking or savings 390, debt collection 365, mortgage 355, credit card 170; these four products drew 306,143 complaints in 2024, of which 147,435 (48.2%) carried a narrative | CDC NCHS: 3,072,666 US deaths in 2024; researcher arithmetic: 1,280 / 3,072,666 = 41.7 per 100,000 deaths; strict series 33.4; checking or savings alone 12.7; scaling by the narrative share gives about 86 per 100,000, an illustration not an incidence estimate | Compiler re-ran the researcher's script (python -I) on the saved archive file and reproduced these counts (see notes)
Implication: Complaint incidence is well under one per thousand deaths, consistent with the objection that the event is rare per customer, but 04_stress.md sets no complaints-per-death threshold for T06, so this neither confirms nor reopens anything; it sizes the survivor-servicing pain as visible but small.
Caveats: Narratives come from an Internet Archive capture (15 Aug 2026 14:13 UTC) of the CFPB bulk file, because the CFPB stopped publishing narratives on 14 Aug 2026 (crosscut-90); the capture was not reconciled to a CFPB-published total. Narratives are opt-in, unverified allegations and a floor on complaints. Term matching is regex, uncoded; estate and deceased capture some non-death uses (one living person wrongly marked deceased is in the count). 2026 is partial and its narrative share lags. Part of the 2023-2025 rise is database-wide volume growth.

Claim: Only 31% of the 2023 to August 2026 death-or-estate complaints sit in checking or savings; the larger share is mortgage servicing in payment trouble and debt collectors pursuing survivors for a decedent's debt.
Evidence: Top product-issue pairs among 4,670 matches: checking or savings / managing an account 825; mortgage / struggling to pay 631; debt collection / attempts to collect debt not owed 611; mortgage / trouble during payment process 581; checking or savings / closing an account 459 | By product 2023-2026: mortgage 1,539; checking or savings 1,462 (31.3%, researcher arithmetic); debt collection 1,107; credit card 562 (450 Credit card plus 112 under the 2023-only Credit card or prepaid card label) | Recurring themes in ten paraphrased narratives: proof-of-death or authority paperwork lost or re-requested, collectors treating the survivor as debtor, and servicing continuing as if the holder were alive (for example billing reminders for two years after an estate account closed)
Implication: The complaint record shows a real survivor-servicing pain but places most of it at mortgage servicers and collectors rather than deposit banks, so for a deposit bank the heir-retention test remains the deciding one and the T06 verdict is left where it was.
Caveats: Same archive provenance and opt-in limits as transfer-92. Mortgage and debt-collection issue labels are broad, so some matches are not death-related servicing failures. The ten examples are a random judgement sample of 120 to 700 character matches, not a coded sample. Whether survivors left the bank is not coded.

Claim: Remitly's FY2025 10-K reports $74.9 billion of send volume, $1.6 billion of revenue and 9.3 million quarterly active customers, so immigrant remittance is already served at consumer scale by a profitable digital specialist.
Evidence: FY2025 send volume $74.9 billion, up 37% from $54.6 billion (2023: $39.5 billion); Q4 2025 active customers 9.3 million, up 19% from 7.8 million; more than 5,300 corridors (Remitly 10-K filed February 2026). | Revenue $1.6 billion (2025), $1.3 billion (2024), $944.3 million (2023); net income $67.9 million in 2025 after losses of $37.0 million (2024) and $117.8 million (2023). | Payments to India, Mexico and the Philippines were about 46% of 2025 revenue (49% in 2024, 55% in 2023). Revenue-to-volume of roughly 2.1% is compiler arithmetic on the rounded $1.6 billion, not a filed figure.
Implication: The money-movement leg of T11 fails the zero-to-one test: a scaled, now-profitable specialist already serves immigrant senders, many of them Debit-Primary Spenders, so a bank remittance offer would be adjacency.
Caveats: Company's own filing. Global figures; the US-originated share was not located. Revenue is stated only to one decimal in billions.

Claim: Wise's FY2026 results (year to 31 March 2026) report 18.9 million active customers, $243.5 billion of cross-border volume and a 0.52% cross-border take rate, with US net revenue of $365.2 million.
Evidence: FY26 active customers 18.9 million (up 21% from 15.6 million); cross-border volume $243.5 billion (up 31% from $185.2 billion); net revenue $2,502.8 million (up 19% from $2,098.9 million). | Cross-border take rate 0.52%, down 6 basis points from 0.58%; almost 50% of net revenue now comes from non-cross-border sources (interest, card, other). | Geographic table: United States net revenue $365.2 million; the roughly 14.6% US share is compiler arithmetic ($365.2M / $2,502.8M). Dateline New York, 25 June 2026.
Implication: A half-percent take rate sets the price a bank remittance offer must meet, so T11 as a transfer product is a price-taker against a scaled low-cost leader and fails the zero-to-one test.
Caveats: Company results release read through Investegate, a regulatory-news relay of the RNS text; the Wise investor site was not fetched, so Confidence is mapped down to Medium. Most Wise volume is not immigrant remittance (multi-currency, business, travel).

Claim: In the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide Issue 51 (Q3 2024), banks were the costliest provider type at 13.64% to send $200, against 5.40% for money transfer operators, 3.87% for digital-only operators and a 6.03% average from the United States.
Evidence: Q3 2024 global average cost 6.62%; digital remittances 4.95% versus non-digital 7.29%; digital services were 29% of services tracked; the digital-only MTO index (Wise, Remitly, WorldRemit, InstaReM, Xoom) was 3.87%. | By provider type: banks 13.64%, post offices 7.66%, MTOs 5.40%, mobile operators 2.84% (under 1% of the sample). Credit or debit card was the cheapest funding method at 5.13%. | US average cost to send rose from 5.79% to 6.03% year on year; Australia was the cheapest G20 sender at 5.35%. Corridors averaging under 5% rose from 17% (Q1 2009) to 83% (Q3 2024); the global average has stayed below 7% since Q1 2019. | For comparison, Capital One's own international send is a $40 branch-only wire (see worldview-06).
Implication: The price gap that exists is the banks' own; non-banks have already closed it, so a deposit bank enters at a price handicap and its possible edge is trust and account integration, not price, for Debit-Primary senders.
Caveats: PDF did not parse through WebFetch; verified against the researchers' local extract (output/worldview/_pdf/rpw.txt). Data collected by FXC Intelligence; a basket of services per corridor, not volume-weighted. Bank figure is a global average including small and foreign banks, not US large banks. The Q3 2025 issue returned 403, so figures are two years old.

Claim: Western Union's FY2025 10-K shows consumer money transfer revenue down 8% to $3,507.4 million on 285.9 million transactions while it agreed to buy Intermex for about $500 million and planned a stablecoin, and MoneyGram was taken private at $11.00 a share on 1 June 2023.
Evidence: Western Union FY2025: total revenue $4,050.7 million (down 4% from $4,209.7 million); Consumer Money Transfer revenue $3,507.4 million (down 8% from $3,798.0 million); transactions 285.9 million (down 1% from 289.9 million); the segment was 87% of revenue (90% in 2024, 92% in 2023). | Agreed 10 August 2025 to buy International Money Express for about $500 million cash, expected to close Q2 2026; announced 28 October 2025 a US-dollar stablecoin (USDPT) on Solana issued by Anchorage Digital Bank, N.A., expected in the first half of 2026; about 360,000 locations active in the prior 12 months. | MoneyGram: press release filed as an 8-K exhibit says funds affiliated with Madison Dearborn Partners completed the all-cash acquisition at $11.00 per share on 1 June 2023.
Implication: The agent-network incumbents are shrinking and consolidating while digital leaders grow, so cross-border transfer is a scale-and-price game with no unserved gap for a deposit bank to enter as a new category.
Caveats: Company filings. The decline mixes enforcement-driven corridor weakness and share loss to digital; the branded-digital and US-originated splits were not located. Intermex closing status as of October 2026 not checked. MoneyGram volumes undisclosed since it went private.

Claim: As of 2026 the large banks' cross-border consumer offer is a wire or an enrolled, branch-started service: Bank of America's fee schedule lists international wires ($45 in US dollars, no fee but an exchange-rate markup in foreign currency) and Wells Fargo's ExpressSend requires an in-branch first transfer and is not on its mobile app.
Evidence: Bank of America Personal Schedule of Fees effective 7 August 2026: international outgoing wire in US dollars $45; in foreign currency no wire fee but exchange rate markups apply; international incoming wire $15. The term SafeSend does not appear in the schedule. | Wells Fargo ExpressSend (Mexico page): the rate includes a markup; the first remittance under each service agreement must be started in person at a branch (some existing customers by phone); not available on the Wells Fargo Mobile app; a Wells Fargo checking or savings account is required; minors cannot enrol; fees vary by network member and amount.
Implication: Large banks treat cross-border send as a legacy, branch-linked, non-mobile service, which leaves a service-quality gap for Debit-Primary immigrant customers but not an empty category.
Caveats: The Bank of America schedule is a PDF that WebFetch still returns as binary; verified against the researcher's local extract (output/worldview/_pdf/boa.txt). The brief's SafeSend pointer was not found and is treated as stale. Wells Fargo fee amounts are not on the page; whether ExpressSend accepts new enrolments was not confirmed.

Claim: Capital One's 360 Checking disclosure limits the account to US citizens or lawful permanent residents who supply either an SSN or an ITIN, its MONEY Teen Checking page asks for an SSN or ITIN without stating a citizenship test, and its only international send is a $40 branch-only wire, while Wells Fargo and Bank of America accept an ITIN and Bank of America opens for US visa holders in person.
Evidence: Capital One 360 Checking disclosure (fetched 26 October 2026): available to US citizens or lawful permanent residents with a US physical address, aged 18 or older, with a US mobile number, with either a valid SSN or an ITIN, and a linked account at a US-chartered bank. The remainder of the disclosure has no further ITIN or residency text; its wire section covers domestic transfers only ($30 outgoing). | Capital One MONEY Teen Checking: joint account with a parent or guardian for ages 6 and up; opening requires a Tax ID Number (SSN or ITIN); no citizenship requirement is stated on the page. Help center: international wires can only be sent through branch locations, $40, not all account types eligible, up to 10 business days, 30-minute hold. | Wells Fargo Everyday Checking: SSN or ITIN for online and branch opening. Bank of America FAQ: US visa holders living in the US may open in person at a financial center with an ITIN and both foreign and local addresses. | Customer identification rule 31 CFR 1020.220(a)(2)(i)(A)(4)(ii): for a non-US person a bank may collect a taxpayer identification number, a passport number and country, an alien ID card number, or another government-issued photo document showing nationality or residence.
Implication: ITIN account opening is already standard at large banks, so T11 cannot rest on it; on its published terms Capital One's adult checking is narrower than Bank of America's for non-resident ITIN holders, and the unbuilt piece at Capital One is a consumer-grade cross-border send, not account access.
Caveats: Resolves the A/B conflict: both researchers were reading the same sentence; it accepts an ITIN, but only within a citizen-or-permanent-resident eligibility rule, so an ITIN holder who is neither is outside 360 Checking on the disclosure's terms. Practice at application may differ and was not tested. Company pages are what the company publishes, not an audit. A second Capital One help page gives 3 to 5 business days for international wires on the receive side. Chase was not verified.

Claim: Investors are funding immigrant neobanks and stablecoin remitters (Comun's $21.5 million Series A in August 2024; Félix Pago's reported $200 million round in September 2026), but none discloses a user count, and Remitly closed its immigrant bank Passbook in 2023 for lack of scale.
Evidence: Comun (TechCrunch, 28 August 2024): $21.5 million Series A led by Redpoint after a $4.5 million round in December 2023; says it is on track for over $1 billion annualised payment volume; customers average 3.1 remittances a month; interchange under half of revenue; accounts open with 100 Latin American ID types; no user count. Competitors named: Tanda, Bloom Money, Majority, Welcome Tech, Maza, Pillar. | Félix Pago (Forkast, 2 September 2026, attributing the split to Bloomberg): $200 million Series B of $87 million equity led by a16z and a $113 million General Catalyst credit facility; over $8 billion processed to date, unattributed; no user count. | Remitly Passbook (Banking Dive, 27 February 2023): launched 2020, closed to new accounts with service ending 1 May 2023 because it would not reach scale fast enough and had little overlap with Remitly's remittance customers; account numbers never disclosed.
Implication: Investor money says a bundled account-plus-remittance offer for Latin American immigrants is a live thesis, but no consumer-scale account count exists and a scaled remitter could not make the bank layer work, which is the layer a deposit bank would bring.
Caveats: A funded startup is investor belief, not demand. Trade press is the only record of these events (no filings); Félix figures are secondhand from Bloomberg via Forkast and the round label varies across outlets. Seis, a reported Spanish-language neobank shutdown, could not be fetched and is excluded.

Claim: Credit-history portability already exists as a B2B utility: Nova Credit says it operates as an FCRA consumer reporting agency that imports credit history from 17 countries and that Chase, HSBC and Scotiabank use its Credit Passport, and the FCRA definitions place no limit on where report data originate.
Evidence: Nova Credit about page: Chase, HSBC and Scotiabank use the Credit Passport to serve newcomers; histories from 17 countries including India, Mexico, Nigeria, the Philippines, South Korea and the UK; it enables 'millions of people' to access credit (no count); Income Navigator has more than 4,000 customers; headline 'Nova Credit Raises $35M Series D' linked to cash-flow underwriting. | Nova Credit homepage: operates as a consumer reporting agency under the FCRA in the US; clients approve, decline and send adverse-action notices; Nova manages disputes; logos include HSBC, SoFi, MoneyLion, Scotiabank and Sallie Mae. | 15 USC 1681a(d) and (f): a consumer report is any communication by a consumer reporting agency bearing on creditworthiness; a consumer reporting agency regularly assembles or evaluates consumer credit information and uses interstate commerce; neither definition limits the source location of the data.
Implication: The credit-history noun in T11 is legally feasible for a bank and already sold to lenders as infrastructure, so it is a vendor a bank can buy, not a white space a bank can own; whether it moves approvals is undisclosed.
Caveats: Vendor marketing pages selling to lenders; no volumes or outcome data; undated. The 'no geographic limit' reading is the compiler's and researcher's reading of the statute (Cornell LII copy), not a CFPB or court statement. Logo lists do not say which partners use Credit Passport. Capital One's own use of foreign-bureau data was not found.

Claim: As of October 2026 parent-visible kids and teen accounts are a crowded category that Capital One already occupies: Greenlight reports 6.5 million family members, Chase First Banking and Capital One MONEY Teen Checking are fee-free parent-linked accounts from age 6, and Acorns bought GoHenry in 2023 for nearly 6 million combined subscribers.
Evidence: Greenlight homepage: 6.5 million family members and counting; plans from $5.99 a month per family; $700 million-plus saved by kids and teens; banking through Community Federal Savings Bank; 'not a bank'. | Capital One MONEY Teen Checking: joint with a parent or guardian from age 6, no fees to open, keep or use, including after 18; Zelle from 13 only with parental consent; balance insured up to FDIC limits; at 18 the teen can move to 360 Checking or keep the account; Capital One's EVERFI page pairs the account with EVERFI's Modern Money course. Chase First Banking: ages 6-17, parent-owned, $0 monthly fee, funded only from the parent's Chase checking, closed at 25 if no other account is chosen. | Acorns and GoHenry (TechCrunch, 3 April 2023): all-equity deal; nearly 6 million combined subscribers; Acorns had over 4.6 million paid subscribers (March 2022) and GoHenry 2 million customers (October 2022). | Law is light: FDIC insures UTMA deposits as the child's single account up to $250,000; the FTC finalized COPPA amendments on 16 January 2025 (separate parental consent for third-party sharing, retention limits, biometric and government identifiers added) with one year from Federal Register publication to comply.
