Implication: The one family-account form the corpus left untested exists at scale and inside Capital One, so a kids product fails both the zero-to-one test and the additive screen for Young Consumers; the open question is whether child holders stay as adults, which no provider discloses.
Caveats: Direction is relative to the white-space proposition and the kids-first candidate (worldview-22). Company pages; Greenlight's 6.5 million is family members, not paying subscribers, and undated; Acorns and GoHenry counts are 2022. Whether COPPA binds a bank's own teen product depends on FTC versus banking-agency jurisdiction, unresolved. No retention or conversion data from any provider.

Claim: Blackbaud disposed of EVERFI, the school financial-education vendor reaching over 7 million students a year, for a nominal amount on 31 December 2024 after a $390.2 million impairment and a $15.2 million loss on disposition, three years after acquiring it.
Evidence: Blackbaud FY2024 10-K: EVERFI disposed of for a nominal amount on 31 December 2024; pre-tax non-cash impairment $390.2 million plus a $15.2 million loss on disposition, $405.4 million in total EVERFI disposition charges. | Blackbaud FY2023 10-K: EVERFI acquired 31 December 2021; curriculum reaches over 7 million students a year at over 25,000 K-12 schools; after the acquisition Blackbaud lost certain employees and saw unexpected delays in realizing anticipated returns. | Same filing's risk factors: financial institutions subscribe to EVERFI and may give it free to schools in low- and moderate-income communities to meet Community Reinvestment Act obligations.
Implication: Worldview formation through schools reached millions of Young Consumers but was paid for by bank sponsorship, partly for CRA credit, and the asset was written off, so it holds a sponsored brand channel at best (Capital One already pairs its teen account with an EVERFI course), not a bank-owned business.
Caveats: Company filings. The buyer and the reason for the sale are not stated. The impairment may reflect Blackbaud's purchase price and integration rather than EVERFI's operating viability. Whether EVERFI programmes continue under new ownership was not checked.

Opportunity: Cross-Border on an Owned International Network
Claim: Discover's network page reports Diners Club at 44+ issuers in 40+ countries, PULSE at over 1.7 million ATMs in 144 countries and territories, and 30+ network alliances, gives no Discover merchant count and lists no person-to-person send feature, and the Discover Deliver push product is described for US debit and prepaid cards only.
Evidence: Discover Global Network reach page, fetched 2026-10-26: Diners Club 44+ issuers in 40+ countries (internal data, January 2026); PULSE over 1.7 million ATMs in 144 countries and territories (internal data to 31 December 2025 and a Datos Insights study to 31 December 2024); 30+ network alliances (signed agreements); partners include JCB, UnionPay and mada; no Discover merchant-location count. | Discover Deliver factsheet (local extract of the PDF saved in sweep 2): push payments to Discover debit and prepaid cards in the U.S.; funds usually available within 30 minutes; Discover Deliver is not a payment app. | A search for a current card-to-card cross-border transfer on Discover, Diners Club or PULSE found only ATM and merchant acceptance.
Implication: Acceptance and ATM counts describe where a card can be used abroad, not where a US sender's money can be delivered to a recipient, so the network gives no cross-border send capability to build an immigrant-sender product on.
Caveats: Edge: none (footprint exists, no send product to monetise it). Network-owned, unaudited counts. The Deliver factsheet was verified against the local extract at output/sweep2/_pdf/P06B-deliver-usecases.txt; its web URL was not recorded, so only the reach page is listed in Source Links. The negative search result is from one researcher's searches.

Opportunity: Cross-Border on an Owned International Network
Claim: Capital One's FY2025 10-K describes its UK and Canada businesses as card lending that takes no deposits, with average international card loans of $7,164 million against $227,309 million of total card loans (about 3%).
Evidence: FY2025 10-K: in the UK the Bank operates through Capital One (Europe) plc, an FCA-authorised payment institution that does not take deposits; Capital One Canada, a branch of an authorised foreign bank, does not take deposits; Diners Club is a network of licensees. | International card businesses: average loans $7,164M (2025), $6,868M (2024), $6,359M (2023); period-end $7,668M; net charge-offs $368M, 5.14% (2024: 5.15%). Total card average loans $227,309M; compiler arithmetic 7,164 / 227,309 = about 3.2%. | Remitly's revenue is concentrated in India, Mexico and the Philippines corridors [worldview-01]; Capital One's own international send is a branch wire [worldview-06].
Implication: The enterprise footprint does not match the flow: US senders go mainly to Mexico, India and the Philippines, and the UK and Canada operations hold no deposits to receive or originate transfers, so the footprint edge in the hypothesis is weak for immigrant senders and Young Consumers alike.
Caveats: Edge: none. Verified against the local 10-K extract at output/franchise/_pdf/cof10k.txt. The International row is a card-loan line, not a segment with its own profit; no UK-Canada split or revenue by country was found in the sections read.

Opportunity: Cross-Border on an Owned International Network
Claim: The P09 kill criteria are largely met at the digital frontier: specialists price cross-border transfers near 0.5% to 2% against a 6.03% US average, section 4475 exempts card- and account-funded transfers for every provider, and the FinCEN customer due diligence proposal ordered by EO 14406 was not found as of October 2026.
Evidence: World Bank RPW Q3 2024: the average cost of sending $200 from the US rose to 6.03%; globally, banks averaged 13.64%, MTOs 5.40%, digital-only MTOs 3.87%, and card funding was the cheapest method at 5.13% [worldview-03]. Wise's FY2026 cross-border take rate was 0.52% [worldview-02]; Remitly revenue over send volume is about 2.1% (compiler arithmetic) [worldview-01]. | 26 USC 4475: 1% tax on remittance transfers made after 31 December 2025, not applying to transfers from an account at a covered financial institution or funded with a US-issued debit or credit card [worldview-11]; the exemption is open to Wise, Remitly and any card issuer alike. | EO 14406 (19 May 2026) section 3(b) directs Treasury to propose stronger risk-based customer due diligence rules within 90 days (by about 17 August 2026, compiler arithmetic), and section 3(a)(vi) says ITIN use in place of an SSN may be identified as an enhanced due diligence risk factor [worldview-13]. The proposal itself was not found. | Reg E subpart B applies to bank remittances [worldview-12]; remittances to Mexico fell 4.6% in 2025 [worldview-16].
Implication: There is no right to win on price or tax: specialists already sit at 0.5% to 2% and the 4475 exemption helps every card- or account-funded sender equally, while the ITIN due-diligence risk falls on immigrant senders whatever network carries the transfer.
Caveats: Edge: none. Correction: the researcher labelled the bank, MTO, digital-only and card-funding figures as US; the RPW report gives them as global averages, and only 6.03% is the US figure. RPW data is Q3 2024. The Remitly ratio mixes rounded revenue with volume. The CDD proposal's date and text are a gap.

Claim: Since 1 January 2026 IRC section 4475 taxes remittance transfers at 1 percent, paid by the sender and collected by the provider, but exempts transfers withdrawn from an account at a covered financial institution or funded with a US-issued debit or credit card, so the tax falls on cash-type funding.
Evidence: Statute (26 USC 4475, added by Pub. L. 119-21 section 70604, 4 July 2025): tax of 1 percent of the amount of any remittance transfer; paid by the sender; applies to transfers made after 31 December 2025; terms take their meaning from EFTA section 919(g). | Section 4475(d): the tax does not apply to funds withdrawn from an account held in or by a qualifying financial institution, or funded with a debit or credit card issued in the United States. The IRS release describes the taxed case as the sender providing cash, a money order, a cashier's check or a similar physical instrument. | Proposed regulations released 10 April 2026 (IR-2026-48; REG-114499-25 per KPMG), comments due 12 June 2026: transfers of $15 or less and certain securities and commodities transfers excluded; anti-avoidance examples cover general-use prepaid cards issued to cash-paying customers; reliance allowed for transfers after 31 December 2025 until final rules apply. | Notice 2025-55: relief from failure-to-deposit penalties for the first three calendar quarters of 2026. No final regulations were located as of 26 October 2026.
Implication: A sender funding from a deposit account escapes the 1 percent tax that cash-funded agent networks must collect, but app-based transmitters funded by debit card escape it too, so the tax gives a bank an edge only over cash channels used by Debit-Primary senders.
Caveats: Statute read on Cornell LII's copy of the US Code. The REG number and the regulatory exclusions come from a KPMG summary (pointer; the Federal Register text 2026-07085 was not fetched); proposed rules are not final. Notice 2025-55 verified against the local extract. The cash share of US remittance funding is unsourced, so the edge cannot be sized.

Claim: Regulation E subpart B applies to any person that provides remittance transfers in the normal course of business, banks included, and the CFPB's 2025 posture was withdrawal of guidance with a September 2024 narrow disclosure amendment still shown as proposed.
Evidence: 12 CFR 1005.30(e)-(f): a remittance transfer is an electronic transfer requested by a sender to a designated recipient; transfers of $15 or less are excluded; a provider is any person providing them in the normal course of business; a person making 500 or fewer transfers in both the prior and current calendar years is outside the rule. | Official commentary 30(e)-3.i: consumer wires executed by a financial institution, international ACH sent by the sender's institution, and scheduled online bill payments by the sender's institution are covered remittance transfers. | CFPB remittance-rule compliance page (last modified 1 July 2025): on 12 May 2025 the Bureau withdrew guidance including Bulletin 2012-08; a 20 September 2024 narrowly tailored disclosure amendment is shown as proposed, with no final action. | Player enforcement, one line: CFPB ordered Wise to pay $2.5 million (order 30 January 2025, superseded by a modified amended consent order 15 May 2025).
Implication: Consumer remittance law neither blocks nor favours a bank, so any bank edge in T11 must come from account integration or the tax exemption, not from disclosure rules.
Caveats: Absence of a final action on one CFPB page last modified July 2025 is not proof the proposal is dead. The CFPB archive page does not describe the Wise conduct or what the May 2025 modification changed.

Claim: Executive Order 14406 (19 May 2026) and a 5 June 2026 joint FinCEN, FDIC, OCC and NCUA advisory say an ITIN used in place of an SSN or work authorization may be identified as a risk factor requiring enhanced due diligence, with customer due diligence and customer identification rule changes ordered to follow.
Evidence: EO 14406, 'Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System' (19 May 2026): Treasury advisory within 60 days, including ITIN use in place of an SSN or work-authorized visa as a possible enhanced-due-diligence risk factor (section 3(a)); CFPB to consider ability-to-repay clarification on deportation and lost wages within 60 days (4(a)); credit-risk guidance from regulators within 60 days (4(b)); proposed Bank Secrecy Act customer due diligence changes within 90 days, where warranted obtaining immigration status and work authorization (3(b)); customer identification changes considered within 180 days, including foreign consular ID cards (3(c)). | FinCEN Advisory FIN-2026-A002 (5 June 2026), issued jointly with FDIC, OCC and NCUA in coordination with the IRS: ITINs do not show legal status or authorize work; the agencies note ITIN use in lieu of an SSN may be a risk factor requiring enhanced due diligence, are particularly concerned by ITIN use to open depository accounts without verified legal presence, and encourage banks to consider ITIN use in risk-based customer due diligence. | The advisory says its red flag indicators do not convey or alter any independent regulatory obligations or supervisory expectations. | Neither the 90-day customer due diligence proposal nor any customer identification proposal was located by the researcher as of 26 October 2026.
Implication: A bank building a T11 product on ITIN accounts now carries explicit federal supervisory attention and reputational exposure it did not carry in 2024, and the cost lands on the Debit-Primary immigrant segment the bank could otherwise serve.
Caveats: Executive and agency guidance, not statute or final rule; it can change. The FinCEN web page names only FinCEN, the PDF names the joint agencies; the PDF was verified against the local extract. The advisory's focus is unlawful employment and shell companies; effects on lawful tax-paying ITIN holders are indirect. Law-firm summaries the researcher cited were not needed and are not used.

Claim: The largest recent AML penalty touching cross-border and peer-to-peer flows fell on a bank (TD Bank, $1.3 billion, FinCEN, 10 October 2024), while 2025 actions against the remittance specialist Wise were $4.2 million (six states) and $2.5 million (CFPB).
Evidence: FinCEN (10 October 2024): $1.3 billion penalty on TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A., the largest against a depository institution in Treasury and FinCEN history; TD admitted willfully failing to maintain a compliant AML program; trillions of dollars of transactions a year went unmonitored; SARs not filed on about $1.5 billion of suspicious transactions; peer-to-peer (Venmo and Zelle) monitoring insufficient; four-year independent monitorship. | NYDFS with Massachusetts, Texas, California, Minnesota and Nebraska (9 July 2025): $4.2 million penalty on Wise US, Inc. for BSA/AML/CFT program inadequacies, with a lookback and remediation. | CFPB: Wise ordered to pay $2.5 million for illegal remittance practices (30 January 2025 order, superseded 15 May 2025).
Implication: For a deposit bank the downside of a high-risk corridor product is priced at the scale of the whole AML programme, so any T11 product must be scoped to corridors and customers the bank's existing monitoring can absorb.
Caveats: TD's case was a bank-wide AML failure (cash, funnel accounts, insider facilitation), not a remittance case; two unlike cases, not a base rate. No OFAC action against a remittance product was found, but the OFAC page returned 404, so that is an absence of evidence.

Claim: The FTC Endorsement Guides (16 CFR 255.5) require clear and conspicuous disclosure of any material connection between an endorser and an advertiser, including payment and free products, and expect advertisers to advise, monitor and train endorsers, so creator marketing is open to any bank or app on the same terms.
Evidence: 16 CFR 255.5: a connection that could materially affect an endorsement's weight and that the audience would not expect must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously; connections include payments and free or discounted products and other benefits. | Examples: an advertiser giving an influencer free product should advise disclosure and have reasonable procedures to monitor the influencer's posts; employers should train employees who post endorsements and monitor posts they directed. | No FDIC or OCC rule specific to influencer marketing of deposit products was found by the researcher. The corpus holds the finance enforcement record (FINRA fined M1 Finance $850,000 in 2024 over per-funded-account influencer pay; worldview-23).
Implication: Social media is a channel any bank or fintech can buy at the cost of disclosure and monitoring, not a bank-specific right to win, and per-account influencer pay carries an enforcement record.
Caveats: Addresses regulation of the channel, not whether social media is where bank choice is shaped. Vintage 2023 is the Guides' last known revision; the eCFR page does not show the amendment date, so it is not verified from the page.

Claim: Remittances to Mexico fell 4.6 percent in 2025 to $61.791 billion while the average amount per remitter rose from $490 to $520, with senders averaging 26 years in the US and a net loss of 533,208 remitters.
Evidence: Inter-American Dialogue: Mexican remittance senders averaged 26 years in the US by 2025; net loss of 533,208 remitters (569,521 exits, 36,313 entrants). | Remittances to Mexico fell from $64.745 billion to $61.791 billion while the average sent per remitter rose $490 to $520, so the loss is from senders exiting, not smaller transfers. | Pew survey of 7,006 Asian American adults (2022-23): 37 percent of Asian immigrants in the US 20 years or less sent remittances in the prior 12 months versus 28 percent of those there longer. | Chicago Fed (2004): reduced US financial-market participation among immigrants from weak-institution countries persists past 32 years for those arriving at 16 or older.
Implication: The corridor pool is real but its most established senders exit with tenure, so T11 as a remittance business decays in its core customers, while the surplus that stays in the US is the Debit-Primary deposit a bank could reach.
Caveats: Corpus row (spot-checked 2026-10-26: all three Dialogue figures confirmed). Single corridor in one volatile year; tenure and enforcement effects are entangled; the Dialogue's Table 4 gives a broader net figure of -402,718. Inter-American Dialogue is a think tank analysing Banxico data. Chicago Fed synthesis is from 2004.

Claim: Global remittances were $818 billion in 2023, $656 billion of it to low- and middle-income countries, with growth forecast at only 2.3 to 2.8 percent a year and about two-thirds of volatility tied to synchronized financial-stress cycles.
Evidence: Federal Reserve analysis of World Bank data: $818 billion global in 2023, $656 billion to LMICs (over three times $223.7 billion of OECD official development assistance); LMIC growth forecast 2.3 percent (2024) and 2.8 percent (2025) to about $690 billion. | Remittances exceed 20 percent of GDP in El Salvador, Honduras, Nepal and Lebanon. | Mexico fell 4.6 percent in 2025 as irregular Mexican migration dropped from 630,202 to about 170,000 and deportations reached roughly 160,000. | About two-thirds of global remittance volatility comes from synchronized movements tied to financial-stress conditions.
Implication: The world pool is large and slow-growing, but US-outbound corridor revenue is volatile and policy-driven, so a remittance line would be lumpy revenue for any consumer bank.
Caveats: Corpus row. World Bank forecasts relayed through the Fed's February 2025 note. Global figures are not US-outbound figures. 2025 enforcement makes the corridor swing unusually large.

Claim: In Pew's survey of 7,006 Asian American adults, 15 percent of second-generation adults sent money to an ancestral homeland in the prior 12 months versus 4 percent of third-or-higher-generation adults.
Evidence: 15 percent of second-generation versus 4 percent of third-or-higher-generation Asian adults sent remittances in the prior 12 months. | Within the immigrant generation the decline is shallower: 37 percent at 20 years or less in the US versus 28 percent beyond 20 years. | 27 percent of Asian adults overall sent remittances, 38 percent among those with immediate family still in the homeland.
Implication: A cross-border customer base is first- and second-generation and does not renew across generations, which limits T11 as a relationship-for-life play for Young Consumers outside immigrant families.
Caveats: Corpus row (spot-checked 2026-10-26: 15 and 4 percent, 27 and 38 percent confirmed). Asian Americans only; do not generalise to other origins. Twelve-month recall self-report; one cross-section. Strong method (address-based sample, seven languages, plus or minus 2.1 points).

Claim: In FDIC's 2019 survey, 36.3 percent of unbanked households cited not trusting banks and 36.0 percent cited privacy, against 48.9 percent citing minimum balance requirements, and older studies find immigrants, especially from Mexico and Latin America, less likely to hold accounts.
Evidence: FDIC 2019 as summarised by the Cleveland Fed: distrust 36.3 percent (16.1 main reason); privacy 36.0 percent (7.1 main); minimum balances 48.9 percent (29.0 main). | Rhine and Greene (2006, SIPP 1996-2000): immigrants significantly less likely than US-born citizens to hold bank accounts, with Mexican and other Latin American immigrants least likely. | Amuedo-Dorantes and Bansak (2006): only 9 percent of Mexican immigrants in their sample held a US bank account.
Implication: A non-price trust barrier among immigrant Debit-Primary households is documented but dated, and cost still outranks it; the 2026 ITIN guidance (worldview-13) plausibly raises the privacy barrier, but no source measures that.
Caveats: Corpus row. The 36 percent figures are general-population, not by nativity; nativity studies are about 20 years old and the 2023 FDIC survey publishes no nativity breakdown.

Claim: A Federal Reserve working paper using state-law variation finds that earlier independent account access for minors raised ownership at ages 16-19 but left banked rates equal by age 24 and was followed by more check cashing, lower credit scores and more delinquencies at ages 21-24.
Evidence: Collins, Larrimore and Urban (FEDS 2021-075): laws permitting minors to own accounts independently raised ownership from 16 through 19; by 24 banked rates matched teens in states without such laws. | Earlier-access young people were more likely to use alternative financial services, particularly check cashing, from 21 through 24. | No short-run credit score effect, but lower credit scores and more loan delinquencies at 21-24.
Implication: The strongest administrative evidence in the territory cuts against youth banking as a worldview-forming first relationship, at least in independent form, so a bank should not expect a capability dividend from Young Consumer accounts.
Caveats: Corpus row (spot-checked 2026-10-26: findings confirmed on the abstract page). Single study; tests independent, not parent-visible, accounts; mechanism not isolated.

Claim: Within-person and randomized evidence shows the same low-income US households look present-biased before payday and not after, and a 135-school savings programme in Ghana relabelled savings without raising total savings.
Evidence: Carvalho, Meier and Wang (AER 2016; 1,191 US households under $40,000 surveyed before or after payday): before-payday respondents moved $10.60 more of a $500 choice to 'sooner'; no differences in cognition or decision quality. | J-PAL and IPA cluster-randomised evaluation in 135 Ghanaian schools (about 5,291 students): savings at school rose 5 to 9 points off a 3 percent base; total savings and attitudes did not move. | Watts, Duncan and Quan (2018): the marshmallow-test correlation is about half the original and shrinks by about two-thirds with family background controls. | Low-income households save under a payroll default but not under a tax-refund default (Chetty et al. 2014).
Implication: Products premised on repairing a childhood-installed saving disposition work on the wrong variable for Debit-Primary Spenders; the lever is surplus and paycheck timing, which belong to the income and rupture territories.
Caveats: Corpus synthesis row; no single study compares disposition and present cash flow. Ghana is not US. Marshmallow figures rest on abstract and summary (full text 403 during corpus verification).

Claim: No sourced evidence shows that a child's first bank relationship yields durable capability or retention: the only administrative study finds independent minor accounts leave no banked advantage by 24 and precede worse credit at 21-24, and parental education outweighs money conversations in early financial skill.
Evidence: Collins, Larrimore and Urban (FEDS 2021-075): no banked-rate advantage by 24; lower credit scores and more delinquencies at 21-24 (worldview-20). | Whitebread and Bingham (2013, Money Advice Service) conclude explicit financial teaching of young children is likely ineffectual; CFPB's 2016 building-blocks model places habits and norms at ages 6-12 and cites the same review. | Fletcher and Wright (2024; UK, 817 children aged 4-6): parental university education carries +23.8 to +26.6 percent against +11.1 to +11.4 percent for discussing the child's own spending. | FDIC: about 15 percent of single-parent households are unbanked and more than half of children in unbanked households live with single parents.
Implication: The kids-and-family-money-as-first-relationship candidate dies as a worldview lever for Young Consumers; with the category already crowded and inside Capital One (worldview-09), only a retention test on Capital One's own MONEY Teen data remains.
Caveats: Corpus candidate assembled from separate corpus rows; no statistic merged. Row 21 tests independent accounts only. The Whitebread and Bingham PDF is a third-party mirror (altorwealth.com) of a UK government report and is a pointer only. UK evidence is correlational. No source measures retention of child account holders as adults.

Claim: Social media is a measured belief-forming channel for thin-asset investors (48 percent of investors with under $50K used it for investing decisions in 2024) and accounts have been bought through it, but no source measures it as the channel where bank choice is made.
Evidence: FINRA Foundation 2024 NFCS Investor Survey: 48 percent of investors with portfolios under $50K used social media and 47 percent followed finfluencers, versus 20 and 15 percent at $500K or more. | OSC and Decision Lab randomized trial (2025; 1,465 Canadian social media users): non-investors bought a promoted asset at 29 percent versus 21 percent for investors after exposure. | Most-used channels among finfluencer followers: YouTube 77 percent, Instagram 51 percent, TikTok 40 percent; Pew teens: YouTube 90 percent, TikTok and Instagram about 60 percent each. | FINRA fined M1 Finance $850,000 (March 2024) over flat per-funded-account influencer pay; about 1,700 influencers generated more than 39,400 funded accounts from January 2020 to April 2023.
Implication: Social media is an acquisition channel any bank or app can buy (worldview-15), not a zero-to-one opportunity, and its influence on bank choice for Debit-Primary Spenders and Young Consumers is unmeasured.
Caveats: Corpus candidate assembled from separate rows; no statistic merged. FINRA data are investor-only and self-reported, so the Debit-Primary base is structurally excluded. OSC study is Canadian, one session, fictional money. Pew measures platform use, not financial content.
